title: Textual [project] detection diverges from tomllib: quoted/dotted/array-of-tables project tables are missed, so a duplicate [project] is appended and `haute init` crashes
description: `_scan_table_headers` only recognises a literal bare `[project]` header. It returns the raw bracket text, so a quoted header `["project"]` yields header name '"project"' (with quotes) and a dotted-key table `project.dependencies = [...]` yields NO header at all. tomllib, however, treats all of these as a `project` table. `_find_project_table_bounds` compares `name == "project"` (exact, unquoted) and therefore returns None for these structurally-valid project tables. `_rewrite_project_dependencies` then takes its `bounds is None` branch (line 241-244) and APPENDS a fresh `[project]\ndependencies = [...]`, producing a file with TWO `project` declarations. tomllib rejects this with `Cannot declare ('project',) twice`, which is raised uncaught from `_ensure_haute_dependency` line 312. Net effect: running `haute init` in a directory whose existing pyproject.toml uses a quoted `["project"]` header or dotted `project.x = ...` keys crashes the command with a raw TOMLDecodeError and exit code 1.
evidence:
Probe via real CLI: pyproject `["project"]
name=...
dependencies=["polars"]` -> `runner.invoke(cli,["init"])` => exit=1, exc=TOMLDecodeError: Cannot declare ('project',) twice (line 7). Same for `project.name=...
project.dependencies=[...]` => Cannot declare ('project',) twice (line 6). `_scan_table_headers('["project"]...')` returns [(0,12,'"project"')] and `_find_project_table_bounds` returns None, while `tomllib.loads(...)['project']['dependencies']==['polars']`.

title: Dependency strings are re-emitted with naive double-quote wrapping; any dependency value containing a quote (env markers) round-trips to invalid TOML and crashes `haute init`
description: Line 264 parses the dependency array slice with tomllib, producing UN-escaped Python strings (e.g. `pkg ; python_version < "3.11"`). Line 269 then re-emits each entry as `f'    "{dep}",\n'` — wrapping in a basic TOML string WITHOUT re-escaping embedded double quotes. So a dependency value that legitimately contains `"` (environment markers such as `"tomli ; python_version < \"3.11\""`, or URLs) is written back as `"pkg ; python_version < "3.11"",`, which is no longer valid TOML. The subsequent re-parse at `_ensure_haute_dependency` line 312 fails with `Unclosed array`, and `haute init` exits 1 with a raw traceback. Environment-marker dependencies with quotes are extremely common in real pyproject files, so this is a high-likelihood, high-impact corruption path. The fix is to emit each dep with a proper TOML string serializer (escape `\` and `"`, or use a TOML writer) rather than an f-string.
evidence: Real CLI probe: existing pyproject with `dependencies = [ "polars", "tomli ; python_version < \"3.11\"" ]` -> `init` => exit=1, exc=TOMLDecodeError: Unclosed array (line 8). Direct trace: `_find_matching_bracket` correctly returns the `]`; `tomllib.loads` slice => ['pkg ; sys_platform == "win32"']; `_rewrite_project_dependencies` output line becomes `    "pkg ; sys_platform == "win32"",` (embedded quote not escaped).

title: `dependencies` key indented inside [project] is not matched, so a duplicate `dependencies` key is inserted, corrupting the file
description:
`_DEPENDENCIES_KEY_RE = re.compile(r'^dependencies\s*=\s*\[', re.MULTILINE)` anchors the key at column 0. TOML permits leading whitespace before a key, so `[project]
  dependencies = [ ... ]` is valid and `_dependencies_contain_haute` sees only the existing deps (not haute). `_rewrite_project_dependencies` then fails to find the array (regex returns None) and takes the line 249-253 branch, INSERTING a second `dependencies = [
    "haute",
]` immediately after the `[project]` header. The result has two `dependencies` keys in one table; tomllib rejects it with `Cannot overwrite a value`, and `haute init` crashes (exit 1, raw traceback).
evidence:
Real CLI probe: `[project]
name=..
version=..
  dependencies = [
    "polars",
]` -> `init` => exit=1, exc=TOMLDecodeError: Cannot overwrite a value (line 9). `_DEPENDENCIES_KEY_RE.search('[project]
  dependencies = [
')` returns None; `_scan_table_headers` still detects the indented [project] header correctly, so bounds is found but the array isn't.

title: `parsed.get('project', {}).get('dependencies', [])` raises AttributeError when [[project]] makes `parsed['project']` a list
description: If the existing pyproject.toml declares `project` as an array-of-tables (`[[project]]`), tomllib parses `parsed['project']` as a list. Line 302 then calls `.get('dependencies', [])` on that list, raising `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` — distinct from the duplicate-append crash, and reached before any rewrite. While `[[project]]` is an unusual pyproject shape, the code claims to be a robust TOML-aware reader and should reject it with a clear error rather than crash with an AttributeError. (`_scan_table_headers` deliberately skips `[[`, so the rewrite path would also mis-handle it, but the crash happens first here.)
evidence: Real CLI probe: pyproject `[[project]]\nname = "p"` -> `init` => exit=1, exc=AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'. Traceback originates at _init_cmd.py line 302.

title: Unreachable defensive guard: `if project_end is None` can never be true after the loop
description: Inside the loop, whenever `name == 'project'` both `project_start` and `project_end` are assigned and the loop breaks. Therefore after the loop, `project_start is None` <=> `project_end is None`. The early return at line 159-160 handles the None case, so by line 161 `project_start` is not None, which means `project_end` is also not None. The `if project_end is None: project_end = len(text)` guard (lines 161-162) is unreachable dead code and can be removed (return `project_start, project_end` directly).
evidence: Lines 151-158: the only assignment to `project_start` (line 152) is paired in the same iteration with an assignment to `project_end` (lines 154/156) before `break`. No path sets `project_start` without also setting `project_end`.
est_reduction: ~2 lines
behavior_preservation: Removing the guard cannot change behavior because the condition is provably always false at that point.

title: Redundant local `import tomllib` shadows the module-level import
description: `tomllib` is already imported at module top (line 14) and is used by the helper functions in this module. `handle_init` adds a local `import tomllib` at line 332, which is redundant — the module-level binding is already in scope. The local import can be deleted; `tomllib.load` at line 372 continues to resolve to the module-level import.
evidence: Line 14: `import tomllib` (module scope). Line 332: `import tomllib` (function scope, inside handle_init). Both refer to the same stdlib module; the function-local one provides no benefit.
est_reduction: 1 line
behavior_preservation: Identical: same module object is bound either way; tomllib has no import side effects beyond binding.

title: Misleading `# noqa: F841` on a loop variable that is actually used
description: `for f in ci_files:  # noqa: F841` suppresses Ruff's 'local variable assigned but never used' warning, but `f` IS used on the very next line (`click.echo(f"  {f}")`). The noqa is stale/incorrect and should be removed; it suppresses nothing real and misleads readers into thinking `f` is unused.
evidence: Line 523 `for f in ci_files:  # noqa: F841` immediately followed by line 524 `click.echo(f"  {f}")` which references `f`.
est_reduction: noqa comment removal
behavior_preservation: Removing the noqa changes no runtime behavior; F841 would not fire because f is used.

title: Create-vs-append .gitignore entry sets diverge, so the final ignore set depends on whether .gitignore pre-existed
description: When .gitignore is missing, the create branch (line 508) writes `__pycache__/, *.pyc, .venv/, .env, *.haute.json, .haute_cache/, mlruns/, data/` but omits `impact_report.md`. When .gitignore exists, the append branch (line 497-505) uses `haute_entries = .env, *.haute.json, impact_report.md, .haute_cache/, mlruns/, data/` — which includes `impact_report.md` but omits `__pycache__/, *.pyc, .venv/`. The two code paths therefore produce inconsistent ignore sets for the same project depending on a pre-existing file. Extracting a single canonical entry list (and merging it in both branches) removes the drift and the duplication.
evidence:
Line 497: `haute_entries = ".env
*.haute.json
impact_report.md
.haute_cache/
mlruns/
data/
"`. Line 508: `"__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
.env
*.haute.json
.haute_cache/
mlruns/
data/
"` (no impact_report.md; has __pycache__/, *.pyc, .venv/).
est_reduction: ~3-5 lines plus removes divergence
behavior_preservation: If unified to the union of both sets, the only behavioral change is that both paths ignore the same files (a deliberate consistency fix); the two literal blocks collapse to one source of truth.

title: `--force` re-init does not remove stale CI files from a previously chosen provider
description: With `--force`, handle_init overwrites haute.toml and scaffold files and writes the CI files for the NEW `--ci` choice, but never deletes CI files from a previous provider. Running `haute init --force --ci gitlab` over a project previously initialised with `--ci github` leaves `.github/workflows/{ci,deploy-staging,deploy-production}.yml` on disk, so the repo ends up with two providers' CI configs. The help text advertises `--force` as 'Overwrite existing scaffold files', and tests only assert single-provider state on fresh directories, so this cross-provider staleness goes unnoticed. Severity is low because it is a re-init convenience gap, not data loss, but it is a real behavioral surprise.
evidence: Lines 442-471 only write the branch matching the current `ci`; there is no removal of `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, or `azure-pipelines.yml` belonging to other providers. test_cli_init.py asserts non-existence of other providers only after a single fresh init (e.g. test_gitlab_ci_creates_gitlab_ci_yml), never after a --force switch.

title: --port is silently broken in dev mode: backend port is never propagated to the Vite proxy
description: The CLI advertises --port as "Backend API port" and uvicorn is correctly started on config.host:config.port. But in dev mode the browser talks to the Vite dev server (localhost:5173), and Vite proxies /api and /ws to a HARDCODED http://127.0.0.1:8000 / ws://127.0.0.1:8000 (frontend/vite.config.ts lines 24,28). _start_vite_subprocess only injects VITE_HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN into the child env (lines 408-412) and passes nothing about the backend port/host; vite.config.ts reads no env var for the proxy target (verified: the only VITE_* var the frontend consumes is VITE_HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN, frontend/src/api/client.ts:238). Consequently `haute serve --port 9000` starts the backend on 9000, the readiness probe correctly waits on 9000, the browser opens localhost:5173, but every /api and /ws request from the frontend is proxied to 127.0.0.1:8000 and fails. The user-facing --port option is therefore non-functional for the primary developer (dev-mode) workflow, with no error surfaced. The echoed banner compounds the confusion: line 454 prints the real backend `http://{config.host}:{config.port}` while line 453 hardcodes `http://localhost:5173`, so the displayed and actually-used values diverge.
evidence: _run_dev_mode: uvicorn.run(host=config.host, port=config.port, ...) (lines 465-472) uses the override, but _start_vite_subprocess builds env = os.environ.copy()/dict(node_env) then only adds env['VITE_HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN'] (lines 409-412) — no HAUTE_BACKEND_PORT / VITE_API_TARGET. frontend/vite.config.ts: server.proxy['/api'].target = 'http://127.0.0.1:8000' and ['/ws'].target = 'ws://127.0.0.1:8000' are string literals, not derived from any env. Dev mode is the live path whenever frontend/node_modules exists (_detect_dev_frontend_dir, lines 330-345).

title: Malformed/whitespace host is misreported as "port already in use" instead of an invalid-host error
description: _port_is_available binds using the raw, unstripped config.host (line 191: probe.bind((host, port))), while every sibling helper that interprets the host strips it first (_is_loopback_host line 87, _socket_family_for_host line 164, _trusted_hosts_for_bind line 290). A host carrying surrounding whitespace — e.g. `--host " 127.0.0.1 "` or a sloppy `haute.toml` value (`_load_toml_server_host` returns the TOML string verbatim, line 143, no strip) — passes the loopback/trusted-host checks (which strip) but fails getaddrinfo inside bind(), raising OSError, which _port_is_available swallows into `return False`. _abort_if_port_in_use then prints "Error: port {port} already in use. Use --port to choose another." and exits 1. The diagnostic is actively wrong: the port is fine; the host string is malformed. The user is sent to chase a non-existent port conflict.
evidence: _socket_family_for_host(host) strips internally (line 164) but _port_is_available passes the original `host` to probe.bind on line 191; `except OSError: return False` (lines 192-193) collapses a getaddrinfo/resolution failure into the same signal as EADDRINUSE; _abort_if_port_in_use turns that into the port-in-use message (lines 323-327).

title: GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY append opens file without encoding='utf-8', can raise UnicodeEncodeError
description: When GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY is set, the report is appended via `with open(github_summary, "a") as f: f.write(md)` with NO explicit encoding, so it uses the platform default (locale-dependent; cp1252 on Windows). The markdown `md` always contains non-ASCII characters — `format_markdown` unconditionally emits the U+2192 right-arrow ('→') on the Staging→Production line (src/haute/deploy/_impact.py:550) and '⚠️' for failed rows (line 557). On any runner whose default text encoding is not UTF-8 (e.g. a self-hosted Windows GitHub Actions runner, or local reproduction of the CI step on Windows), `f.write(md)` raises UnicodeEncodeError and the command crashes. This is internally inconsistent: the portable artifact two lines earlier (line 166) is written with explicit `encoding="utf-8"`, but the step-summary append is not.
evidence: Line 166: `report_path.write_text(md, encoding="utf-8")` (explicit utf-8). Lines 171-173: `with open(github_summary, "a") as f: f.write(md)` (no encoding -> locale default). `md` = format_markdown(report); format_markdown (deploy/_impact.py:549-551) always inserts '→' (U+2192). U+2192 is unrepresentable in cp1252, so on a cp1252 default the write raises UnicodeEncodeError.

title: First-deploy ImpactReport counts staging rows without unwrapping quote envelopes
description: In the first-deploy branch the report is hand-assembled with `scored_rows=len(staging_preds)` and `failed_rows=len(records) - len(staging_preds)` directly on the RAW `staging_preds` returned by `_impact_databricks`/`_impact_http`. The non-first-deploy path goes through `build_report`, which first calls `_unwrap_prediction_envelopes(staging_preds)` (deploy/_impact.py:416) before counting. The codebase explicitly supports serving endpoints that return a Haute 'quote envelope' dict wrapping N rows (that is the whole reason `_unwrap_prediction_envelopes`/`_is_haute_quote_envelope` exist). For the Databricks transport, `score_endpoint_batched` returns `resp.predictions` per batch and `_run_batched` APPENDS a non-list (a single envelope dict) rather than extending it — so when an endpoint returns envelopes, `len(staging_preds)` counts envelopes/batches, not scored rows. Consequently a first-deploy report shows a wrong `scored_rows` and a wrong (possibly large positive, or negative) `failed_rows`, whereas the identical predictions on a non-first deploy would be counted correctly via build_report. The mismatch is purely in reported metrics (it does not change scoring or the deploy gate), hence low severity, but it is a genuine cross-path inconsistency.
evidence: build_report unwraps before counting: deploy/_impact.py:416-421 `staging_preds = _unwrap_prediction_envelopes(staging_preds); ... scored = min(len(staging_preds), len(prod_preds))`. First-deploy branch does NOT: cli/_impact.py:143-144 `scored_rows=len(staging_preds), failed_rows=len(records) - len(staging_preds)` on the raw list. `_run_batched` (deploy/_impact.py:110-114) appends non-list preds, so an envelope dict counts as 1 regardless of row count.

title: _is_http_not_found matches 'HTTP 404' anywhere in the message, including a non-404 error body
description: `_is_http_not_found` returns True when the substring 'HTTP 404' appears anywhere in `str(exc)`. The RuntimeError produced by the only intended source, `score_http_endpoint_batched`, has the shape `f"HTTP {exc.code} from {quote_url}: {error_body}"` (deploy/_impact.py:163) where `error_body` is the raw upstream response body. If a real failure returns a non-404 status whose body literally contains the text 'HTTP 404' (e.g. a 500/502 proxy error page that says 'upstream returned HTTP 404', or any echoed request text), the message becomes e.g. 'HTTP 502 from .../quote: ... upstream HTTP 404 ...' and `_is_http_not_found` mis-classifies a genuine transport failure as a first-deploy signal — exactly the silent-misclassification the fail-loudly contract (test_cli_fail_loudly.py::TestImpactProdExistsFailsLoudly) was written to prevent. A robust check would anchor on the status the wrapper emits (the 'HTTP {code} from' prefix) rather than scanning the whole message including attacker/server-controlled body text.
evidence: cli/_impact.py:246 `return "HTTP 404" in str(exc)` (unanchored substring over the full message). Message construction includes the upstream body verbatim: deploy/_impact.py:161-163 `error_body = exc.read().decode(...); raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {exc.code} from {quote_url}: {error_body}")`. A 5xx whose body mentions 'HTTP 404' therefore passes the 404 test.

title: --sample accepts negative values and silently treats them as 'all', unlike --batch-size which uses IntRange
description: `--sample` is declared `type=int` with no range, and the gate is `if config.sample > 0 and total_rows > config.sample`. A negative value (e.g. `--sample -5`) is accepted by Click and silently falls into the 'no sampling -> score the entire dataset' path — the same behaviour documented for `--sample 0`. The help text only documents '0 = all', so a negative is an undocumented, silently-different input. This is asymmetric with the sibling option `--batch-size`, which correctly uses `type=click.IntRange(min=1)` to reject non-positive values at parse time. For a tool whose stated purpose is gating production deploys, silently scoring the full (possibly very large) dataset instead of erroring on an obviously-invalid `--sample` is a minor robustness gap; using `click.IntRange(min=0)` would reject negatives loudly and match the existing convention.
evidence: cli/_impact.py:178-183 `--sample` is `type=int` (no IntRange); cli/_impact.py:184-188 `--batch-size` is `type=click.IntRange(min=1)`. Gate at line 101 `if config.sample > 0 and total_rows > config.sample` makes any value <= 0 a no-op (= score all). Help string (line 182) only mentions '0 = all'.

est_reduction: ~14 lines
behavior_preservation: The first-deploy ImpactReport is hand-built field-by-field, duplicating the construction that build_report already performs for the non-first-deploy case (total_rows/sampled_rows/scored_rows/failed_rows population and ImpactReport instantiation). Routing the first-deploy case through a single shared constructor — e.g. having build_report accept the staging-only / is_first_deploy=True scenario, or extracting a small `_first_deploy_report(...)` helper that itself calls `_unwrap_prediction_envelopes` — removes the divergent second copy. This is the same divergence that produces the envelope-counting bug reported separately; consolidating both paths through one code path fixes the metric inconsistency for free while shrinking handle_impact.
title: First-deploy branch duplicates ImpactReport assembly already encapsulated by build_report
description: handle_impact contains two near-parallel report-construction paths: the `if not prod_exists` branch (lines 135-147) manually instantiates ImpactReport with the same shape build_report returns, and the `else` branch (lines 149-158) delegates to build_report. The manual branch re-derives total_rows/sampled_rows/scored_rows/failed_rows by hand and, unlike build_report, skips `_unwrap_prediction_envelopes`. Collapsing the first-deploy case into the shared builder removes the duplicated field wiring and eliminates the source of the count-inconsistency defect.

title: CLI pipeline_file override clobbers the resolved path, breaking directory-discovery in the no-toml deploy path
description: In the no-haute.toml branch, handle_deploy correctly resolves the user-supplied pipeline argument through resolve_pipeline_file (which accepts a directory and discovers the project pipeline inside it, returning an absolute file path) and feeds that resolved path into DeployConfig.from_cli_args. But immediately afterwards the override step at lines 117-124 unconditionally puts the RAW, unresolved CLI argument back: `if config.pipeline_file: overrides["pipeline_file"] = Path(config.pipeline_file)` followed by `deploy_config = deploy_config.override(**overrides)`. This discards the resolution. For a regular file argument the effect is merely cosmetic (the unresolved relative path still reads from cwd), but when the argument is a DIRECTORY (a documented, supported form per resolve_pipeline_file: '`haute run ./rating` is symmetric with `cd rating && haute run`'), the override replaces the discovered file with the directory itself. resolve_config then calls parse_pipeline_file(<directory>) -> read_user_text(<directory>) -> Path.read_text() which raises IsADirectoryError/PermissionError, caught by the broad `except Exception` at line 133 and surfaced as a confusing 'Resolution failed: [Is a directory]' SystemExit. So `haute deploy ./somedir` (no toml) is broken even though the equivalent `haute run ./somedir` / `haute lint ./somedir` work, because _run.py/_lint.py correctly use the `resolved` value (e.g. RunConfig(pipeline_file=resolved)) and never re-wrap the raw arg. The fix is to apply the already-resolved path (use `resolved` in the override, or skip the pipeline_file override entirely in the no-toml branch since from_cli_args already received the resolved path).
evidence: Trace for `haute deploy ./somedir` with no haute.toml and ./somedir a directory containing a discoverable pipeline: (1) line 93-95 resolve_pipeline_file(Path('./somedir')) -> _project.py:286-287 path.is_dir() True -> _resolve_default_in returns abs '/cwd/somedir/main.py'; (2) line 96-99 from_cli_args(pipeline_file='/cwd/somedir/main.py') sets deploy_config.pipeline_file to the discovered file; (3) line 118 config.pipeline_file=='./somedir' is truthy -> overrides['pipeline_file']=Path('./somedir'); (4) line 124 override() (_config.py:425-431, val is not None and hasattr -> setattr) sets deploy_config.pipeline_file=Path('./somedir') (the DIRECTORY); (5) line 132 resolve_config -> _config.py:543 parse_pipeline_file(Path('./somedir')) -> parser.py:91 read_user_text -> _io.py:461 Path('./somedir').read_text() raises IsADirectoryError; (6) caught at _deploy.py:133 -> 'Resolution failed' SystemExit(1). Contrast _run.py:99 `config = RunConfig(pipeline_file=resolved)` which uses the resolved path and is unaffected.

title: Empty test-quote file produces cryptic 'division by zero' on HTTP/container smoke target
description: In _smoke_http, each quote file is loaded via load_test_quote_file(jf) into `cleaned`, then scored with score_http_endpoint_batched(endpoint_url, cleaned, batch_size=len(cleaned)). A test-quote JSON file containing an empty array `[]` is accepted by the loader (_load_test_quote_cases checks only isinstance(raw, list); the comprehension over an empty list yields []), so `cleaned == []` and `batch_size == 0`. score_http_endpoint_batched delegates to _run_batched, whose first statement is `n_batches = math.ceil(len(records) / batch_size)` = math.ceil(0 / 0), which raises ZeroDivisionError. The per-file `except Exception as exc` at _smoke.py:215 catches it and prints `  ✗ <file>.json: division by zero` then sets all_ok=False. The smoke run fails (exit 1) with a message that names neither the real cause (an empty quote file) nor anything HTTP-related. The Databricks path (_smoke_databricks) is unaffected because it does not batch: an empty `cleaned` is passed straight to ws.serving_endpoints.query as empty dataframe_records.
evidence: _smoke.py:209-217 loop -> line 212 batch_size=len(cleaned)=0 for cleaned=[]. _impact.py:104 `n_batches = math.ceil(len(records) / batch_size)` => math.ceil(0/0). Reproduced: `math.ceil(0/0)` raises ZeroDivisionError('division by zero'). Caught at _smoke.py:215 and reported as a per-file failure with the bare exception text.

title: config_update enum compared to bare string 'NOT_UPDATING' is always unequal, making the guard dead
description: In _smoke_databricks the readiness check on line 140 correctly normalises the Databricks enum: `update_str = str(config_update).rsplit('.', 1)[-1]` and breaks when `update_str in ('', 'NOT_UPDATING')`. But the status-message guard on line 144 compares the RAW value: `if config_update and config_update != "NOT_UPDATING":`. config_update from the SDK is an EndpointStateConfigUpdate enum whose str() is the fully dotted 'EndpointStateConfigUpdate.NOT_UPDATING', and `enum != 'NOT_UPDATING'` is always True (verified live: `EndpointStateConfigUpdate.NOT_UPDATING != 'NOT_UPDATING'` -> True). In the test suite config_update is the dotted string 'EndpointStateConfigUpdate.NOT_UPDATING', which is likewise != 'NOT_UPDATING'. So `config_update != "NOT_UPDATING"` is effectively always True whenever config_update is truthy, and the intended suppression of NOT_UPDATING from the not-ready status line never occurs: an endpoint in state ready!=READY, config_update=NOT_UPDATING would still print `, config_update=EndpointStateConfigUpdate.NOT_UPDATING`. The condition should use the already-normalised `update_str` (e.g. `if update_str and update_str != 'NOT_UPDATING'`) to match line 140.
evidence: _smoke.py:137-148: line 139 builds normalized update_str; line 140 uses `update_str in ('', 'NOT_UPDATING')` (correct); line 144 uses raw `config_update != "NOT_UPDATING"`. Live SDK check: str(EndpointStateConfigUpdate.NOT_UPDATING)=='EndpointStateConfigUpdate.NOT_UPDATING' and (enum != 'NOT_UPDATING') is True. Effect is confined to the cosmetic status line printed at _smoke.py:146-148 on the not-ready branch.

title: Unreachable true-branch in SCENARIO_EXPANDER outputs merge (`if outputs is None`)
description: In `overlay_declared_contract`, the SCENARIO_EXPANDER output-merge guard is entered only when `builder.outputs is not None`. By that point `outputs` was assigned `declared.outputs if declared.outputs is not None else builder.outputs`, so when `builder.outputs is not None` the else-branch already guarantees `outputs is not None` (it falls back to the non-None `builder.outputs`). Therefore inside the guard `outputs is None` can never be true, making the ternary's consequent `builder.outputs` dead. The expression only ever evaluates the else-branch `outputs | builder.outputs`. The branch is a behavior-preserving no-op that can be simplified to `outputs = outputs | builder.outputs`.
evidence:
Line 596-599:
  inputs = declared.inputs if declared.inputs is not None else builder.inputs  # (596)
  outputs = declared.outputs if declared.outputs is not None else builder.outputs  # (597)
  if node.data.nodeType == NodeType.SCENARIO_EXPANDER and builder.outputs is not None:  # (598)
      outputs = builder.outputs if outputs is None else outputs | builder.outputs  # (599)
Trace: entering 598 requires builder.outputs is not None. Two cases for `outputs` from line 597: (a) declared.outputs is not None -> outputs = declared.outputs (a frozenset, not None); (b) declared.outputs is None -> outputs = builder.outputs which is not None here. In both cases `outputs is None` is False, so the `builder.outputs` consequent at line 599 is unreachable. (The early-return path in `_empty_declared_contract_should_defer_to_builder` (614-615) handles the empty-declared SCENARIO_EXPANDER case before line 598 is reached, so it cannot make `outputs` None either.)
est_reduction: ~1 line / one dead conditional arm; replace ternary with `outputs = outputs | builder.outputs`.
behavior_preservation: The dead consequent is `builder.outputs`; the live arm is `outputs | builder.outputs`. Since `outputs is None` is provably never true inside the guard, the observable result is unchanged for all inputs. Removing the unreachable arm preserves behavior exactly.

location: src/haute/projection.py:1212-1218 (_unordered_expression_demands, filter branch); contrast the correct ordered branch at :1118-1126; manifests through SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule.parent_demands (:1277-1299)
title: Unordered demand walk omits filter keyword-constraint columns, under-demanding the parent for df.filter(col='value')
description: In _unordered_expression_demands the `filter` branch only collects columns via _referenced_polars_columns(ast_node), which recognises pl.col(...) references. It never accounts for Polars keyword-constraint filters such as df.filter(segment='A'), where the keyword name `segment` IS a required column (df.filter(seg='A') is sugar for df.filter(pl.col('seg')=='A')). The ordered branch already handles this exact case (line 1125 adds `{kw.arg for kw in call.keywords if kw.arg is not None}` with the comment "Keyword constraints (df.filter(segment='A')) name columns"), so the two demand walks are inconsistent. Code containing only df.filter(segment='A') has no rename/select/derived-reference, so _single_parent_polars_expression_demands routes it straight to the unordered walk (not the ordered one), returning a parent demand that omits `segment`. compute_prepared_plan writes routed_demands.by_parent verbatim into edge_demands (projection.py:2253-2256), so the parent scan is narrowed to exclude `segment`; the filter then fails at execution with ColumnNotFoundError on otherwise-valid user code (or, if the column is genuinely present upstream and pruned, the filter loses a required input). This breaks a very common single-parent feature-engineering shape.
evidence: Verified at the in-scope rule contract. SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule().parent_demands(node='df = df.filter(segment=\'A\')', parent_ids=['p1'], my_needed={'premium'}) returns by_parent={'p1': {'premium'}} -- 'segment' is MISSING. The ordered extractor for the same code returns {'premium','segment'} (correct). Polars confirms the column is required: df.filter(segment='A') on a frame lacking 'segment' raises ColumnNotFoundError("unable to find column 'segment'"). Root cause: _unordered_expression_demands filter branch (1212-1218) never reads call.keywords, whereas the ordered branch (1118-1126) does. Mixed shapes are equally affected: 'df = df.with_columns((pl.col(\'x\')+1).alias(\'y\'))\ndf = df.filter(seg=\'B\')' with needed={y} returns {'x'} (drops 'seg') because the derived-reference router does not detect a keyword-named column and the unordered walk drops it.

location: src/haute/projection.py:789-802 (_referenced_polars_columns) used by in-scope _select_output_to_input (:845-847), _unordered_expression_demands (:1204,1213) and _ordered_expression_demands via _call_argument_columns; manifests through SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule.parent_demands
title: String-argument Polars aggregation shortcuts (pl.sum('a'), pl.mean('a'), ...) contribute zero column references, silently under-demanding the parent
description: _referenced_polars_columns only treats pl.col('name') as a column reference and returns None (forcing the safe full-width boundary) ONLY for a dynamic/unknown `.col(...)`. Polars top-level aggregation shortcuts that name a column by string argument -- pl.sum('a'), pl.mean('a'), pl.min/max/first/last/std/var/median/count/n_unique('a') -- are NOT pl.col calls, so _referenced_polars_columns silently returns an empty set for them instead of bailing. This contradicts the module's stated design (bail to full width on anything unprovable). Several of these are row-preserving when used inside with_columns (e.g. df.with_columns(pl.sum('a').alias('s')) broadcasts the column sum across all rows and is a valid single-parent shape), so they legitimately reach the demand walks. The with_columns ordered guard at line 1145 does NOT bail because the expression is aliased (_alias_name is not None). The result is a parent demand that omits the referenced column; the narrowed parent scan then fails at execution with ColumnNotFoundError on valid user code. Unlike finding 1 this affects BOTH the ordered and unordered walks (and _select_output_to_input), because they share _referenced_polars_columns.
evidence: Rule-level: SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule().parent_demands(node='df = df.with_columns(pl.sum(\'a\').alias(\'s\'))', parent_ids=['p1'], my_needed={'s'}) returns by_parent={'p1': set()} -- 'a' MISSING. _select_output_to_input(parse('df.select(pl.sum(\'a\').alias(\'s\'))')) yields {'s': set()} (should be {'s': {'a'}}). Polars confirms requirement: df.with_columns(pl.sum('a').alias('s')) on a frame lacking 'a' raises ColumnNotFoundError. By contrast the pl.col form df.select(pl.col('a').sum().alias('s')) is captured correctly (returns {'a'}), showing the gap is specifically the string-argument shortcut functions. Safe alternative would be to return None from _referenced_polars_columns (or bail in the branch) when a pl.<func>(<string>) expression cannot be proven column-free, matching the existing dynamic-pl.col() bail at lines 796-801.

location: src/haute/projection.py:1396-1403 (_raise_if_unbounded_user_code_is_terminal); sole call site at :2268-2273 in compute_prepared_plan
est_reduction: ~8 lines removed (function body + the 5-line call) and one misleadingly-named indirection eliminated
behavior_preservation: Exact. The function body is `_ = node, parent_ids, strict_projection; return` -- it has no side effects and ignores all arguments, returning None unconditionally. Removing both the function and its call (lines 2268-2273, leaving the surrounding `if my_needed is None:` block that writes the opaque contribution) cannot change any observable behaviour. No test references it (grep over *test*.py finds none).
title: _raise_if_unbounded_user_code_is_terminal is a no-op whose name promises a guard it never performs
description: _raise_if_unbounded_user_code_is_terminal accepts (node, parent_ids, *, strict_projection) and its entire body is `_ = node, parent_ids, strict_projection` followed by `return`. It never raises and never inspects anything. It is called once, in compute_prepared_plan's `if my_needed is None:` branch, immediately before unconditionally writing an opaque ParentDemandResult. The name strongly implies a loud guard (consistent with the project's fail-loudly philosophy) that does not exist, which is misleading to readers and a maintenance trap. It appears to be leftover scaffolding (introduced in commit 33b41036 'backend hardening and optimisation'). Either it should be implemented to actually raise when terminal unbounded user code would silently widen, or both the no-op and its call site should be deleted.

title: _freeze_plan rebuilds dict(node_reasons) once per opaque boundary inside the comprehension
description: In _freeze_plan the opaque_reasons MappingProxyType is built with a dict comprehension `{node_id: dict(node_reasons or {}).get(node_id, <default>) for node_id in opaque_boundaries}`. The expression `dict(node_reasons or {})` is re-evaluated on EVERY iteration, materialising a fresh copy of the entire node_reasons mapping for each opaque boundary. With O(n) opaque boundaries and an O(m) node_reasons map this is O(n*m) allocation/copy work to perform what is logically n lookups. node_reasons is already a Mapping (Mapping[str, ProjectionReason] | None), so `(node_reasons or {}).get(node_id, default)` performs the identical lookup with zero copies, and the surrounding code already separately builds the canonical copy once at line 2390 (node_reasons=MappingProxyType(dict(node_reasons or {}))). The per-iteration default ProjectionReason(rule='opaque_demand', message='opaque demand') is likewise reconstructed each iteration but could be hoisted to a module constant since ProjectionReason is frozen.
evidence: Line 2380: `node_id: dict(node_reasons or {}).get(node_id, ProjectionReason(...))` sits inside `for node_id in opaque_boundaries` (line 2387). dict(...) copies the whole mapping per node_id. node_reasons is typed Mapping (param annotation line 2367), so .get works without the dict() wrapper; the same value is copied again standalone at line 2390. No mutation of node_reasons occurs between, so the repeated copy is pure waste.
est_reduction: ~2-3 lines net plus removing O(n*m) copies; replace with a single hoisted `reasons = node_reasons or {}` (and a module-level default ProjectionReason) used inside the comprehension.
behavior_preservation: Identical output: dict(M).get(k, d) and M.get(k, d) return the same value for any Mapping M; node_reasons is not mutated during the comprehension, so hoisting the copy out (or dropping it entirely in favour of the original Mapping) is byte-for-byte behaviour-preserving. The default ProjectionReason is frozen/immutable so sharing one instance is equivalent to constructing fresh ones.

title: join_parent_demands attributes a suffix-stripped column to BOTH join parents, over-demanding the left and risking a spurious loud failure
description: For a simple inferred join with a non-empty suffix, join_parent_demands walks the demanded output_columns and, for every column ending in `join.suffix`, strips the suffix and adds the resulting `parent_column` to BOTH `join.left_parent` and `join.right_parent` (lines 2055-2056). In Polars only the RIGHT operand's colliding column is renamed to `<col><suffix>`; the LEFT operand keeps `<col>` under its original name. Therefore `<col><suffix>` is owned solely by the right parent, and demanding `<col>` from the left parent is an over-demand. In the common case the left parent physically has `<col>` (that is exactly why the collision/suffix arose), so this only widens the left scan harmlessly. But when the left parent does NOT physically produce `<col>` (e.g. the suffixed name collides with a right-only column whose base name the left lacks), the edge projection guard in _execute_lazy._apply_edge_projection (`missing = demand - schema_set`, raises ContractMismatchError) turns a perfectly valid join into a loud 'columns missing from the parent frame' failure. The mis-attribution to the left is provably present; it is over-demand (never a silent mispricing) but can convert a valid graph into a spurious hard error. This is distinct from the known passthrough-parent misroute (catalog #57 / known item 2), which concerns simple_left_join_passthrough_parent / unambiguous_passthrough_parent routing UN-suffixed collision columns; here the defect is in the SUFFIXED-column branch of join_parent_demands which neither of those known items touches.
evidence: Lines 2049-2057: `for column in output_columns - handled: if not column.endswith(join.suffix): continue; parent_column = column[:-len(join.suffix)]; ...; demands.setdefault(join.left_parent, set()).add(parent_column); demands.setdefault(join.right_parent, set()).add(parent_column)`. Both left and right get parent_column. join_parent_demands has exactly one caller: PolarsFanInRule.parent_demands (line 1482) for the uncovered `missing` set under a declared inputs_by_parent contract; its result is OR'd into by_parent (lines 1488-1491) and then validated per-parent against the parent's PHYSICAL schema by _apply_edge_projection (_execute_lazy.py:1044-1056), which raises ContractMismatchError when demand - schema_set is non-empty. Polars suffix semantics (confirmed in catalog #57's ground-truth check): the right copy becomes `<col><suffix>`, the left keeps `<col>`.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Expression renderer drops required parentheses around Compare/BoolOp/IfExp/UnaryOp operands and around equal-precedence right-Pow, so the human-readable formula re-parses to a DIFFERENT value
description: _binop only adds parentheses when a child is itself an ast.BinOp (lines 223 and 225 both guard on `isinstance(node.left/right, ast.BinOp)`), and uses strict `<` precedence. This produces formulas that, when read by a human or re-parsed, compute a different number than the original Polars expression. Confirmed manifestations: (1) Compare operand inside arithmetic: `(pl.col('a') > pl.col('b')) + 1` renders as `a > b + 1`, which re-parses as `a > (b + 1)` (a boolean vs an arithmetic compare). (2) Unary-minus as power base: `(-pl.col('a')) ** 2` renders as `-a ** 2`, which Python parses as `-(a**2)` (sign flips for even powers). (3) Right-associative `**`: `(pl.col('a') ** pl.col('b')) ** pl.col('c')` renders as `a ** b ** c`, which re-parses as `a ** (b ** c)` (because the left-paren rule uses `<`, not `<=`, for the right-associative Pow). (4) IfExp operand: `(a if c else b) + 1` renders as `a if c else b + 1` -> reparses as `a if c else (b + 1)`. (5) BoolOp precedence in _boolop: `(a or b) and c` renders as `a or b and c`, which reparses as `a or (b and c)` because _boolop never wraps a lower-precedence `or` child inside an `and`. The rendered `expression_text` (and the parallel substituted_text) is written into user-facing trace lineage (`step.calculation`/`source_info`, per catalog finding 38), so the actuary is shown a formula that does not match the actual computation. This is the project's explicit fail-loud-vs-silent-wrong concern: a confidently-wrong formula with no error.
evidence: Ran the real _ExprConverter: `(a > b) + 1` -> 'a > b + 1'; `(-a) ** 2` -> '-a ** 2'; `(a ** b) ** c` -> 'a ** b ** c'; `(a if c else b) + 1` -> 'a if c else b + 1'; `(a or b) and c` -> 'a or b and c'. Each rendered string re-parses with different operator grouping than the source. Root cause: _binop paren guards at lines 223/225 test only `isinstance(..., ast.BinOp)` so Compare/UnaryOp/IfExp/BoolOp children are never parenthesized; and line 223 uses `_op_prec(node.left.op) < _op_prec(node.op)` (strict `<`) which omits parens for an equal-precedence left Pow that right-associativity actually requires. _boolop (257-260) joins values with no precedence awareness. Existing tests (test_expression_parser.py:189-207) only pin `+/-/*` precedence; none cover Compare-in-BinOp, unary-in-Pow, Pow associativity, IfExp-in-BinOp, or and/or mixing, so these slipped through.

title: _name recurses into symbol-table entries with no visited-guard, so a self-/mutually-referential top-level assignment causes RecursionError (masked to a silently-opaque expression)
description: _name resolves a variable by recursively calling self.convert(self._symbol_table[name]) (lines 280-283) with no cycle/visited tracking. The feeding symbol tables (_build_safe_symbol_table:792-808 and _build_symbol_table:776-789) capture any top-level `name = <non-df-expr>` assignment, including self-referential ones like `factor = factor * 2` and mutually-referential pairs like `a = b + 1; b = a + 1`. When such a variable is used in the with_columns target expression, _name -> convert(BinOp) -> _binop -> convert(Name) -> _name loops until Python's recursion limit, raising RecursionError. parse_expression's broad `except Exception` (988-1003) then swallows it and returns an `expression_type='opaque'` result with no columns/constants/formula. Net effect: an otherwise-parseable expression is silently downgraded to opaque (all lineage lost) after burning a full deep recursion stack, instead of being resolved or cleanly skipped. This is distinct from the catalogued catch-all finding (which documents that the catch-all masks failures); here the specific defect is the unbounded recursion inside in-scope _name, which has no business looping.
evidence:
End-to-end via the real public entry: parse_expression('factor = factor * 2
df = df.with_columns(factor.alias("out"))', 'out') returns expression_type='opaque', referenced_columns=[] (the formula `factor * 2` and the column are lost). Mutual case ('a = b + 1
b = a + 1
...with_columns(a.alias("out"))') likewise -> opaque. Direct converter call on a symtab {'x': <BinOp x+1>} converting Name('x') raises RecursionError. _build_safe_symbol_table:797-803 confirms `x = x + 1` is captured (ast.Assign, Name target, RHS BinOp is not a df-assignment). RecursionError subclasses Exception, so the parse-boundary catch-all converts the crash into the opaque sentinel.

title: f-string format specs and conversions (:fmt, !r/!s/!a) are silently dropped — wrong RESOLVED ALIAS (column name) via _try_eval_fstring, and lossy formula text via _joinedstr
description: Both f-string handlers ignore FormattedValue.format_spec and FormattedValue.conversion. In _joinedstr a FormattedValue is rendered as `{<value>}` (line 334), dropping any `:.2f`/`!r`. More seriously, _try_eval_fstring (used by _strip_alias to statically evaluate an f-string ALIAS into the target column name) folds a FormattedValue by appending only str(resolved-constant) (lines 736-747), ignoring the format spec. So an alias `pl.col('a').alias(f"col_{idx:02d}")` with idx=3 resolves to 'col_3' instead of the actual Polars output column name 'col_03'. The parser then attributes the expression to the wrong column name, so target-column matching/lineage is mis-labelled (a correctness defect, not merely display).
evidence: Real _strip_alias on `pl.col('a').alias(f"col_{idx:02d}")` with symbol table {'idx': Constant(3)} returns alias='col_3'; Python's f'col_{3:02d}' is 'col_03' -> mismatch. Real _ExprConverter on `f"{x:.2f}"` -> 'f"{x}"' and on `f"{x!r}"` -> 'f"{x}"' (spec/conversion dropped). _try_eval_fstring lines 736-745 only branch on ast.Name (symtab Constant) and ast.Constant and never inspect v.format_spec / v.conversion.

location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:300-303 (_subscript) — missing ast.Slice handler in convert (152-186)
title: Sliced subscripts render as raw ast.dump garbage (e.g. 'a[Slice(lower=Constant(value=1), upper=Constant(value=2))]') because convert has no ast.Slice case
description: _subscript renders the slice via self.convert(node.slice). For a plain index `a[0]` node.slice is a Constant (handled), but for a slice `a[1:2]` node.slice is an ast.Slice, which convert (152-186) does not dispatch on — it falls through to the `return ast.dump(node)` fallback (line 186). The resulting human-readable text contains a raw AST repr ('Slice(lower=Constant(value=1), upper=Constant(value=2))') instead of '1:2'. Polars expressions can produce subscript-with-slice (e.g. Expr.__getitem__ slicing or struct/array indexing), so this leaks internal AST text into the user-facing formula.
evidence: Real _ExprConverter on `a[1:2]` returns 'a[Slice(lower=Constant(value=1), upper=Constant(value=2))]'. convert() (152-186) lists handlers for BinOp/UnaryOp/Compare/BoolOp/Call/Constant/Name/Attribute/Subscript/List/Tuple/Dict/IfExp/JoinedStr/Starred/Expr but not Slice, so node.slice of type ast.Slice hits ast.dump at line 186.

title: _constant does not escape embedded double-quotes, producing malformed/ambiguous formula text
description: _constant renders a str literal as f'"{val}"' (line 271) without escaping any `"` characters inside val. A column/string compared against a value containing a double quote (e.g. `pl.col('a') == 'he said "hi"'`) renders as `a == "he said "hi""`, which is not valid/round-trippable text and is ambiguous to a human reader. The same unescaped pattern is repeated in _pl_lit (line 494). Lower severity (display fidelity), but it is the formula surfaced to actuaries and breaks any consumer that re-parses the text.
evidence: Real _ExprConverter on `pl.col('a') == 'he said "hi"'` returns 'a == "he said "hi""' (the inner quotes are emitted verbatim, closing the string early on re-parse). Source line 271 `return f'"{val}"'` performs no escaping; repr(val) (which would escape) is used only for the non-str int/float/other branches.

title: ast.walk BFS ordering breaks 'last match wins' for chained .with_columns(...).with_columns(...) that redefine the same column, selecting the shadowed (overwritten) definition
description: _find_with_columns_calls collects with_columns/select calls via ast.walk(tree). ast.walk is breadth-first, so for a single chained expression df.with_columns(A).with_columns(B) the OUTER call (B, which Polars applies LAST and which therefore wins) is yielded BEFORE the inner call (A). parse_expression (and _compute_result_impl and _evaluate_conditional_branches) iterate wc_calls and keep the LAST alias match ('last match wins', comment at line 1078). Because walk order is reverse-of-execution for chained calls, the loop's 'last' is actually the inner/earliest (shadowed) definition A, not the effective definition B. The displayed formula, expression_type, referenced_columns AND the computed result_value all reflect the overwritten definition. No exception is raised, so the broad except-catch-all (known finding #23) is NOT involved — this is a confidently-wrong value/formula. Note the equivalent code written as two SEPARATE statements works correctly, because there the two Assign/Call nodes are siblings at the same depth and ast.walk preserves their source order; only the chained form is wrong.
evidence: Executed repro (uv run, Polars 1.39.2) on the real public API. code = 'df = df.with_columns((pl.col("a") + 1).alias("out")).with_columns((pl.col("a") + 100).alias("out"))'. _find_with_columns_calls walk order prints the +100 call FIRST then the +1 call. parse_expression(code,'out').expression_text == 'a + 1' (WRONG; Polars effective is a+100). evaluate_expression(code,'out',{'a':10}).result_value == 11 and substituted_text == '10 + 1' (WRONG; Polars truth = 110). Control: the same logic as two separate statements yields expression_text=='a + 100' and result_value==110 (correct), isolating the chained form + ast.walk ordering as the cause.

location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1171-1181 (_expr_references_vars), reached from _parse_expression_impl:1138-1147; interacts with _find_control_flow_assigned_vars:843-851 and _build_safe_symbol_table:792-808
title: _expr_references_vars's 'and child.id not in symbol_table' guard defeats the opaque bailout when a control-flow-reassigned variable also has a top-level binding, silently dropping the conditional reassignment
description: _parse_expression_impl uses cf_assigned = _find_control_flow_assigned_vars(stmts) and, if the matched expression references any of those vars, returns an opaque ParsedExpression (the intent: an expression depending on a conditionally-assigned variable is not statically resolvable — comment lines 1057-1058). But _expr_references_vars only returns True when a referenced name is in var_names AND 'child.id not in symbol_table'. When the SAME variable is assigned both at top level and reassigned inside an if/for/try (e.g. `factor = pl.col("base")` then `if region=="north": factor = pl.col("base") * 2`), the name is present in symbol_table (from the top-level assignment), so _expr_references_vars returns False, the code is NOT marked opaque, and the variable is resolved to its TOP-LEVEL value only — the conditional reassignment is silently discarded. The parser therefore emits a confidently-wrong formula/result that omits the branch logic, rather than the correct opaque fallback.
evidence: Executed repro: with the top-level binding present, _build_safe_symbol_table -> {'factor'}, _find_control_flow_assigned_vars -> {'factor'}, 'factor' in symbol_table == True, and _expr_references_vars(Name('factor'), {'factor'}, st) == False. parse_expression(code,'out').expression_text == 'base' (type 'arithmetic', refs ['base']) — the `*2` conditional branch is dropped. Contrast: identical code WITHOUT the top-level `factor = pl.col("base")` line yields _expr_references_vars == True and parse_expression(...).expression_type == 'opaque' (correct). This isolates the 'also has a top-level binding' case as the trigger and shows the guard clause `and child.id not in symbol_table` is the defect.

title: _substitute_values corrupts an already-substituted string value when a later (shorter) column name matches a word inside the inserted string literal
description: _substitute_values replaces column names in expression_text one at a time, sorted by name length descending (to avoid prefix collisions). _format_value renders a string column value as a quoted literal (e.g. '"base rate"'). The length-sort only protects against one column name being a prefix of another; it does NOT protect already-inserted VALUES. After substituting a string-valued column, the inserted literal can contain a token equal to another (later-processed) column name; _replace_column_name then matches that token (via \bname\b word boundaries, where spaces are word boundaries) inside the quoted string and overwrites it, producing a corrupted user-facing 'calculation' text. The substituted_text is surfaced to the actuary as the computed calculation (written into step.calculation/source_info by _trace_enrichment), so the displayed formula is demonstrably wrong even though result_value is computed independently.
evidence: Executed end-to-end via the public evaluate_expression: code='df = df.with_columns(pl.concat_str([pl.col("label"), pl.col("rate")]).alias("out"))', row={'label':'base rate','rate':5}. expression_text='concat_str(label, rate)', input_values={'label':'base rate','rate':5}, but substituted_text='concat_str("base 5", 5)' — the literal "base rate" was mangled to "base 5" because column name 'rate' matched the word 'rate' inside the already-substituted string. Direct call _substitute_values('x + b', {'x':'a b','b':5}) likewise yields '"a 5" + 5'. Not covered by the known evaluator-divergence findings (#28/#29), which concern result_value, not the substitution-text rendering order.

est_reduction: ~22 LOC (two orphaned helper functions removed)
