title: Outer .otherwise() containing a nested when corrupts outer branch metadata (reports wrong taken_branch/index/dimmed)
description: In _BranchTrackingEvaluator._eval_clauses, the `then` path sets `self._is_outer = False` (line 2094) before recursing into the then value, but the `otherwise` path (lines 2107-2113) sets taken_branch/taken_branch_index/dimmed_branches WITHOUT clearing `self._is_outer`. So when the outer `.otherwise()` value itself contains a nested when-chain, `self.evaluate(clause['otherwise'])` (line 2113) recurses into the inner chain's _eval_clauses with `is_outer = self._is_outer` still True. The inner chain then overwrites taken_branch/taken_branch_index/dimmed_branches with ITS OWN (inner) values, clobbering the outer's. The trace therefore reports that the outer THEN clause fired when in fact the outer OTHERWISE fired. This metadata is serialized verbatim into step.calculation via dataclasses.asdict(evaluated) (_trace_enrichment.py:1523) and drives which clause the explainability UI highlights/dims, so the user is shown the wrong branch as taken.
evidence: Executed repro (polars 1.39.2). Code: out=pl.when(pl.col('a')>0).then(99).otherwise(pl.when(pl.col('b')>0).then(1).otherwise(2)); row a=-1,b=1. _compute_result_impl returns 1 (correct: outer-otherwise -> inner-then). But _evaluate_conditional_branches returns {'taken_branch':'then','taken_branch_index':0,'dimmed_branches':[1],'nested_branches':[]} — claiming the outer THEN (value 99, index 0) was taken, which is false; the outer OTHERWISE (index 1) fired. Root cause: otherwise branch lacks the `self._is_outer = False` that the then branch has at line 2094, so the nested evaluate() overwrites the just-set outer metadata.

title: nested_branches always records "then" for a nested conditional, regardless of which inner branch actually fired
description: When the taken outer `.then()` contains a nested when-chain, lines 2098-2100 append `self.taken_branch` to `nested_branches` intending to capture the inner branch that fired. But `self._is_outer` was set False at line 2094 BEFORE `self.evaluate(then_node)` runs at line 2096, so the nested _eval_clauses invocation sees `is_outer=False` and never updates `self.taken_branch`. At line 2100 `self.taken_branch` is therefore still the outer's "then", and `self.taken_branch or 'then'` always appends "then". The inner-otherwise case is thus mislabelled as inner-then. nested_branches is surfaced to the trace UI (EvaluatedExpression.nested_branches -> dataclasses.asdict). The intended semantics (record the inner branch kind) are never achievable with the current ordering.
evidence: Executed repro. Code: out=pl.when(pl.col('a')>0).then(pl.when(pl.col('b')>0).then(1).otherwise(2)).otherwise(3). With a=1,b=-1 the inner OTHERWISE fires (result_value=2, confirmed via _compute_result_impl), yet _evaluate_conditional_branches returns nested_branches=['then'] (expected ['otherwise']). With a=1,b=1 (inner then) it also returns ['then'] — so the field is constant 'then' whenever a nested-in-then conditional is taken, carrying no real information. Additionally, a nested when inside the OTHERWISE branch is never recorded in nested_branches at all (the append only exists in the cond/then path), confirmed: a=-1,b=1 gives nested_branches=[].

title: Unary ~ (Invert) does Python bitwise-not on booleans instead of Polars logical-not (~True shown as -2)
description: _unaryop maps ast.Invert to `return ~val`. For boolean inputs this is Python bitwise complement: `~True == -2`, `~False == -1`. But in Polars `~pl.col('mask')` on a Boolean column is LOGICAL negation (`~True -> False`, `~False -> True`), and `~pl.col('flag')` is one of the most common Polars idioms for negating a predicate/mask. The evaluator therefore displays a meaningless signed integer (-1/-2) as the computed value for a negated boolean in the trace waterfall, instead of the boolean Polars actually produces. This null/bool divergence is not one of the broad categories the catalog enumerates (the replace finding lists null-propagation / branch-selection / string-coercion / aggregation; unary boolean ~ is none of these) and is far more commonly hit than the horizontal-func edge cases already catalogued.
evidence: Executed repro (polars 1.39.2). Code: out=~pl.col('flag'). flag=True -> evaluator result_value=-2, real Polars=False. flag=False -> evaluator=-1, real Polars=True. The AST for ~pl.col('flag') is UnaryOp(op=Invert), routed to line 1647-1648 which returns ~True == -2.

title: _compare silently treats unsupported comparison operators (is/is not/in/not in) as passing, returning True
description: _compare builds cmp_map for Eq/NotEq/Lt/LtE/Gt/GtE only. For any other comparison operator (ast.Is, ast.IsNot, ast.In, ast.NotIn) `fn = cmp_map.get(type(op))` is None, the `if fn:` block is skipped, the loop advances `left = right`, and the function ultimately falls through to `return True`. So an unsupported comparison is silently treated as satisfied rather than failing loudly or returning None. This is a latent correctness hole: any future code path (or a chained comparison mixing a supported and an unsupported op) would silently report True. Reachability through valid Polars expression source is essentially nil (Polars uses .is_in()/.is_null() methods, not Python `in`/`is`), so impact today is low, but the swallow-and-pass behaviour contradicts the project's fail-loud preference and the None-propagation contract used elsewhere in this class.
evidence: Executed repro: _ExprEvaluator({'a':1,'b':2}).evaluate(ast.parse('a is b').body[0].value) -> True (1 is 2 is False); evaluate(ast.parse('a in b').body[0].value) with {'a':9,'b':[1,2,3]} -> True (9 in [1,2,3] is False). The supported chained case 1<5<3 correctly returns False, confirming only the unsupported-op arm is affected.

title: Subclass override of _eval_when_from_then_or_otherwise is byte-identical to the parent and adds nothing
description: _BranchTrackingEvaluator overrides _eval_when_from_then_or_otherwise with a body that is byte-identical to _ExprEvaluator._eval_when_from_then_or_otherwise (both do `clauses = self._collect_eval_clauses(node); return self._eval_clauses(clauses)`). The docstring claims 'Override to track nested branches', but the override changes no behaviour: the branch-tracking happens entirely inside _eval_clauses, which is independently overridden, and Python already dispatches `self._eval_clauses`/`self._collect_eval_clauses` to the subclass via normal MRO. The override can be deleted with zero behavioural change. This is distinct from SIMP-7 (which covers the _eval_when_chain/_eval_chained_when stubs and the _eval_clauses duplication, not this redundant override).
evidence: AST comparison of the two method bodies (docstring stripped) shows identical statement lists: Assign(clauses = self._collect_eval_clauses(node)); Return(self._eval_clauses(clauses)). Equal == True. Removing the subclass method leaves the inherited parent method, which already calls the subclass's overridden _eval_clauses/_collect_eval_clauses, so output is unchanged.
est_reduction: ~4 LOC (one redundant method)
behavior_preservation: Deleting the override leaves the identical inherited implementation, which already dynamically dispatches to the subclass's _eval_clauses and _collect_eval_clauses; no call site or output changes.

title: all_horizontal / any_horizontal are in the horizontal dispatch set but unimplemented in _eval_horizontal, always returning None
description: _HORIZONTAL_FUNCS (lines 114-123) includes 'all_horizontal' and 'any_horizontal', so _call routes them to _eval_horizontal (line 1733-1734). But _eval_horizontal only has branches for max_horizontal/min_horizontal/sum_horizontal/mean_horizontal/coalesce; all_horizontal and any_horizontal hit the final `return None`. Unlike the catalogued sum/mean/concat_str null-edge divergences, these are TOTALLY unimplemented — they return None for ALL inputs, not just edge cases, so the trace shows None where Polars returns a real boolean. The catalog's known horizontal finding enumerates only sum_horizontal(all-null), mean_horizontal(one-null), and concat_str; it does not mention all_horizontal/any_horizontal, and these route through the dispatch set rather than being merely unhandled functions. (Reported with low confidence as it may be considered subsumed by the broad 'horizontal funcs diverge' title.)
evidence: Executed repro (polars 1.39.2): out=pl.all_horizontal(pl.col('a'),pl.col('b')) with a=True,b=False -> evaluator result_value=None, real Polars=False. out=pl.any_horizontal(...) same inputs -> evaluator=None, real Polars=True. The function names are present in _HORIZONTAL_FUNCS so they reach _eval_horizontal, which has no matching arm and returns None at line 2017.

title: Falsy `source` is handled three different ways inside _execute_lazy (raw for graph pruning, coerced to "live" for cache-key validation and checkpoint scenario) — latent inconsistency
description: _execute_lazy receives `source: str = "live"`. Graph preparation / live-switch pruning uses the RAW value (`_prepare_graph_with_edges(graph, target_node_id, source=source)` at lines 709-713, which flows into `projection_planner.prune_live_switch_edges` where `source not in input_scenario_map.values()` and `mapped != source` compare against the raw string). However, two other sites in the SAME function silently coerce a falsy source to "live": the dataframe-cache-key source check computes `effective_source = source or "live"` (line 807) and validates `cache_key.source != effective_source`, and the checkpoint-decision scenario passes `node_source_overrides.get(nid, source or "live")` (line 1360). Node builders, meanwhile, receive the raw `source` (via `_build_funcs` `node_source_overrides.get(nid, source)`). If a caller ever passes `source=""` (or any falsy string), the graph would be pruned and node functions built under `""`, while cache admission and checkpoint MODEL_SCORE-skip logic would behave as if `"live"` — three divergent interpretations of one argument. This is a contract inconsistency, not a crash.
evidence: Line 709-713 `_prepare_graph_with_edges(graph, target_node_id, source=source)` → projection.py prune_live_switch_edges compares raw `source`. Line 807 `effective_source = source or "live"` then `if cache_key.source != effective_source: raise`. Line 1360 `_checkpoint_decision(..., node_source_overrides.get(nid, source or "live"))`; _checkpoint_decision (line 440) skips MODEL_SCORE only when `scenario != "live"`. Line 1484 in _build_funcs uses `node_source_overrides.get(nid, source)` (raw). The presence of the defensive `source or "live"` coercion at exactly two of the three sites shows a falsy source was anticipated but not handled uniformly.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1903-1904 (multi-port emit branch of _execute_eager_core), consumed at src/haute/executor.py:1131-1137 (_column_infos_for_node)
title: Multi-port apiInput source node reports zero columns in its own preview (empty output_columns shadows the first-port fallback)
description: In the multi-port emit branch of `_execute_eager_core`, a source that returns `dict[port_label, DataFrame]` has `output_columns[nid] = []` and `available_columns[nid] = []` hard-set (lines 1903-1904). That empty list flows out as `EagerResult.output_columns` and becomes `output_cols` in `executor._eager_execute`. When the preview builder renders the source node itself, `_column_infos_for_node` (executor.py:1131) does `full_output = output_cols.get(node_id)`, gets `[]`, and because `[] is not None` is True it sets `columns = []` and never reaches the `elif df is not None` branch (line 1134) that would derive columns from the representative first-port DataFrame. The result: the multi-port apiInput node's NodeResult has `column_count == 0` and `columns == []` even though `df = next(iter(df.values()))` (executor.py:1182-1185) is a real DataFrame with columns and `row_count` is reported correctly. This directly defeats the documented intent at executor.py:1179-1181 ('use the first port's frame as a representative'). Single-port apiInput is unaffected because it returns a bare DataFrame and takes the normal path that populates `output_columns` (line 1933).
evidence: _execute_eager_core multi-port branch: `output_columns[nid] = []` (line 1904) then `continue` (line 1907), so the normal `output_columns[nid] = full_output_columns` (line 1933) is skipped. executor._column_infos_for_node: `full_output = output_cols.get(node_id)` -> `[]`; `if full_output is not None:` is taken for an empty list, so `columns = [ColumnInfo(n,d) for n,d in []] == []`; the `elif df is not None` first-port fallback is dead for this node. Existing test test_apiinput_multi_port_runtime.py::test_two_consumers_different_ports_dont_collide_on_column_cache only asserts columns on the POLARS *consumer* nodes (c_policies/c_drivers, lines 411-420), and the single-port test (lines 184-189) asserts only status/row_count on `api` — no test asserts `results['api'].columns`/`column_count` for a multi-port source, so the gap is uncovered.

title: explain_null_value is dead code — fully implemented and tested but never called by any production path
description: explain_null_value is a public-looking enricher that produces human-readable null-origin explanations, but nothing in src/ ever calls it. It is not invoked by enrich_steps or any node-type enricher, not re-exported via haute.trace or haute.__init__, and not reached by any dynamic/string dispatch. Its only references are its own definition and a dedicated test class (tests/test_trace_enrichment.py:2601+). It therefore inflates the module and its line/branch coverage without contributing to any traced behaviour. Per the project's dead-code guidance (raise coverage by deleting dead code, not by gaming the gate), this is a removal candidate (function + its tests).
evidence: Repo-wide search for non-definition, non-test references returns nothing: `grep -rn explain_null_value --include=*.py . | grep -v tests/ | grep -v 'def explain_null_value'` => only the def at line 62. No hit in src/haute/trace.py or src/haute/__init__.py. No getattr/string-keyed dispatch references it (the only `null_value`/`fill_null` hits are unrelated, in chunking.py:439/455). The five other private banding/payload helpers in this file (_banding_factor_for_column, _banding_*_payload, _focus_banding_factor, _copy_banding_factor_summary) all have real callers at lines 462/584/586/1101-1104/1207-1212; explain_null_value uniquely has none.
est_reduction: ~38 lines in src (the function + its module section header) plus the associated test class; net coverage neutral-to-positive since the removed code currently only pads coverage via its own tests.
behavior_preservation: Removing the function and its tests changes no runtime behaviour because no production code imports or calls it. (If it is intended as public API, it should instead be wired into the null-explanation path or exported and documented — currently it is neither.)

title: _enrich_single_table returns matched=True while status='unmatched_value', so a value the trace cannot attribute to any entry or the default is still flagged as a match
description: The returned `matched` field (line 177: `matched and not default_used`, where `matched = rate_value is not None`) is derived purely from value-presence, but `status` (lines 161-168) is derived from `matched_entry is not None`. These diverge for the `unmatched_value` branch: when the rating join produced a NON-null `rate_value` that (a) Python's `normalise_rating_key` walk could not attribute to any `entries` row AND (b) does not equal a usable finite `default_val`, the code sets status='unmatched_value' yet matched=True (and default_used=False). The frontend warning-chip contract relies on `matched`/`default_used` to flag suspicious rows (cf. tests/test_optimiser_apply_trace_enrichment.py:450-451 'frontend warning-chip contract'), so an unattributable value — exactly the suspicious case — is hidden behind matched=True. The single-table convenience path propagates this upward: enrich_rating_step sets result['matched']=t['matched'] (line 248), and the multi-table path ORs t['matched'] (line 256), so the top-level rating detail also reports matched=True for an unmatched_value row. Reachable cases: (1) the documented Float32 non-integer factor-key gap (normalise_rating_key docstring at src/haute/_rating.py:329-333 explicitly excludes non-integer Float32 columns from the engine-agreement guarantee — the engine matches an entry and fills its value, but normalise_rating_key formats the float differently and finds no entry); (2) a non-finite/non-numeric configured defaultValue that the engine nonetheless used (e.g. defaultValue='inf' => default_val=None at lines 132-133 => default_used can never become True at line 155, so a real defaulted miss with a non-null fill becomes status='unmatched_value', matched=True).
evidence: Trace for defaultValue='inf', input miss, engine fills a non-null value v: line 127 has_default truthy; line 129 default_val=float('inf'); line 132 not isfinite => default_val=None. matched_entry stays None (no entry matched / or miss). line 153 matched = (v is not None) = True. line 155 guard `default_val is not None` is False => default_used stays False. Status ladder: not default_used, matched_entry is None, rate_value is not None => line 168 status='unmatched_value'. Return line 177: `matched and not default_used` = True. => {status:'unmatched_value', matched:True, default_used:False}. The existing test test_default_value_infinity (tests/test_trace_enrichment.py:3260) only asserts default_value is None and uses a value (0.5) that isn't the inf fill, so it never checks matched/status for an actually-used non-finite default. The engine-agreement harness assert_engine_and_enrichment_agree (tests/test_rating_key_agreement.py:565-577) only ever asserts the matched/default/no_match trichotomy and has no branch for 'unmatched_value', so this internally-inconsistent state is entirely unguarded.

title: enrich_steps builds input_frames / source_names / source_ids with DIFFERENT filter predicates, so a missing/None parent output desynchronises the positional alignment and optimiserApply trace selects the wrong parent DataFrame (or raises a spurious index ValueError)
behavior_preservation: n/a (correctness bug, not a simplification)
description: In the optimiserApply branch of enrich_steps the three positionally-correlated argument lists are derived from the same parent_ids list but with non-matching guards: input_frames keeps `pid` only when `pid in eager_outputs and eager_outputs[pid] is not None`, while source_names and source_ids keep `pid` when `pid in node_map`. A parent that failed to execute is ABSENT from eager_outputs (trace.py:768 builds `eager_outputs = {nid: df ... if df is not None}`, so failed/None nodes are dropped) but is still PRESENT in node_map (node_map holds every node). When such a parent precedes a real one, input_frames drops it while source_ids/source_names retain it, so the frames tuple is shorter than / shifted relative to source_ids. The downstream selector _select_optimiser_apply_input (_builders.py:1409-1415) does `index = source_ids.index(ratebook_input); return dfs[index]`, which assumes dfs and source_ids are positionally aligned. Result: in ratebook mode the wrong parent frame is selected, or `index >= len(dfs)` raises the misleading 'expected ratebook_input at index N but received M input(s)' ValueError; in online mode _select_optimiser_apply_input returns `dfs[0]`, so a dropped first parent silently makes dfs[0] the SECOND parent's frame, yielding a confidently-wrong optimiser explanation. The engine's own non-trace build path (_builders.py:1013-1016) deliberately rebuilds dfs in declared-source order to keep dfs/_src_names/_src_ids consistent; the trace path here does not, diverging from that contract. Because the call is wrapped in the per-node try/except, the failure surfaces as a node_detail error marker or a wrong explanation rather than a hard crash.
evidence: Lines 1724-1742: `parent_ids = parents_of.get(step.node_id, [])`; `input_frames = [eager_outputs[pid] for pid in parent_ids if pid in eager_outputs and eager_outputs[pid] is not None]`; `source_names = [_sanitize_func_name(node_map[pid].data.label) for pid in parent_ids if pid in node_map]`; `source_ids=[pid for pid in parent_ids if pid in node_map]`. The `eager_outputs[pid] is not None` guard proves the author anticipated absent/None frames, yet that filter is not applied to source_ids/source_names. _select_optimiser_apply_input (_builders.py:1383-1415) selects `dfs[0]` for online mode and `dfs[source_ids.index(ratebook_input)]` for ratebook mode, both requiring dfs[i] to correspond to source_ids[i]. eager_outputs values are never None / failed nodes are absent (trace.py:768), but node_map contains all nodes (trace.py:_assemble_steps reads node_map[nid] for every ordered node), so a failed/absent parent satisfies `pid in node_map` but not `pid in eager_outputs` — desynchronising the lists. Reachable on the partial-execution trace path (trace.py:514-524 assembles steps for nodes even when the target failed) and whenever an optimiserApply node has ≥1 parent missing from eager_outputs.
est_reduction: n/a

title: Banding column contract declares produced output even when the factor has no rules (runtime skips it)
description: _banding_columns reports a factor's outputColumn as a produced column whenever both 'column' and 'outputColumn' are non-empty: `produced = {f["outputColumn"] for f in factors if f.get("outputColumn")}`. But the runtime _apply_banding_factors skips any factor whose rules are empty: `if not col or not out or not rules: continue`. So a banding factor with column+outputColumn set but an empty/absent `rules` list is declared as produced by the contract yet is never created at runtime. The projection demand-propagation subtracts produced columns from upstream demand (projection.py:2321 `base_contribution = (my_needed - produced) | referenced`), so if a downstream node demands that outputColumn, the demand is removed at the banding node (contract claims ownership) but no column is materialised -> downstream select/reference fails with column-not-found in projected/bounded profiles. The contract must apply the same `rules` guard as the executor.
evidence: _banding_columns (l.762) has no rules check; _apply_banding_factors (_rating.py l.244) skips factors with empty rules; projection.py l.2321 subtracts `produced` from upstream demand for concrete contracts (BANDING is concrete, registered via columns=_banding_columns at l.767).

title: Rating-step column contract declares produced output for tables with no factors/entries (runtime skips them)
description: _rating_step_columns adds a table's outputColumn to `produced` for any table with a non-empty outputColumn (l.794-797: `out = t.get("outputColumn", ""); if out: produced.add(out)`), ignoring whether the table has usable `factors`/`entries`. The runtime _apply_rating_table returns the frame unchanged (no column produced) when factors or entries are empty: `if not factors or not entries or not output_col: return lf`. So a rating table with outputColumn set but empty entries (an in-progress config) is declared produced by the contract but never materialised. As with banding, projection.py:2321 subtracts the over-declared `produced` from upstream demand, so a downstream consumer of that outputColumn gets it pruned away yet the runtime never creates it -> column-not-found at materialisation in projected profiles. The contract should mirror the executor's factors/entries guard before declaring a table output as produced.
evidence: _rating_step_columns l.794-797 declares produced from outputColumn presence only; _apply_rating_table (_rating.py l.517) skips tables with empty factors or entries; demand subtraction at projection.py l.2321 applies (RATING_STEP concrete contract via columns=_rating_step_columns at l.807). normalise_rating_tables (_rating_step_config.py l.304) does not drop such tables.

title: scenario_expander step_column contract diverges from runtime when step_column is empty/None
description: The contract reads `sc = config.get("step_column", "scenario_index")` then only adds it to produced if truthy, whereas the builder uses `_step_col = config.get("step_column") or "scenario_index"`. These differ exactly when `step_column` is present but falsy ("" or None): the contract yields `""`/None (falsy) and omits the produced column, while the builder coalesces to "scenario_index" and always produces it. Result: the contract under-declares the produced step-index column for an explicitly-empty step_column. Under-declaring produced means the planner does not treat "scenario_index" as created here; if it happens to exist upstream the demand routing/ownership for it is wrong, and checkpoint projection metadata is inaccurate. Use the same `or` coalescing in the contract (matching the builder) so both agree.
evidence: Contract l.845: `sc = config.get("step_column", "scenario_index")` (default only applies when key absent); builder l.863: `_step_col = config.get("step_column") or "scenario_index"` (default applies for absent, "" and None). Divergence for explicit empty/None step_column.

title: live_switch kwarg path mis-indexes when an upstream frame is absent from dfs_by_name
description: In the kwarg branch, `dfs = tuple(dfs_by_name[name] for name in input_names if name in dfs_by_name)` compacts to only the present names, but the selection loop later indexes the compacted tuple using the position of the matching name within the FULL input_names list: `for i, name in enumerate(input_names): if name == inp: return dfs[i]`. If any earlier input name is missing from dfs_by_name, `i` is offset relative to the compacted `dfs`, so the wrong frame is returned (or IndexError when i >= len(dfs)). The executor itself always calls the function positionally (_execute_lazy.py:1206 `fn(*input_lfs)` and :1856 `result = fn(*input_lfs)`), so this path is only reached by direct kwarg callers (tests/future callers) -- hence the low real-world severity -- but the kwarg contract is silently wrong. The index should be computed against the same filtered name list used to build `dfs`.
evidence: Builder l.645 filters names present in dfs_by_name; l.651-653 indexes dfs by position in unfiltered input_names. Executor passes positional args only (_execute_lazy.py:1206, 1856), so the kwarg branch is exercised solely by direct callers.

title: OUTPUT contract (_passthrough_columns) ignores the fields-based select for non-terminal output nodes
description: output_fn narrows its frame to config['fields'] (`if fields: lf = lf.select(fields)`), but OUTPUT is registered with _passthrough_columns (reads nothing, produces nothing => models full pass-through). The projection layer compensates only when the OUTPUT node is TERMINAL: projection.py:2166-2168 seeds `needed` from fields for childless OUTPUT nodes. For a non-terminal OUTPUT (one that has downstream children), the special case does not apply and the contract claims pass-through; the planner therefore propagates child demand through unchanged, but the runtime select(fields) drops any demanded column not in `fields`, causing a downstream column-not-found. This is a latent gap that only manifests for the unusual topology of an OUTPUT node feeding further nodes; if such topologies are intentionally rejected elsewhere this is moot, but the contract/runtime divergence is concrete and unguarded.
evidence: output_fn l.753-755 selects fields; registration l.743 uses columns=_passthrough_columns; projection.py terminal-only fields seeding at l.2165-2168 (guarded by `if not children`). No fields handling for non-terminal OUTPUT.

title: Stale sys.path comment in _compile_preamble describes idempotent gated inserts the code no longer performs
description: The block comment in _compile_preamble (lines 421-427) states: 'We add both cwd and the pipeline's parent directory ... These inserts are idempotent (gated on `not in sys.path`) so the list doesn't grow on every call.' This is doubly inaccurate. (a) _compile_preamble itself performs NO sys.path mutation — the only sys.path edit in the whole module is in _prioritise_preamble_import_paths (lines 279-280), reached via _compile_preamble_cached. (b) That actual mutation is `sys.path[:] = [existing for existing in sys.path if existing != path]` followed by `sys.path.insert(0, path)` — a remove-then-reinsert, NOT an insert 'gated on `not in sys.path`'. The remove-then-reinsert is what actually prevents growth, while also re-prioritising the entry to position 0 each call (a behaviour the comment does not mention and would be surprising to a maintainer who trusts the 'gated on not in sys.path' description). The stale comment can mislead a maintainer reasoning about import-precedence/ordering during the preamble compile.
evidence: grep for `sys.path` in executor.py returns exactly lines 131 (doc), 279-280 (the only mutation, in _prioritise_preamble_import_paths), and 426 (the stale comment). _compile_preamble's body (380-454) contains no sys.path access; it only computes cwd/pipeline_dir_str/fingerprint and delegates to _compile_preamble_cached, which calls _prioritise_preamble_import_paths under _preamble_lock. The mutation removes all matching entries then inserts at index 0 — neither 'gated on not in sys.path' nor located in _compile_preamble.
est_reduction: ~7 comment lines corrected/removed (no logic change)
behavior_preservation: Comment-only; deleting or correcting it does not alter runtime behaviour.

title: Redundant `import os` inside _compile_preamble shadows the module-level import with the same module
description: Line 428 executes `import os` inside _compile_preamble even though `os` is already imported at module scope (line 22) and is referenced elsewhere in the module (e.g. _positive_int_from_env at line 92, _compile_preamble_cached/_exec via cwd). The local statement re-binds the identical module object to the same name with no effect and no shadowing benefit — nothing in the function between its start (380) and line 428 rebinds or deletes `os`. It is leftover from an earlier refactor (the surrounding comment about 'spawned by uvicorn reload' refers to behaviour now handled by _prioritise_preamble_import_paths).
evidence: Module top: line 22 `import os`. Inside _compile_preamble: line 428 `import os` then line 430 `cwd = os.getcwd()`. The module-level `os` is already in scope and usable; the function-local import is a no-op rebind to the same module.
est_reduction: 1 line
behavior_preservation: Removing line 428 leaves `os` resolved to the module-level import; `os.getcwd()` on line 430 behaves identically.

title: _utility_module_candidates duplicates _cache._utility_candidates_for_dir's utility-path enumeration
description: _utility_module_candidates (executor.py) and _utility_candidates_for_dir (_cache.py) implement the same algorithm: build candidate utility roots from [pipeline_dir?, cwd], then for each base yield `base/'utility.py'` and `base/'utility'`, resolve each, and de-duplicate via a `seen` set preserving order. They produce identical resolved candidate lists. The only textual difference is that _cache's version pre-resolves the pipeline_dir base (`Path(pipeline_dir).resolve()`) while executor's appends `Path(pipeline_dir_str)` unresolved — immaterial because each candidate is resolved in-loop (`candidate.resolve()` resolves the full chain). The two copies serve adjacent concerns (fingerprinting in _cache, on-disk pyc eviction in executor) so they will drift if one is changed (e.g. adding a `utility/` nesting rule) without the other. Consolidating to a single shared helper removes the duplicated dedup/enumeration logic.
evidence: Side-by-side: both functions construct `bases=[pipeline_dir?, cwd.resolve()]`, loop `for candidate in (base/'utility.py', base/'utility')`, `resolved=candidate.resolve()`, skip if in `seen`, else append. Trace shows identical outputs for any input because in-loop `.resolve()` makes the executor's unresolved base immaterial. _utility_module_candidates is consumed only by _evict_utility_import_state (executor.py:256); _utility_candidates_for_dir only by preamble_execution_fingerprint (_cache.py:394).
est_reduction: ~16 lines (one copy of the enumeration body), modulo a cross-module import
behavior_preservation: Both functions already yield byte-identical resolved candidate lists; routing both call sites through one helper preserves the candidate set and ordering, so eviction targets and fingerprint inputs are unchanged.

title: _cached_output_names raises AttributeError on multi-port apiInput parents (dict output has no .columns)
description: _cached_output_names is the schema-warning helper used when an instance node (config['instanceOf']) is present: it sums the columns feeding the instance and the original by calling _cached_output_names(pid) for each parent. For a multi-port apiInput source, _execute_eager_core stores output_columns[nid] = [] and available_columns[nid] = [] (an EMPTY list, not absent) while eager_outputs[nid] is a dict[port_label, DataFrame] (src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1900-1904). In _cached_output_names, `cached = output_cols.get(node_id)` yields [], so `if cached:` is False and it falls through to `df = eager_outputs.get(node_id)` which is the per-port dict, then executes `set(df.columns)` (line 1107). dict has no .columns attribute, so this raises AttributeError. This loop runs inside execute_graph's try/finally that only manages the cache pin — it is NOT covered by the per-node error swallowing of _eager_execute(swallow_errors=True) — so the exception propagates out of execute_graph and fails the entire preview/trace request (HTTP 500) rather than degrading one node. Trigger: a multi-port apiInput wired as a direct parent of any node carrying instanceOf (or of the referenced original). Multi-port apiInput sources and instance nodes are both shipped features and nothing structurally forbids wiring them together.
evidence: executor.py:1103 `cached = output_cols.get(node_id)` -> [] for multi-port; 1104 `if cached:` False (empty list falsy); 1106 `df = eager_outputs.get(node_id)` -> dict (the `materialised` bundle); 1107 `set(df.columns)` -> AttributeError because df is a dict. Population proof: _execute_lazy.py:1900 `eager_outputs[nid] = materialised` (a dict), 1903 `available_columns[nid] = []`, 1904 `output_columns[nid] = []`. Reached via executor.py:1116 / 1120 `_cached_output_names(pid)` for parents of an instanceOf node.

title: _column_infos_for_node reports column_count=0 / columns=[] for a multi-port apiInput's own NodeResult despite a non-empty representative frame
description: For the multi-port apiInput source node, output_columns[nid] is stored as [] (empty list) by the eager core (_execute_lazy.py:1904). In _column_infos_for_node, `full_output = output_cols.get(node_id)` is [] and the guard is `if full_output is not None:` — an empty list is NOT None, so the function takes the empty branch and sets columns = [], never reaching the `elif df is not None:` branch (line 1134) that would correctly read the representative first-port frame's columns. Meanwhile the main results loop (line 1182-1184) reduces the dict to the first port and builds a real preview from it: row_count = len(first_port_df) > 0, preview rows carry the port's columns, and preview_columns is non-empty (line 1208-1221). The resulting NodeResult is internally inconsistent: column_count=0 and columns=[] while preview/preview_columns/row_count reflect a frame that has columns. tests/test_apiinput_multi_port_runtime.py only asserts the CONSUMER nodes' columns, never the multi-port source node's own result, so this silent misreport is untested. This is a classic 'empty-list is not None' bug: the intended fallback to df.columns is dead for the [] case.
evidence: executor.py:1131 `full_output = output_cols.get(node_id)` -> [] ; 1132 `if full_output is not None:` True for [] ; 1133 `columns = [...]` over [] -> columns=[] ; line 1134 `elif df is not None:` (which would read first_port_df.columns) is unreachable when output_cols is []. df passed in is the first-port frame (executor.py:1182-1185). Contrast: a normal node legitimately producing zero columns also hits this branch correctly; only the multi-port case is wrong because its frame has columns but output_columns is [].
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: _eager_execute rebuilds node_map manually instead of using the cached graph.node_map property
description: Line 1327 constructs `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` inside the preamble-error injection block. PipelineGraph already exposes `node_map` as a @cached_property whose body is exactly `{n.id: n for n in self.nodes}` (src/haute/_types.py:697-700), and execute_graph itself uses `graph.node_map` (executor.py:1082). The manual rebuild duplicates that logic and rebuilds the dict on every preamble-error path instead of reusing the memoised mapping. Replacing it with `node_map = graph.node_map` is behaviour-preserving (the cached_property returns the same mapping for the same instance) and removes the hand-rolled comprehension.
evidence: executor.py:1327 `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` vs _types.py:698-700 `@cached_property def node_map(self): return {n.id: n for n in self.nodes}`. The surrounding loop (1328-1331) only reads node_map.get(nid), so the cached property suffices.
est_reduction: 1 line (replace comprehension with cached-property access); avoids a redundant dict build on preamble-error paths.
behavior_preservation: Identical mapping content; cached_property is computed from the same graph.nodes and is read-only here.

title: Module constants _VARIABLE_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES and _UNKNOWN_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES are defined but never referenced
description: Lines 201-202 define `_VARIABLE_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES = 64` and `_UNKNOWN_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES = 64`. Neither name is used anywhere in the module or the test suite. The byte-budget width estimation path uses `_DEFAULT_PROJECTED_COLUMN_BYTES` (line 180, also 64) for both the unknown-column fallback in `_estimate_projected_row_bytes` (line 649) and the unmapped-dtype fallback in `_dtype_estimated_width` (line 691). These two constants are leftover scaffolding from an apparently abandoned width-classification design (variable-width vs unknown-width) that was never wired up. They also silently duplicate the value 64 three ways, creating drift risk if someone later edits one but not the others.
evidence: Grep across the entire repo (`src/haute` and `tests`) for `_VARIABLE_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES` / `_UNKNOWN_WIDTH_COLUMN_BYTES` returns matches ONLY at the definition site src/haute/chunking.py:201-202 (one file, two lines, the definitions themselves). By contrast `_DEFAULT_PROJECTED_COLUMN_BYTES` is referenced at lines 649 and 691. The width-estimation functions (`_estimate_projected_row_bytes` 629-651, `_dtype_estimated_width` 690-691) never read the two constants.
est_reduction: -2 LOC (delete the two unused constants); removes a 3-way duplicated literal/drift hazard
behavior_preservation: The constants are never read by any code path, so deleting them cannot change behavior. `_estimate_projected_row_bytes` and `_dtype_estimated_width` continue to use `_DEFAULT_PROJECTED_COLUMN_BYTES` unchanged.

title: validate_chunk_capability_declarations silently substitutes the global registry for an explicitly-passed empty mapping (truthiness fallback)
description: Line 348 does `registry = declarations or _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS`. The intent (per the `Mapping | None = None` signature) is 'use the global registry when the caller passes None'. But the `or` test is on truthiness, not `is None`: an explicitly-passed EMPTY mapping `{}` is falsy and is therefore silently replaced by the global `_CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS`. As a result `validate_chunk_capability_declarations({})` validates the global registry (and passes), instead of validating the empty mapping the caller actually handed in (which should fail loudly: it is missing every NodeType). This conflates two distinct inputs ('not provided' vs 'an empty registry') and is precisely the kind of silent fallback the project's CLAUDE.md forbids ('code should be allowed to fail loudly... a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice'). A validator that cannot detect a completely-empty registry is a contract hole: a future refactor that builds the registry dynamically and accidentally yields `{}` would pass this guard rather than being caught.
evidence: Line 348: `registry = declarations or _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS`. For `declarations={}`: `{} or _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS` evaluates to `_CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS` because `{}` is falsy, so `expected - observed` (line 351-352) is computed against the full global registry and `missing`/`extra` are both empty -> no RuntimeError raised. The drift test at tests/test_chunk_plan.py:99-104 only ever passes a 17-entry dict (POLARS popped from the 18-entry registry), which is still truthy, so it never exercises the empty-mapping path; the empty case is unguarded. The correct, fail-loud form is `registry = _CHUNK_CAPABILITY_DECLARATIONS if declarations is None else declarations`, which would raise the existing 'must mention every node type exactly once' RuntimeError for `{}` (Missing=all 18 node types).

title: Manual unlink of dest/.parquet.tmp in _write_chunk_checkpoint failure path is unreachable-as-effective; atomic_write already guarantees removal
description: On a checkpoint write failure, _write_chunk_checkpoint's except block calls `path.unlink(missing_ok=True)` and `path.with_suffix('.parquet.tmp').unlink(missing_ok=True)` before rmdir. Neither call can ever find a file to remove. `atomic_write` (src/haute/_polars_utils.py:288-293) wraps the write in `try: yield tmp; tmp.replace(dest) except BaseException: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise`, so on ANY exception inside the `with` body (the only failure point is `frame.write_parquet(tmp, ...)`) the temp file is already unlinked by atomic_write before control returns to _write_chunk_checkpoint. The final `dest` is created only by the atomic `tmp.replace(dest)`, which runs solely on the success path and is itself atomic (os.replace cannot partially create dest), so `path` (dest) never exists on the failure path either. Thus both unlink calls are guaranteed no-ops. The only load-bearing cleanup in this block is the `checkpoint_dir.rmdir()` (which removes the now-empty owned dir on a first-chunk failure). The redundant unlinks are confirmed non-load-bearing by the passing regression test test_chunk_runner_cleans_partial_checkpoint_write_failure (tests/test_chunk_runner.py:890-914), which writes a partial tmp file then raises and still passes purely via atomic_write's own cleanup.
evidence: _polars_utils.py atomic_write: `try: yield tmp; tmp.replace(dest) except BaseException: tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise` -> tmp always removed on failure, dest never created on failure. chunking.py:1552-1556: `with atomic_write(path) as tmp: frame.write_parquet(...) except BaseException: path.unlink(missing_ok=True); path.with_suffix('.parquet.tmp').unlink(missing_ok=True); ...` -> at this point tmp is already gone and dest absent, so both unlinks match nothing in every reachable path (write_parquet failure, or the atomic replace failure).
est_reduction: -2 LOC (drop the two redundant unlink statements at 1555-1556; keep the rmdir cleanup). Net: removes dead defensive cleanup, leaving atomic_write as the single source of temp/dest cleanup.
behavior_preservation: Behavior is identical: the two unlinks are provable no-ops in all reachable failure paths because atomic_write unconditionally unlinks the temp file and never creates dest on failure. The kept rmdir and the outer _cleanup_written_checkpoints path are unaffected. test_chunk_runner_cleans_partial_checkpoint_write_failure already proves cleanup succeeds without relying on these unlinks.

title: streaming_collect is re-imported locally inside iter_chunked_frames though it is already imported at module level
description: iter_chunked_frames performs a function-local `from haute._polars_utils import (bounded_collect_batches, streaming_collect, temporary_streaming_chunk_size)`. However `streaming_collect` is already imported at module scope on line 27 (`from haute._polars_utils import DEFAULT_STREAMING_CHUNK_SIZE, streaming_collect`) and is used elsewhere in the module at lines 670 and 1029 via that module-level binding. The local re-import of `streaming_collect` shadows the identical module-level name with no behavioral difference. Only `bounded_collect_batches` and `temporary_streaming_chunk_size` genuinely need the local import (they are not imported at module level). This is incidental redundancy, not a correctness issue.
evidence: Line 27: `from haute._polars_utils import DEFAULT_STREAMING_CHUNK_SIZE, streaming_collect`. Line 864 re-imports the same `streaming_collect` inside iter_chunked_frames. grep of `streaming_collect` in chunking.py shows usages at 670 and 1029 (both resolvable from the module-level import) plus the redundant local import at 864.
est_reduction: -1 name from the local import tuple (drop `streaming_collect` from line 864, keeping bounded_collect_batches and temporary_streaming_chunk_size which are not module-level).
behavior_preservation: Identical: the module-level streaming_collect (line 27) is the same object; removing the shadowing local re-import leaves all call sites bound to the same function. No call site references differ.

title: Type-mismatch list silently truncated to 10 with no "... and N more" indicator (inconsistent with the missing-features block)
description: _format_feature_mismatch renders the missing-feature block with an explicit overflow line (`if n_missing > 20: lines.append(f'  ... and {n_missing - 20} more')`, lines 179-180) but the type-mismatch block iterates `type_mismatches[:10]` (line 185) with NO equivalent overflow notice. When a wide model is scored with more than 10 declared-categorical columns each supplied as a numeric dtype, the operator is told to 'fix the upstream schema or re-train' but the diagnostic shows only the first 10 offending columns and gives no signal that further columns are also mis-typed. The truncation is real: the type-mismatch raise (lines 256-267) fires precisely when `usable` is non-empty and nothing is missing, i.e. all expected features are present but >=1 categorical was passed numeric — a wide model can easily exceed 10 such columns. The result is a fail-loud error whose remediation guidance is silently incomplete, so the operator may fix the 10 shown columns, re-run, and hit the same error again on the next 10.
evidence: Lines 175-187: missing block has `for name in missing[:20]: ...` followed by `if n_missing > 20: lines.append(f'  ... and {n_missing - 20} more')`. Type block (183-187): `lines.append('Type mismatch(es):'); for col, expected_type, actual_type in type_mismatches[:10]: lines.append(...)` then `lines.append('')` — no `if len(type_mismatches) > 10` overflow line. `n_missing` is computed (line 167) but there is no `n_type_mismatches`. The header count uses `n_expected`/`n_available` only, so the total type-mismatch count is never surfaced anywhere in the message.

title: categorical_levels is re-normalised three times along the batched scoring path
description: On the batched scoring path the declared categorical value domains are passed through _normalise_runtime_categorical_levels (each of which calls modelling._feature_contract.normalise_categorical_levels, iterating/validating/sorting every level list) at three nested boundaries: _run_score_pipeline (line 869) normalises and forwards the result into _score_batched_standalone; score_frame (line 798) re-normalises the already-normalised mapping; and _batch_score_to_parquet (line 1333) normalises it a third time before per-chunk validation. normalise_categorical_levels is idempotent (it sorts and de-dupes, so a second/third pass yields the same dict), so behaviour is unchanged, but the work is repeated. Each boundary re-validates its own input because score_frame and _batch_score_to_parquet are independently-tested public/internal entry points, which makes the redundancy defensible as input-hardening rather than a clear defect.
evidence: _run_score_pipeline L869 computes normalised_levels and passes it to _score_batched_standalone (L915-923). _score_batched_standalone -> score_frame(categorical_levels=normalised_levels). score_frame L798 again calls _normalise_runtime_categorical_levels(categorical_levels, features=features) on that already-normalised value, then passes the result to _score_batched_unified, which forwards it (unchanged) to _batch_score_to_parquet, where L1333 normalises a third time. normalise_categorical_levels (_feature_contract.py:380-385) sorts/de-dupes, so passes 2 and 3 are no-ops.
est_reduction: ~0 LOC (drop the L798/L1333 re-normalisation only if the boundaries are documented as already-normalised); primary benefit is removing repeated O(n_levels log n_levels) work, not line count.
behavior_preservation: Fully behaviour-preserving: normalise_categorical_levels is idempotent on its own output (sorted, de-duped, feature-filtered), so eliminating the 2nd/3rd pass produces the identical mapping. Only safe if the contract that score_frame/_batch_score_to_parquet receive an already-normalised mapping is made explicit; as standalone testable entry points they currently normalise defensively.

title: _normalise_frontier_range_pair raises raw Python float() messages (TypeError / unprefixed ValueError) on the config-side path, breaking its documented "error messages match" contract
description: The function's docstring states it is the 'single source of truth for both the request-body schema layer and the config-side path' so error wording is shared. That promise holds for the tested cases (missing keys, non-finite, min>max) because they are explicit string-keyed raises. It does NOT hold when a min/max value is a non-numeric scalar or a nested value, because float(raw_min)/float(raw_max) on line 63-64 raise Python's own exceptions instead of a field-prefixed ValueError. Two concrete cases on the config path (which passes RAW, un-coerced JSON values from config['frontier_ranges'] into _normalise_frontier_range in _optimiser_service._auto_frontier_ranges_from_config): (a) a string min/max, e.g. frontier_ranges={'volume': ['abc','def']}, yields ValueError 'could not convert string to float: \'abc\'' rather than 'frontier_ranges.volume must contain ...'; (b) a nested min/max, e.g. {'volume': {'min': [1,2], 'max': 3}}, raises TypeError 'float() argument must be a string or a real number, not \'list\''. The request-body path (OptimiserFrontierRequest.threshold_ranges) is NOT affected because pydantic's list[float] coercion runs before the mode='after' validator and rejects/converts those inputs first (verified: validator only ever sees pre-coerced floats). So this is config-path-only. The TypeError is ultimately caught by the broad `except Exception` at _optimiser_service.py:2232 and surfaced as a non-fatal 'Frontier unavailable: <raw msg>' frontier_error, so it does not crash the worker, but the user sees an internal float() message instead of the intended, consistent field-scoped diagnostic the function was written to provide.
evidence: Line 63-64: `min_value = float(raw_min); max_value = float(raw_max)` with no try/except; the structured ValueErrors only guard None (line 60-61), shape (line 57-58), finiteness (line 65-66) and ordering (line 67-68). Confirmed at runtime: `_normalise_frontier_range_pair(['abc','def'], field='threshold_ranges.volume')` -> ValueError "could not convert string to float: 'abc'"; `_normalise_frontier_range_pair({'min':[1,2],'max':3}, field='frontier_ranges.volume')` -> TypeError (not a ValueError, so it escapes the function's own error model). Config-side caller: _optimiser_service.py:1386 ranges[...] = _normalise_frontier_range(configured_ranges[cname], ...) on raw dict values; wrapped by `except Exception` at line 2232.

title: _normalise_frontier_range_pair silently accepts booleans as range bounds (e.g. [False, True] -> (0.0, 1.0)) on the config path, inconsistent with the sibling _reject_bool_chunk_size policy
description: Because bool is a subclass of int, float(False)==0.0 and float(True)==1.0, and booleans pass the finiteness and ordering checks. So a frontier-range value of [False, True] (or {'min': False, 'max': True}) is silently normalised to the numeric range (0.0, 1.0) instead of being rejected as a malformed payload. This is the opposite policy from the file's own sibling validator _reject_bool_chunk_size (lines 21-24), which was deliberately added to reject bool for streaming_chunk_size on the grounds that a bool is almost certainly a client bug rather than a real number. As with finding 1, the request-body path (OptimiserFrontierRequest.threshold_ranges, list[float]) is unaffected because pydantic coerces [False,True] to [0.0,1.0] before the after-validator runs; the silent acceptance is reachable on the config-side path (_auto_frontier_ranges_from_config) where raw JSON booleans flow straight in. Severity is low because boolean range bounds in an optimiser config are a degenerate, low-probability input, but it is a genuine validation gap and an inconsistency with the module's stated bool-rejection stance for numeric fields.
evidence: Runtime: `_normalise_frontier_range_pair([False, True], field='x')` returns (0.0, 1.0); `_normalise_frontier_range_pair({'min': False, 'max': True}, field='x')` returns (0.0, 1.0). No isinstance(..., bool) guard exists in the function, whereas the adjacent _reject_bool_chunk_size (line 22) does `if isinstance(value, bool): raise ValueError(...)`. isinstance(True, int) is True, so the int-based float() coercion accepts bools.

title: _format_contract_source silently overwrites inputs_by_parent when a parent-id key and that parent's emitted func-name appear as two separate declared keys
description: When serialising a declared contract's inputs_by_parent, each declared key is reclassified: an id present in parent_name_by_id is remapped to its emitted func-name (line 142-143), while a key already equal to one of the emitted func-names is kept verbatim (line 144-145). Both branches then write `inputs_by_parent[emitted_parent] = ...` (line 149). If the same physical parent is represented by BOTH its node-id key (e.g. 'left-uuid') AND its already-resolved func-name key (e.g. 'Left_Input') in the declared contract, both reduce to emitted_parent='Left_Input' and the loop assignment last-writer-wins, silently dropping one entry's column set. The winner is decided purely by `sorted(contract.inputs_by_parent.items())` key order, so which columns survive is arbitrary and the loss is silent (no warning, no error) — exactly the silent-wrongness class the project guidelines forbid.
evidence: Loop at 139-149: parent_id in parent_name_by_id -> emitted_parent = name (143); elif parent_id in parent_names (the set of func-names, line 136) -> emitted_parent = parent_id (kept, 145); line 149 `inputs_by_parent[emitted_parent] = None if columns is None else sorted(columns)`. With declared inputs_by_parent = {'left-uuid': [A], 'Left_Input': [B]} and parent_name_by_id = {'left-uuid':'Left_Input'} (per test_graph_to_code_remaps_inputs_by_parent_ids_to_function_names, tests/test_codegen_fail_loudly.py:104-155, distinct labels guarantee distinct func-names via _error_on_name_collisions): 'Left_Input' is in parent_names so it is kept; 'left-uuid' remaps to 'Left_Input'; both assign inputs_by_parent['Left_Input'], so sorting puts 'Left_Input' before 'left-uuid' and the id-derived [A] overwrites the name-keyed [B] (or vice versa depending on inputs). No collision detection exists; the result is emitted as the file's contract and consumed by projection.declared_inputs_by_parent (projection.py:1784-1821), so the wrong/narrowed parent-column ownership is persisted. A mixed id+name keyed inputs_by_parent is reachable by re-saving a file whose inputs_by_parent was already name-keyed by a prior save while config still carries an id-keyed entry, or by a hand-authored/partially-migrated contract.

title: Dead `if declared is not None:` branch in _format_contract_kwarg — Contract.from_user_declared can never return None once declared_raw is not None
description: Line 96 already guards `if declared_raw is not None:` before calling `declared = Contract.from_user_declared(declared_raw)` (line 97). Contract.from_user_declared returns None ONLY for a None input (haute/_contracts.py:65); every other input either returns a Contract or raises ValueError (it never returns None for a non-None value). Therefore line 98 `if declared is not None:` is always True, and the implicit else (fall through to the get_column_contract path) is unreachable. The defensive guard suggests a fall-through that cannot occur, obscuring the actual control flow (a malformed declared contract raises, it does not silently fall through to contract recomputation).
evidence: _contracts.py Contract.from_user_declared: `if value is None: return None` (65) is the sole None return; '' -> raises (78), {} -> raises (93-96), [] -> raises (105), any unknown type -> raises (105). Given codegen.py:96 already excludes None, `declared` at line 98 is never None. The branch's else (continuing to line 100 try/get_column_contract) can never be taken when declared_raw is truthy.
est_reduction: ~1 line (collapse the redundant guard) + removes a misleading apparent fall-through path
behavior_preservation: Replacing `if declared is not None: return _format_contract_source(...)` with an unconditional `return _format_contract_source(...)` is behaviour-identical because declared is provably non-None here; no input reaches the recompute path via this branch today.

title: graph_to_code() silently returns the FIRST submodel file (not the main pipeline) when given a graph with submodels
description: graph_to_code delegates to graph_to_code_multi and does `return next(iter(files.values()))`, documented as 'returns the single generated file's code'. That assumption only holds for submodel-free graphs. When the graph has submodels, graph_to_code_multi returns a multi-entry dict whose submodel files are inserted FIRST (line 1097, inside the per-submodel loop) and the main pipeline file LAST (line 1262). Since Python dicts preserve insertion order, next(iter(files.values())) returns the first submodel module's source, NOT the main pipeline. The public API thus returns the wrong artifact with no error. The unstated single-file precondition is neither asserted nor handled: it should either fail loudly when len(files) != 1 or explicitly select the main file. This is the kind of silent-wrong-result that should fail loudly per the project's 'no incorrect fallbacks' rule.
evidence: graph_to_code: files = graph_to_code_multi(...); return next(iter(files.values())). In graph_to_code_multi the submodel branch builds files[sm_file] = ... at line 1097 (loop over submodels, runs first), then files[main_key] = ... at line 1262 (runs last). With submodels present, iter(files.values()) yields the submodel code first. The sole production caller (src/haute/routes/_save_pipeline.py:517-535) guards with `if graph.submodels: graph_to_code_multi(...) else: graph_to_code(...)`, so production is safe; but graph_to_code is exported in __all__ (codegen.py:49-52) and is a documented public entry point, so a direct caller passing a submodel graph silently gets the wrong file. Tests only call graph_to_code on flat graphs (e.g. tests/test_submodel.py:231 uses flat_graph), so this path is currently unexercised.

title: Submodel cross-boundary handle validation is hand-rolled twice, duplicating _resolve_submodel_endpoint
description: graph_to_code_multi validates submodel boundary handles in three places that share identical logic: (a) the inline input loop at 1013-1043 (checks handle.startswith('in__'), slices child_id, checks membership in sm_child_ids, raises the same two ParseError messages), (b) the inline output-validation loop at 1044-1068 (same for 'out__'), and (c) the _resolve_submodel_endpoint closure at 1117-1150 which performs exactly this validation for both prefixes and raises the same two ParseError messages. The closure was clearly introduced to centralize this, but the two earlier loops were never folded into it. location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1199-1221 (infer_v2_schema_from_data column assembly; the object-table branch `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` at :1213) interacting with the reserved sentinel `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF` (:72) consumed in shred_to_buffers._walk at :629-632
title: A literal JSON key named "$value" collides with the reserved scalar-array sentinel, so inference emits a $value-leaf column on an OBJECT table and shred_to_buffers silently drops EVERY record of that table
description: The module reserves the leaf token `$value` (`_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`) to mean "the scalar element itself" for scalar-array child tables, and the header comment (lines 70-71) asserts "a JSON key can't be `$value` in this path grammar, so there's no collision with a real field." That assertion is false. `infer_v2_schema_from_data` builds an object column's path as `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with NO escaping/guarding of `col_name`, so a record carrying a real key `"$value"` yields an object-table column with path `$[*].$value`. At shred time `parse_column_path` returns the leaf `$value`, which EQUALS `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`. In `shred_to_buffers._walk`, `is_scalar_table = any(leaf == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF ...)` (line 629) then becomes TRUE for what is actually an OBJECT table, so the shape guard `if is_scalar_table != (not is_dict)` (line 630) treats every dict record as a shape mismatch and `continue`s past it (counting it as a skipped row). The whole table emits ZERO rows. Because validate_v2_schema accepts `$value` as a legal leaf and `_v2_fingerprint` sees a distinct path, the cache is judged valid/fresh; the only signal is the skipped-rows counter (which the user must notice). This is distinct from the catalogued 'scalar-value-column-fixed-name-ambiguity' finding (that is about output-port identity / a real field named `value` being indistinguishable downstream); here the *sentinel* `$value` causes total, silent row loss on the build path.
evidence: Reproduced end-to-end: records=[{"$value":10,"other":1},{"$value":20,"other":2}] -> infer_v2_schema_from_data emits root column path '$[*].$value'; parse_column_path('$[*].$value','$[*]') == '$value' == _SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF (True). build_per_port_cache + load_per_port_cache -> root frame height=0 (columns ['$value','other']) from 2 source records; shred_to_buffers skip stats = {'records':0,'rows_by_table':{'$[*]':2}}. Trace: _walk line 629 is_scalar_table=True for a dict record (is_dict=True), line 630 True != (not True=False) -> True -> _count_row_skip + continue, so no row is ever appended.

location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1203/1213 (infer_v2_schema_from_data builds column path `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with an unescaped key) consumed by _resolve_leaf dotted-walk at :526-536
title: infer_v2_schema_from_data manufactures a dotted column path for a JSON key that literally contains a dot, so the shred silently resolves the value to None (value lost, not even counted as a skip)
description: Inference emits an object column whose path is `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with no escaping of `col_name`. For a record with a key that itself contains a dot (e.g. `"a.b": 42`), this yields column path `$[*].a.b`, and `parse_column_path` returns the leaf `a.b`. The dotted leaf is then interpreted by `_resolve_leaf` (lines 526-536) as a NESTED path: it walks `value.get("a")` then `.get("b")`, which is absent (the real key is the single string `"a.b"`), so the column resolves to None. The original value is silently lost and the row is still emitted with None (so it is not surfaced by skip accounting either). The schema also round-trips through validate_v2_schema cleanly, hiding the problem. This shares the `_resolve_leaf` dotted-ambiguity root with catalogued finding #12/BUG-N3 (a list at an intermediate dotted segment), but the NEW angle is that inference itself fabricates these ambiguous flat-key-as-dotted-path columns with no guard, making it reachable from the ordinary Infer Tables -> Cache as Parquet flow rather than only from hand-authored configs.
evidence: Reproduced: records=[{"a.b":42,"ok":1}] -> infer column path '$[*].a.b' -> build+load root frame: column 'a.b' value = [None] (source had 42); 'ok' = [1]. _resolve_leaf({'a.b':42}, 'a.b'): '.' in leaf -> split ['a','b'] -> cur=value.get('a')=None -> returns None. The value is dropped with no skip count (object record IS a dict, so the row is emitted, just with a None cell).

title: Generated GitLab CI uv cache never caches anything (wrong cache path)
description: gitlab_ci_yml() emits a default cache block with `paths: - .cache/uv`, but uv does NOT write its cache to a project-relative `.cache/uv` directory. By default uv caches to a home/XDG location (`~/.cache/uv` on Linux, confirmed `uv cache dir` -> AppData/.cache outside the repo). GitLab CI `cache.paths` are resolved relative to `$CI_PROJECT_DIR`, and paths outside the build directory cannot be cached, so the configured cache silently captures an empty/nonexistent directory and every pipeline re-downloads dependencies. The GitHub and Azure templates do not have this problem (GitHub uses `astral-sh/setup-uv@v4` with `enable-cache: true`, which targets uv's real cache dir; Azure configures no uv cache). The fix is to point uv at the cached dir, e.g. add `UV_CACHE_DIR: .cache/uv` to the top-level `variables`/`default.variables` so uv actually writes there.
evidence: default.cache.paths = ['.cache/uv'] (lines 606-609) and before_script runs `pip install "uv>=0.5,<1" && uv sync --frozen` (line 611) with no UV_CACHE_DIR set. `uv cache dir` resolves to C:\Users\...\AppData\Local\uv\cache (home, not project); on Linux runners it is ~/.cache/uv, outside $CI_PROJECT_DIR, so GitLab cannot persist it. test_caching only asserts the literal '.cache/uv' substring is present, never that caching is effective.

title: _ModelCacheWithCascade.put skips the validation-cache cascade when a key is overwritten in place
description: `_ModelCacheWithCascade.put` detects evicted models by diffing the pre-put key snapshot (`before`) against the post-put key set (`after_keys`) and treating `k not in after_keys` as 'was evicted'. This correctly catches LRU capacity evictions (the evicted key disappears from `_data`), but it MISSES the case where `put` is called with a key that already exists and a *different* `ScoringModel` value. The base `LRUCache.put` overwrites in place (`self._data[key] = value`, lines _lru_cache.py:160-164), so the key remains in `after_keys`; the diff yields no evicted models, and `_ms._invalidate_feature_validation_cache_for(old_model)` is never invoked for the replaced object. Consequently the feature-validation cache in `_model_scorer` retains entries keyed on `id(old_model)` (key shape `(id(scoring_model), contract, schema)`, _model_scorer.py:72/317-321). Those entries are now unreachable garbage that linger until LRU pressure or a full `clear()` removes them — the exact leak the targeted cascade was built to prevent (docstring _model_scorer.py:138-148: 'purge them so the table does not fill with dead id() values'). The method's own docstring (lines 144-147) promises 'every eviction triggers the targeted ... hook', so the in-place-replacement value drop is a contract violation.
evidence: Override put (lines 157-171): `before = dict(self._data); super().put(key, value); after_keys = set(self._data); evicted_models = [v for k, v in before.items() if k not in after_keys]`. For an overwrite of an existing key K, K is in both `before` and `after_keys`, so `evicted_models` is empty even though `before[K]` (the old ScoringModel) was just dropped by base put's `self._data[key] = value`. The validation entries keyed on `id(before[K])` are never invalidated. Tests in tests/test_feature_validation_cache.py (TestValidationCacheCascadeEviction) exercise LRU eviction, targeted invalidation, and full clear, but never the same-key overwrite path, so the gap is untested.
behavior_preservation: Reachability through load_mlflow_model is low because the get-then-put sequence is serialized under _artifact_io_lock(run_id, artifact_path) and same-key callers see a get-hit before reaching put; production therefore rarely (if ever) overwrites a live key with a new object. The defect is a latent contract gap in the general-purpose put method (leak, not wrong result, since a stale id-keyed entry only produces a false get-hit if the reused id ALSO collides on contract+schema). A correct fix would diff on value identity for retained keys (e.g. invalidate when before[k] is not self._data[k]) and add a same-key-overwrite cascade test.

title: Fast-path cache key drops `version` while the canonical key keeps it, so run-sourced catboost/rustystats models load from disk twice and leave a permanently-orphaned duplicate cache entry (and skewed hit/miss counters); pyfunc loses the fast path entirely

description: load_mlflow_model has two cache-key construction sites that disagree for `source_type="run"` whenever a non-empty `version` is supplied. The fast-path (lines 893-900) hardcodes `version=""`, so `_model_cache_key` (lines 311-313: truthy version -> 5-tuple, else 4-tuple) returns the 4-tuple `("run", run_id, artifact_path, task)`. The slow-path (lines 968-974) passes `version=resolved_version`, and for a run source `resolve_mlflow_source` returns `resolved_version = version` unchanged (_mlflow_utils.py:101,109-111). Production callers ALWAYS pass `version=config.get("version", "latest")` even for run sources (src/haute/_builders.py:1196; src/haute/_model_explainability.py:569; threaded through ModelScorer._load_scoring_model_uncached at _model_scorer.py:1063-1070). The two keys can never coincide. CONSEQUENCES for catboost/rustystats (the only in-repo producers): call 1 (cold) misses the 4-tuple, finds no disk file, falls to the slow path, downloads + loads + put(5-tuple); call 2 misses the 4-tuple again (model is under the 5-tuple), now finds the disk file present and re-loads it from disk via the disk-cache fast path, put(4-tuple) — so the model is deserialized from disk TWICE before steady state, TWO cache MISSES are recorded for one logical model (skewing get_model_cache_stats hit-rate), and the 5-tuple entry becomes dead weight that the steady-state fast path never hits again, permanently consuming one of only _MODEL_CACHE_MAX_SIZE=16 slots until LRU-evicted (effectively halving cache capacity for run-sourced models). No price-correctness impact (same model bytes, same run_id+artifact_path), but it is a real cache-coherence defect: redundant disk loads, a permanently duplicated/orphaned cache entry, defeated fast-path, and inaccurate observability counters.

title: _sanitize_description's leading-\n heuristic corrupts single-line descriptions that have leading whitespace, and still drops trailing newlines/blank-lines (cleandoc strips them); these input classes are outside the existing round-trip test matrix
description: The sanitiser prepends a newline when `'\n' in desc or desc != desc.strip()` to neutralise inspect.cleandoc's first-line handling. But cleandoc ALSO strips the minimum common indentation of every line after the first. For a single-line description with leading whitespace (e.g. ' hello'), the prepend makes that text the 'second line', so cleandoc strips its leading indent and the leading whitespace is silently lost on round-trip. Trailing newlines / trailing blank lines / trailing tabs are likewise dropped or rewritten (cleandoc removes trailing blank lines and right-strips each line). Because the parse direction (ast.get_docstring with the default clean=True) applies the same cleandoc, the corruption lands on the FIRST save and is stable thereafter — a user editing a node description with leading indentation or a trailing newline in the GUI sees it change under them. The module docstring scopes its round-trip guarantee to inputs 'covered by the docstring round-trip tests', and those specific inputs are not in tests/test_codegen_docstring_roundtrip.py, so this is an unguarded extension of the known (xfail-tracked) round-trip limitation rather than a contract the code claims to meet — hence low severity.

Via real `_node_to_code` + ast.get_docstring: ' leading-space' -> 'leading-space' (FAIL); 'a
b

b' (FAIL); 'line	' -> 'line    ' (FAIL); 'x
