title: _gen_model_score drops runtime-affecting categorical_levels and feature_contract_path from the emitted decorator, silently losing categorical-domain / feature-contract validation on a parse->re-save round-trip
description: _gen_model_score builds decorator_kwargs from a HAND-PICKED allowlist (sourceType/run_id/artifact_path/registered_model/version/task/output_column, plus optional run_name/experiment_name/experiment_id) and never emits two persisted ModelScoreConfig keys that DO affect scoring: categorical_levels (_types.py:180) and feature_contract_path (_types.py:179). Both are consumed at runtime by score_from_config (_model_scorer.py:1252-1253: feature_contract_path=cfg.get('feature_contract_path') or None; categorical_levels=cfg.get('categorical_levels') or None), which drives categorical value-domain enforcement and feature-contract checks in ModelScorer. At the FIRST save the sidecar JSON is written from the node config via _prepare_config_for_sidecar (both keys are in VALID_KEYS[MODEL_SCORE] because categorical_levels is a _UNIVERSAL_KEY and feature_contract_path is a ModelScoreConfig field), so the runtime body recovers them from the sidecar and behaves correctly. The loss is silent and occurs on any parse->re-save cycle: when the generated .py is re-parsed by parse_pipeline_source, _config_builder._build_config (_config_builder.py:111-116) rebuilds the model_score config from decorator kwargs ONLY (it does not read the existing sidecar). Because the decorator omitted both keys, the rebuilt node config lacks them; on the next save, _prepare_config_for_sidecar derives the sidecar from that now-incomplete config and the sidecar loses categorical_levels/feature_contract_path -> score_from_config stops applying categorical-domain / feature-contract validation. categorical_levels is the stronger half: the parser explicitly supports restoring it (MODEL_SCORE_CONFIG_KEYS at _types.py:487-499 includes categorical_levels), and _gen_api_input demonstrably PRESERVES categorical_levels (asserted by tests/test_codegen_builders.py:115-128 'test_api_input_preserves_categorical_levels_in_shared_reader'), so the omission in _gen_model_score is an inconsistency, not an intentional design choice. (feature_contract_path is additionally absent from MODEL_SCORE_CONFIG_KEYS, so even were it emitted the parser would not restore it -- but the runtime-affecting drop is identical.)
evidence: _gen_model_score decorator_kwargs construction (lines 622-646) lists only source_type/run_id/artifact_path/registered_model/version/task/output_column [+ run_name/experiment_name/experiment_id]; neither 'categorical_levels' nor 'feature_contract_path' appears. ModelScoreConfig (_types.py:163-183) declares both categorical_levels and feature_contract_path. score_from_config reads both from the sidecar config (_model_scorer.py:1252-1253). Parser rebuild path _config_builder.py:111-116 only copies MODEL_SCORE_CONFIG_KEYS from decorator_kwargs and never loads the sidecar, so any key the decorator omits is gone after parse. codegen.py never handles categorical_levels (grep: no matches) and the emitted contract kwarg carries only inputs/outputs/inputs_by_parent (_format_contract_source, codegen.py:122-176) -- so there is no recovery path. Round-trip test tests/test_model_score_codegen.py::TestParserRoundTrip.test_codegen_parses_back (lines 266-318) only exercises sourceType/run_id/artifact_path/task/output_column, leaving this drop uncovered. Contrast: _gen_api_input round-trips ALL config keys via _data_source_runtime_config_expr (lines 300-303) and is tested to preserve categorical_levels.

title: _match_source silently drops the first user statement when a DataSource body has no recognized source-load line
description: _source_load_boilerplate_end_index scans the cleaned body, skipping leading import lines and source-load statements. If it never sees a source-load statement (saw_source_load stays False) but idx is still in range, the final branch returns `_statement_end_index(cleaned, idx)` instead of `idx`/0. That advances PAST the first non-boilerplate user statement and reports it as boilerplate, so _match_source's start_idx skips it and extract_user_code drops it from the result. The effect is silent corruption of user code: (a) a single-statement no-load source body returns '' (ALL user code lost); (b) a multi-statement body drops the FIRST statement, e.g. `a = 1` / `df = df.with_columns(x=a)` / `return df` extracts only `df = df.with_columns(x=a)`, which now references an undefined `a` (broken code); (c) `import numpy as np` + one transform returns '' (import treated as boilerplate, then the lone transform skipped). This contradicts the function's own contract and the sibling codegen-side helper _strip_source_load_boilerplate_from_code (lines 407-409), which correctly guards `has_source_load = any(...)` and returns the code UNCHANGED when no load is present. _match_external also handles the no-load case correctly (lines 642-645 rewind to first_import_idx). Only the source path regresses. Reachable for hand-authored / legacy / externally-produced DataSource pipeline files parsed via _config_builder.py:251 (_extract_source_user_code); the normal codegen round-trip is unaffected because _gen_data_source always emits `df = read_data_source(...)` which is in _SOURCE_LOAD_PREFIXES.
evidence:
Lines 495-496: `if not saw_source_load and idx < len(cleaned): return _statement_end_index(cleaned, idx)` returns the end-index of the FIRST user statement rather than its start. Probe via .venv python: `_extract_source_user_code('    """d"""
    df = df.with_columns(x=1)
    return df')` -> '' (whole body lost). `_extract_source_user_code(body where lines = a=1 / df=... / return df)` -> 'df = df.with_columns(x=a)' (a=1 dropped). `_source_load_boilerplate_end_index(['a = 1','df = df.with_columns(x=a)','return df'])` -> 1, dropping cleaned[0]. Contrast `_strip_source_load_boilerplate_from_code('df = df.head()
df = df.tail()')` -> 'df = df.head()
df = df.tail()' (preserved). No existing test in tests/test_parser_helpers.py (TestExtractSourceUserCode, all use a scan_parquet/read_data_source load) or tests/test_ast_return_boundaries.py covers the no-load source body.

title: ModelScore/RatingStep boilerplate matchers anchor on the wrong line when the generated-call token appears in a string literal or comment
description: _match_model_score finds the scoring boilerplate by `"score_from_config(" in stripped and not stripped.startswith(("from ", "import "))`. This is a raw substring test over the textual line, so a comment or string literal containing the token before the real call line is matched first. It then walks parentheses from that wrong line and treats the REAL `result = score_from_config(...)` line (and anything between) as user code, which _finalise_model_score then rewrites `result`->`df`, leaking `df = score_from_config(...)` into the saved user code box. _match_rating_step has the identical defect for `apply_rating_step_from_config(`. Unlike the return-boundary detection (which the module docstring deliberately migrated to an AST walk to avoid exactly this class of string/comment confusion), these matchers remain stringly-typed. Severity is low because it requires a user comment/string containing the exact generated-call token positioned before the real call, but the failure is silent and corrupts round-tripped code.
evidence: Probe via .venv python: body with a comment `# call score_from_config(...) below` preceding the real `result = score_from_config(source, config="s.json")` -> _extract_model_score_user_code returns 'df = score_from_config(source, config="s.json")\ndf = df.head()', i.e. the generated scoring line was NOT stripped and was rewritten into user code. Same with a string literal: `note = "uses score_from_config(x)"` preceding the real call -> identical leak. Line 538: `if "score_from_config(" in stripped and not stripped.startswith(("from ", "import "))`. Line 555: `if "apply_rating_step_from_config(" not in stripped: continue` (same substring approach).

title: Count-based column fallback subtracts len(excluded) without checking presence, silently under-estimating columns (and thus RAM) when excluded names are not in the resolved schema
description: When _resolve_target_columns_detail returns None but the simpler count walker _resolve_target_columns returned a column count, the ELSE branch at line 928 computes `n_columns = max(n_columns - len(excluded - preserved_excluded_join_keys), 1)`. It subtracts the *cardinality* of the exclude list from the count with no verification that those excluded names actually exist among the counted columns. If `exclude` contains any name absent from that schema (a user typo, or a feature produced by a downstream transform the count walker stopped before reaching, or - per the existing SIMP-4 verdict - the non-string-selected_columns / diamond-revisit cases where detail aborts to None while the count still resolves), the subtraction removes more columns than are really excluded. The result is an undercounted n_columns -> undercounted base_bytes_per_row/peak_bytes (lines 941-953) -> an over-optimistic RAM estimate that can skip a needed downsample and allow an OOM. This is precisely the silent-incorrect-fallback the project's CLAUDE.md warns against. The asymmetry is telling: the IF branch (line 913-921, when detail IS available) filters over the ACTUAL resolved columns (`if column not in excluded`), so absent excluded names are correctly ignored there; only the count-based ELSE branch over-subtracts. Note this is a distinct *correctness* defect, not the SIMP-4 simplification (which only evaluated merging the two walkers and treated the ELSE branch as an intentional weaker fallback without flagging the over-subtraction).
evidence: Line 905-909 builds `excluded` from the target's exclude config; line 928 does `max(n_columns - len(excluded - preserved_excluded_join_keys), 1)`. Contrast the detail path at 916-920 which iterates `for column in target_columns.columns if column not in excluded` (presence-checked). Reachability of the ELSE branch is pinned by tests/test_ram_estimate.py:569-576 (patches _resolve_target_columns->4, _resolve_target_columns_detail->None, asserts probe_columns==2 for exclude=['a','b']); with exclude=['a','zzz'] (zzz absent) the same path would yield probe_columns=2 instead of the correct 3, under-counting by 1. SIMP-4 verdict (review/03-simplification/findings-raw.json:3212) confirms this ELSE branch runs 'precisely when the detail walker yields None' and the int count is load-bearing there.

location: src/haute/trace.py:262-271 (_find_target_row_index) and its use in execute_trace at 489-491
title: _find_target_row_index silently returns the first of multiple matching rows, unlike the hardened ambiguity handling in _correlate_rows_posthoc
description: When execute_trace's positional row-identity check fails (cold trace after the preview cache was evicted and joins reordered rows), it relocates the clicked row via _find_target_row_index(target_df, row_values). That helper intersects row_values with target_df.columns ('shared') and returns the index of the FIRST row whose shared columns all match, with no detection of multiple matches. This is the exact anti-pattern the post-hoc correlation layer was explicitly hardened against: _find_matching_row / _correlate_rows_posthoc record an 'ambiguous_row_match' diagnostic and return None rather than silently selecting a row when >1 candidate matches (see _trace_correlation.py:355-368, 387-397). The relocated row_index is then used as the anchor for all upstream correlation, so an ambiguous relocation silently produces a trace for the wrong row instead of raising the existing 'Trace data does not match the preview row' ValueError or surfacing a diagnostic.
evidence: trace.py:264 `shared = [col for col in row_values if col in df.columns]`; 268-271 loops and `return idx` on the first all-match, no count of further matches. Contrast _trace_correlation.py:357-368 where exact_row_indices with len>1 calls _record_ambiguous_row_match and returns None,-1. execute_trace.py:489-491 `matched_index = _find_target_row_index(...); if matched_index is not None: row_index = matched_index` — accepts the first-match index unconditionally. Realistic trigger is narrow: row_values normally equals the target node's own visible columns, so 'shared' is usually the full row and identical rows yield an identical trace; the conflation requires row_values to carry a key absent from the (changed) target_df AND two rows colliding on the remaining shared columns. Impact is therefore low, but the silent first-match selection is inconsistent with the module's stated 'fail loudly rather than show wrong data' contract.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Column-origin regex \b{column}\s*= false-matches an equality comparison (column ==) as an assignment
description: In the failed-execution fallback, _prune_to_column_relevance scans each node's raw config code and treats the node as an origin of the traced column when the code contains '.with_columns(' AND re.search(rf'\b{re.escape(column)}\s*=', code) matches. Because the pattern stops at the first '=', it also matches the leading '=' of a comparison operator: a bare `premium == 5`, `premium >=`-no(only '='), specifically `premium ==`/`premium =` both match. A node that merely COMPARES the column (e.g. filters on it) but does not assign it is then added to origin_ids and force-tagged column_relevant=True, broadening the referenced-column ancestor walk. The effect is over-inclusion of steps in the trace, never wrong cell values, so impact is low; and the most common Polars form `pl.col("premium") == 5` does NOT match (the column name is quoted, so the `==` is not directly adjacent to the identifier), which further narrows the trigger to bare-identifier comparisons.
evidence: trace.py:874 `if rc and ".with_columns(" in rc and re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(column)}\s*=", rc):` then 875-876 `origin_ids.add(s.node_id); s.column_relevant = True`. Verified empirically with the project venv: for column='premium', 'premium == 5' -> True (false positive), 'premium=5' -> True, but 'pl.col("premium") == 5' -> False, 'premium != 2' -> False, 'premium >= 1' -> False, 'net_premium = 3' -> False. A stricter pattern (e.g. requiring `=` not followed by `=`, or matching `<col>\s*=\s*` excluding `==`) would eliminate the comparison false-positive.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: checkpoint() skips memory-pressure-event evaluation when only rss_limit_bytes is set (gate ignores rss_limit_bytes), diverging from the budget check that honours it
description: checkpoint() samples RSS only when `self.memory_limit_bytes is not None or self._active_stage_stack()` (lines 705-709); it does NOT consider `self.rss_limit_bytes`. When the sample is skipped, rss_bytes stays None and `_observe_rss` is not called (lines 710-711) - and `_observe_rss` is the SOLE path to `_record_memory_pressure_events` (line 851). Therefore, for an ExecutionContext that has `rss_limit_bytes` set but `memory_limit_bytes is None` and no active stage on the current thread, a bare `checkpoint()` call evaluates the hard budget (because `_check_memory_budget` re-samples at line 867 and `_effective_rss_limit_bytes()` returns `rss_limit_bytes`) but silently performs NO memory-pressure threshold evaluation. This is an internal inconsistency: `_check_memory_budget`, `_record_memory_pressure_events`, and `_effective_rss_limit_bytes` all treat `rss_limit_bytes` as a valid limit source, but the checkpoint() sampling gate alone does not, so the 50/75/90% advisory pressure events (and their callback/publish side effects) are never produced for such a context at checkpoint boundaries.
evidence: Line 705-709: `rss_bytes = self.memory_sampler() if self.memory_limit_bytes is not None or self._active_stage_stack() else None` - omits `self.rss_limit_bytes`. Line 710-711: `if rss_bytes is not None: self._observe_rss(...)`. `_observe_rss` (835-856) is the only caller of `_record_memory_pressure_events` (851). Meanwhile `_effective_rss_limit_bytes` (950-952) returns `self.rss_limit_bytes` first, so a context with `rss_limit_bytes` set and `memory_limit_bytes=None` HAS an effective limit; `_check_memory_budget` (863-869) re-samples via `self.memory_sampler()` when rss_bytes is None and enforces it - proving the limit is live, yet pressure events are skipped. Reachability: in the shipped codebase admitted contexts (create_admitted_execution_context, _execution_admission.py:455-457) always co-set memory_limit_bytes AND rss_limit_bytes, so checkpoint() samples; the gap is only hit by direct ExecutionContext(rss_limit_bytes=...) construction, which is why this is latent rather than active.

title: ExecutionStageMetric and ExecutionStageSummary duplicate ~16 identical fields with a 20-line manual field-copy in to_summary()
description: ExecutionStageMetric (lines 143-191) and ExecutionStageSummary (lines 194-237) declare the same ~16 fields (name, operation, profile, elapsed_ms, node_id, job_id, rss_start/end/peak_bytes, rows_in/out, bytes_read/written, columns_scanned, n_collects, n_checkpoints, schema_version) differing only in that the summary adds a materialised rss_delta_bytes field (the metric exposes it as a property) and reorders elapsed_ms vs node_id. to_summary() (171-191) then manually re-lists all 17 keyword arguments to copy one into the other. Any field added to the timed metric must be added in three places (metric field, summary field, to_summary copy) or it silently fails to surface in the public trace. The split could be collapsed (e.g. summary derives from the metric via a single helper that injects rss_delta_bytes, or the property is computed in to_dict) to remove the parallel field list and the hand-written copy.

The only real transformation is `rss_delta_bytes=self.rss_delta_bytes` (line 181), which the property at 165-169 already computes.
