Risk is real because the frozen public summary is a stable serialization contract validated by ExecutionMetricsPayload and frontend fixtures, so any merge must keep field order/defaults and the materialised rss_delta_bytes exactly; this is why confidence is low - the split may be an intentional internal-vs-public boundary.

title: get_status.changed_files mangles renamed files into a single 'old -> new' string
description: When a file has been renamed, `git status --porcelain` emits a single line of the form `R  old.py -> new.py` (status code 'R', two-char status + space, then 'old -> new'). The parser does `line[3:].strip().strip('"')`, which yields the literal string `old.py -> new.py` as ONE entry in `changed_files`, instead of the new path `new.py`. Consequently the status panel shows a nonsensical pseudo-filename for every rename, and any consumer treating entries as real paths (e.g. opening the file) breaks. The same line[3:] slice also fails to C-unescape git's quoted paths (git emits `"my file.py"` / backslash-escaped octal for non-ASCII and special chars); `.strip('"')` removes only the outer quotes and leaves embedded escapes intact. Note save_progress/_auto_commit are unaffected because they parse `git diff --cached --name-only`, which prints each path on its own line with no arrow form — only get_status uses the porcelain arrow format.
evidence: Reproduced: `git mv a.py b.py; git status --porcelain` -> `R  a.py -> b.py`. With this single line, the loop appends `('R  a.py -> b.py')[3:]` = `'a.py -> b.py'` (after strip) to changed_files. Expected entry is `b.py`. No test in tests/test_git.py exercises a rename, so this is uncovered.

title: _get_user_slug falls back to os.getlogin(), which raises OSError when stdin is not a TTY (servers/containers)
description: When `git config user.name` is unset/empty, `_get_user_slug` falls back to `os.getlogin()`. `os.getlogin()` reads the controlling terminal and raises `OSError: [Errno 25] Inappropriate ioctl for device` (or similar) in any environment without a controlling TTY — daemonized servers, many Docker containers, systemd services, and some CI runners. Because `_get_user_slug` is called inside `get_status`, `create_branch`, and `list_branches`, an unconfigured git identity in such an environment turns into an UNCAUGHT OSError that escapes the GitError funnel and becomes a generic HTTP 500, rather than a clean, branch-able username. The codebase already has the correct, robust idiom for exactly this in src/haute/deploy/_utils.py:get_user(), which uses `getpass.getuser()` wrapped in `except (KeyError, OSError)`. getpass.getuser() consults LOGNAME/USER/LNAME/USERNAME env vars before falling back, so it works headless; os.getlogin() does not. This helper is inconsistent with that established pattern and is the fragile choice.
evidence: Line 202: `return _slugify(os.getlogin())`. Contrast src/haute/deploy/_utils.py:15-20 `get_user()` -> `try: return getpass.getuser() except (KeyError, OSError): return 'unknown'`, whose tests (tests/test_deploy_utils.py:96-104) explicitly cover `OSError('no tty')` and `KeyError('no user')`. _git has no analogous guard and uses the more failure-prone os.getlogin().

est_reduction: 1 line (the unreachable `else f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{branch}"` arm)
behavior_preservation: exact — str.split never returns an empty list, so the else arm is never taken; removing it (use `parts[-1]` unconditionally) preserves behavior identically.
title: archive_branch has an unreachable `else` fallback on `parts = branch.split('/')`
description: `parts = branch.split('/')` is then used as `archive_name = f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{parts[-1]}" if parts else f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{branch}"`. `str.split('/')` ALWAYS returns a non-empty list (e.g. `'x'.split('/') == ['x']`, `''.split('/') == ['']`), so `if parts` is unconditionally truthy and the `else` arm is dead code. Additionally, `branch` is non-empty here because `_validate_ref_name(branch)` (line 875) rejects empty names, so `parts[-1]` is always a real value. The ternary can be reduced to `archive_name = f"{_ARCHIVE_PREFIX}/{parts[-1]}"`.
evidence: Line 886-888. `branch.split('/')` cannot yield [] for any str input; `_validate_ref_name` already guarantees branch != ''. Hence the else branch is unreachable.

title: Continuous banding silently overwrites the source float column, destroying NaN/Inf for all downstream nodes
description: In the continuous-banding path, when the banded column is Float32/Float64, _apply_banding rewrites the column with `pl.when(col.is_nan() | col.is_infinite()).then(pl.lit(None)).otherwise(col).alias(column)` and assigns the result back into `lf` (lines 110-116). Because this `alias(column)` targets the SAME column name (not a temporary), the returned frame carries a permanently mutated source column: every NaN and +/-Inf in the input column is replaced by null. The output band column is produced separately, so the mutation is a pure side effect on the input factor. Any downstream node (or the user's post-banding code) that reads the original column afterwards sees null where the data was Inf/NaN, with no log, no warning, and no record that a value was dropped. The docstring frames this as an internal step to make NaN/Inf 'fall cleanly to the default' for the band, but the implementation leaks that nulling into the frame returned to callers. This reaches both the GUI executor (executor re-exports _apply_banding, used by _apply_banding_factors) and the standalone codegen path via apply_banding_from_config. It only matters when output_column != column (when they are equal the final band overwrite makes the intermediate moot). This is the silent-corruption class the project's CLAUDE.md explicitly forbids ('code should be allowed to fail loudly... far superior to a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice').
evidence: Reproduced via public entry point: apply_banding_from_config(pl.DataFrame({'si':[inf,100.0]}).lazy(), {factors:[{banding:'continuous',column:'si',outputColumn:'si_band',rules:[{op1:'>=',val1:0,op2:'<',val2:1e9,assignment:'band'}]}]}).collect()['si'] -> [None, 100.0]; the input Inf is gone. Also via _apply_banding(lf x=[nan,1.0,inf,5.0], 'x','band','continuous',...): result['x'] == [None,1.0,None,5.0] while only result['band'] should have been derived. Code trace: line 116 reassigns `col = pl.col(column)` after the mutating with_columns at 110-115, and nothing restores the original column before `return lf` at 133. No test asserts the source column is preserved after continuous banding of NaN/Inf — existing tests (e.g. test_inf_in_banding_sanitized_to_default) only assert the band output, so the regression is unguarded.

title: Linear chain validation checks full node_map, not the routing-pruned set, so a pruned/non-ancestor parent is silently dropped from wiring
description: build_linear_execution_chain_functions validates base_node_id and chain_node_ids membership against node_map returned by _prepare_graph, raising ValueError('... not in the prepared graph') for anything missing. But _prepare_graph returns prepared.node_map == graph.node_map (the FULL graph: see projection.prepare_graph lines 2116/2130), whereas the actual wiring downstream relies on id_to_name, which contains ONLY the nodes in `order` = topo-sort of `needed` (ancestors of target_node_id that survived live-switch/source pruning; projection.py:2126-2128). The 'missing' check therefore does not match its stated contract: a node that is present in node_map but absent from id_to_name (because it was pruned by prune_live_switch_edges under routing_source='batch', or is simply not an ancestor of target_node_id) passes the check. It is then passed to _build_funcs as a chain parent via chain_parents, and _build_funcs computes src_ids = [pid for pid in parents_of.get(nid, []) if pid in id_to_name] (_execute_lazy.py:1475). Because the parent is filtered out by `if pid in id_to_name`, the first chain node is built with an EMPTY source list and no error is raised — a silently mis-wired chain that produces a wrong frame instead of failing loudly. The sole current caller (_optimiser_service.py:3967) derives base/chain as single-parent ancestors of body.node_id, so it is usually safe, but a source/live-switch-pruned branch under routing_source='batch' can still remove a chain node from id_to_name while leaving it in node_map, making this reachable. The validation should be performed against the routing-scoped set (id_to_name / order), not the full node_map, so a chain node that did not survive routing fails loudly.
evidence: execution.py:747-757 -> node_map,_order,_parents_of,id_to_name = _prepare_graph(graph, target_node_id, source=routing_source); missing = [n for n in (base_node_id,*chain_ids) if n not in node_map]. projection.py:2116 node_map = graph.node_map (FULL); 2126-2128 order/id_to_name scoped to `needed` (target ancestors, post-prune). _execute_lazy.py:1475 src_ids filters parents by `pid in id_to_name`, and 1477 src_names = [id_to_name[pid] ...] — a parent absent from id_to_name is silently dropped, not errored.

title: dataframe_paths_input_fingerprint is exported but has no caller; deploy uses its own stat-gated duplicate instead
description: dataframe_paths_input_fingerprint is defined and listed in __all__ (execution.py:84) but is never called anywhere in src/ or tests/ (grep over all .py files finds only its definition and the __all__ entry). The structurally-identical consumer that one would expect to use it, deploy/_scorer.py, instead defines and uses its own private _deploy_artifact_paths_input_fingerprint (_scorer.py:199-209) with byte-for-byte identical key/value validation and the same payload shape — differing only in calling _stat_gated_runtime_path_fingerprint instead of the non-gated _runtime_path_fingerprint. So the public function is dead within the repo and is duplicated by the deploy variant, signalling the intended consumer never adopted it. Either delete the unused export, or unify the two (parameterise stat-gating) so there is a single named-path fingerprint helper.
evidence: grep 'paths_input_fingerprint' over *.py: only execution.py:84 (__all__), execution.py:369 (def), _scorer.py:199 (def of _deploy_artifact_paths_input_fingerprint), _scorer.py:793 (its sole call). No reference to dataframe_paths_input_fingerprint outside its own definition/__all__. The two bodies are identical except _runtime_path_fingerprint(Path(raw_path).resolve()) vs _stat_gated_runtime_path_fingerprint(Path(raw_path)).
est_reduction: ~12 lines (remove unused export) or consolidate two ~10-line helpers into one
behavior_preservation: Removing an unused exported function changes no runtime behaviour; consolidating would preserve the deploy call's stat-gated semantics.

title: dataframe_graph_input_fingerprint hand-rolls json.dumps instead of the mandated single canonical_json encoder
description: The digest here is produced with json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(',',':')).encode() rather than haute._cache.canonical_json. canonical_json's docstring is explicit that it is THE only canonical-JSON encoder for digest material and that adding a second divergent encoder is how silent cache collisions / phantom invalidations arise ('do not add a second one; import this'). The sibling module _dataframe_execution_cache.py follows this (dataframe_execution_policy_fingerprint and dataframe_execution_cache_key both use canonical_json), and ALGO_VERSION v5 exists specifically to record that the two divergent encoders were unified. For the payload this function actually builds (str keys, dict/list/scalar values only) json.dumps and canonical_json emit identical bytes, so this is behaviour-preserving today; but it re-introduces a forbidden second encoder and leaves a latent divergence for any future extra_fingerprints value that is a set/tuple or a non-finite float, where the two encoders disagree (canonical_json normalises sets and emits deterministic Infinity/NaN/array ordering). Replace with: content_hash_bytes(canonical_json(payload).encode()) and drop the local json import use here.
evidence: execution.py:509 returns content_hash_bytes(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(',',':')).encode()). _cache.py:71-100 canonical_json docstring mandates single encoder; _dataframe_execution_cache.py:212 and :288 use canonical_json for the very keys this fingerprint feeds into. _cache.py:46 ALGO_VERSION v5 comment: the two divergent encoders were replaced by canonical_json.
est_reduction: 1 line changed; removes one of two JSON-digest encoders the codebase forbids
behavior_preservation: Byte-identical digest for all current inputs (str-keyed dict/list/scalar payloads); only diverges for set/tuple/non-finite values, which this function does not currently receive.

title: OnlineSolveResultLike and RatebookSolveResultLike re-declare baseline_objective/baseline_constraints already inherited from SolveResultLike
description: Both `OnlineSolveResultLike(SolveResultLike, Protocol)` (lines 451-453) and `RatebookSolveResultLike(SolveResultLike, Protocol)` (lines 476-478) re-declare `baseline_objective -> float` and `baseline_constraints -> dict[str, float]`. These two members are already declared on the shared base `SolveResultLike` (lines 431-434) with byte-identical signatures, so each subclass inherits them. The re-declarations add no typing or runtime information: structural (Protocol) membership and `runtime_checkable` isinstance checks consider the inherited members regardless. The duplication is also mildly misleading: each subclass docstring frames its extra members as solver-specific (e.g. "attributes specific to the online solver" / "baseline values" for ratebook), yet `baseline_objective`/`baseline_constraints` are the common, not the specific, attributes — they live on the base by design. Removing the four redundant stubs leaves each subclass declaring only its genuinely-specific members (dataframe/iterations/n_quotes/n_steps/history/grid for online; factor_tables/cd_iterations/clamp_rate for ratebook).
evidence: SolveResultLike (lines 425-436) declares `@property def baseline_objective(self) -> float: ...` and `@property def baseline_constraints(self) -> dict[str, float]: ...`. OnlineSolveResultLike (line 440) and RatebookSolveResultLike (line 467) both subclass SolveResultLike and re-state the identical two property stubs at lines 451-453 and 476-478 respectively. Identical signatures => the re-declarations are no-ops for both static type checking and runtime_checkable isinstance.
est_reduction: 4 lines (two property stubs in each of two Protocols)
behavior_preservation: Fully preserving: inherited Protocol members are identical in signature, so static type-checking results and runtime_checkable isinstance behaviour are unchanged after removing the duplicates.

title: x-request-id header is dropped on the 500 error path, breaking log/response correlation exactly when it matters most
description: The middleware binds a request_id (from the client's x-request-id header or a generated value) and logs every request with it, but it only echoes that id back to the client via response.headers['x-request-id'] on the SUCCESS path (line 396). When call_next raises, the except branch (lines 380-392) returns a fresh JSONResponse(status_code=500, ...) and returns immediately WITHOUT setting the x-request-id header. So for every unhandled-exception 500 - the one case where a user most needs to correlate the response with the server-side traceback that was logged under that request_id - the response carries no request id at all. A client-supplied x-request-id is likewise lost on errors, silently violating the 'custom request id preserved' contract that test_custom_request_id_preserved (test_server.py:2242) only verifies for 2xx.
evidence: dispatch(): rid computed at line 370; logger.error('unhandled_exception', ...) logs WITH the bound rid at lines 382-388; the returned JSONResponse at 389-392 never gets response.headers['x-request-id']=rid. Only the non-exception path sets it (line 396). Tests test_request_id_header_passthrough (2236) and test_custom_request_id_preserved (2242) both hit 200 responses, so the error-path omission is unpinned. structlog contextvars are bound but the HTTP response surface loses the id.

title: serve_spa compares a fully-resolved file path against an UN-resolved STATIC_DIR, so on any symlinked install path real static assets silently fall through to the SPA shell
description: STATIC_DIR is defined as Path(__file__).parent / 'static' WITHOUT .resolve() (line 74). In serve_spa, file_path = (STATIC_DIR / full_path).resolve() IS resolved (line 724), then the guard is file_path.is_relative_to(STATIC_DIR) (line 725) against the un-resolved STATIC_DIR. If any component of the package install directory is a symlink (e.g. the package is symlinked into site-packages, or installed under a path that traverses a symlinked home/temp dir - common on macOS where /tmp and /var are symlinks, and in some container/uv/editable layouts), file_path's realpath will not be relative_to the un-canonicalised STATIC_DIR, the is_relative_to check returns False, and a legitimately existing asset (e.g. /favicon.ico, /robots.txt, or anything mounted at the SPA root) is served as the index.html SPA shell with media_type text/html instead of via FileResponse with its correct type. This is a silent wrong-content/wrong-mimetype response rather than a clean 404/200. The mount at line 705 also uses the un-resolved STATIC_DIR/'assets'.
evidence: Line 74: STATIC_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / 'static' (no resolve). Line 724: file_path = (STATIC_DIR / full_path).resolve(). Line 725: if file_path.is_relative_to(STATIC_DIR) and file_path.is_file(): -> resolved-vs-unresolved comparison. When the prefixes differ only by symlink canonicalisation, is_relative_to is False and control reaches the final 'return _serve_index_html()' (line 730), serving HTML for an existing static file. Contrast _wire_source_file (line 182) which deliberately resolves BOTH sides (Path.cwd().resolve()).

location: src/haute/_trace_correlation.py:186-189 (_build_value_match_expr); crash surfaces via _match_columns_by_row_index:255-261 and _find_matching_row:349, called unguarded from _correlate_rows_posthoc:650
title: _build_value_match_expr crashes the whole trace on dtype-asymmetric shared columns (numeric value vs string column, or NaN/inf value vs non-float column)
description: _build_value_match_expr only reconciles dtypes in ONE direction: when the match value is a str it casts the column to Utf8 (line 188), so 'string-value vs numeric-column' works. But when the value is numeric and the parent column is a string, control falls to `pl.col(column) == value` (line 189), and Polars raises ComputeError: 'cannot compare string with numeric type'. Symmetrically, when the value is a raw float NaN/inf the function emits `pl.col(column).is_nan()` / `is_infinite()` (lines 177-185), which raise InvalidOperationError if that same column is non-float (e.g. Utf8) in the parent. Because the value-matching path runs the expression inside `indexed.select(...)` (_match_columns_by_row_index, lines 255-261) and `_correlate_rows_posthoc` calls `_find_matching_row` WITHOUT any try/except (trace.py:504 and _trace_correlation.py:650), the exception propagates out of the entire post-hoc correlation, turning a 'click a price to trace' request into a hard 500 for any pipeline whose graph changes a shared column's dtype across a non-1:1 transform. This is a realistic shape: a node that casts a string code/id column to Int64 (or vice-versa) while also filtering/aggregating (so the same-row-count positional fast path at line 634 is bypassed and value matching is reached). Note the fast path itself is safe because it uses the pure-Python `_trace_values_match` (line 644), so the trigger is precisely: value-matching fallback + a shared column whose dtype differs between parent and child.
evidence: Reproduced end-to-end against the real function: parent_df = pl.DataFrame({'code':['10','20','30'],'v':[1,2,3]}); child_df = parent_df.filter(pl.col('v')>1).with_columns(pl.col('code').cast(pl.Int64)); _correlate_rows_posthoc({'p':parent_df,'c':child_df}, ['p','c'], {'c':['p']}, 'c', 0, node_map=...) raises `ComputeError: cannot compare string with numeric type (i32)` from `[(col("code")) == (dyn int: 20)]`. Direct expr check: df=pl.DataFrame({'x':['1','2','3']}); df.select(_build_value_match_expr('x',2)) -> ComputeError. And df=pl.DataFrame({'s':['a','b']}); df.select(_build_value_match_expr('s',float('nan'))) -> InvalidOperationError `is_nan` not supported for dtype `str`. The string-value-vs-numeric-column direction works because of the cast at line 188; the numeric-value-vs-string-column direction has no equivalent guard and hits line 189. No existing test covers a dtype-asymmetric shared column (grep of tests/ for the build_value_match_expr / 'cannot compare string with numeric' shows none), so loud-crash here is not an intended contract — the function is meant to either match (it casts in the mirror case) or fall through to the (None,-1) 'no match' result, not to abort the trace.
behavior_preservation: Fix should cast the column to Utf8 and compare stringwise (mirroring line 188) whenever the column dtype and the value type are incompatible — or guard with a dtype check so a non-matching dtype yields a False predicate rather than an exception — so correlation degrades to 'no match' (the function's documented fail-soft) instead of crashing the whole trace.

title: _find_matching_row's required `fallback_index` parameter is never used
description: `_find_matching_row` declares a required positional parameter `fallback_index: int` (line 318) but the function body never references it. The docstring's strategy (lines 332-339) explicitly returns `(None, -1)` on no match and never consults a fallback index; the implementation only ever returns either a value-matched row's real index or `(None, -1)`. The parameter is vestigial from an earlier design that positionally fell back to a row. The sole production caller (_correlate_rows_posthoc, line 650-653) computes `child_row_idx` and passes it as `fallback_index` purely as dead plumbing, and every unit test passes a literal `0` while asserting only value-match-derived indices (e.g. test_trace.py:169-179 returns idx 1/2 by value, never the passed-in 0). The unused required arg adds noise and invites a future caller to assume a fallback-to-position semantic that does not exist.
evidence: Grep for `fallback_index` in src/haute/_trace_correlation.py returns exactly one line — the signature at 318 — proving zero uses in the body. The function's only return statements are `_jsonify_row(df.row(idx, named=True)), idx` (lines 370, 385) and `None, -1` (lines 368, 397, 407); none involve `fallback_index`. Tests at test_trace.py:173-179 confirm the result is driven entirely by value matching, not by the (0) passed as fallback_index.
behavior_preservation: Removing the parameter (and dropping the `child_row_idx` argument at the call site) is behaviour-preserving: it is read nowhere, so no code path changes. Update the unit-test call sites that pass a positional 0 accordingly.
est_reduction: ~1 parameter + the dead argument at the call site; clarifies the no-silent-fallback contract

title: Online trace resolves quote id from hardcoded literal "quote_id" with precedence over the configured qid_col, contradicting the filter on line 185
description: In `_explain_online`, the artifact's quote-id column is read via `qid_col = _required_artifact_column(artifact, "quote_id", default="quote_id")` (line 156) and is what both the price_contour applier (`ApplyOptimiser(quote_id=qid_col)`, line 173) and the candidate filter (`explained.filter(pl.col(qid_col).cast(pl.Utf8) == str(quote_id_value))`, line 185) operate on. But the *value* used in that filter is resolved on line 179 as `quote_id_value = output_row.get("quote_id", output_row.get(qid_col))`, which gives the literal key `"quote_id"` precedence over the configured `qid_col`. When the artifact configures a non-default quote-id column (e.g. `quote_id="policy_ref"`), and the output row also carries a literal `quote_id` column (which the route layer can legitimately add — see `routes/_optimiser_service.py:1971-1972` preferring a literal `quote_id` when present), the value taken from the wrong column is then filtered against the *correct* `qid_col` column on line 185, so no rows match and the trace raises a spurious `OptimiserApplyTraceError("no optimiser candidates found for quote_id=...")`. A second facet: because `dict.get("quote_id", default)` only uses the default when the key is *absent*, a present-but-null literal `quote_id` (value `None`) shadows a valid configured-column value and forces the `quote_id_value is None` branch (line 180-183) to raise even though the configured column holds a real id. Correct behaviour is to prefer the configured `qid_col` and only fall back to the literal `"quote_id"`, i.e. `output_row.get(qid_col, output_row.get("quote_id"))`, and to treat null as missing.
evidence: L156 qid_col=_required_artifact_column(artifact,"quote_id",default="quote_id") -> may be e.g. "policy_ref". L179 quote_id_value=output_row.get("quote_id", output_row.get(qid_col)) -> picks literal-quote_id value (or None if key present but null) BEFORE the configured column. L185 explained.filter(pl.col(qid_col).cast(pl.Utf8)==str(quote_id_value)) -> filters on policy_ref using the quote_id-column value; mismatch => quote_rows.is_empty() => L189 raise 'no optimiser candidates found'. All tests (test_optimiser_apply_trace_enrichment.py) use qid_col=='quote_id', so the divergent-column path is unexercised.

title: materialize_lazy_frame_with_cache computes _profile_value(profile) and discards it; the profile argument is otherwise unused and never reconciled with key.profile
description: The `profile` parameter of `materialize_lazy_frame_with_cache` is used only at line 593 (`_profile_value(profile)`) whose return value is discarded. The sink (`bounded_sink`, lines 601-606) takes no profile, and cache identity is already fully baked into `key` (which carries `key.profile`, set when `dataframe_execution_cache_key` was built). The function never compares the passed `profile` against `key.profile`, so a caller passing a profile that disagrees with the key is silently accepted. The line therefore exists purely as a fail-loud parse guard (`ExecutionProfile(profile)` raises ValueError on an unknown string via `dataframe_execution_cache_profile`). In the sole production caller (_execute_lazy.py:1300-1308) the profile passed is the live `execution_context.profile`, and the genuine key/profile agreement is already enforced upstream at _execute_lazy.py:814 (`cache_key.profile != effective_cache_profile` -> ValueError) before materialize is ever called. The argument is thus redundant beyond a parse-check that the upstream path already covers, making it read like a no-op and inviting confusion about whether `profile` affects materialization (it does not).
evidence: Line 587 declares `profile: ExecutionProfile | str`. Line 593 `_profile_value(profile)` -> `dataframe_execution_cache_profile` -> `ExecutionProfile(profile)` (raises on bad string) but the str result is not bound or used. Lines 594-621 never reference `profile` again; `bounded_sink(lf, path, fast_checkpoint=..., streaming_chunk_size=...)` has no profile param. `key.profile` (set at dataframe_execution_cache_key line 297) is the actual identity; it is validated against the execution profile at _execute_lazy.py:814-819 prior to the materialize call at _execute_lazy.py:1300. No test exercises a bad-profile raise from line 593 (grep of tests/test_dataframe_execution_cache.py and tests/test_execute_lazy_dataframe_cache.py found none).
behavior_preservation: Deleting line 593 and the `profile` parameter is NOT fully behavior-preserving in isolation: it removes the parse-check that raises on an unknown profile string at this entry point. Safe-equivalent options: (a) keep the parameter but assert agreement with key, e.g. raise if `_profile_value(profile) != key.profile` (turns a silent mismatch into a loud error and gives the line a real purpose), or (b) drop the parameter entirely since the upstream caller already validates profile/key agreement and the cache key alone determines identity. Either makes the intent explicit without changing the cached output.
est_reduction: 1 line plus one parameter from the public signature (or convert the discarded call into a 1-line assertion).

title: _normalise_dtype accepts any pl attribute as a dtype, bypassing the documented SchemaMismatchError for unsupported dtypes
description: _normalise_dtype is the single validation chokepoint for declared source dtypes (via _normalise_schema_overrides / _schema_overrides_from_config / read_source schema_overrides). For a string value it first checks _POLARS_DTYPE_ALIASES, then does `dtype = getattr(pl, dtype_name, None); if dtype is not None: return dtype`, and only raises SchemaMismatchError("Unsupported declared source dtype") when getattr returns None. The polars top-level namespace exposes many public names that are NOT dtypes -- e.g. `col`, `lit`, `len`, `sum`, `Series`, `DataFrame`, `read_csv`. getattr returns those objects (non-None), so they are accepted as a 'dtype' and the documented SchemaMismatchError is never raised. The malformed value then leaks downstream: for CSV/NDJSON it is passed to pl.scan_csv/scan_ndjson(schema_overrides=...) which raises a confusing `TypeError: cannot parse input ... into Polars data type`; for JSON/parquet (which never pass overrides to the reader) it is compared in _validate_declared_schema via `actual_dtype != declared_dtype`, which is always unequal and surfaces a spurious 'Declared source schema mismatch' instead of an 'unsupported dtype' error. Either way the function violates its contract (raise SchemaMismatchError for unsupported declared dtypes) and gives the user a misleading diagnostic for a simple config typo. Note: an attribute that does NOT exist on pl (e.g. 'NotAType') is handled correctly (the existing test test_io.py:211 only covers that case), so the gap is specifically the 'valid pl attribute but not a DataType' class of input and is currently untested.
evidence:
_normalise_dtype: `dtype = getattr(pl, dtype_name, None)
    if dtype is not None:
        return dtype
    raise SchemaMismatchError("Unsupported declared source dtype.", ...)`. Probe with venv polars 1.39.2: _normalise_dtype('col') -> polars.functions.col.Col (no raise); _normalise_dtype('Series') -> <class Series>; _normalise_dtype('lit')/('len')/('sum')/('read_csv') all return non-dtype callables/classes without raising. Passing pl.Series/pl.lit/pl.len to pl.scan_csv(schema_overrides=...) raises `TypeError: cannot parse input ... into Polars data type` (wrong exception type; contract promises SchemaMismatchError). Fix: after getattr, assert the resolved object is a Polars dtype, e.g. `isinstance(dtype, pl.DataType) or (isinstance(dtype, type) and issubclass(dtype, pl.DataType))`, else raise the SchemaMismatchError.

title: _validate_csv_declared_schema_for_profile returns a header list/None that its only caller discards
description: _validate_csv_declared_schema_for_profile is annotated `-> list[str] | None` and threads a `return None` (early exit) plus `return header` (success) and bare `return` after raising paths. Its sole caller (read_source, line 501) invokes it purely for its validation side effects and discards the return value entirely; a repo-wide search confirms no other caller. The CSV read path independently re-derives the schema via _select_columns(lf, ...). The header return value is therefore dead: the function exists only to raise on mismatch. The signature can be simplified to `-> None`, dropping the `header_set`/`return header` plumbing that exists only to satisfy the unused return contract, with no behavior change.
evidence: Grep for `_validate_csv_declared_schema_for_profile` yields exactly two hits: the def (line 227) and the call at line 501, where the result is not assigned: `        _validate_csv_declared_schema_for_profile(\n            path=path_string, ...)`. The function returns `header` (line 283) / `None` (line 236) but nothing consumes it.
est_reduction: ~3-5 lines and a simpler `-> None` signature
behavior_preservation: Pure side-effect (validation/raise) is unchanged; only the unused return value is removed.

title: _assert_finite_glm_record silently accepts None/missing required GLM fields; only a bare assert guards them, so malformed records raise AssertionError (or TypeError under -O) instead of ModelExplanationError
description: `_as_float` short-circuits `None` to `None` BEFORE the strict branch (lines 25-26), so `_as_float(value, strict=True)` raises ModelExplanationError only for non-numeric/non-finite values, never for `None`. `_assert_finite_glm_record` validates every required numeric field via `_as_float(record.get(field), strict=True)` (lines 317-318) and discards the result. Because `record.get(field)` returns `None` when the key is absent or explicitly null, a GLM record that is MISSING `base_value`/`sum_contributions`/`prediction_from_contributions`/`prediction_value` (or carries an explicit `None`) passes `_assert_finite_glm_record` without error, despite its name/docstring asserting finiteness. Downstream, `explain_rustystats_glm_prediction` re-parses these fields with `strict=True`, gets `None`, and the ONLY thing catching it is a bare `assert ... is not None` (lines 386, 458, 459, 460; also 420 for each contribution). That assert raises `AssertionError` — not the module-contract `ModelExplanationError` — and is stripped entirely when Python runs under `-O`/PYTHONOPTIMIZE, in which case `_prediction_tolerance(None)` -> `abs(None)` raises `TypeError`. The whole module is documented/built to fail with `ModelExplanationError`, and the sole production caller `enrich_model_score` (src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py:712) catches ONLY `ModelExplanationError` to emit structured per-method error metadata via `explanation_error_metadata_for_config`. An `AssertionError`/`TypeError` instead falls through to the broad `except Exception` (line 725), producing a generic 'model score enrichment failed' detail with `prediction_value=None` and `error_type='AssertionError'` — an observable degradation of the trace for a malformed-record case the validation function exists specifically to handle cleanly.
evidence: _as_float: line 25 `if value is None: return None` executes before the strict finite check (33-36), so strict=True returns None for None input rather than raising. _assert_finite_glm_record (317-318) does `_as_float(record.get(field), field_name=field, strict=True)` with no presence check -> a missing/None `sum_contributions` is not rejected. explain_rustystats_glm_prediction line 447-460 then: `sum_contributions = _as_float(record.get('sum_contributions'), strict=True)` (=None) ; `assert sum_contributions is not None` -> AssertionError, not ModelExplanationError. _trace_enrichment.enrich_model_score line 712 `except _model_explainability.ModelExplanationError` does not catch AssertionError; broad `except Exception` at 725 produces the generic failure detail.

title: Identical rank-by-abs-contribution, truncate, and re-number blocks duplicated across the CatBoost and RustyStats explainers
description: Both `explain_catboost_prediction` (231-259) and `explain_rustystats_glm_prediction` (412-443) build a list of contribution dicts carrying a private `_feature_index`, sort by `(-abs_value, _feature_index)`, apply the same `max_contributions`/`truncated`/`omitted_count` truncation, then re-iterate to pop `_feature_index` and assign `rank` starting at 1. The sort key field name differs (`abs_shap_value` vs `abs_contribution`) but both dicts also carry the other alias (the CatBoost item has `abs_shap_value`; the RustyStats item sets both `abs_contribution` and `abs_shap_value`), so a single shared helper `rank_and_truncate(items, *, abs_key, max_contributions)` would collapse ~30 lines of near-verbatim logic into one call site each, removing a maintenance hazard where one copy can drift from the other (e.g. a tie-break or truncation-accounting fix applied to only one).
evidence: Lines 243-245 sort `key=lambda item: (-float(item['abs_shap_value']), int(item['_feature_index']))`; lines 427-429 sort `key=lambda item: (-float(item['abs_contribution']), int(item['_feature_index']))`. Lines 247-252 and 431-436 are byte-identical truncation logic. Lines 254-259 and 438-443 are identical pop-`_feature_index`/assign-`rank` loops.
est_reduction: ~25-30 lines
behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving if the shared helper keeps the exact tie-break (descending abs value, then ascending original index), the same truncation arithmetic (omitted_count = len - max), and 1-based rank numbering; the differing abs key name must be passed as a parameter.

title: First in-flight admission is refused whenever a single profile's memory LIMIT exceeds (available_ram - os_reserve), even with default fixed budgets on a modestly-sized machine
description: The in-flight gate refuses an admission when `reserved + reservation_bytes > limit_bytes`. With an empty ledger (`reserved == 0`) this reduces to `reservation_bytes > limit_bytes`, and there is no clamp guaranteeing that at least the first reservation is admitted. `reservation_bytes` is the configured per-profile LIMIT (`budget.memory_limit_bytes`), while `limit_bytes = _in_flight_limit_bytes(budget) = max(available - reserve, 1)` (available RAM minus the OS reserve, default 2 GiB). For any in-flight profile whose LIMIT is larger than `available - os_reserve`, the very FIRST and ONLY job of that profile is refused with reason `in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded`, despite real RSS being near zero. This is DISTINCT from the known accumulation/leak finding (which requires 2-3 lingering un-released reservations to sum past the limit and is gated on close()/GC): here a single fresh reservation on an empty ledger is rejected, so the defect persists even after the known leak is fixed.
evidence: Trace with DEFAULT fixed policy, LAZY_SINK (default LIMIT = 4*1024*_MIB = 4 GiB at line 36), on a 5 GiB box: _resolve_required_budget -> _fixed_default_memory_limit -> ExecutionBudget(memory_limit_bytes=4 GiB, available_ram_bytes=None, os_reserve_bytes=None). create_admitted_execution_context -> _reserve_in_flight_budget: profile LAZY_SINK in _IN_FLIGHT_PROFILE_SET (line 198). limit_bytes=_in_flight_limit_bytes(budget): available=available_ram_bytes()=5 GiB (line 549), reserve=min(_resolve_os_reserve_bytes()=2 GiB, max(5GiB//2,1)=2.5 GiB)=2 GiB (line 554), return max(5GiB-2GiB,1)=3 GiB. reservation_bytes=4 GiB (line 510). Under _IN_FLIGHT_LOCK: reserved=sum(...)=0 (empty ledger, line 512); 0 + 4 GiB > 3 GiB is True (line 513) -> raises ExecutionAdmissionError(reason='in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded') (lines 514-523). So the first heavy job is refused on any box with available_ram < profile_limit + os_reserve (~6 GiB for LAZY_SINK). Existing test test_heavy_execution_admission_counts_in_flight_budget (tests/test_execution_context.py:262) only checks the TWO-reservation accumulation case (10 GiB RAM, two adaptive OPTIMISER_SETUP contexts); no test covers a single reservation exceeding the in-flight limit, and no clamp in _reserve_in_flight_budget guarantees admission of the first reservation.

title: _IN_FLIGHT_RESERVATIONS stores (profile, reservation_bytes, operation) tuples but only reservation_bytes is ever read; profile and operation are never consumed
description: The process-wide ledger `_IN_FLIGHT_RESERVATIONS: dict[int, tuple[ExecutionProfile, int, str]]` is written at line 525 with `(profile, reservation_bytes, operation)`, but the only read site (line 512) destructures and uses solely the middle `amount` (`sum(amount for _profile, amount, _operation in ...)`). The `profile` and `operation` fields are never surfaced anywhere: the ExecutionAdmissionError for `in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded` reports only the aggregate `reserved` sum and the `limit_bytes`, not a per-reservation breakdown by profile/operation. The ledger value could be just the int `reservation_bytes`, simplifying the type and the write. (The repro at review/02-findings/repro likewise reads only `amount`.)
evidence: Grep for _IN_FLIGHT_RESERVATIONS across the repo (*.py) shows exactly: declaration (line 209), read at line 512 `sum(amount for _profile, amount, _operation in _IN_FLIGHT_RESERVATIONS.values())`, write at line 525, pop at line 541, clear at line 561. The two underscore-prefixed binders (`_profile`, `_operation`) at the only read site confirm those tuple fields are intentionally discarded; no other code path reads them.
behavior_preservation: Storing `reservation_bytes` directly as the dict value (or keeping the tuple but documenting it as reserved-for-diagnostics) produces identical admission decisions, since only the summed amount is read. No externally observable behavior depends on the stored profile/operation.
est_reduction: -2 fields of stored state per reservation; simpler ledger value type

title: Empty HAUTE_EXECUTION_MEMORY_POLICY="" hard-fails every execution admission instead of falling back to the unset default
description: `_memory_policy_name` reads the env var with a default of `_ADAPTIVE_MEMORY_POLICY_NAME` for the UNSET case, but when the variable is set to an EMPTY string it does not fall back: `raw=''`, `policy=''.strip().lower()==''`, which is not the alias and is not in the allowed set, so it raises RuntimeError. Because this function is called on every budget resolution (execution_budget_for_profile -> _resolve_required_budget -> _memory_policy_name) for preview/sink/train/optimiser/deploy, an empty env var (a common shell/orchestrator artifact for 'unset to default', e.g. `export HAUTE_EXECUTION_MEMORY_POLICY=`) makes ALL bounded executions crash, whereas a truly-unset variable defaults to adaptive. Treating empty-string differently from unset (crash vs. default) is an inconsistency; whether the loud failure is intended is ambiguous.
evidence: Line 339: `raw = os.environ.get(_MEMORY_POLICY_ENV, _ADAPTIVE_MEMORY_POLICY_NAME)`. With the var set to '', os.environ.get returns '' (not the default). Line 340: policy=''. Line 341: '' != _ADAPTIVE_MEMORY_POLICY_ALIAS. Lines 343-347: '' not in {local_adaptive, fixed, strict_server} -> True -> raise RuntimeError (lines 348-352). The unset path would have used the default 'local_adaptive' and returned successfully. No normalization maps '' to the default.

title: C8 display-consistency guard silently accepts any multiply factor when the prior cumulative is 0.0
description: For an `operation == "multiply"` step, `_check_display_consistency` validates the displayed factor by computing `reapplied = prev_cumulative * display_value` and comparing it to the observed value. When `prev_cumulative == 0.0` (or -0.0), `reapplied` is `0.0` for ANY `display_value`, so the comparison `abs(reapplied - observed) > tolerance` is satisfied (passes) for an arbitrary, wrong factor as long as `observed` is also 0.0. The module-level/C8 docstring explicitly promises that feeding a wrong multiply amount in 'must fail loudly', but here a bogus factor is accepted and rendered (e.g. an entry displaying 'x999.0' on a value that did not change). This is reachable through the public `build_waterfall(steps)` entry point (which is part of the module's tested public surface, exercised directly with hand-authored step lists in the test suite).
evidence: Verified by running the public API: build_waterfall([{label:'Base',operation:'base',value:0.0,cumulative:0.0},{label:'Bogus',operation:'multiply',value:999.0,cumulative:0.0},{label:'End',operation:'add',value:5.0,cumulative:5.0}]) returns a result with the 'Bogus' entry value=999.0 and does NOT raise WaterfallReconciliationError, because line 263 `reapplied = prev_cumulative * display_value` = 0.0*999.0 = 0.0 and line 270 `abs(reapplied - observed)` = abs(0.0-0.0) = 0.0 <= tolerance. The analogous 'add' branch does not have this hole (reapplied = prev_cumulative + display_value is sensitive to display_value). Note the production trace path (build_waterfall_from_steps -> _classify_contribution) never emits a multiply step when value_before==0 (it returns 'add' at lines 403-412), so this gap is confined to the hand-authored build_waterfall path, hence low severity.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

location: src/haute/_ast_helpers.py:203-231 (_strip_docstring), specifically the single-line branch at :219-221 (`if stripped.count(opening_quote) >= 2 and stripped.endswith(opening_quote)`) and the close test at :215
title: _strip_docstring swallows the entire function body when a single-line docstring has a trailing comment after the closing triple-quote
description: When a function's docstring is a single-line triple-quoted string followed by a trailing comment on the same line (e.g. `"""Doc."""  # note`), `_strip_docstring` discards the docstring AND every subsequent line of the body, returning only the docstring's leading whitespace lines (effectively []). This is valid Python and `ast.get_docstring` recognises it as the docstring, so the body the heuristic is meant to preserve (`x = 1; return x`, etc.) is silently lost. The single-line fast-path at :221 requires `stripped.endswith(opening_quote)`; with a trailing comment the line ends with the comment text, not `"""`, so the `else` branch sets `in_docstring = True`. From then on, line 215 looks for a line that *contains* `opening_quote`, but the only such line was the (now consumed) opener, so the loop `continue`s past every remaining body line (line 218) without ever appending them. This corrupts the extracted user code that `_code_extraction._extract_user_code` (src/haute/_code_extraction.py:964) persists into the node config box, so a round-trip (parse -> codegen) drops the user's logic. This is DISTINCT from known finding #4: that finding was about mixed/embedded triple-quote runs *inside* a multi-line docstring body and was REFUTED by review/03-simplification/repro/parser__NEWBUG-03.py (its 10 valid-Python cases all matched the AST oracle); none of them placed a comment or any content after the closing quote on the docstring's own line. A second, rarer variant of the same root cause: a first statement that is a triple-quoted string *concatenation/BinOp* (e.g. `"""a""" + foo`) is NOT a docstring per ast, yet _strip_docstring treats the opener line as a docstring start and swallows the statement plus all following lines.
evidence:
Source: `def f():
    """Doc."""  # trailing comment
    x = 1
    return x`. ast.get_docstring(func) == 'Doc.' and func.body[0] is an Expr (a real docstring). _extract_function_bodies(...)['f'] == '    """Doc."""  # trailing comment
    x = 1
    return x'. _strip_docstring(body.splitlines()) == [] (verified by running it in the project venv). AST ground truth (ast.get_docstring + docstring node end_lineno, the same oracle used by parser__NEWBUG-03.py) keeps ['x = 1', 'return x']; _strip_docstring returns [] -> AGREE: False. No existing test in tests/test_parser_internals.py::TestStripDocstring or tests/test_parser_helpers.py covers a trailing comment after the closing quote.
behavior_preservation: The behavior-preserving fix is to derive the docstring boundary from the AST (ast.get_docstring + func.body[0].end_lineno) — already available because the parser passes the parsed tree into _extract_function_bodies — instead of the line-scanning heuristic; this also subsumes known finding #4's concern.

title: _topo_order length-mismatch guard is unreachable for cycles/disconnects and emits a misleading empty-set error on the only path that reaches it
description: Inside Pipeline._topo_order the block `if len(sorted_ids) != len(self._nodes): missing = {n.name for n in self._nodes} - set(sorted_ids); raise ValueError(f"Cycle detected or disconnected nodes: {missing}")` is dead/misleading. topo_sort_ids (delegating to graphlib.TopologicalSorter) registers every node via sorter.add(nid) and returns list(sorter.static_order()), which yields ALL added nodes including fully disconnected ones; a genuine cycle raises CycleError inside topo_sort_ids and propagates, never returning a short list. Therefore len(sorted_ids) == len(self._nodes) for every cycle-free graph, and cycles never reach this line at all. The only way to make len(sorted_ids) < len(self._nodes) is duplicate node names (two functions with the same __name__, which _register_node silently allows because it overwrites _node_map but appends both to _nodes). In that case `missing = {names} - set(sorted_ids)` is the EMPTY set (the duplicated name is present in sorted_ids), so the error reads 'Cycle detected or disconnected nodes: set()' — it names neither the real cause (duplicate node name) nor any node. So the branch is unreachable for its stated purpose and actively misleading for the one input that triggers it.
evidence: topo_sort_ids (_topo.py:51-69): `for nid in node_ids: sorter.add(nid)` then `return list(sorter.static_order())`; CycleError is raised before returning. Verified with graphlib: disconnected nodes ['a','b','c','d'] with only a->b yields static_order ['a','c','d','b'] (len 4 == input 4, branch not taken); duplicate ['x','x','y'] yields ['x','y'] (len 2 < 3, branch taken) and {names}-set(sorted) == empty set. test_topo_order_cycle_raises / test_self_loop_detected assert CycleError (from topo_sort_ids), not this ValueError; no test ever exercises line 304.
behavior_preservation: Removing the branch is behaviour-preserving for all currently reachable inputs (cycles still raise CycleError from topo_sort_ids; disconnected nodes are still caught downstream by run()/score()'s 'no inbound edges' guard). Duplicate node names are a distinct latent defect that this branch obscures rather than reports; if desired they should be rejected explicitly at registration with the offending name, not via a set-difference that yields the empty set.
est_reduction: ~4 lines removed; or replace with an explicit duplicate-name guard at registration that actually names the colliding node.

kind: duplicated transform-execution loop across run() and score()
title: run() and score() duplicate the non-source node execution block (input resolution + missing-input check + no-inbound-edges raise)
description: The per-non-source-node execution logic is copy-pasted between Pipeline.run() and Pipeline.score(): both compute `input_names = self._get_inputs(n.name)`, build `missing = [name for name in input_names if name not in outputs]`, raise the identical 'Node ... is missing input(s) from: ...' ValueError, gather `input_dfs = [outputs[name] for name in input_names]`, call `outputs[n.name] = n(*input_dfs)`, and otherwise raise the identical 'Node ... has no inbound edges' ValueError. The two copies are byte-for-byte equivalent apart from run() handling sources inline in the same loop while score() seeds sources in a separate prior loop. This duplication risks the two execution paths silently diverging (e.g. a future fix to the missing-input message or ordering applied to only one).
evidence: run() lines 343-357 vs score() lines 393-407 contain the same input_names/missing/input_dfs/raise structure verbatim. The only structural difference is source handling, which can be hoisted: a shared private helper, e.g. `_run_transforms(order, outputs)` iterating non-source nodes, would be called by both after each method seeds `outputs` for sources in its own way.
behavior_preservation: Extracting the shared non-source loop into one helper preserves behaviour exactly (same ordering via _get_inputs, same error messages, same _scenario_ctx token still set by each caller). Covered by existing tests: test_run, test_score, test_diamond_dependency, test_run_no_edges_raises, test_score_no_edges_raises, test_no_edges_multiple_nodes_raises.
est_reduction: ~15-18 duplicated lines collapse to a single ~10-line helper.

title: safe_joblib_load captures original_find_class OUTSIDE the lock, permanently leaking a restricted find_class onto NumpyUnpickler under concurrent loads
description: safe_joblib_load monkeypatches NumpyUnpickler.find_class with a restricted closure inside `with _joblib_lock`, then restores `original_find_class` in finally. But `original_find_class = NumpyUnpickler.find_class` is read at line 452, OUTSIDE the lock. If thread B enters safe_joblib_load while thread A holds the lock (A has already replaced find_class with its restricted closure), B captures A's restricted function as its 'original'. When B later acquires the lock, runs, and hits its finally, it restores find_class to A's restricted closure rather than the genuine NumpyUnpickler.find_class. The result is that after the interleaving, NumpyUnpickler.find_class is left permanently pointing at a dead `safe_joblib_load.<locals>._restricted_joblib_find_class`, so EVERY subsequent joblib.load process-wide (including plain joblib.load calls outside the sandbox) silently uses a restricted find_class belonging to a leaked closure. Repeated races can also stack nested restricted wrappers. The single-threaded tests (test_safe_load_does_not_break_subsequent_loads, test_safe_load_restored_after_error) do not cover this concurrent path. Reachable via _io.load_external_object(file_type='joblib'), which servers can invoke concurrently for model loading.
evidence: Executed repro: two threads call safe_joblib_load; thread A is held inside the lock (slow joblib.load) while thread B executes line 452 and reads NumpyUnpickler.find_class == A's restricted closure. After both join, `NumpyUnpickler.find_class is _Unpickler.find_class` -> False; it equals `safe_joblib_load.<locals>._restricted_joblib_find_class` (RESTORED to true original: False; LEAKED restricted patch: True). Root cause is the capture at line 452 being outside the `with _joblib_lock:` block at line 465; the allow_imports=True path is unaffected only because this is joblib-specific.

title: safe_globals default path returns ns['__builtins__'] aliasing the shared module-global _SAFE_BUILTINS; mutation leaks across all subsequent exec namespaces (inconsistent with the allow_imports branch)
description: _SAFE_BUILTINS is a module-global dict whose '__builtins__' key is set to itself at line 109. In safe_globals, the default (allow_imports=False) path does `ns = dict(_SAFE_BUILTINS)` (a shallow copy of the entries) but the copied '__builtins__' value still points at the original _SAFE_BUILTINS object. So ns['__builtins__'] IS the shared module-global, not a per-call copy. Any mutation through ns['__builtins__'] (e.g. side effects of exec that add/remove a builtins entry, or any code path that writes through the builtins mapping) permanently corrupts _SAFE_BUILTINS for every subsequent exec() in the entire process. This is a shared-mutable-state hazard and a contract violation for a function whose purpose is to hand back an isolated namespace. It is also internally inconsistent: the allow_imports=True branch (line 125) deliberately builds a FRESH dict `{**_SAFE_BUILTINS, '__import__': ...}` for ns['__builtins__'], so the two branches have asymmetric isolation guarantees for no stated reason.
evidence: Executed: `g = safe_globals(pl=...)`; `g['__builtins__'] is _SAFE_BUILTINS` -> True. `g['__builtins__']['LEAKED'] = 'pwned'` then `'LEAKED' in _SAFE_BUILTINS` -> True, and a fresh `safe_globals()` call sees 'LEAKED' at both top level and under '__builtins__'. The AST validator currently blocks direct `__builtins__[...]=` in user code, but safe_globals is a public reusable helper (used by executor and preamble) whose isolation contract is violated and whose two branches disagree.

title: Allowlist entries ('builtins','True'), ('builtins','False'), ('builtins','None') are unreachable — pickle never calls find_class for these
description: The pickle protocol encodes True/False/None with dedicated opcodes (NEWTRUE / NEWFALSE / NONE), never as global references, so Unpickler.find_class is never invoked with name in {'True','False','None'}. _pickle_global_is_allowed therefore can never be reached with those (module,name) pairs from any real pickle stream, making those three two-segment allowlist entries dead. (Note: the type-constructor entries like int/float/str/set/list/tuple/bytes are NOT dead — those can legitimately appear as global references inside custom __reduce__ outputs — only True/False/None are provably unreachable.)
evidence: Executed: pickletools.genops(dumps(True/False/None)) -> ['PROTO','NEWTRUE'/'NEWFALSE'/'NONE','STOP']; a recording Unpickler subclass shows find_class is called zero times when loading True, False, None (and also int/float/str scalars). Hence the three ('builtins','True'/'False'/'None') tuples in _ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES can never satisfy the `len(prefix)==2 and module=='builtins' and name in {...}` branch.
est_reduction: 3 lines
behavior_preservation: Removing the three entries cannot change behavior because find_class is never invoked for True/False/None; the allowlist outcome for every reachable pickle global is identical.

title: _ASTValidator docstring overstates protection: claims it blocks lambda definitions and star-expression assignments, but neither is rejected
description: The class docstring lists 'Class, async, and lambda definitions' and 'Star expressions in assignments (a, *b = ...)' among the blocked constructs. The validator has no visit_Lambda and no visit_Starred, so `f = lambda x: x+1` and `a, *b = [1,2,3]` both pass validation. (This is a documentation defect, not a security hole: the validator still recurses via generic_visit into lambda/def bodies, so dunder access and reflection calls inside a lambda are still caught — e.g. `lambda o: getattr(o,'x')` and `lambda o: o.__class__` are correctly blocked.) The inaccuracy is harmful because a maintainer relying on the docstring would wrongly believe lambda/star definitions are themselves rejected, weakening reasoning about the sandbox's structural guarantees.
evidence: Executed via validate_user_code: 'f = lambda x: x + 1' -> ALLOWED; 'a, *b = [1, 2, 3]' -> ALLOWED. Source grep confirms no visit_Lambda / visit_Starred in _ASTValidator (only Attribute/Call/Subscript/Import/ImportFrom/ClassDef/AsyncFunctionDef/Global/Nonlocal). Recursion check: 'f = lambda o: getattr(o, "x")' -> BLOCKED, 'f = lambda o: o.__class__' -> BLOCKED, confirming generic_visit recursion is intact and the gap is purely the stale docstring claim.

title: _validate_user_code_cached docstring claims chain-syntax fragments are wrapped as `df = (df <code>)` and re-parsed; no such wrapping exists
description:
The docstring states: 'Code that cannot be parsed as standalone Python (e.g. chain syntax .filter(...)) is wrapped as `df = (
 df
 <code>
)` and re-parsed before giving up — this mirrors how the executor wraps user code fragments.' The actual implementation calls _try_parse_code, which does a single ast.parse(code) and immediately raises UnsafeCodeError (wrapping the SyntaxError) on failure — there is no df=(...) wrapping or retry. Moreover the executor it claims to mirror (_user_exec._exec_user_code) does not wrap fragments either: it validates and execs the raw `code` directly. So a bare fragment like '.filter(...)' is rejected with a syntax error, contrary to the documented fallback. This is a stale/incorrect docstring describing a non-existent fallback path — exactly the 'incorrect and hard to notice' hazard the project guidelines warn against.
evidence: Executed: validate_user_code('.filter(pl.col("age") > 25)') -> UnsafeCodeError 'Cannot validate code with syntax errors (line 1): invalid syntax'; same for '.select(...)' and '.with_columns(...)'. _try_parse_code body is a single try/except around ast.parse with no wrapping branch; _user_exec._exec_user_code execs raw `code` (no fragment wrapping), so the 'mirrors the executor' claim is also inaccurate.

title: Streaming-incompatibility detection is a naive 'stream' substring match that misclassifies unrelated Polars errors
description: _is_streaming_compatibility_error(exc) decides whether a Polars ComputeError/InvalidOperationError/SchemaError is a streaming-engine incompatibility purely by `"stream" in str(exc).lower()`. Any genuine data/schema/compute error whose rendered message happens to contain the substring 'stream' (e.g. a column named `upstream_premium`, `stream_id`, `quote_stream`, or a message that references an 'upstream' plan node) is misclassified. Consequences: (1) in bounded_sink (via _is_streaming_sink_error) a real schema/compute failure is swallowed and re-raised as BoundedMemoryUnsupportedError('Bounded streaming sink failed'), masking the true root cause; (2) in streaming_collect with allow_broad=True a real data error containing 'stream' silently triggers the high-memory broad collect fallback instead of surfacing; (3) conversely a real streaming-incompatibility error whose message does NOT contain 'stream' is treated as a non-streaming error and propagates raw (no typed BoundedMemoryUnsupportedError), defeating the bounded-memory contract. The whole bounded/broad routing hinges on this single substring.
evidence: Line 43-44: `message = str(exc).lower(); return "stream" in message`. streaming_collect line 77 `if not _is_streaming_compatibility_error(exc): raise`; bounded_collect_batches line 146 same; bounded_sink line 256 `if not _is_streaming_sink_error(exc): raise` (and _is_streaming_sink_error just calls _is_streaming_compatibility_error). The existing tests (test_polars_utils.py:126-147) deliberately craft non-streaming messages WITHOUT the word 'stream' (e.g. 'conversion from str to f64 failed') to exercise the propagate path, demonstrating the classification depends entirely on the literal substring; a ComputeError('column \'upstream_id\' not found') would be wrongly wrapped as a bounded-memory failure.

title: read_parquet_metadata produces wrong per-column byte map and column_count for nested (struct/list) parquet columns
description: The function builds `columns` from the Arrow top-level schema names (one entry per top-level field), but accumulates per-column byte totals using `column.path_in_schema`, which for nested types is a dotted leaf path (e.g. struct field 's' yields leaf columns 's.x', 's.y'). column_uncompressed_size_bytes/column_compressed_size_bytes are pre-seeded with top-level names via dict.fromkeys(columns,0); the leaf-path accumulation therefore (a) leaves the top-level struct key (e.g. 's') at 0 bytes despite the struct holding data, and (b) injects NEW dotted keys ('s.x','s.y') that are absent from `columns`. So the returned per-column map keys disagree with `columns` and attribute zero bytes to nested columns. Separately, `column_count` returns meta.num_columns (the leaf count, e.g. 3 for {a, struct{x,y}}) which disagrees with len(columns)=2. Aggregate totals (uncompressed_size_bytes/compressed_size_bytes) remain correct since they sum all leaves. _ram_estimate._detailed_parquet_metadata consumes both meta['column_count'] (over-counted) and meta['column_uncompressed_size_bytes'] (mis-keyed, struct columns => 0 width), so RAM estimation under-counts and mis-attributes width for any user-supplied parquet source node containing struct/list columns (reachable via the /api/files schema path and DATA_SOURCE parquet inputs). Flat tabular parquet is unaffected, which is why all existing tests (only flat schemas) pass.
evidence: Reproduced with the project venv: `pl.DataFrame({'a':[1,2],'s':[{'x':1,'y':2},{'x':3,'y':4}]}).write_parquet(p)` then `pq.read_metadata(p).num_columns == 3`, `pq.read_schema(p).names == ['a','s']` (len 2), and row_group column path_in_schema values are ['a','s.x','s.y']. Code: line 314 `columns = {name: ... for name in arrow_schema.names}` (top-level), lines 317-318 `dict.fromkeys(columns,0)`, line 327 `column_name = str(column.path_in_schema)` (leaf-dotted), lines 328-332 `.get(column_name,0)+...` adds dotted keys; line 335 `"column_count": meta.num_columns`. _ram_estimate.py:228 uses meta['column_count'] and :231-234 maps column_uncompressed_size_bytes by name.

title: _is_streaming_sink_error is a pure pass-through alias of _is_streaming_compatibility_error
description: _is_streaming_sink_error(exc) does nothing but `return _is_streaming_compatibility_error(exc)`. title: _get_credentials: `if resolved_http_path is None` branch is provably unreachable
description: After `resolved_http_path = http_path or os.getenv("DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH", "")` the value can never be None: `os.getenv` is called with a non-None default `""`, so the right-hand operand of `or` is always `str`, and `http_path or <str>` therefore always yields a `str`. Moreover, the `missing` aggregation a few lines above already raised `DatabricksConfigError` when `resolved_http_path` was falsy (empty string), so at line 138 it is guaranteed to be a non-empty `str`. The subsequent `if resolved_http_path is None: raise RuntimeError(...)` can never fire and the RuntimeError is dead. mypy already narrows the type to `str` here, so the guard adds no type-safety value either.
evidence: Line 114: `resolved_http_path = http_path or os.getenv("DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH", "")` — type is `str` (both `or` operands are `str`; getenv default is `""`). Lines 121-129: if `not resolved_http_path` (i.e. empty), `missing` is non-empty and `DatabricksConfigError` is raised, returning early. Therefore at line 138 `resolved_http_path` is a non-empty `str`; `resolved_http_path is None` is always False and the `raise RuntimeError(...)` on line 139 is unreachable.
est_reduction: 2 lines (remove the dead `if ... is None: raise RuntimeError(...)` guard).
behavior_preservation: Pure removal of an unreachable branch; the function's return value and all reachable behavior are identical. No caller can observe the difference because the branch never executes.

title: Backtick-quoted table names map to a different cache file than their unquoted form (cache-key inconsistency / fragmentation)
description: `_TABLE_NAME_RE` (line 33) explicitly permits optionally backtick-quoted identifiers per part: `^`?[\w-]+`?\.`?[\w-]+`?\.`?[\w-]+`?$`, so both `cat.schema.table` and `` `cat`.`schema`.`table` `` (and partially-quoted mixes) pass validation in `fetch_and_cache` and in the route gates (databricks.py:39, files.py:194). `_cache_path_for`, however, only normalizes `.`, `/` and `\` to underscores (line 163) and leaves backticks intact. As a result the same logical table produces two distinct cache files: `cat_schema_table.parquet` versus `` `cat`_`schema`_`table`.parquet ``. A user who fetches the table using the quoted form and later reads it (or whose stored config later switches quoting) gets a `CacheNotFoundError` / a second redundant fetch instead of a cache hit, and two GUI configs that differ only by backtick-quoting silently maintain separate caches for identical data. The backtick character is a legal filename character on both Windows and POSIX, so this fails silently (no exception) rather than loudly. Note the cache directory itself is consistent (both go through `_cache_path_for`), so the divergence is purely keyed on the exact table string supplied by each call site.
evidence: Regex at line 33 accepts ```cat`.`schema`.`table```. `_cache_path_for` line 163: `safe_name = table.replace(".", "_").replace("/", "_").replace("\\", "_")` — no `.replace("`", ...)`. So `cat.schema.table` -> `cat_schema_table` while ```cat`.`schema`.`table``` -> ```cat`_`schema`_`table```; `result.parent` is still the cache dir so the path-traversal guard (line 166) passes and no error is raised. read_cached_table (line 442) and fetch_and_cache (line 310) both key off the raw `table` string, so a quoted fetch + unquoted read miss each other. Existing tests cover Unicode/homoglyph collisions (test_databricks_io.py:844-887) but never the backtick case.

title: _validate_select_clause rejects legitimate SELECTs whose string/identifier literals contain a denylisted word (e.g. WHERE status = 'DELETE')
description: `_DANGEROUS_SQL_RE` matches the denylisted keywords on bare `\b` word boundaries anywhere in the stripped query, with no awareness of SQL string literals or backtick-quoted identifiers. A perfectly valid, read-only SELECT that merely references one of these words as data is rejected with a `ValueError`. Examples: `SELECT * FROM t WHERE status = 'DELETE'`, `SELECT * FROM t WHERE event = 'UPDATE'`, `SELECT * FROM t WHERE op IN ('CREATE','GRANT')`, or a backtick-quoted column whose name is exactly one of the keywords (`` SELECT `update` FROM t `` — backtick is a non-word char so `\bUPDATE\b` fires). Because the `query` field is GUI-editable free text and string-literal filters are a normal thing for a pricing analyst to write, this is a real usability/correctness limitation: legitimate queries are blocked. It is consistent with the module's fail-loud philosophy (it raises rather than silently mis-handling), and the keyword set is deliberately conservative, so the severity is low — but the matcher's inability to distinguish keywords-as-syntax from keywords-as-data means valid input is refused.
evidence: Line 36-39: pattern is `\b(DROP|DELETE|INSERT|UPDATE|ALTER|TRUNCATE|EXEC|EXECUTE|CREATE|GRANT|REVOKE|UNION|LATERAL)\b` with IGNORECASE, applied via `_DANGEROUS_SQL_RE.search(stripped)` (line 82) over the whole query with no string-literal stripping. `'DELETE'` inside a SQL single-quoted literal still presents `DELETE` flanked by `'` (a non-word char) on both sides, so `\bDELETE\b` matches and line 84 raises `ValueError(f"Query contains forbidden SQL keyword: {match.group()!r}")`. Substring-style names like `update_ts` are correctly NOT matched (trailing `_` keeps the word boundary closed), confirming the matcher only over-blocks the exact-word-as-literal case, which is the realistic failure.

title: _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions is never called (dead code)
description: The function _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions (lines 259-275) builds and returns a tuple of recoverable exception classes, but it is never imported or invoked anywhere in src/ or tests/. The only live consumer of the parse-time fallback logic is the predicate form _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception (line 278), which is called at _config_builder.py:335 inside _validate_user_contract and re-derives the same isinstance check inline. The tuple-builder variant is not in __all__ (which lists only _copy_config_keys, _build_node_config, _attach_code_from_body, _resolve_node_config) and has no callers. It mirrors _execute_lazy._compute_boundary_check_exceptions, which IS used there to build an `except` tuple — but in _config_builder the tuple form was never wired up; only the predicate form is used. It is pure dead code.
evidence: Grep for `_compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions` across the whole repo returns only: (a) its own definition at _config_builder.py:259, and (b) review/metrics JSON files. Zero import sites (the only `from haute._config_builder import ...` statements pull _resolve_node_config, _attach_code_from_body, _build_node_config). Its sibling predicate _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception is the one actually called (line 335). __all__ at lines 39-44 does not export it.
est_reduction: ~17 LOC (the entire function body plus its lazy mlflow import block)
behavior_preservation: Deleting the function removes no behaviour: it has no callers, so no code path changes. The live fallback decision is made solely by _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception at line 335.

title: Parse-time contract fallback swallows ImportError/RuntimeError that the runtime boundary check was deliberately narrowed to re-raise (silent-failure drift)
description: Both _compute_contract_resolve_fallback_exceptions (line 268: `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]`) and the live predicate _is_contract_resolve_fallback_exception (line 284: `isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError))`) treat ImportError and RuntimeError as recoverable 'fall back to opaque contract' conditions. Their docstrings explicitly claim they mirror the runtime boundary check: line 262-263 says 'Matches ``_execute_lazy._BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS`` — the parse-time fallback must not swallow more than the runtime boundary check would', and line 281-282 says 'Matches ``_execute_lazy``'. That invariant is now VIOLATED. The runtime sibling (_execute_lazy._compute_boundary_check_exceptions / _is_boundary_check_exception) was deliberately narrowed in commit 34aff403 ('Phase 3 audit — narrow 4 exception catches') from `[ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]` down to `(ConfigError, OSError, MlflowException)`, with a detailed rationale in its docstring (_execute_lazy.py:140-150): RuntimeError ('Persistently corrupt model artifact' from _load_with_bounded_retry) and ImportError (missing catboost/rustystats backend) are real deploy/infra bugs that must surface loudly, NOT be silently downgraded to an opaque contract. The parse-time copy in _config_builder.py was not updated in that commit (34aff403 touched only _execute_lazy.py), so it still carries the old wide set. Consequence: if a node declares `contract=...` and _derive_parse_time_contract raises ImportError or RuntimeError (e.g. a contract function that imports an optional backend, or a corrupt-artifact RuntimeError), _validate_user_contract (line 334-346) catches it and silently treats the builder as fully opaque (Contract.opaque()), so a genuinely drifted/wrong user contract annotation passes parse-time validation unflagged — exactly the silencing the runtime narrowing was meant to prevent. The referenced symbol `_BOUNDARY_CHECK_EXCEPTIONS` in the docstring does not even exist (the real names are _compute_boundary_check_exceptions / _is_boundary_check_exception), confirming the docstring drifted from reality.
evidence: git show 34aff403 -- src/haute/_execute_lazy.py shows the line `-    exc_types: list[...] = [ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError]` replaced by `+    exc_types: list[...] = [ConfigError, OSError]`, with commit body 'Dropped RuntimeError and ImportError from the tuple. Kept: (ConfigError, OSError, MlflowException)'. `git show 34aff403 --name-only` lists only src/haute/_execute_lazy.py (config_builder untouched). Runtime predicate _execute_lazy.py:171 now reads `if isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError)):` whereas parse-time _config_builder.py:284 still reads `if isinstance(exc, (ConfigError, OSError, ImportError, RuntimeError)):`. The two are no longer in sync despite the docstring asserting they are, and the parse-time set is a strict SUPERSET, so it 'swallows more than the runtime boundary check would' — the exact condition the docstring says must not happen.

title: canonical_json is NON-deterministic for sets/frozensets containing NaN floats — violates the documented order-independence contract for unordered containers
description: canonical_json's contract (module docstring lines 81-99 and _canonicalise docstring lines 119-123) promises that sets/frozensets 'whose elements are the same regardless of the order they were inserted' encode identically because unordered containers are sorted. This is broken when a set/frozenset contains two or more NaN floats. _canonicalise (line 141-143) calls sorted(members, key=_sort_key); _sort_key maps every float (NaN included) to ('2_num', value). Because all NaN comparisons return False, sorted() cannot impose a total order on the NaN members and leaves them in their incoming (hash-/insertion-determined, hence arbitrary) relative positions. Distinct NaN objects also have distinct, effectively-arbitrary hashes, so the set's iteration order — and therefore which slots the surrounding non-NaN elements occupy relative to the NaN run — varies. Result: two logically-equal sets produce DIFFERENT canonical JSON, so two identical configs/policies yield different fingerprints (phantom cache misses), and the digest is unstable across processes/insertion orders. This is silent: sorted() does not raise, so the 'fail loud, never silent' guarantee the surrounding code advertises is bypassed for this case. The property test deliberately excludes NaN (tests/test_caching_correctness.py:504-510 uses allow_nan=False with a comment that NaN breaks equality), confirming the case is unhandled rather than intentionally specified. canonical_json is THE digest encoder (used by _graph_base_fingerprint node configs, runtime_input_extra_keys, and _dataframe_execution_cache execution_policy/payload, the last of which the code comments explicitly note may contain sets).
evidence: Cross-process reproduction (3 separate interpreter runs, each 2000 trials shuffling [nan,nan,nan,1.0,2.0,3.0] before set()): each run produced TWO distinct outputs — '[1.0,2.0,3.0,NaN,NaN,NaN]' and '[1.0,2.0,NaN,3.0,NaN,NaN]'. A 7-element variant produced 4 distinct outputs in one run. Trace: _canonicalise(set) -> members=[..NaN..,1.0,..] -> sorted(members, key=_sort_key); _sort_key(NaN)=('2_num', nan); pairwise key comparisons against nan are all False so Timsort performs no reordering of nan-adjacent elements -> output order == set-iteration order, which is governed by per-object NaN hashes and insertion. By contrast canonical_json([nan,1.0,nan]) is stable across 50 runs (lists preserve order), isolating the defect to the unordered-container (set/frozenset) sort path.

location: src/haute/_cache.py:198-201 (_graph_base_fingerprint node line) and 429-432 (graph_fingerprint extra_keys/context join)
title: Node-line and extra-key fingerprint serializations use unframed pipe/newline joins and are NOT injective — a node id or extra key containing '|' or '\n' collides distinct inputs to one fingerprint
description: _graph_base_fingerprint builds each node line as f"{n.id}|{n.data.nodeType}|{canonical_json(config)}" (line 200) and joins all node+edge lines with "\n".join(parts) (line 218). GraphNode.id is an unvalidated bare str (src/haute/_types.py:605 — no pattern/validator), so an id containing a newline lets ONE node masquerade as the concatenation of TWO different node lines, making two structurally-different graphs hash identically. The same non-injective pattern recurs in graph_fingerprint (line 431): combined = "\n".join([*extra_keys, *context_parts, base]) — an extra_key containing a newline collides with a different extra_keys tuple. The module deliberately framed EDGES with canonical_json arrays specifically to be collision-proof (see the lines 205-217 comment: 'quoting/escaping rules out separator-content collisions'), but the NODE line and the graph_fingerprint join were left in the unframed delimiter form — an internal inconsistency. Consequence: cache cross-contamination — preview/trace/dataframe-execution entries for one graph (or one set of execution params) served as fresh for a genuinely different one. This is DISTINCT from the known duplicate-node-id finding (findings.json:906, which is about node_map collapsing two same-id nodes); here the colliding ids/keys are different strings and the collision is in the digest material itself.
evidence: Reproduced: PipelineGraph with a single node id='a|polars|{}\nb' (POLARS, config {}) yields the SAME _graph_base_fingerprint (75c649bf6c837eaa) as a two-node graph with ids 'a' and 'b' — the crafted id reconstructs both 'a|polars|{}' and 'b|polars|{}' lines after the join. Separately, graph_fingerprint(g, 'k1\nk2') == graph_fingerprint(g, 'k1', 'k2') (both v5:9bc49183309e7af8) because the single newline-bearing key reproduces the two-key join.
