Reachability: node ids and extra keys (e.g. trace.py:383 passes target_node_id raw as an extra key) originate from raw graph JSON / source, which is not constrained to exclude '|' or newlines; only the pipe-with-newline cross-line case is needed (pipe-only within one line does not collide because the config-JSON boundary differs — verified). Fix is uniform with the existing edge handling: encode the node line as canonical_json([id, str(nodeType), config]) and frame extra keys/context similarly, which also removes the bespoke f-string format (minor simplification).

title: parse_column_path accepts array-crossing column paths (tail containing '[*]'), producing a silent-None leaf instead of loud-failing
description: parse_column_path only checks that column_path starts with the raw table_path string and that the immediate tail begins with a dot. It never inspects the tail for further '[*]' array iterators. A column path that descends through a NESTED array (a deeper iteration depth than the table) is therefore accepted as if it were a flat leaf, in direct violation of the function's documented contract: 'Raises ApiInputSchemaError if the column's path doesn't sit cleanly under the table's iteration depth.' The returned 'leaf' then carries the literal '[*]' substring, and the downstream resolver (_json_shred._resolve_leaf) splits it on '.' and does dict.get('licenses[*]') against keys that are never literally named with '[*]', so the value resolves to None. The malformed config thus yields silently-null column data at shred/cache-build time rather than the structured 422 that validate_v2_schema's whole purpose (the on-the-wire contract, B3) is meant to produce. This is exactly the 'silent failure that's incorrect and hard to notice' the project guidelines warn against. validate_v2_schema calls parse_column_path at line 366 as its only column-path validity gate, so the gap propagates straight through validation.
evidence: parse_column_path: `if not column_path.startswith(table_path): raise`; `tail = column_path[len(table_path):]`; `if not tail: raise`; `if not tail.startswith('.'): raise`; `return tail.removeprefix('.')`. No check rejects '[*]' inside `tail`. Trace: parse_column_path('$[*].drivers[*].licenses[*].id', '$[*].drivers[*]') -> startswith True, tail='.licenses[*].id', starts with '.', returns 'licenses[*].id'. Then _json_shred._resolve_leaf(value, 'licenses[*].id') (src/haute/_json_shred.py:509-534): '.' in leaf -> splits to ['licenses[*]','id'] -> cur = value.get('licenses[*]') which is None (real key is 'licenses', and it is a list, not a scalar) -> column silently None for every row. Contrast parse_table_path (line 210), which DOES enforce every segment ends with '[*]'; parse_column_path enforces the opposite end (a leaf) but forgets to forbid intermediate array iterators. Existing tests (tests/test_v2_codec_and_shred.py:66-82) cover only a clean leaf and an unrelated-prefix rejection; no test exercises a tail containing '[*]'.

title: row_id_column may reference an unselected (non-emitted) column, yielding a silent None row id in the trace UI
description: The row_id_column membership check tests `row_id_column not in seen_col_names`, where seen_col_names is populated from EVERY column's name regardless of its `selected` flag (built in the column loop at lines 351-360 before any selected filtering). But only `selected: True` columns are emitted into the per-port parquet (see _json_shred.shred_to_buffers line 572: `if not col.get('selected'): continue`), so a row_id_column that names an existing-but-unselected column passes validation yet is absent from the materialised frame. The runtime trace consumer reads it with `target_row.get(row_id_column)` (src/haute/trace.py:560), which then silently returns None — the trace UI shows no row identity instead of the configured one, with no error anywhere. The validator's stated job is to loud-fail invariant violations so the cache route can return a structured 422; here a configuration that cannot work as intended is accepted silently. Confidence is medium because the literal docstring wording (line 275: 'it references a column name in the same table') is satisfied — the defect is that the contract is too weak: it should require the referenced column to be a SELECTED/emitted one.
evidence: validate_v2_schema builds seen_col_names from all columns (line 360 `seen_col_names.add(cname)`) with no `selected` gate; the row_id check at line 397 is `if row_id_column not in seen_col_names: raise`. Emission gate is elsewhere: _json_shred.shred_to_buffers line 572 `if not col.get('selected'): continue` and build path line 817 same, so unselected columns never reach a parquet buffer. Consumer: src/haute/trace.py:558-560 `if n.data.nodeType == NodeType.API_INPUT and n.data.config.get('row_id_column'): row_id_column = ...; row_id_value = target_row.get(row_id_column)` -> None when the column was not emitted. Result surfaced at trace.py:602/988 (row_id_column/row_id_value) -> UI shows null identity, no error.

title: Unreachable None/invalid-handle checks inside validate_edge_join_target_handles loop
description: The per-edge loop at lines 132-145 re-checks `target_handle is None` (lines 133-138) and `config_key is None` (lines 140-145), but both branches are provably unreachable given the validation that runs immediately before the loop. By line 132 the function has already established: (a) `len(present_handles) == len(target_handles)` (else it raises at line 117), so NO element of `target_handles` is None; and (b) `set(present_handles) == set(_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY)` i.e. `{'base','join'}` (else it raises at line 125). Because no element was filtered out by the `if handle is not None` comprehension at line 114, `set(present_handles) == set(target_handles)`, so every element of `target_handles` is exactly 'base' or 'join'. Therefore `target_handle is None` (line 133) can never be true, and `_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY.get(target_handle)` (line 139) can never return None (line 140). The only reachable raise in the loop is the genuine role/source mismatch at lines 147-154, which the tests exercise.
evidence: _ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY = {'base': 'baseInput', 'join': 'joinInput'} -> set is {'base','join'}. Line 117 guarantees no None remains; line 125 (`if set(present_handles) != set(_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY): raise`) guarantees every handle ∈ {'base','join'}. The sole caller, resolve_edge_join_role_indices line 96, forwards target_handles unchanged, and the function is not invoked elsewhere (grep over src/ shows only def + that one call). An invalid non-None handle such as ['base','xyz'] is rejected at line 125 before the loop; a None such as ['base', None] is rejected at line 117. Tests test_edge_join_builder_rejects_target_handle_role_mismatch / test_edge_join_codegen_rejects_target_handle_role_mismatch only reach the line-147 mismatch raise.
est_reduction: ~13 lines (drop the `if target_handle is None` and `if config_key is None` blocks; replace `_ROLE_HANDLE_TO_CONFIG_KEY.get(target_handle)` with a direct `[target_handle]` index since membership is guaranteed).
behavior_preservation: Removing the two unreachable branches preserves behavior exactly: no input that reaches the loop can trigger them, and the surviving line-147 comparison plus the pre-loop checks at 107-130 fully cover all validation outcomes. The error messages they raise are duplicated by the earlier line-117/line-125 raises for the equivalent malformed inputs.

title: Top-level `_`-prefix filter in _prepare_config_for_sidecar is fully subsumed by the immediately-following _strip_internal_keys call
description: `_prepare_config_for_sidecar` first builds `filtered = {k: v for k, v in config.items() if k not in _CODE_KEYS and not k.startswith("_")}` (line 135), then on line 136 immediately runs `filtered = _strip_internal_keys(filtered)`. `_strip_internal_keys` already drops every dict key that is a str starting with `_` at the top level (and recursively). So the `and not k.startswith("_")` sub-condition on line 135 is dead: any `_`-prefixed key it would remove is removed again one line later. Only the `k not in _CODE_KEYS` part (dropping `code`, which does not start with `_`) is load-bearing on line 135. The inline comment claims line 135 is "Kept first so α's allowlist sees a smaller candidate set", but removing the redundant `_`-check does not change that: `_strip_internal_keys` on line 136 still runs before the VALID_KEYS allowlist (lines 149-158), so the allowlist sees the identical smaller set either way.
evidence: Line 135: `filtered = {k: v for k, v in config.items() if k not in _CODE_KEYS and not k.startswith("_")}`. Line 136: `filtered = cast(dict[str, Any], _strip_internal_keys(filtered))`. `_strip_internal_keys` (line 71-76) returns `{k: v ... for k,v in obj.items() if not isinstance(k,str) or not k.startswith("_")}` for a dict — i.e. it strips top-level `_`-prefixed string keys. Therefore the `not k.startswith("_")` clause on line 135 removes nothing that line 136 would not also remove.
est_reduction: ~1 clause (simplify line 135 predicate to `k not in _CODE_KEYS`)
behavior_preservation: Behavior-identical: the set of keys surviving lines 135-136 is unchanged because line 136 strips the same `_`-prefixed top-level keys; downstream allowlist and compaction see the same dict.

title: `json.JSONDecodeError` is redundant in the except tuple in find_config_by_func_name (it is a subclass of ValueError, already listed)
description: `find_config_by_func_name` wraps the load in `except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError, ValueError) as exc`. `json.JSONDecodeError` is a subclass of `ValueError` (CPython: `class JSONDecodeError(ValueError)`), and `ValueError` is already present in the same tuple, so `json.JSONDecodeError` can never be the catching type independently — it is dead in the handler list. The tuple is equivalent to `(OSError, ValueError)`. This also makes the intent slightly misleading (it reads as if JSON-decode errors are handled by a distinct branch when they are caught by the broad `ValueError`).
evidence: Line 305: `except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError, ValueError) as exc:`. In CPython `json.JSONDecodeError` derives from `ValueError`; since `ValueError` is in the same tuple, listing `json.JSONDecodeError` adds nothing. `_load_json_object` raises plain `ValueError("duplicate JSON key ...")` / `ValueError("Node config JSON must contain an object")` and `json.loads` raises `json.JSONDecodeError`, both of which are caught by the `ValueError` entry; `read_user_text` file errors raise `OSError`.
est_reduction: 1 redundant exception type in the except tuple
behavior_preservation: Behavior-identical: removing `json.JSONDecodeError` leaves `(OSError, ValueError)`, which catches exactly the same set of exceptions (JSONDecodeError is a ValueError subclass).

title: Large worker results deadlock: parent joins the child before draining the result queue (classic mp.Queue feeder-pipe deadlock)
description: run_isolated_worker fully waits for the child to exit (_wait_for_worker loops on process.join until not process.is_alive()) BEFORE it ever reads the result queue (_read_worker_payload -> result_queue.get). With multiprocessing.Queue, the child's put() hands the serialized object to a background feeder thread that writes it into an OS pipe with a finite buffer (~64 KiB on Linux). If the pickled result exceeds the pipe buffer, the feeder blocks on the pipe write until the parent reads. But the parent never reads during the wait phase; it only join()s. At interpreter shutdown the child blocks in Queue._finalize_join waiting for the feeder, so the child never exits, and the parent's join() never returns. This is the exact deadlock documented in the stdlib ('a process that has put items in a queue will wait before terminating until all the buffered items are fed... if you join such a process you may get a deadlock'). The module never calls cancel_join_thread and never drains the queue before joining, so the pattern is unconditional.
evidence: Order in run_isolated_worker: (1) _wait_for_worker(process, worker_config) at line 211 -> while process.is_alive(): ...; process.join(timeout=wait_seconds) (lines 329-344), parent NEVER calls result_queue.get here. (2) only after the loop returns does line 213 call _read_worker_payload -> result_queue.get(timeout=1.0) (line 309). result_queue = ctx.Queue(maxsize=1) (line 194) with no cancel_join_thread. Child entrypoint does result_queue.put(('ok', function(...))) then returns (lines 270, 266). For a result larger than the pipe buffer the feeder blocks -> child cannot exit -> is_alive() stays True -> with default timeout_seconds=None the parent loops forever in _wait_for_worker. The docstring promises 'return its pickled result' (line 176) with no size bound, so the primitive is defective for large results; existing tests only return tiny dicts (tests/test_worker_isolation.py:25-26), so this is untested.

title: stop_reason() returning 'completed' raises an uncaught ValueError and silently skips cleanup callbacks
description: stop_reason is typed Callable[[], WorkerTerminalReason | None], and 'completed' is a member of WorkerTerminalReason. If a caller's stop_reason returns 'completed', _wait_for_worker first calls _terminate_process(process) (killing the worker) and then constructs IsolatedWorkerStoppedError(terminal_reason='completed'), whose __init__ raises ValueError('completed is not a valid stopped-worker reason'). That ValueError is NOT an IsolatedWorkerError, so the 'except IsolatedWorkerError' arm in run_isolated_worker (line 236) does not catch it. It propagates out through the finally (queue closed) and skips the entire cleanup section (lines 245-251) -> parent-owned cleanup_callbacks never run, contradicting the module contract that 'the parent ... always runs them after the child reaches a terminal state' (lines 178-180). The validation that rejects 'completed' is placed in the exception constructor (after termination) instead of where stop_reason is read, turning a guard into a cleanup-bypassing crash.
evidence: _wait_for_worker lines 331-334: reason = config.stop_reason(); if reason is not None: _terminate_process(process); raise IsolatedWorkerStoppedError(terminal_reason=reason). IsolatedWorkerStoppedError.__init__ lines 116-117: if terminal_reason == 'completed': raise ValueError(...). run_isolated_worker line 236 catches only IsolatedWorkerError; the ValueError bypasses lines 245-251 so _run_cleanup_callbacks is never invoked. WorkerTerminalReason (lines 17-25) includes 'completed', so the offending return value is type-valid.

title: Cleanup-failure details are lost when a primary worker error is also present (only a count is surfaced)
description: When the worker fails (primary_error set) AND one or more cleanup callbacks also fail, run_isolated_worker attaches only str(cleanup_error) as a note to primary_error and then discards cleanup_error. But str(IsolatedWorkerCleanupError) is just 'Isolated worker cleanup failed in N callback(s)' -- it contains neither the underlying exception types nor their messages/tracebacks. The actual cleanup exceptions live in cleanup_error.errors, which is dropped (not chained as __cause__/__context__, not attached to primary_error). So in the common 'worker failed and its temp-dir cleanup also failed' case, the operator sees only a count and cannot tell what cleanup broke. (When primary_error is None the cleanup_error is raised directly and callers can still inspect .errors, so the loss is specific to the dual-failure path.)
evidence: Lines 246-249: if primary_error is not None: if cleanup_error is not None: primary_error.add_note(str(cleanup_error)); raise primary_error. IsolatedWorkerCleanupError.__init__ (lines 139-144) sets the message to f'Isolated worker cleanup failed in {len(errors)} callback(s)' and stores self.errors = tuple(errors); only the message (the count) reaches add_note, and cleanup_error (holding .errors) is never re-raised or chained on this path.

title: Final 'raise IsolatedWorkerCrashedError' after has_result check is unreachable
description: The trailing 'raise IsolatedWorkerCrashedError(...)' at lines 254-257 can never execute. To reach it, control must pass lines 246 (primary_error is None) and 250 (cleanup_error is None) and 252 (has_result is False). But has_result is set True iff status == 'ok' (line 220); every other status raises an IsolatedWorkerError inside the try (status=='error' -> line 226; else-branch -> line 232), which is caught and stored in primary_error. Hence primary_error is None implies status was 'ok' implies has_result is True implies the function already returned at line 253. The same CrashedError is already raised defensively (and pragma-no-cover'd) at lines 231-235 for the impossible non-'ok' status, making lines 254-257 a redundant unreachable duplicate (and, unlike line 231, it is not even pragma-excluded).
evidence: has_result only set True at line 220 under 'if status == "ok"'. 'elif status == "error"' raises at 226; 'else' raises at 232 (both IsolatedWorkerError, caught at 236 -> primary_error). Therefore at line 252 primary_error is None <=> status was 'ok' <=> has_result True <=> returns at 253; lines 254-257 are never reached.
behavior_preservation: Removing lines 254-257 (the unreachable branch) preserves behavior; the live defensive crash path is the pragma-excluded else-branch at 231-235.
est_reduction: 4 lines

title: Unpicklable worker result is misreported as a generic crash (and can be misclassified as memory_limited) instead of a clear pickling error
description: _isolated_worker_entrypoint does result_queue.put(('ok', function(...))). multiprocessing.Queue.put returns immediately; serialization happens later on the feeder thread. If the function's return value is not picklable, the feeder raises PicklingError on the child's feeder thread (printed to the child's stderr) and never delivers the item; the child then exits 0. The parent's _read_worker_payload waits 1.0s, times out (queue.Empty), and raises IsolatedWorkerCrashedError with exitcode=0 and no indication that the real cause was an unpicklable result. Worse, IsolatedWorkerCrashedError feeds exitcode into _exitcode_looks_memory_limited; while a clean exitcode 0 won't trip it, any exit signal coincidence could mislabel this as memory_limited. Net effect: a clear 'result is not picklable' contract violation is surfaced as an opaque crash, costing a fixed 1s delay and hiding the root cause. (Partly an inherent mp.Queue limitation, but the primitive could detect the empty-queue-after-clean-exit case and report it specifically; the 'error' path already proves cross-process delivery of failure detail is feasible.)
evidence: Line 270 put(('ok', function(*args, **kwargs))) with no pre-serialization/picklability check. _read_worker_payload lines 308-314: result_queue.get(timeout=1.0) -> on queue.Empty raises IsolatedWorkerCrashedError(exitcode=exitcode, ...). The error message (line 95) only reports exitcode, never that delivery failed due to pickling. The sibling 'error' branch (lines 271-281) deliberately sends only plain strings precisely so failures are deliverable, showing the asymmetry.

title: Verbatim string factor labels that look like int-like floats are silently corrupted on compact->expand round trip
description: The compact-write side (`_compact_entry_rows` -> `_canonical_sidecar_key` -> `normalise_rating_key`) keeps string factor labels VERBATIM (strings are never collapsed by `normalise_rating_key`). But the expand-read side (`_expand_entries_map.walk` -> `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`) applies a 'legacy float-string migration' that collapses any int-like float-string map key: '25.0'->'25', '1.0'->'1', '1e1'->'10', '5.'->'5'. So a legitimate, non-numeric string label such as a price band '25.0' (or any banding/categorical label that happens to parse as an int-valued float) is silently rewritten after a single save/load cycle. The rating lookup join keys on the exact label, so after `collect_node_configs` (compact write) + `parse_pipeline_source` (expand read) the table entry's key changes and the row STOPS MATCHING -- a silent wrong-result defect, not an error. The `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key` docstring frames this as scoped legacy migration, but it cannot distinguish a legacy float that `str()` wrote as '25.0' from a genuine verbatim string label '25.0', and `normalise_rating_key`'s own docstring explicitly promises 'String keys are deliberately verbatim -- 25.0 is a label, not a number, and never collapses', which the expand path violates.
evidence: Inline trace via .venv python: `_canonical_sidecar_key('25.0')` -> '25.0' (compact write keeps it) but `_normalise_compact_sidecar_key('25.0')` -> '25' (expand read collapses). Full round trip: cfg tables[0].factors=['band'], entries=[{'band':'25.0','value':7.0}] -> compact map {'25.0':7.0} -> expand -> entries=[{'band':'25','value':7.0}] (label changed from '25.0' to '25'). 3-factor variant ({'a':'1.0',...}) likewise yields a='1' after round trip. Values in the leaf position are correctly NOT migrated (only keys), confirming the asymmetry is key-specific. The compact/expand pair is the real save (`_config_io._prepare_config_for_sidecar` line 163) and load (`_config_io._normalise_loaded_config` line 120) path, so this is reachable in production.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar can emit a sidecar that expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar then rejects (write/read asymmetry)
description: Because the compact-write key normaliser (`_canonical_sidecar_key`, line 201) does NOT apply the int-like float-string migration while the expand-read normaliser (`_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`, line 225) DOES, two distinct row-array labels that differ only in float-string formatting (e.g. '5.' and '5', or '25.0' and '25') are written by `_compact_entry_rows`/`_insert_entry_value` as two distinct, non-colliding map keys (no duplicate raised on the write side). When that same compact sidecar is later loaded, `_expand_entries_map.walk` migrates both '5.' and '5' to '5' and raises a collision ValueError. The result is a save operation that SUCCEEDS but produces a JSON sidecar that can never be loaded again -- the pipeline becomes un-parseable until the user hand-edits the file. The two normalisation helpers are contradictory contracts for the same key space.
evidence: Trace: cfg entries=[{'band':'5.','value':1.0},{'band':'5','value':2.0}] -> `compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar` returns {'5.':1.0,'5':2.0} (write OK, _insert_entry_value sees two distinct leaf_keys '5.' and '5'). Feeding that compact map to `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` raises: "ratingStep tables[0].entries factor 'band' compact key '5' collides with existing key '5.' after legacy key migration to '5'". Root cause confirmed inline: _canonical_sidecar_key('5.')='5.' vs _normalise_compact_sidecar_key('5.')='5'.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Unreachable list-type guard in normalise_rating_tables
description: `normalise_rating_tables` calls `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar(config)` and then re-checks `if tables is None: return []` (308-309) and `if not isinstance(tables, list): raise` (310-311). But `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` already guarantees its returned `tables` is exactly `None` or a `list` (it returns early with `tables=None`, raises if not a list, otherwise assigns `result['tables']=expanded` which is a list). After the `None` case is handled at 308-309, `tables` is provably a list, so the `not isinstance(tables, list)` branch at 310-311 can never execute. It is unreachable defensive code that duplicates a guarantee made one call up.
evidence: expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar (286-301): `tables = result.get('tables'); if tables is None: return result; if not isinstance(tables, list): raise; ...; result['tables'] = expanded`. Therefore post-call `tables in {None, list}`. normalise_rating_tables handles None at 308-309, leaving only `list`, so 310-311 is dead.
est_reduction: 2 lines
behavior_preservation: Removing lines 310-311 preserves behavior: the only inputs that could reach them already raised inside expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar, and the None case is handled at 308-309.

title: _normalise_entry_rows redundantly re-validates factors already validated by its sole caller
description: `_normalise_entries_for_table` computes `factors = _validate_factors(result, table_index)` at line 276, then on the list branch calls `_normalise_entry_rows(entries, result, table_index)` (line 281), which immediately calls `_validate_factors(table, table_index)` AGAIN at line 154 on the same dict. `_normalise_entry_rows` is only ever called from this one site, so the second validation is pure redundant work. It also makes the signature asymmetric with the parallel `_compact_entry_rows`, which correctly takes a pre-validated `factors: list[str]` parameter. Passing `factors` into `_normalise_entry_rows` (mirroring `_compact_entry_rows`) would remove the duplicate validation and the unused `outputColumn` re-derivation divergence, and align the two row-processing helpers.
evidence: Line 276 `_normalise_entries_for_table`: `factors = _validate_factors(result, table_index)`. Line 281 passes `result` to `_normalise_entry_rows`. Line 154 inside `_normalise_entry_rows`: `factors = _validate_factors(table, table_index)` -- second call on the identical dict. Contrast `_expand_entries_map`/`_compact_entry_rows` which receive `factors` as a parameter and do not re-validate.
est_reduction: ~3 lines plus a clearer contract
behavior_preservation: _validate_factors is a pure function of the dict; calling it once vs twice yields identical results and identical raises, so removing the duplicate (passing factors in) is behavior-preserving.

title: Empty-entries early return skips factor validation, silently accepting/serialising invalid factor lists
description: Both `_normalise_entries_for_table` (272-274) and `_compact_table_for_sidecar` (323-326) short-circuit when `entries == []` BEFORE calling `_validate_factors`. As a result a table whose `factors` is structurally invalid -- e.g. `['', '  ']` (blank/whitespace names) or non-string elements -- is accepted without error as long as its entries list is empty, and `_compact_table_for_sidecar` even emits `entries: {}` for it (because the blank-name list is truthy). The same table with one entry would be rejected by `_validate_factors`. This is an inconsistent contract: validity of `factors` should not depend on whether `entries` happens to be empty. The asymmetry can let a malformed table pass save/load unnoticed and only fail later (or differently) once a row is added.
evidence: Trace: cfg tables[0]={'name':'T','factors':['','  '],'outputColumn':'out','entries':[]} -> compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar returns the table with entries={} and the invalid factors ['','  '] untouched (no ValueError). expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar returns entries=[] likewise unvalidated. With a non-empty entries list, _validate_factors (lines 26-29) would raise "factors[0] must be a column name".
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: cache_state_signature_for_graph catches OSError/ValueError but _path_hash raises RuntimeError on unresolvable ~ paths, so the defensive skip is bypassed and the function crashes preview-key computation
description: In cache_state_signature_for_graph the per-node hash is computed defensively: `try: cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path) except (OSError, ValueError): continue`. The intent is to skip any apiInput whose configured path cannot be hashed. But _path_hash calls `Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()`, and pathlib.Path.expanduser() raises **RuntimeError** (not OSError/ValueError) when a leading `~`/`~user` cannot be resolved to a home directory. RuntimeError is not in the except tuple, so it escapes the `continue` and propagates out of cache_state_signature_for_graph. That function is invoked from execution.py:613 while composing the preview/trace cache key for EVERY preview/trace request (`json_cache_signature = cache_state_signature_for_graph(graph)`), so a single apiInput node whose config path is e.g. `~missinguser/data.json` (or `~/data.json` in a deploy with HOME unset and no pwd entry) turns every preview/trace request that includes that graph into an unhandled-exception 500, instead of the node simply being skipped as designed. The node.data.config['path'] value is free-form user input and is read raw at line 193 with no prior expanduser/normalisation on this code path, so the bad path reaches _path_hash unmodified.
evidence: CPython 3.11.13 pathlib source (inspected via the project's .venv): `def expanduser(self): ... homedir = os.path.expanduser(self._parts[0]); if homedir[:1] == '~': raise RuntimeError('Could not determine home directory.')`. _path_hash (line 90): `os.path.normcase(str(Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()))`. cache_state_signature_for_graph (lines 197-200): `try: cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path) except (OSError, ValueError): continue` — RuntimeError not caught. Caller execution.py:613 has no guard either.

location: src/haute/_json_flatten.py:276-290 (no-op trapdoor reads committed/meta.json via _read_cache_meta) + 151-159 (_read_cache_meta raises on corrupt/non-dict meta)
title: A corrupt committed/meta.json makes mirror_cache_to_committed raise at the no-op-trapdoor read, aborting BEFORE the copytree that would overwrite it — so committed/ corruption is self-perpetuating and silently never repaired
description: mirror_cache_to_committed reads the committed-layer meta for its no-op trapdoor at line 277: `committed_meta = _read_cache_meta(committed_dir) if committed_dir.exists() else None`. _read_cache_meta does `orjson.loads(meta_path.read_bytes())` with NO error handling and additionally raises ValueError if the payload is not a dict. So if committed/<hash>/meta.json is truncated/garbled (e.g. a crash during a prior mirror's copytree, or external tampering) the read raises orjson.JSONDecodeError or ValueError at line 277 — which is BEFORE the atomic copytree-and-swap at lines 293-310 that would otherwise replace the whole committed/ directory (including the bad meta) with a fresh, valid working/ snapshot. The repair path is therefore unreachable while committed/ is corrupt. The save caller (_save_pipeline._mirror_api_input_caches, lines 626-633) wraps the call in `except Exception` and only logs `json_cache_mirror_failed`, so save does not crash but committed/ is left corrupt indefinitely: every subsequent save re-raises and re-logs without ever promoting the good working/ snapshot. This is asymmetric with the rest of the cache subsystem, where a garbled/missing meta is treated as 'stale -> rebuild' (e.g. _data_file_matches returns False on a non-dict signature, is_per_port_cache_valid invalidates pre-W2 caches). Note this is distinct from known finding #13 (which is about the missing build lock / bare rename during the copytree); here the failure occurs at the meta read and prevents the copytree from ever running.
evidence: _read_cache_meta (lines 156-158): `payload = orjson.loads(meta_path.read_bytes()); if not isinstance(payload, dict): raise ValueError(...)` — no try/except. mirror line 277 calls it unconditionally when committed_dir exists, before the copytree at line 297. Caller _save_pipeline.py:626-633 swallows the exception and only logs. Contrast _data_file_matches (_json_shred.py:261 `if not isinstance(recorded, dict): return False`) which degrades to 'stale -> rebuild'.

title: cache_state_signature_for_graph hashes the same path three times per apiInput node (one explicit _path_hash + two via _json_cache_dir), each a resolve() syscall plus SHA-256
description: Per apiInput node, cache_state_signature_for_graph computes `cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path)` at line 198, then calls `_json_cache_dir(data_path, _LAYER_WORKING)` (line 201-203) and `_json_cache_dir(data_path, _LAYER_COMMITTED)` (line 204-206). _json_cache_dir internally calls `_path_hash(data_path)` again at line 98. So _path_hash — which does `Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()` (a filesystem syscall) plus a SHA-256 over the canonical path — runs 3 times for the same path on every preview/trace cache-key build, for every apiInput in the graph. The already-computed cache_hash could be reused to build both layer directory paths directly (e.g. `Path.cwd()/_CACHE_DIR/<layer>/f'json_{cache_hash}'`), collapsing 3 hashes to 1. Behaviour is identical because _json_cache_dir's hash is the same cache_hash value; only the redundant resolve() syscalls and hash recomputation are removed.
evidence: Line 198 `cache_hash = _path_hash(data_path)`; lines 201-206 each call `_json_cache_dir(data_path, ...)`; _json_cache_dir line 98 `... f"json_{_path_hash(data_path)}"`. Three _path_hash invocations, each invoking Path.resolve() + hashlib.sha256, for one data_path.
est_reduction: ~2 resolve() syscalls + 2 SHA-256 computations per apiInput per preview key (no LOC change required, or a few lines reorganised)
behavior_preservation: Identical output: the layer directory hash equals the already-computed cache_hash; only redundant recomputation is eliminated.

title: Negative `ttl` is not validated and silently turns the cache into a permanent always-miss
description: The constructor validates `max_size >= 1` and `max_bytes >= 1` and the byte/size_of cross-dependencies, but performs NO lower-bound validation on `ttl`. A negative `ttl` (e.g. `LRUCache(ttl=-5)`) is accepted silently. Because `time.monotonic()` is non-decreasing, for any stored entry the expiry check in `get` is `(_time.monotonic() - stored_at) > self._ttl`, and `elapsed >= 0 > negative_ttl` is always True. Every `get` therefore takes the expiry branch, calls `_remove_key`, and returns `None` — so `put` keeps inserting entries that the very next `get` immediately evicts. The cache becomes a no-op that never serves a hit, with no error raised. This is exactly the silent-failure class the project's CLAUDE.md warns against ('code should be allowed to fail loudly'), and it diverges from an existing codebase convention: `src/haute/routes/_job_store.py:76-79` rejects `ttl_seconds < 0` with `ValueError("ttl_seconds must be >= 0")`. The fix is a one-line guard mirroring the other params, e.g. `if ttl is not None and ttl < 0: raise ValueError(f"ttl must be >= 0, got {ttl}")`.
evidence: Lines 93-100 validate max_size and max_bytes but never reference `ttl`. Line 101-102 stores it unchecked: `self._ttl = ttl`. get() lines 127-131: `if self._ttl is not None: stored_at = self._timestamps.get(key, 0.0); if (_time.monotonic() - stored_at) > self._ttl: self._remove_key(key); return None`. For ttl=-5 and any entry stored at t0, at any later get the elapsed `>=0` satisfies `>-5`, so the entry is always removed and None returned. Contrast _job_store.py:76 `if ttl_seconds < 0: raise ValueError("ttl_seconds must be >= 0")`. No test in tests/test_lru_cache.py or tests/test_lru_cache_contracts.py exercises a negative ttl (TestTTLEdgeCases only covers ttl=0).

title: Chained and keyword-form pipeline.submodel(...) calls are silently dropped, discarding entire submodels
description: extract_submodel_calls only recognises the single, positional, non-chained form `pipeline.submodel("path")`. It requires the call's `func.value` to be a bare `ast.Name` equal to "pipeline" and reads only `call.args[0]`. Two valid, runtime-supported spellings are therefore silently ignored, returning an empty path list so every referenced submodel (and all of its nodes and edges) vanishes from the parsed graph with no warning: (1) the documented chained form `pipeline.submodel("a.py").submodel("b.py")`, and (2) the keyword form `pipeline.submodel(file="a.py")`. Chaining is explicitly documented in the runtime (`Pipeline.submodel` returns `self`, docstring at src/haute/pipeline.py:477 says "Can be chained: pipeline.submodel(\"a.py\").submodel(\"b.py\")") and is exercised by tests/test_pipeline.py:786 and :792. The sibling helper _extract_connect_calls (src/haute/_ast_helpers.py:336-381) walks method chains down to the base receiver and accepts positional-or-keyword source/target; extract_submodel_calls does neither, so the two paths disagree. Codegen always emits one `pipeline.submodel(\"...\")` per line (codegen.py:1241) so GUI round-trips are unaffected, but any hand-authored pipeline file that uses the documented chaining (or the keyword) syntax silently loses its submodels. This is a silent contract violation that drops graph content rather than failing loudly, contrary to the project's fail-loud policy.
evidence: Confirmed by execution: `extract_submodel_calls(ast.parse('pipeline.submodel("modules/a.py").submodel("modules/b.py")'))` returns `[]`; `extract_submodel_calls(ast.parse('pipeline.submodel(file="modules/a.py")'))` returns `[]`; while the one-per-line form returns `['modules/a.py','modules/b.py']`. Code trace: for the chained expression the outer Call's `func.value` is itself a Call (the inner `.submodel("a.py")`), so `isinstance(func.value, ast.Name)` at line 52 is False and the whole expression is skipped (lines 49-54). For the keyword form `call.args` is empty so the `if call.args and isinstance(call.args[0], ast.Constant)` guard at line 55 is False. Runtime support: src/haute/pipeline.py:470-480 `def submodel(self, file: str) -> Pipeline: ...; return self`; tests/test_pipeline.py:786 asserts `p.submodel('a.py').submodel('b.py')` yields `submodel_files == ['a.py','b.py']`.

title: Direct edge between children of two different submodels loses its boundary handle: dropped on flatten, breaks codegen on re-save
description: When the main pipeline file directly connects an OUTPUT child node of one submodel to an INPUT child node of another submodel (e.g. `pipeline.connect("a_out", "b_in")` where a_out is a child of submodel A and b_in is a child of submodel B), merge_submodels produces a corrupt boundary edge. The cross-boundary edge is first reconstructed as `a_out -> b_in` (lines 143-168), then rewire_edges is applied once per submodel in sequence (line 194). Submodel A's pass sees src_inside → rebuilds the edge as `submodel__A -> b_in` with sourceHandle='out__a_out'. Submodel B's pass then sees tgt_inside and rebuilds a FRESH GraphEdge with target=submodel__B and targetHandle='in__b_in' but does NOT copy the existing sourceHandle, so the result is `submodel__A -> submodel__B` with targetHandle='in__b_in' and sourceHandle=None. Two downstream failures result, neither caught at parse time: (a) flatten=True path — flatten_graph (src/haute/_flatten.py:63-78) only rewrites the source side when sourceHandle is truthy; with sourceHandle=None the source stays 'submodel__A', the edge still references a submodel node at line 77, and the edge is dropped entirely, so the executor runs with the a_out→b_in data dependency silently removed (wrong execution order / missing data flow). (b) flatten=False (GUI/hierarchical) path — codegen later requires every edge whose source is a submodel placeholder to carry an 'out__<child>' sourceHandle and raises ParseError otherwise (codegen.py:1050-1057), so saving the parsed pipeline throws and the round-trip is broken. validate_pipeline_graph_shape_contracts does not detect it: _iter_submodel_child_contexts (src/haute/_graph_shape.py:115-118) computes `_boundary_child_id(None, prefix='out__')` → None and silently skips, so parse appears to succeed. Reachable directly from parse_pipeline_source: explicit pipeline.connect() pairs are passed verbatim as parent_edges to _merge_submodels.
evidence: Confirmed by execution against the real code. flatten=False: merge_submodels with two single-child submodels A={a_out}, B={b_in} and parent_edges=[('a_out','b_in')] yields exactly one edge `submodel__A -> submodel__B sh=None th=in__b_in` (out__a_out handle lost), with submodels['A']['outputPorts']==['a_out'] and submodels['B']['inputPorts']==['b_in'] (so classify_ports correctly identified both ports, but the edge handle was dropped). flatten=True: the same input produces `graph_flattened ... edge_count=0` — zero edges; nodes ['a_out','b_in'] are present but the a_out→b_in dependency is gone. Trace of the loss: _submodel_graph.rewire_edges lines 116-125 (target-side rewrite) constructs GraphEdge(source=e.source, target=sm_node_id, targetHandle=f'in__{e.target}') with no sourceHandle argument, discarding the 'out__a_out' set by A's earlier source-side pass at lines 126-135.

title: normalise_banding_factors silently returns [] for malformed non-list factors instead of failing loudly
description: normalise_banding_factors guards with `if not isinstance(factors, list): return []`. For a malformed config where `factors` is a non-list, non-None value (e.g. a dict, string, or number), this silently returns an empty list, so banding produces zero factors and the node becomes a silent no-op with no error. This diverges from the two sibling functions in the same module — expand_banding_config_from_sidecar (line 80-81) and compact_banding_config_for_sidecar (line 198-199) — which both explicitly `raise ValueError("banding factors must be a list")` for exactly the same malformed input. It also contradicts the project's stated principle (CLAUDE.md: 'code should be allowed to fail loudly... a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice' is to be avoided). There is no upstream schema validation forcing `factors` to be a list (src/haute/_config_validation.py has no `factors` check; src/haute/_builders.py::_banding_columns also uses the lenient `config.get('factors') or []`). The runtime callers (src/haute/_rating.py:225, src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:1807, src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py:506) therefore silently drop all banding for a corrupted/non-list factors blob rather than surfacing the corruption.
evidence: normalise_banding_factors: `factors = config.get('factors'); if not isinstance(factors, list): return []`. Compare expand_banding_config_from_sidecar: `factors = result.get('factors'); if factors is None: return result; if not isinstance(factors, list): raise ValueError('banding factors must be a list')`. Same input class (non-list, non-None) -> one returns [] silently, the other raises. A `None` factors is correctly an empty no-op in both; only the non-list-non-None case diverges.

title: upstream_node_ids docstring 'nearest parents first' is false for DAGs/diamonds
description: The docstring states the result is ordered 'nearest parents first', but the algorithm is a pre-order DFS (pop from the front of `stack` while prepending each node's parents to the front via `stack[0:0] = ...`), not a breadth-/distance-ordered traversal. In any diamond/DAG topology a more-distant ancestor can be emitted before a nearer direct parent. Trace: parents_of = {D:[B,C], B:[A], C:[A]}; upstream_node_ids(D) yields [B, A, C] — A (distance 2 from D) is emitted before C (a direct parent, distance 1), violating 'nearest parents first'. The returned set of ancestors is correct and complete (no node is missed or duplicated), and every current caller is order-insensitive — they either wrap the result in set() (execution.py:489, _dataframe_execution_cache.py:218, _optimiser_service.py:583) or feed it to merge_categorical_level_declarations, which keys results by column and is order-independent (modelling/_feature_contract.py:389, raises on any conflict regardless of declaration order). So there is no current functional impact; the defect is purely a false documented contract that could mislead a future caller who relies on the stated ordering.
evidence: Loop: `stack = list(parents_of.get(node_id, []))`; `current = stack.pop(0)`; `stack[0:0] = parents_of.get(current, [])` — this is DFS pre-order, not nearest-first BFS. Concrete counterexample parents_of={D:[B,C],B:[A],C:[A]} produces [B,A,C], placing grandparent A before direct parent C.

title: Wildcard trusted-host patterns are matched case-sensitively against a force-lowercased host, so any mixed-case '*.' pattern (e.g. HAUTE_TRUSTED_HOSTS=*.Internal.Corp) rejects every host
description: LocalTrustedHostMiddleware normalises (lowercases) exact-match patterns and the incoming Host header, but deliberately leaves wildcard patterns un-normalised. The two sides of the wildcard comparison therefore disagree on case, so a wildcard pattern containing any uppercase letter can never match a real host. Exact patterns are case-insensitive while wildcard patterns are case-sensitive against an always-lowercased host -- an internal inconsistency that silently denies service to legitimately-configured hosts (fail-closed, not a security hole, but a contract bug).
evidence: In __init__ (line 119-122): `self._normalised_allowed_hosts = [pattern if "*" in pattern else _normalise_host_value(pattern) for pattern in self.allowed_hosts]` -> a wildcard like `*.Internal.Corp` is stored verbatim; an exact `Example.com` becomes `example.com`. In __call__ (line 129): `host = _normalise_host_value(Headers(...).get("host",""))` always lowercases the host. The wildcard branch (line 131): `(pattern.startswith("*.") and host.endswith(pattern[1:]))` evaluates `"foo.internal.corp".endswith(".Internal.Corp")` -> False. Contrast starlette's reference TrustedHostMiddleware (.venv/.../trustedhost.py:40,44) which compares both sides raw (consistently case-sensitive); Haute added lowercasing only on the exact-match and host sides. HAUTE_TRUSTED_HOSTS is a documented user knob (_local_security.py:26, server.py:360-363) and the `*.` branch exists specifically to serve it.

title: Positional-only and keyword-only @pipeline node parameters are silently dropped (only ast.arguments.args is read), losing implicit edges and corrupting user-code/config extraction
description: _extract_decorated_nodes builds param_names from `stmt.args.args` only. Python's ast.arguments splits parameters into posonlyargs (before `/`), args (positional-or-keyword), kwonlyargs (after `*`), vararg, and kwarg. Reading just `args` means a pipeline node written as `def node(a, /, b, *, claims_aggregate):` exposes only `b`. Every parameter that names an upstream node but lives in the posonly/kwonly buckets is invisible: its implicit param-name edge is never created by _build_edges, its input-extraction line is not recognised as boilerplate by extract_user_code (mis-extracting the saved code), and for LIVE_SWITCH/CONSTANT-style nodes it is missing from config['inputs']. No error is raised -- a silent contract violation in the same family as the known async-def and submodel-edge drops, but distinct from them and not covered by any known finding. (Machine-generated codegen never emits `/` or `*`, so this only bites hand-edited pipelines, but those are an explicitly supported edit surface.)
evidence: src/haute/_graph_builders.py:73 `param_names = [arg.arg for arg in stmt.args.args]` -- a project-wide grep shows `posonlyargs`/`kwonlyargs` are referenced nowhere in src/haute, so these parameter kinds are never recovered on the healthy AST path. Downstream: _build_edges (line 143-154) derives implicit edges from `node_info['param_names']`; _config_builder._build_node_config sets `config['inputs'] = param_names` for LIVE_SWITCH (line 108) and passes param_names into _extract_user_code/_extract_rating_step_user_code/etc (lines 180,183,203,218,223,249-255), which use them to strip the codegen input-extraction lines. n_params=len(param_names) (line 74) is likewise undercounted. Example: `@pipeline.polars` over `def transform(claims, *, adjustments): ...` where `adjustments` is another node -> the (adjustments, transform) edge is dropped and the `adjustments = inputs[...]` boilerplate line is treated as user code.

title: Implicit param-name edges are not de-duplicated among themselves, so a duplicated parameter name (reachable via the regex fallback) yields two GraphEdges with an identical id
description: The implicit-edge loop dedups each candidate only against the explicit_edges set; it never guards against producing the same implicit edge twice. If a node's param_names contains the same name twice and that name matches an upstream node, two GraphEdge objects with the identical id `e_{src}_{tgt}` are appended. The healthy AST path cannot produce duplicate params (Python rejects `def f(a, a)` at parse time), but the regex fallback path (_parser_regex._find_function_blocks) builds param_names by naively splitting the parameter text on commas with no de-duplication, and that path runs precisely on malformed source. The result is a duplicate React Flow edge key and a parent listed twice in build_parents_of. The explicit-edge branch already prevents its own duplicates via explicit_edges; the implicit branch lacks the symmetric guard.
evidence: src/haute/_graph_builders.py:143-154 iterates `for param in node_info['param_names']` and appends an edge with `id=f"e_{pair[0]}_{pair[1]}"` whenever `pair not in explicit_edges`, with no seen-set across implicit edges. src/haute/_parser_regex.py:532-539 builds param_names via `for p in params_text.split(','): ... param_names.append(name)` (no de-dup). A regex-fallback node `def f(source, source)` with an upstream node `source` would emit two `e_source_f` edges. Low likelihood (requires already-broken source) but a concrete asymmetry with the explicit-edge de-dup.

title: Local-origin check compares the raw origin host string against a fixed set, so a non-canonical IPv6 loopback origin (e.g. http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]) is rejected
description: _is_local_origin tests `origin_host in _LOCAL_ORIGIN_HOSTS` where the set is the literal `{'localhost','127.0.0.1','::1'}`. _normalise_host_value returns the bracket-stripped inner address verbatim (lowercased) without canonicalising it through ipaddress, so the fully-expanded loopback form `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` does not equal the compressed literal `::1` and the origin is treated as non-local (403). The comparison is naive string equality rather than an ip_address-normalised compare. Fails closed (rejects a valid loopback), so it is a robustness/correctness gap rather than a bypass; browsers almost always emit the compressed `[::1]` form, which is why this is low-impact.
evidence: src/haute/_local_security.py:32 `_LOCAL_ORIGIN_HOSTS = {'localhost','127.0.0.1','::1'}`; line 64-82 _normalise_host_value returns `host[1:closing]` (the inner address, never canonicalised); line 147 `return origin_host in _LOCAL_ORIGIN_HOSTS or origin_host in _configured_origin_hosts()`. Origin `http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]:5173` -> origin_host `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` != `::1` -> not local. _is_ipv6_literal already exists and ip_address(...).compressed would canonicalise both sides.

title: rewire_edges silently drops the external endpoint's port handle on cross-boundary edges, corrupting multi-port wiring
description: When rewire_edges replaces a cross-boundary edge, it correctly synthesises the SUBMODEL-side boundary handle (in__<child> / out__<child>) but throws away the handle on the *external* side of the edge. In the External->internal branch it builds GraphEdge(source=e.source, target=sm_node_id, targetHandle=f'in__{e.target}') with no sourceHandle=e.sourceHandle, so an external multi-output source node feeding a submodel child loses its output-port selector. Symmetrically, the Internal->external branch sets sourceHandle=f'out__{e.source}' but omits targetHandle=e.targetHandle, dropping the external target's input-port role. The module's sibling reconstruction code in _parser_submodels.py:159-167 deliberately preserves these handles (sourceHandle=source_port, targetHandle=target_port) precisely so that 'later rewiring replaces true submodel boundary handles with in__/out__ markers' (comment at _parser_submodels.py:139-142) -- i.e. only the boundary side should be replaced, not the far side. The flatten round-trip (_flatten.py) only restores the target side, and ONLY for edge-join roles via build_edge_join_boundary_target_roles (_flatten.py:30-33, 74); there is NO recovery path for a dropped source-side handle (when a submodel is the SOURCE, _flatten.py:67 sets new_sh=None unconditionally). Consequently a graph that wires an external multi-output node (e.g. a model node emitting frequency/severity frames, or a multi-port apiInput) into a node inside a newly-created submodel ends up, after flatten-for-execution, with an edge from that multi-port node carrying sourceHandle=None, which _execute_lazy.py:103-108 rejects with ValueError 'Edge from multi-port node X has no sourceHandle'. Worse, in the hierarchical (flatten=False) saved graph the wiring intent is silently lost with no error at all. Both callers are affected: routes/_submodel_ops.py:90 passes real GraphEdge objects (cross_edges) straight from graph.edges with handles intact, and _parser_submodels.py:194 passes parent_edge_list whose cross edges carry the preserved source_port/target_port.
evidence: _submodel_graph.py:117-125 (External->internal) constructs the rewired GraphEdge with only targetHandle set; e.sourceHandle is never forwarded. _submodel_graph.py:127-135 (Internal->external) sets only sourceHandle; e.targetHandle is never forwarded. Contrast _parser_submodels.py:159-167 which builds the pre-rewire cross edge WITH sourceHandle=source_port and targetHandle=target_port, and the comment at 139-142 stating only the boundary handle should be replaced. _flatten.py:60-74 recovers a target-side handle only through edge_join_boundary_target_roles (join roles) and sets new_sh=None for submodel-source edges (line 67) -- no source-side handle recovery exists. _execute_lazy.py:103-108 raises ValueError when a multi-port source edge has sourceHandle is None. The existing tests (tests/test_submodel_graph.py:177-285) construct edges via a helper that never sets any handle, so this loss is entirely unguarded.

title: Contract dataclass, _freeze, and _freeze_mapping are duplicated near-verbatim in _builders.py instead of imported from _contracts.py
description: src/haute/_builders.py defines its own Contract dataclass (with opaque/from_tuple/to_tuple/from_user_declared), _freeze, and _freeze_mapping that are functionally identical to the ones in the in-scope src/haute/_contracts.py (confirmed: _builders.py contains no `from haute._contracts import` for these symbols; it redeclares Contract at line 162 and the two helpers at 274/296). The bodies match line-for-line including the redundant first disjunct in _freeze (`isinstance(value,(set,list,tuple)) or (isinstance(value,Iterable) and not isinstance(value,(str,bytes)))`, where the first clause is fully subsumed by the second). _contracts.py was created expressly as the lightweight import surface (module docstring: 'parser/codegen callers need the contract dataclass ... without paying for the full executor-side builder module import'). That goal is exactly served by having _builders.py re-export Contract/_freeze/_freeze_mapping from _contracts.py rather than maintaining a second copy. The duplication is a real maintenance hazard: the two classes are distinct types, so a behavioural change to one (e.g. a new accepted user-declared form, or tightening _freeze) silently diverges, and Contract.from_user_declared's `isinstance(value, Contract)` fast-path (line 67) does not even fire for the other module's Contract (it falls through to the hasattr duck-typing branch). Note this is NOT the known SIMP-7 (which concerns _optimiser_io.py cache-info logging) nor the known codegen _format_contract_kwarg item.
evidence: _builders.py:162 `class Contract:` with opaque@182, from_tuple@187, to_tuple@203, from_user_declared@209; _freeze@274; _freeze_mapping@296 -- bodies identical to _contracts.py:36/44/49/56/63 and 111/133. `grep -n _contracts src/haute/_builders.py` returns only comment/string hits (lines 157, 344), proving no import of these symbols. The redundant set/list/tuple disjunct appears identically at _contracts.py:117 and _builders.py:280.
est_reduction: ~110 duplicated lines removed from _builders.py (Contract + _freeze + _freeze_mapping) by importing from _contracts.py; the deliberate lightweight-import boundary is preserved because _contracts.py imports nothing heavy.
behavior_preservation: Re-exporting from _contracts.py yields one canonical Contract type. Behaviour is preserved for every caller; the only observable change is that the two previously-distinct Contract classes collapse into one, which removes the latent isinstance-fast-path divergence rather than introducing risk. test_column_contracts (which asserts callable identity per _builders.py:344) and the codegen/projection contract round-trip tests should be run to confirm.

title: export_trace reports a source column's `origin` as the most-DOWNSTREAM carrier (usually the target node), not its true upstream origin
description:
In the `sources` section, the per-column origin is computed by iterating ALL steps and keeping the LAST step whose `output_values` contains the column:

    origin_node = None
    for s in steps:
        if col in s.output_values:
            origin_node = s.node_name
    sources.append({"column": col, ..., "origin": origin_node})

`output_values` is the FULL output row of each node (every column present at that node's output, including columns merely carried through), not just newly-added columns — confirmed at trace.py:833 `output_values=output_row` where `output_row` is the whole correlated row. Consequently `col` is present in the `output_values` of every step from the column's creation point all the way through to the traced target step. Because the loop overwrites `origin_node` on each match and does NOT break, it returns the LAST (most-downstream) step that still carries the column — which is the target node itself (or the final step), i.e. the OPPOSITE of an origin. The field is named `origin`, the module docstring describes `sources` as 'input columns and their origins', and the test `test_export_includes_input_sources` (test_trace_hero_tdd.py:796) documents the intent as 'Lists each input column and its origin node'. So the value returned is silently semantically wrong. A correct implementation would select the FIRST producing step (e.g. the first step where `col in s.schema_diff.columns_added`, or simply `break` on the first `output_values` match for upstream-most carrier).
evidence: _trace_export.py:62-66 keeps the LAST match (no break) over steps that are in pipeline order; trace.py:833 sets output_values to the full output row (carried-through columns included), so `col in s.output_values` is True for every downstream step including the target; the existing export_trace tests (test_trace_coverage.py:1017-1084, test_trace_hero_tdd.py:796-820) assert only the column NAMES in `sources`, never the `origin` value, so the defect is untested. Note also export_trace has no production caller (grep over src/ outside review/ shows only the definition; all other references are tests), which limits blast radius but the stated contract is still violated.

location: src/haute/deploy/_scorer.py:605-704 (MODEL_SCORE branch of _intercept) + fall-through to haute._builders._build_model_score
title: Misconfigured modelScore node deploys and serves as a SILENT passthrough — the 'no model artifact' fail-loud guard is bypassed when neither model nor contract is bundled
description: The deploy scorer's stated invariant (lines 673-702) is that 'deployed scoring cannot produce predictions without a model artifact' and 'Deploy scoring must never manufacture null predictions when no real model artifact is available.' This guard (model_score_missing_artifact, raising RuntimeError) ONLY fires when a feature contract was bundled (`if bundled_contract_path is not None`, line 677). If a modelScore node is misconfigured so that the bundler skips it entirely (no model AND no contract bundled), the intercept's MODEL_SCORE branch finds remapped_path=None and bundled_contract_path=None, returns None (line 733), and falls through to the base `_build_node_fn` -> `_build_model_score`, which returns `_passthrough_fn` for unconfigured sources (_builders.py:1170-1175). The deployed node then passes its input through UNCHANGED, producing an API response that silently omits the model's prediction column, with NO error raised at build, serve, or contract-enforcement time.
evidence: Trace: (1) Bundler `collect_artifacts` (_bundler.py:70-103) defaults sourceType to 'run'; for sourceType=='run' with empty run_id or artifact_path it does `continue` (lines 90-91), and for sourceType=='registered' with empty registered_model it logs a warning and `continue`s (lines 79-83) — in both cases NO `{nid}__<model>` artifact and NO `{nid}__feature_contract.json` are added to the artifact map. (2) At serve time HauteModel.predict (_model_code.py:49-57) calls score_graph with exactly the bundled artifact_paths and the manifest's output_fields (which may be None). (3) In _scorer.py _intercept, for that node remap has no `{nid}__...` keys, so `bundled_contract_path` (line 606) and `remapped_path` (line 607) are both None; neither the model_score_fn branch (line 629) nor the model_score_missing_artifact branch (line 677) is entered; the function returns None at line 733. (4) wrap_builder then calls the base `_build_node_fn`; `_build_model_score` (_builders.py:1163-1175) returns `_passthrough_fn` because `source_type=='run' and not _run_id`. (5) In _execute_lazy the node runs `fn(*input_lfs)` = passthrough -> input returned unchanged; `is_passthrough_runtime = fn is _passthrough_fn` (line 1128) causes the output-contract boundary check to be SKIPPED (`and not is_passthrough_runtime`, line 1239-1244), so even ENFORCE_CONTRACTS does not catch the missing prediction column. (6) score_graph_lazy applies `.select(output_fields)` only when output_fields is truthy (line 825-827); when output_fields is None the missing column is never surfaced. validate_deploy (_validators.py:231-318) performs no per-modelScore configuration/bundling check; it would only catch the missing prediction column if the operator happened to supply test quotes whose `expected` mapping references that column (lines 198-208). tests/test_deploy_scorer_artifact_cache.py:255 covers the WITH-contract fail-loud path; the no-contract/no-model silent-passthrough case is unguarded and untested.

title: Near-verbatim duplicate of haute._builders._declared_categorical_levels_for_model_score (different first arg only)
description: This deploy helper and `_builders._declared_categorical_levels_for_model_score` (_builders.py:1132-1149) implement the same logic: seed one declaration for the modelScore node's own config, build candidate_ids via `list(dict.fromkeys([*source_ids, *(upstream_ids or [])]))`, append each candidate node's `config.get('categorical_levels')` when present, and call `merge_categorical_level_declarations`. The only differences are cosmetic: the deploy version takes a `node` (uses `node.id`/`node.data.config`) and seeds the owner label as `node.id`, while the builders version takes `config` and seeds the owner label as the literal `'modelScore'`; the owner label only affects the message in a conflict error. The two could share a single implementation (e.g. parameterised by an owner label), removing one of the duplicated bodies.
evidence: Deploy (line 310-317): `declarations = [(node.id, node.data.config.get('categorical_levels'))]; candidate_ids = list(dict.fromkeys([*source_ids, *(upstream_ids or [])])); declarations.extend((source_id, node_by_id[source_id].data.config.get('categorical_levels')) for source_id in candidate_ids if source_id in node_by_id); return merge_categorical_level_declarations(declarations)`. Builders (line 1141-1149): `declarations = [('modelScore', config.get('categorical_levels'))]; candidate_ids = list(dict.fromkeys([*source_ids, *(upstream_ids or [])])); ... (source_id, node_map[source_id].data.config.get('categorical_levels')) ... ; return merge_categorical_level_declarations(declarations)`. Identical control flow and merge call; only the seed owner label and the parameter shape differ.
est_reduction: ~12 lines (consolidate two ~14-line helpers into one shared helper parameterised by owner label)
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-preserving: merge output is identical for any inputs since the owner label only appears in the FeatureMismatchError raised on a conflicting declaration (source_node=owner); a shared helper can keep the deploy label as node.id and the builders label as 'modelScore' to preserve even those error messages verbatim.

title: build_report reports post-truncation length as sampled_rows, breaking the sampled = scored + failed invariant
description: When staging and production prediction lists differ in length, build_report truncates input_df to `scored` (line 427) and then reports `sampled_rows=len(input_df)` (line 449) using the already-truncated length. However `failed` (line 422) is computed against the ORIGINAL input_df length. The result is a self-contradictory report where sampled_rows != scored_rows + failed_rows: the header line in format_terminal/format_markdown shows '(N of total sampled)' with the wrong (too-small) N while simultaneously printing 'M rows failed to score', so a reviewer sees fewer sampled rows than the scored+failed rows actually accounted for. sampled_rows should be captured from the input length BEFORE truncation (the number of rows actually submitted for scoring).
evidence: Line 421 `scored = min(len(staging_preds), len(prod_preds))`; line 422 `failed = len(input_df) - scored` (original length); lines 424-427 truncate `input_df = input_df.head(scored)`; line 449 `sampled_rows=len(input_df)` now reads the truncated length. Empirically confirmed with stg=[1 item], prd=[2 items], inp=2 rows -> ImpactReport(sampled_rows=1, scored_rows=1, failed_rows=1); invariant sampled==scored+failed is False (1 != 2). The existing test test_failed_rows_counted asserts only scored_rows/failed_rows and so does not catch the sampled_rows contradiction.

title: build_report only aligns input_df to predictions when staging != prod length, causing an unhandled ShapeError (and negative failed_rows) when equal-length predictions are shorter than input_df
description: The truncation guard at line 424 keys input_df alignment off `len(staging_preds) != len(prod_preds)` rather than off `scored < len(input_df)`. If staging and production predictions unwrap to the SAME length L but L < len(input_df) (e.g. both endpoints/envelopes return the same reduced row count, or an endpoint returns fewer predictions than inputs), input_df is left at its original length while stg_df/prd_df have L rows. _segment_breakdown (line 360) then builds pl.DataFrame({'seg': input_df[col], 'chg': change, ...}) with mismatched column heights and raises an unhandled polars ShapeError instead of a domain error or a consistent truncation. The same mismatch also makes `failed = len(input_df) - scored` correct only when truncation occurs; here failed stays positive but input_df is never trimmed, so segments crash. The fix is to always set input_df/preds to `scored` (and capture sampled_rows beforehand) regardless of staging-vs-prod equality.
evidence: Reproduced: stg=12 identical dicts, prd=12 identical dicts (equal -> branch at line 424 skipped, input_df NOT truncated), inp=20 rows with a qualifying categorical column ('region' A*10+B*10). build_report raises `ShapeError: could not create a new DataFrame: height of column 'chg' (12) does not match height of column 'seg' (20)` from _segment_breakdown. No existing test exercises equal-length predictions shorter than input_df.

est_reduction: ~3 lines / one redundant O(n) pass + redundant validation
behavior_preservation: Result-identical: _percent_change_series is a pure function of (stg, prd, name); computing it once for the primary column and passing the series into _segment_breakdown yields the same change values and the same zero-baseline/non-finite raises (which already fire identically in _column_stats run first).
title: Primary-column percent change is computed twice (in _column_stats and again in _segment_breakdown)
description: build_report calls _column_stats(stg_df[primary], prd_df[primary], primary) which computes _percent_change_series (line 309), then calls _segment_breakdown for the same primary output_col which recomputes _percent_change_series on the identical columns (line 356), re-running _raise_for_non_finite_predictions and _zero_baseline_change_count a second time over the full series. The change series (or the precomputed ColumnStats source) could be threaded through to _segment_breakdown to avoid the duplicate pass and duplicate validation. Low impact but genuinely redundant on the hot path (full dataset width).

title: _validate_base_image_pinning accepts newline-bearing base_image values (anchors use $ not \Z, and [^@] matches newlines)
description:
The two pinning regexes use the `$` anchor and a `[^@]*` body that matches newline characters, so values containing newlines pass the 'is pinned' check. Concretely: (a) a trailing newline is accepted because `$` matches just before a final `
` (e.g. `'python:3.11.9-slim
'` -> accepted; `'python@sha256:'+'a'*64+'
'` -> accepted via _DIGEST_PINNED_RE.search); and (b) because the negated class `[^@]` (unlike `.`) DOES match `
`, a value such as `'python:3.11.9
RUN evil:latest'` is also accepted by _PATCH_PINNED_RE.match — the trailing `[^@]*` consumes the newline and following text, and `$` then matches end-of-string. This contradicts the function's own docstring, which states it 'Raises DeployError for every other form' and is the construction-time gate. The correct anchors are `\A`/`\Z`, and the body should exclude newlines (e.g. `[^@
]`).
evidence:
Reproduced with the module's exact regexes: `_PATCH_PINNED_RE = ^[^:]+:[^@]*\d+\.\d+\.\d+[^@]*$` matches 'python:3.11.9-slim
' (span 0..19) and matches 'python:3.11.9
RUN evil:latest' (whole string). `_DIGEST_PINNED_RE = @sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$` matches 'python@sha256:'+'a'*64+'
'. In Python, `$` (no re.MULTILINE) matches at end-of-string OR immediately before a trailing newline, and `[^@]` includes `
`. The docstring at lines 55-62 promises rejection of 'every other form'.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Unreachable else-branch in _check allowed-keys computation (`_self` is always a set)
description: In the dict-schema branch of `_check`, `top_keys = schema.get("_self", set())` always yields a `set` — every `_self` entry in the module-level `_VALID_TOML_SCHEMA` is a `set[str]`, and the default is `set()`. Therefore `allowed = top_keys | sub_sections if isinstance(top_keys, set) else sub_sections` can never take the `else sub_sections` path. The `isinstance(top_keys, set)` guard and its else arm are dead/unreachable defensive code for a shape the schema (and its type annotation `dict[str, set[str] | dict[str, set[str]]]`) never produces. The line can be simplified to `allowed = top_keys | sub_sections`.
evidence: `_VALID_TOML_SCHEMA` (lines 151-181): every nested schema's `_self` value is a literal set (e.g. `"deploy": {"_self": {"target", ...}, ...}`, `"safety": {"_self": {"impact_dataset"}, ...}`, `"ci": {"_self": {"provider"}, ...}`). `schema.get("_self", set())` thus returns a set in all cases, so the ternary condition at line 201 is invariantly True and the `else` branch is unreachable.
est_reduction: ~1 line (collapse ternary to a single expression)
behavior_preservation: Identical: the `else` arm is never evaluated for any value of `_VALID_TOML_SCHEMA`; replacing the ternary with `top_keys | sub_sections` preserves all observable behavior.

title: _validate_base_image / _validate_model_name accept a trailing newline (re.match + '$' anchor instead of fullmatch / \Z)
description:
Both validators use `_RE.match(value)` against a pattern anchored with `^...$`. In Python, `$` matches at the end of the string OR immediately before a single trailing newline, so `re.match(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9._:/@-]+$', 'python:3.11.9-slim
')` returns a match. Consequently `_validate_base_image('python:3.11.9-slim
')` and `_validate_model_name('motor
')` both PASS even though the value contains a control character the validators are meant to forbid. The docstrings state these exist to 'prevent command injection' / 'path traversal / injection', so silently admitting a trailing newline is a contract weakness. Practical blast radius is limited (a single trailing newline in `FROM {base_image}` only yields a blank Dockerfile line, and a multi-line `value
RUN ...` is still correctly rejected because text after the newline defeats the `$`), but the validators do not deliver the strict character whitelist they advertise. The existing test suite only covers an *interior* newline ('image
injection') and shell metacharacters, never a trailing newline, so the gap is unguarded.
evidence:
Lines 25-26: `_VALID_BASE_IMAGE_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9._:/@-]+$")`, `_VALID_MODEL_NAME_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$")`. Lines 39 & 45 call `.match(...)`. Verified with the project venv: `base.match('python:3.11.9-slim
')` -> truthy, `name.match('motor
')` -> truthy, whereas `base.fullmatch('python:3.11.9-slim
')` -> None. Fix: use `re.fullmatch` (or anchor with `\A...\Z`). base_image then flows into Dockerfile `FROM {base_image}` (line 461) and model_name into the image tag `f"{model_name}:{git_sha}"` (line 142).
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: build_and_push_image reuses a non-cleared .haute_build dir, baking stale artifacts from a prior run into the new image
description: The build dir is created with `build_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` and `artifacts_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)`, and is only removed in the `except BaseException` cleanup (lines 165-167). A SUCCESSFUL build therefore leaves `.haute_build/` (and `.haute_build/artifacts/`) on disk. A subsequent `build_and_push_image` call in the same working directory reuses that directory without clearing it: the manifest, Dockerfile and app.py are overwritten, but artifact files are only ever *added* (`shutil.copy2(artifact_path, artifacts_dir / artifact_name)`), never pruned. If the artifact set changes between runs (e.g. a model file is renamed, or a `.pkl` is replaced by a `.cbm`), the orphaned file from the previous run survives and is copied wholesale into the image by the Dockerfile's directory-level `COPY artifacts/ artifacts/` (line 471). The result is a container that silently ships a stale model artifact that is not referenced by the current manifest. Note the sibling MLflow path (`_mlflow.py`) is immune because it logs the live `artifact_path`s rather than copying into a reused directory, so this staleness is specific to the container target's copy+COPY model.
evidence: Line 97-98 create/reuse build_dir; line 101-102 reuse artifacts_dir with exist_ok=True; lines 121-124 copy each current artifact in but nothing deletes pre-existing files; line 471 `COPY artifacts/ artifacts/` bundles everything in the dir; cleanup (rmtree) only runs in the `except BaseException` branch (166), so on success the dir persists for the next invocation. Tests `test_artifacts_copied_to_build_dir` and `test_cleanup_on_exception` only cover the single-run and exception paths, not a second run with a different artifact set.
behavior_preservation: n/a

est_reduction: ~3 lines -> 1
title: Artifact-remap loop unpacks an unused `artifact_path`; reducible to a dict comprehension over keys
description: The remap loop iterates `resolved.artifacts.items()` and binds `artifact_path`, but the body only uses `artifact_name`. The whole block is a key-only transform and is more clearly written as a comprehension, avoiding the dead binding (which also masks the fact that the value is intentionally discarded).
evidence: Lines 109-113: `container_artifacts: dict[str, str] = {}` then `for artifact_name, artifact_path in resolved.artifacts.items(): container_artifacts[artifact_name] = f"artifacts/{artifact_name}"`. `artifact_path` is never referenced. Equivalent: `manifest["artifacts"] = {name: f"artifacts/{name}" for name in resolved.artifacts}`.
behavior_preservation: Identical output dict; pure refactor of a key-only mapping, no behavioral change.

title: Serving signature silently maps every unrecognized Polars dtype (Decimal/Time/Duration/List/Struct/Binary/Object/Null) to string, producing a wrong serving contract
description: `_to_colspecs` builds the MLflow ModelSignature from the resolved input/output schema dicts, whose values are `str(polars_dtype)` strings (see `infer_input_schema`/`infer_output_schema` in src/haute/deploy/_schema.py:71,141). It takes `base_type = dtype_str.split('(')[0]` and then `dtype_map.get(base_type, DataType.string)`. `dtype_map` only covers integers, floats, String/Utf8, Boolean, Date, Datetime. Any other Polars dtype the pipeline legitimately produces -- `Decimal(...)` (e.g. a premium/money column), `Time`, `Duration`, `List(...)`, `Struct(...)`, `Categorical`, `Enum`, `Binary`, `Null`, `Object` -- has a base name not in the map and is SILENTLY coerced to `DataType.string`. The deployed Databricks Model Serving signature then advertises those columns as string, so the endpoint's input validation/coercion is wrong for those fields (a numeric Decimal column is described as text). This directly contradicts the project's 'fail loudly, no incorrect silent fallbacks' principle, and notably the sibling builder src/haute/modelling/_signature.py RAISES `ValueError('Unknown polars dtype ...')` on the very same dtype families (cataloged finding `signature-build-aborts-mlflow-run-on-temporal-decimal-features`) -- the deploy path takes the opposite, silent-and-wrong behavior. Evidence: `dtype_map.get(base_type, DataType.string)` at line 244 with no membership check; e.g. `str(pl.Decimal(18,2))` -> 'Decimal(precision=18, scale=2)' -> base 'Decimal' -> not in dtype_map -> DataType.string.
evidence: line 244: `mlflow_type = dtype_map.get(base_type, DataType.string)` -- unknown base names default to string with no error. dtype_map (lines 221-237) lacks Decimal/Time/Duration/List/Struct/Categorical/Enum/Binary/Null/Object. Schema values are Polars `str(dtype)` strings (_schema.py:71 `{col: str(dtype) ...}`).

title: Registered model version is re-derived via max(search_versions) instead of the value returned by log_model -- races to the wrong version and silently guesses "1" when the search is empty
description: `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(...)` returns a `ModelInfo` whose `registered_model_version` is the exact version just created (confirmed present in the installed mlflow 3.10.0: `ModelInfo.registered_model_version`). The code discards that return value and instead re-queries ALL versions of the UC model with `search_versions(client, uc_model_name)` and takes `max(versions, key=lambda v: int(v.version)).version`, falling back to the string `"1"` when `versions` is empty. Two defects: (1) Race/shared-state -- if another deploy of the same UC model registers a higher version between this `log_model` call and the `search_versions` call, `max()` returns that OTHER deploy's version, which is then passed as `model_version=int(latest_version)` to `_create_or_update_serving_endpoint` (line 152), so the live serving endpoint is bound to the wrong model version, and the wrong `v{model_version}` is reported to the user (cli/_deploy.py:201). (2) Silent incorrect fallback -- after a SUCCESSFUL `log_model` there is always at least one version; an empty `search_versions` result indicates a genuine registry problem, yet the `else: latest_version = "1"` branch fabricates version 1 and proceeds to serve/return it, masking the failure.
