The backend (_rating.py _apply_banding) explicitly skips categorical rules with empty assignment (lines 88-92, `replace_strict` remap only includes non-empty assignments) and skips continuous rules with empty assignment (lines 124-126, `if not assignment: continue`). A rule that has a value/interval but a blank label thus contributes to the preview's matched count even though those rows actually fall through to the Default at runtime. This makes the preview over-report matches and under-report the unmatched figure for a partially-filled rule.
evidence: Frontend categorical: previewRows.filter(row => String(row[column] ?? '') === cat.value).length — no check on cat.assignment. Frontend continuous: matchesContinuousRule(val, cont) — bandingUtils only parses ops/values, ignores assignment. Backend _rating.py: categorical builds remap only when assignment is non-empty (line 91); continuous chain does `if not assignment: continue` (line 126). So {value:'London', assignment:''} matches 0 rows server-side but is counted in the preview.

title: removeFactor adjusts the active tab using safeIdx instead of the removed index, so deleting a tab before the active one silently moves the selection
description: removeFactor filters out `idx` then only re-clamps the active index with `if (safeIdx >= next.length) setActiveIdx(next.length - 1)` (lines 113-114). It never accounts for removing a factor positioned BEFORE the currently-active one. When `idx < safeIdx` and `safeIdx` is still < next.length, no adjustment runs, so `activeIdx` keeps its old numeric value while every factor after the removed one shifted down by one — the highlighted/edited factor silently becomes a different column.
evidence: factors [A,B,C,D], active index 2 (C). User clicks remove on tab A (idx 0). next=[B,C,D] (length 3). safeIdx=2 which is < 3, so the guard does not fire and activeIdx stays 2 => now resolves to D, not the C the user was editing. The active selection jumps to the wrong factor. Correct handling would decrement activeIdx when removing an index <= the active one.

title: Histogram never draws boundary lines in continuous mode
description: The histogram is rendered for both continuous and breakpoints modes (condition at line 209 allows banding==='continuous' || banding==='breakpoints'). But the boundaries array is only populated for breakpoints: the loop at lines 220-226 pushes `Number(bp.boundary)` solely inside `if (factor.banding === 'breakpoints')`. For continuous rules (which carry explicit cut points in val1/val2), no boundaries are ever extracted, so BandingHistogram receives boundaries=[] and renders the value distribution with no cut markers. BandingHistogram fully supports drawing boundary lines (BandingHistogram.tsx lines 88-104), so the continuous histogram is silently missing the visual cues that make it useful, an inconsistency with the breakpoints rendering.
evidence: histogramData boundaries loop: `for (const r of (factor.rules||[])) { if (factor.banding==='breakpoints') { ...push Number(bp.boundary) } }` (lines 220-226). No branch reads ContinuousRule.val1/val2. Yet the gating condition at line 209 includes continuous, so a continuous factor with rules and previewRows shows bars but zero boundary lines.

title: Type toggle has no selected/focusable option when factor.banding is 'continuous'
description: The Type ToggleButtonGroup only offers options 'breakpoints' and 'categorical' (lines 354-357), but a factor's banding can legitimately be 'continuous' (the default from normaliseBandingFactors, from addFactor/duplicateFactor, and from older/pasted configs). When such a configured factor is shown, `value={factor.banding}` ('continuous') matches neither option, so in ToggleButtonGroup every button has aria-checked=false and tabIndex=-1 (ToggleButtonGroup.tsx lines 49-56). The radiogroup then has no keyboard-focusable member, and the user sees a toggle with nothing selected even though the factor is in a real mode. Switching away is possible by click, but the control misrepresents and is not Tab-reachable in that state.
evidence: options=[{key:'breakpoints'},{key:'categorical'}] (lines 355-356). ToggleButtonGroup computes active=value===opt.key and sets tabIndex={active?0:-1}; with value='continuous' both actives are false => all tabIndex=-1, none aria-checked. addFactor creates banding:'continuous' (line 91) and duplicateFactor copies src.banding; a duplicated/added factor that later gets a column set reaches shouldShowTypeToggle while still 'continuous'.

title: Paired key edits/removals normalize leftOn and rightOn independently, persisting unequal-length arrays the backend rejects
description: In paired-key mode, both updatePairedKey (lines 113-117) and removePairedKey (lines 127-133) call normalizeKeyRows() separately on the left array and the right array. normalizeKeyRows trims TRAILING empty strings only. When a user clears the last cell on just one side (or removes a row that leaves a trailing blank on only one side), the two arrays are trimmed to different lengths and written to config that way. This violates the Polars left_on/right_on equal-length contract: the backend (src/haute/_edge_join.py:182-184) raises ConfigError('edgeJoin leftOn and rightOn must contain the same number of keys.') and the frontend analyzer (edgeJoinValidation.ts:147-149) emits 'leftOn and rightOn must contain the same number of keys.' So a single ordinary cell edit produces a malformed, runtime-rejectable config plus a spurious diagnostic, instead of keeping the pair aligned.
evidence: Start paired config leftOn=['a','b'], rightOn=['c','d'] (2 rows). User clears Join key 2 (right side, index 1) to ''. updatePairedKey('right',1,''): nextLeft = replaceAt(['a','b'],1,pairedRows[1].left='b') = ['a','b']; nextRight = replaceAt(['c','d'],1,'') = ['c','']. Then onUpdate({on:[], leftOn:normalizeKeyRows(['a','b'])=['a','b'], rightOn:normalizeKeyRows(['c',''])=['c']}). Result leftOn length 2 != rightOn length 1 -> ConfigError at runtime. The fix is to keep paired arrays aligned (pad to the max length, or only drop a row when both sides are blank) rather than trimming each side independently.

title: Component-level nodeMap duplicates the map already built inside analyzeEdgeJoinNode and is used only for two role-edge labels
description: EdgeJoinEditor builds `new Map(allNodes.map(...))` on every render (line 61) solely to resolve the source label of baseRoleEdge and joinRoleEdge via nodeLabel() in the two RoleDisplay instances. analyzeEdgeJoinNode already constructs an identical nodeMap internally (edgeJoinValidation.ts:92) and already returns baseRoleEdge/joinRoleEdge plus a connectedInputs list that carries each source's resolved label. So the full node map is built twice per render (O(N) over all graph nodes) just to look up two labels that the analysis pass could surface directly. RoleDisplay is not memoized, so passing the fresh Map costs nothing extra, but the second full map build and the local nodeLabel helper (lines 518-520) are redundant with the analyzer.
evidence: Line 61 `const nodeMap = new Map(allNodes.map((node) => [node.id, node]))`; line 62 calls analyzeEdgeJoinNode which at edgeJoinValidation.ts:92 builds the same map. nodeMap is consumed only at lines 184/191 (RoleDisplay nodeMap prop) -> RoleDisplay line 383 `nodeLabel(roleEdge.source, nodeMap)`. The analysis return already exposes baseRoleEdge/joinRoleEdge and connectedInputs[].label, which could provide the two needed labels without a second map over every node.
est_reduction: ~3-6 lines (drop local nodeMap + nodeLabel helper; pass precomputed labels from analysis)
behavior_preservation: Identical rendered labels: nodeLabel falls back to id when a node is missing, exactly matching analyzer's connectedInputs label semantics (edgeJoinValidation.ts:340-342).

title: handleCellClick has no request-sequence / abort guard — out-of-order trace responses desync tracedCell vs traceResult and can clobber a newer trace with a stale one
description: handleCellClick synchronously sets tracedCell = {rowIndex, column} for the just-clicked cell, then fires an async traceCell() request whose .then sets traceResult. There is no AbortSignal, no in-flight request tracking, and no "is this still the latest request" check. If a user clicks cell A then cell B before A resolves, both requests run concurrently; whichever resolves LAST wins setTraceResult. When A resolves after B, the node/edge decorations and trace panel (driven by traceResult) show A's trace while the highlighted cell (driven by tracedCell, App.tsx -> DataPreview line 365 isTraced) shows B — a user-visible inconsistency, and the freshly-requested B trace is silently overwritten by the stale A trace.
evidence: Line 210 setTracedCell({rowIndex,column}) updates immediately; lines 211-220 call traceCell({...}) WITHOUT passing args.signal even though TraceCellArgs supports `signal?: AbortSignal` (api/client.ts:541) and traceCell forwards it to post() (client.ts:550). The .then at 221-228 calls setTraceResult(data.trace) unconditionally on success with no guard that this response corresponds to the most recent click. Two overlapping calls resolve in completion order, not request order, so traceResult can reflect an earlier click than tracedCell. App.tsx:598-599/642-643 wire handleCellClick -> onCellClick and tracedCell straight through with no upstream debounce/guard. DataPreview highlights the cell from tracedCell (line 365) while traceResult separately drives nodesWithStatus/edgesWithTrace decorations and the trace detail panel, so the two can disagree.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

title: Duplicated prune-cache-by-seenIds logic between the node projection cache (inlined) and the edge projection cache helper
description: nodesWithStatus inlines a 'if (cache.size > seenIds.size) { for (const id of cache.keys()) if (!seenIds.has(id)) cache.delete(id) }' block (417-421) that is structurally identical to the standalone pruneEdgeProjectionCache helper (144-149). The two operate on different Map value types (CachedProjection vs CachedEdgeProjection) but the prune algorithm is byte-identical. A single generic helper `pruneCacheBySeenIds<T>(cache: Map<string,T>, seenIds: Set<string>)` could back both, removing the duplicated loop. This is distinct from SIMP-04, which targets the per-mode iterate/seen/prune scaffold inside edgesWithTrace, not the node-cache prune.
evidence: Lines 144-149 define pruneEdgeProjectionCache(cache, seenIds) with the exact `if (cache.size <= seenIds.size) return; for (const id of cache.keys()) if (!seenIds.has(id)) cache.delete(id)` body. Lines 417-421 re-implement the same loop inline against projectionCache. Both gate on the size comparison and delete keys absent from seenIds. Behaviour is identical because the algorithm is the same; only the Map's value generic differs, which a generic helper parameterises.
est_reduction: ~5 LOC plus one fewer copy of the prune idiom; net small
behavior_preservation: Generic helper deletes exactly the same keys (those in cache but not seenIds) under the same size guard, so cache contents, reference identities of retained projections, and array outputs are unchanged.

title: emitTablesSig uses '|' delimiter that collides for labels containing '|', so handle re-measure can be skipped on a multi-port retopology
description: `emitTablesSig = emitTableLabels.join("|")` is the value-equality proxy that drives the `useEffect` calling `updateNodeInternals(id)` (lines 241-243) whenever the emit-port set changes. Port labels are RAW table labels and may legally contain the pipe character: the backend (`validate_v2_schema` in src/haute/_api_input_schema.py) only rejects blank/duplicate/sanitised-collision labels, and sanitisation (`_FILESYSTEM_SAFE_RE`) is applied to the parquet *filename* only, never to the label/handle id. Therefore two genuinely different label arrays can produce an identical signature — e.g. `["a", "b|c"]` and `["a|b", "c"]` both join to `"a|b|c"`. When a config commit transitions between two such topologies (handle ids change from `a`,`b|c` to `a|b`,`c`), the effect's deps do not change, `updateNodeInternals(id)` is NOT fired, and React Flow does not re-measure the relabelled right-edge handles, so already-connected edges keep routing to stale handle anchors until an unrelated re-measure occurs. This is exactly the delimiter-collision hazard that the sibling helper `shallowNodeHash.ts` (line 96, `parts.join("")`) deliberately avoids by using a non-printable delimiter; PipelineNode regresses that established convention.
evidence: Line 226-229: emitTableLabels memo = apiInputEmitPortLabels(config) (returns raw labels, only deduped). Line 236: emitTablesSig = emitTableLabels.join("|"). Lines 241-243: useEffect(() => updateNodeInternals(id), [id, emitTablesSig, edgeJoinJoinHandlePosition, updateNodeInternals]). apiInputPorts.ts isPortableLabel only checks trim().length>0 — '|' is permitted. Contrast shallowNodeHash.ts:96 which uses '' precisely to avoid adjacent-value collisions.

title: apiInputEmitPortLabels(config) is computed twice per render for apiInput nodes (once memoized, once inside _SourceHandles)
description: For an apiInput node the port label list is derived twice on every render: once in the `emitTableLabels` useMemo (line 226-229, used for the effect signature and the body label column) and again inside `_SourceHandles` via `apiInputEmitPortLabels(config)` (line 118, used to render the handles). The two call sites are documented as a shared source of truth, but they recompute the same value from the same `nodeData.config` rather than the render passing the already-memoized `emitTableLabels` down to `_SourceHandles`. Threading the memoized array (or its emptiness) into `_SourceHandles` for the apiInput branch would remove the redundant second derivation while keeping the single-source-of-truth guarantee. Pure presentational change; identical handles/labels render. Marginal (the computation is O(tables) and cheap), hence low confidence that it is worth changing.
evidence: Line 118 (_SourceHandles): const labels = apiInputEmitPortLabels(config). Line 226-229 (component body): const emitTableLabels = useMemo(() => isDeployInput ? apiInputEmitPortLabels(nodeData.config) : [], ...). Both consume the same config; _SourceHandles is invoked with the same config object (line 248).
est_reduction: ~3 lines / one redundant O(tables) pass per apiInput render
behavior_preservation: Identical rendered handles and body labels; only removes a duplicate derivation of an already-memoized value.

title: Pattern grouping keeps only the first column's dtype; siblings with a different dtype are misrepresented by the row's dtype badge
description: buildGroups collapses columns that share a numeric-segment pattern (e.g. arr.0, arr.1 -> arr.*) into one PatternRow and records a single dtype. The dtype is captured once on first insertion into patternMap and never reconciled against later columns sharing the same pattern. When sibling columns under the same pattern have heterogeneous dtypes (entirely possible for struct/array-derived flattened columns, e.g. arr.0=Int64, arr.1=Float64), the collapsed row shows only the FIRST concrete column's dtype, silently hiding that the group mixes types.
evidence: Lines 60-62: `if (!patternMap.has(pat)) patternMap.set(pat, { cols: [], dtype: col.dtype }); patternMap.get(pat)!.cols.push(col.name)`. The dtype is written only inside the `!patternMap.has(pat)` branch; subsequent same-pattern columns only `cols.push(col.name)`, never updating dtype. PatternRow.dtype (line 70) therefore equals concreteColumns[0]'s dtype regardless of siblings. It is rendered as the row badge at lines 503-507 via getDtypeColor(row.dtype). Columns arrive from the backend as arbitrary {name,dtype} pairs (types/node.ts ColumnInfo; usePipelineAPI.ts:123-124 sets _columns/_availableColumns verbatim from the API), with no same-pattern dtype-uniformity guarantee.

title: Strip-prefix can author a column_renames entry whose target collides with an existing column, producing a runtime Polars duplicate-name error with no UI guard
description: Stripping a group prefix (or a mid segment) writes column_renames[old] = stripped without checking that `stripped` does not collide with another existing (non-renamed) column. The backend (_execute_lazy._apply_column_renames) builds `valid = {old:new for ... if old in all_cols and old != new}` then calls `frame.rename(valid)`; if two columns end up mapped to the same target, or a rename target equals an untouched existing column name, Polars raises a DuplicateError when the node runs. Because stripGroupPrefix only iterates the rows of one ColumnGroup, it cannot see a same-named column living in a different top-level group, so cross-group collisions are entirely unguarded. The UI lets the user author this invalid config and surfaces the failure only at execution time.
evidence: stripGroupPrefix (191-198) sets `newRenames[col] = stripSegments(col,1)` for each column with no collision check. Concrete collision: columns `licence.type` (top prefix `licence`) and a separate top-level column `type` (top prefix `type`) live in two different ColumnGroups; clicking 'strip licence prefix' yields rename `licence.type -> type`, colliding with the existing `type`. Backend src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:470-472 then does `frame.rename({'licence.type':'type'})` while `type` is already present -> Polars duplicate-column error. No frontend code path validates rename targets against the full column universe (allNames at line 185 is available but unused for this check).

title: Restoring a stripped mid-segment is unreachable when the segment after the group prefix equals the group-prefix name (display says 'stripped' but clicking re-strips)
description: SegmentedName decides whether a segment is stripped by removing the group prefix from the rename value (renamedShort = renamed without leading `groupPrefix.`) and comparing against the pattern, whereas toggleSegmentStrip decides strip-vs-restore from the rename value VERBATIM (currentAfterGroup = newRenames[col] as-is). When the reconstructed rename still begins with the group-prefix segment, these two disagree: the UI strikes the segment through (stripped) but the toggle still finds the target segment present and strips it again (a no-op), so the user can never restore it.
evidence: For group prefix `a` and column `a.a.b` (shortPattern `a.b`), stripping index 0 ('a') reconstructs newFull = groupPrefix + '.' + newAfter = `a.b` (line 251), stored as newRenames['a.a.b']='a.b'. SegmentedName (117-119) computes renamedShort = `a.b`.slice(2) = `b`, parts=['b'], len 1<2 -> marks segment 0 stripped (struck through, line 144-153). On the restore click, toggleSegmentStrip (231-233) sets currentAfterGroup = newRenames['a.a.b'] = `a.b` (verbatim, NOT re-sliced), afterSegments=['a','b']; targetSeg = shortPattern[0]='a'; indexOf('a')=0 and 0<length-1 -> takes the STRIP branch (246-256) again, recomputes newFull='a.b' (unchanged) -> no restore. Restore branch (257-267) is never reached for this column. (For non-coincident names like `g.b.c.d` the verbatim value `g.c.d` no longer contains 'b', so restore works -- confirming the defect is specific to the group-name/segment coincidence.)

title: Loop-invariant, duplicated locals (exampleOriginal / originalFull / groupPrefix) recomputed every iteration inside toggleSegmentStrip
description: Inside `for (const col of row.concreteColumns)`, the code recomputes exampleOriginal = row.concreteColumns[0], originalFull = exampleOriginal (an exact alias), and groupPrefix = topPrefix(originalFull) on every iteration. None depends on the loop variable `col`; all concrete columns of a PatternRow share the same top prefix by construction (they map to one pattern with one topPrefix). exampleOriginal and originalFull are identical, and the whole block is loop-invariant, so it should be hoisted above the loop and the redundant alias removed.
evidence: Lines 226-228: `const exampleOriginal = row.concreteColumns[0]; const originalFull = exampleOriginal; const groupPrefix = topPrefix(originalFull)`. exampleOriginal is referenced nowhere except to initialise originalFull; originalFull is used only to compute groupPrefix. groupPrefix is then used at 233, 250, 251, 260, 261 -- but its value is constant across iterations because buildGroups (66-70) groups by topPrefix(pat), so every col in concreteColumns yields the same topPrefix.
est_reduction: ~2 lines plus per-iteration recomputation
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: hoist `const groupPrefix = topPrefix(row.concreteColumns[0])` above the loop and delete the exampleOriginal/originalFull aliases; identical values are produced for every iteration, so all downstream branches behave identically.

title: Redundant column-completion reconfigure dispatched on every mount
description: The mount effect (line 343) already configures the column-completion compartment when the EditorView is created (lines 381-385), reading the same `availableColumns` prop. Because effects run in declaration order, the mount effect runs before the `[availableColumns]` effect (line 474). On mount, `viewRef.current` is already set, so the `[availableColumns]` effect immediately dispatches a `columnCompartment.reconfigure(...)` that produces a functionally identical compartment value (a fresh `autocompletion(...)` instance built from the very same prop). This is one extra no-op reconfigure transaction on every component mount. It could be avoided by gating the effect to skip the first run (e.g. an `didMount` ref) or by reconfiguring only when the column set actually differs from what the mount already installed.
evidence: Mount effect lines 381-385 build `columnCompartment.current.of(availableColumns?.length ? autocompletion({override:[columnCompletionSource(availableColumns)]}) : autocompletion())`. Effect at 474-483 then runs on mount (viewRef set) and dispatches `effects: columnCompartment.current.reconfigure(<identical expression>)`. Same `availableColumns` reference in the same render => identical intended config, yet a new extension instance forces CM to apply the reconfigure.
est_reduction: ~1 no-op transaction per mount; ~3 lines if a first-run guard is added
behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving: the compartment ends in the same configured state; only the extra mount-time reconfigure transaction is eliminated.

title: useRef initializers (Annotation.define / new Compartment) re-evaluated on every render
description: `useRef(Annotation.define<boolean>())` (251), `useRef(new Compartment())` (259) and `useRef(new Compartment())` (260) evaluate their argument on every render even though React keeps only the first result. Each render therefore allocates a throwaway Annotation type and two throwaway Compartment objects that are immediately discarded. The allocations are cheap so the runtime cost is negligible, but it is the well-known `useRef(eagerInit())` anti-pattern; the idiomatic lazy form is `useRef<T>()` populated on first use, or `useState(() => ...)[0]` / a `useMemo` with a stable init so the constructor runs once.
evidence: Line 251 `const externalSyncAnnotation = useRef(Annotation.define<boolean>())`; lines 259-260 `useRef(new Compartment())`. The expression inside useRef(...) is a function-call argument, so JS evaluates it on each render before useRef ignores it past the first.
est_reduction: 3 discarded allocations per render eliminated (no LOC change required if switched to a lazy-init helper)
behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving: the retained ref values are identical; only the per-render throwaway allocations are removed.

title: Removing a factor leaves orphaned interaction references that flip backend include_main semantics
description: removeFactor() deletes a column only from `terms`, never from `interactions`. Any interaction row that referenced the removed factor is left dangling. This is not merely cosmetic: the dropdown's `value={interaction.factors[n]}` now points to a value absent from the option list (the select renders an inconsistent/blank selection while config still holds the stale factor name), AND the stale name is persisted and sent to the backend.
evidence: removeFactor (l.135) does `const { [name]: _removed, ...rest } = terms; onUpdate("terms", rest)` — interactions untouched. includedFeatures (l.196) is derived only from addedFactors, so the removed name disappears from both dropdowns (l.420, l.430) while interaction.factors still contains it. Backend _build_interactions (src/haute/modelling/_rustystats.py:82-95): a factor not in `terms` takes the fallback `{"type": "categorical"}` (l.86-87) and forces `all_in_terms=False`, so `include_main` is read from config (l.95) and can be True — the exact path the same function's docstring (l.69-74) warns causes main-effect duplication / singular-matrix failure. So removing a factor can silently re-introduce an unconfigured categorical main effect and/or break training with a singular matrix.

title: Interaction dropdowns permit and persist a degenerate self-interaction (same factor on both sides)
description: Dropdown 1 (l.413-421) lists ALL includedFeatures with no filter, while dropdown 2 (l.423-433) filters out only `factors[0]`. If the user picks factor A in dropdown 2 first (factors[1]=A) and then picks A in dropdown 1 (factors[0]=A), the config becomes `factors: ["A","A"]`. Nothing rejects or repairs this. Dropdown 2 then renders `value="A"` against an option list that no longer contains A, so the displayed selection is inconsistent with stored state.
evidence: l.420 renders every `includedFeatures.map(...)` for select-1 (no exclusion of factors[1]). l.430 select-2 does `includedFeatures.filter(f => f !== interaction.factors[0])`. updateInteractionFactor (l.185-193) writes the chosen value unconditionally with no equality guard. Resulting `["A","A"]` reaches backend _build_interactions (src/haute/modelling/_rustystats.py:77-97): len(factors)<2 is False so it is NOT skipped, and the per-factor loop builds a dict keyed by name (l.82-84) which collapses the duplicate to a single key `{"A": {...}, "include_main": False}` — a malformed one-term 'interaction'.

title: df input uses parseInt without radix instead of the project's safeParseInt helper
description: The degrees-of-freedom input parses with `parseInt(e.target.value)` (no radix argument), whereas configField.ts already exports `safeParseInt(raw, fallback)` used elsewhere in the codebase. Using the shared helper (with radix 10 and NaN-safety) is consistent with the sibling prior_weight input on l.301 which already uses safeParseFloat, and avoids the latent missing-radix smell flagged by lint rules.
evidence: l.287: `onChange={(e) => updateTermField(col.name, "df", e.target.value ? parseInt(e.target.value) : undefined)}`. Compare l.301 prior_weight: `safeParseFloat(e.target.value, 1.0)`. safeParseInt is defined in utils/configField.ts:26-29 (the file already imported on l.4 for configField/safeParseFloat) but not used here.
est_reduction: ~1 line / consistency
behavior_preservation: Equivalent for valid numeric-input strings; safeParseInt additionally pins radix 10 and avoids emitting NaN.

title: Row virtualization start index lacks the upper clamp that column virtualization has, so a stale scrollTop can blank the table after switching to a shorter preview
description: The vertical (row) virtualization computes startIdx with only a lower bound: startIdx = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT) - OVERSCAN), and endIdx = Math.min(totalRows, ...). There is no upper clamp keeping a full window of rows visible (no equivalent of getColumnWindow's `maxStartIdx = Math.max(0, columnCount - windowSize)` / `startIdx = Math.min(maxStartIdx, ...)`). The scroll div is a persistent, non-keyed element (setScrollContainer is a stable callback ref; the component is not remounted when data.nodeId changes), so scrollTop state survives a data swap. When the user has scrolled a tall preview down (large scrollTop) and the selected node / preview then changes to one with far fewer rows, on the first render with the new data scrollTop still holds the stale large value while totalRows is small. Then startIdx can exceed endIdx, so data.preview.slice(startIdx, endIdx) is empty, topPad = startIdx*ROW_HEIGHT is large, and bottomPad = (totalRows-endIdx)*ROW_HEIGHT = 0 — the body renders only a giant empty top spacer with no data rows. The browser clamps the DOM scrollTop on content shrink and fires a scroll event that eventually corrects the React state, so the blank state is transient (up to one paint), but it is a real flicker and the authors explicitly hardened the analogous column path against exactly this scrolled-then-shrunk scenario (see the dedicated test 'clamps the visible column window when a scrolled preview changes to fewer columns'), making the missing row-side clamp an inconsistency.
evidence: Lines 297-300: `if (shouldVirtualize) { startIdx = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT) - OVERSCAN); endIdx = Math.min(totalRows, Math.ceil((scrollTop + effectiveViewHeight) / ROW_HEIGHT) + OVERSCAN) }`. Compare getColumnWindow (lines 116-119) which clamps: `const maxStartIdx = Math.max(0, columnCount - windowSize); const startIdx = Math.min(maxStartIdx, Math.max(0, rawStart - COLUMN_OVERSCAN))`. With e.g. previous scrollTop=10000 (≈357 rows down) and new totalRows=5: startIdx = max(0, 357-10)=347, endIdx = min(5, ...)=5, slice(347,5)=[] -> blank body, topPad=347*28.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Invalid coordinate-less touch drop throws instead of being ignored (point computed before isValid guard)
description: In the source-to-source branch of onConnectEnd, connectionEndPoint(event) is evaluated on line 247 BEFORE the `if (connectionState.isValid === false) return` guard on line 248. connectionEndPoint throws 'Connection end touch event did not include pointer coordinates' when a TouchEvent has empty touches and changedTouches. Therefore an INVALID connection (isValid === false) that happens to be a coordinate-less touch end will throw an uncaught error inside the React event handler, instead of being silently discarded as an invalid gesture should be. Hoisting the `isValid === false` early-return above the connectionEndPoint(event) call fixes this and is behaviour-preserving for every currently-tested path.
evidence: Lines 242-248: branch entered when fromHandle.type==='source' && toHandle.type==='source' && targetNodeId. Line 247 `const point = screenToFlowPosition(connectionEndPoint(event))` runs first; connectionEndPoint (lines 61-68) throws when both event.touches[0] and event.changedTouches[0] are undefined. Line 248 `if (connectionState.isValid === false) return` only runs after. The existing throw test (test line 1261) uses isValid:true; the invalid-drop test (test line 392) uses a MouseEvent with coordinates, so the isValid:false + coordinate-less-touch combination is uncovered and would crash.

title: Re-reads connectionState.fromHandle?.id instead of the already-captured non-null fromHandle local
description: Inside the edge-drop branch, the insertEdgeJoinNode call passes `sourceHandle: connectionState.fromHandle?.id ?? null`. The local `fromHandle` (captured on line 219 as `connectionState.fromHandle`) is the same object, and its source type was just verified on line 289 (`if (fromHandle?.type !== 'source') return`), so `fromHandle` is guaranteed non-null here. The sibling source-to-source and node-to-node branches already use the captured local (e.g. lines 259, 283 use `fromHandle.id ?? null` / `toHandle.id ?? null`). Using `fromHandle.id ?? null` here removes the redundant optional-chain re-dereference and keeps the branch consistent with its siblings.
est_reduction: 1 line edited (no net line change); removes a redundant property re-read
behavior_preservation: Identical: connectionState.fromHandle and the fromHandle local reference the same object, and fromHandle is non-null past the line 289 guard, so `fromHandle.id ?? null` evaluates to exactly the same value.

title: Transient UI key `_id` is persisted into the saved banding config and sent over the wire
description: `ensureRuleIds` injects a frontend-only `_id` field into each rule object, and the id-assignment effect persists it back via `onUpdateFactor({ rules })`. This patch flows through BandingEditor.updateFactor -> onUpdate('factors', next) into the saved pipeline config. `normaliseBandingFactors` (bandingUtils.ts:3-7) returns the persisted factors array verbatim and never strips `_id`, and the backend rule reader (_banding_config.py uses plain dict.get, no extra='forbid') simply ignores the unknown key. Net effect: a purely-presentational React key (only needed for <tr key=...>) leaks into the persisted domain model and the request payload. It does not crash anything, but it pollutes saved configs with non-deterministic values (`rule_<seq>_<Date.now base36>`), which also defeats config diffing/equality and round-trips junk to disk/server. The id is a render concern and should be derived/held outside the persisted `rules` (e.g. a WeakMap keyed by rule object, or a ref-held parallel id list), not merged into the wire object.
evidence: Line 27: `return { ...r, _id: nextRuleId() }`. Line 214: `onUpdateFactor({ rules })` persists ids. bandingUtils.ts:5 `if (Array.isArray(raw) && raw.length > 0) return raw` — no _id stripping. _banding_config.py:70 `result['rules'] = normalise_banding_rules(...)` keeps original rule dicts (including _id) when no categorical expansion happens.

title: Stable-id assignment uses two refs plus a dependency-less effect performing a render-phase state write-back
description: Stable row keys are produced by: (a) calling `ensureRuleIds(rawRules)` on every render, (b) a `prevRulesRef`/`didAssignIds` ref pair plus a `[rawRules]` effect to reset a guard, and (c) a second effect with intentionally no deps that runs after every render to fire `onUpdateFactor({ rules })`. This is a side-effecting write-back of persisted state purely to obtain React keys, and its correctness depends on the parent round-tripping `_id` unchanged and not memo-stripping it. The whole mechanism can be replaced by deriving keys without persisting them — e.g. a module-level `WeakMap<rule, string>` assigned lazily inside `ruleKey`, or `useMemo` mapping rule identity to ids — which removes both refs, both effects, the eslint-disable on the no-dep effect, and the parent write-back entirely. That also resolves finding #1 (no `_id` ever enters the wire model).
evidence: Lines 201-216: `didAssignIds`/`prevRulesRef` + `useEffect(...,[rawRules])` reset + `useEffect(() => { if (rules !== rawRules && !didAssignIds.current) { ...; onUpdateFactor({ rules }) } })` with comment '// intentionally no deps — runs on every render'. `ruleKey` (line 33-35) already falls back to `fallback_${index}` so keys never hard-depend on persisted `_id`.
est_reduction: ~15-20 lines (remove ensureRuleIds persistence, two refs, two effects, one eslint-disable)
behavior_preservation: Row keys remain stable across edits/reorders via object-identity map; deletion/insert behavior and all existing tests on _id presence would need updating since _id would no longer be emitted to onUpdateFactor (behavioral change limited to the synthetic key, not rule data).

title: onPaste handlers on the operator <select> elements never fire (paste is not dispatched on <select>)
description: The lower/upper operator cells render `<select ... onPaste={(e) => handleCellPaste(e, i, 0|2)}>`. Native HTML <select> elements do not receive `paste` events in Chrome/Firefox/Safari (paste only targets editable text controls), so these two handlers are effectively dead and there is no way to range-paste starting from an operator column via the cell path. The whole-grid container paste (`handlePaste`) still covers operator data because it parses full rows, so functionality is not lost — the cell-level handlers on selects are simply unreachable code carrying the `fieldIndex` 0/2 mapping for op columns.
evidence: Line 304: `<select value={rule.op1 || ''} ... onPaste={(e) => handleCellPaste(e, i, 0)}>`; line 321: same for op2 with fieldIndex 2. handleCellPaste relies on a `paste` event that <select> never emits. Compare TwoWayGrid.tsx where onPaste is only attached to <input> cells (lines 250, 321), not selects.

title: hasSelectedColumn uses strict `selected === true`, diverging from the backend's truthiness check on malformed/legacy configs
description: `hasSelectedColumn` decides whether a table contributes a port by testing `(c).selected === true` (strict). The backend predicate this module explicitly claims to mirror — `_json_shred.table_is_emitting` — instead uses Python truthiness: `any(isinstance(col, dict) and col.get("selected") for col in columns)`. For the common, editor-produced configs the two agree (the editor's `writeV2` always persists `selected` as a strict boolean, and a missing/`false` key is falsy on both sides). They diverge only for a column whose `selected` is truthy-but-not-`true` (e.g. `selected: 1`, `selected: "y"`, `selected: {}`): the backend counts such a table as emitting (renders/binds a port at runtime), while `hasSelectedColumn` returns false, so `apiInputEmitPortLabels` omits the port and `_SourceHandles` won't render it. Because the same function gates BOTH frontend rendering and the backend's runtime port set, a desync here is precisely the silent-orphan / missing-port class the module's header says it exists to prevent. The config reaches this code unnormalised: `nodeData.config` is stored opaquely and only coerced lazily by `readV2` when the editor opens, so a hand-authored or legacy on-disk config with a non-boolean `selected` flows straight into `hasSelectedColumn`.
evidence: apiInputPorts.ts:46 `(c as { selected?: unknown }).selected === true` vs _json_shred.py:176 `return any(isinstance(col, dict) and col.get("selected") for col in columns)`. Reachability: App stores config verbatim; readV2 (apiInputSchema.ts:120) only normalises when the editor is open. Note readV2 itself treats missing `selected` as selected (`cc.selected !== false`), a third interpretation, underscoring that `selected` truthiness is handled inconsistently across the three sites.

title: Zustand stores subscribed without selectors, re-rendering the host (App) on every unrelated UI/toast change
description: The hook destructures `const { setSyncBanner } = useUIStore()` and `const { addToast } = useToastStore()` with no selector argument. Calling a Zustand store hook with no selector subscribes the consuming component to the ENTIRE store object, so it re-renders on ANY state change in that store. useUIStore holds high-churn UI state (hoveredNodeId, paletteOpen/utilityOpen/importsOpen/gitOpen toggles, nodePanelWidth, per-node editor section maps, nodeSearchOpen, syncBanner). useWebSocketSync is mounted directly in App.tsx (App.tsx:278), so App and its whole subtree re-render on every hover-highlight change, panel toggle, and toast push, even though this hook only ever needs the two stable action functions. The project's own selector contract is documented verbatim in useGraphStore.ts ("Consumers MUST subscribe via selectors so unrelated state changes do not trigger re-renders ... `useGraphStore()` // BAD — re-renders on any change"); these two lines violate it. The fix is `useUIStore((s) => s.setSyncBanner)` and `useToastStore((s) => s.addToast)`.
evidence: Trace: useUIStore (stores/useUIStore.ts) is `create<UIState>()((set) => ({...}))` with many fields incl. hoveredNodeId/setHoveredNodeId (108-109) updated on hover. `const { setSyncBanner } = useUIStore()` (line 93) reads the whole store → component subscribes to all of it → any `set(...)` (e.g. setHoveredNodeId) triggers a re-render of the hook's host. App.tsx:278 calls `useWebSocketSync({...})` at the top level of App, so App re-renders. The actions themselves (setSyncBanner at useUIStore.ts:87, addToast in useToastStore) are stable refs defined once in `create`, so the effect dep array [..., setSyncBanner, addToast] does NOT change and the WebSocket is NOT torn down — confirming this is a render-cost/contract issue, not a reconnect bug. The remedy (selector subscription) is exactly the pattern useGraphStore.ts documents and that other call sites follow.
est_reduction: ~0 LOC (change 2 lines to selector form); eliminates App-subtree re-renders on every UI-store and toast-store mutation
behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving: selectors return the identical stable action references the hook already uses; only the over-broad subscription (and resulting redundant re-renders) is removed. No change to WebSocket lifecycle, message handling, or any user-visible behavior.

title: FileBrowser cache-hit path does not clear a stale error, leaving a successfully-loaded directory hidden behind a stale error banner
description: In the FileBrowser effect, the cache-hit fast path (`if (cached) { setItems(...); setLoading(false); return }`) returns without calling `setError(null)`. Only the cache-miss branch resets the error (line 189). Because the render checks `error` BEFORE `items` (lines 250-251), a stale error from a previously-failed directory persists and masks the cached content of a different, successfully-loaded directory.
evidence: Reachable sequence: (1) User is in directory B which loads OK and is cached (setFileListCache, line 195; cache TTL 30s per useSettingsStore.getFileListCache). (2) User navigates into subdir A; A's listFiles rejects -> catch sets error + items=[] (lines 200-201); note A is NOT cached on failure. (3) User clicks goUp back to B; goUp sets loading(true) then setDir(B) (lines 211-212). (4) Effect re-runs for B, getFileListCache(B) hits -> setItems(B), setLoading(false), `return` at line 187 WITHOUT setError(null). Render at lines 250-251 evaluates `error ? <error> : items...`, so B's valid cached rows are hidden behind A's stale error banner until the 30s cache expires or `extensions` changes. The cache-miss branch clears error (line 189) but the cache-hit branch does not.

title: InputSourcesBar uses non-unique varName as React key, causing key collisions and mis-targeted delete buttons when two upstream sources share a sanitized name
description: InputSourcesBar renders `inputSources.map((src) => <span key={src.varName} ...>)`. `varName` is NOT unique: in NodePanel.tsx (line 636) it is computed as `sanitizeName(nodeMap[e.source]?.data.label || e.source)`, derived from the upstream node label. sanitizeName is many-to-one, so distinct upstream nodes whose labels collapse to the same identifier produce identical `varName` values and therefore duplicate React keys. The struct already carries a guaranteed-unique `edgeId` (e.g. used as the delete payload `onDeleteInput(src.edgeId)`), which is the correct key.
evidence: Producer (NodePanel.tsx lines 632-639): `upstreamEdges.map((e) => ({ sourceNodeId: e.source, varName: sanitizeName(nodeMap[e.source]?.data.label || e.source), sourceLabel: ..., edgeId: e.id }))`. sanitizeName (utils/sanitizeName.ts:18-19) replaces `[\s-]` with `_` and strips non-alnum/underscore, so labels like `"Age Band"`, `"Age-Band"`, `"Age_Band"`, and `"Age Band!"` all sanitize to `"Age_Band"`. Two upstream nodes with such labels yield two inputSources entries with identical `varName` -> `key={src.varName}` collides. React then logs a duplicate-key warning and, on reconciliation, can associate the click handler / DOM of the wrong entry; clicking one delete-X may remove the other source's edge (both call onDeleteInput but the reconciled element identity is ambiguous). Fix: `key={src.edgeId}` (edgeId = e.id, unique per edge).

title: Duplicate React key when a categorical column contains both SQL null and the literal string "__null__"
description: In CategoricalSummaryCard, each distinct-value chip is keyed by `${profile.field}:${item.value ?? "__null__"}`. A genuine missing value arrives over the wire as `item.value === null` (the backend `_format_display_value` returns Python None for nulls, serialised as JSON null), so its key becomes `field:__null__`. If the same column also contains the ordinary string value "__null__" (a perfectly legal string after the backend's `.cast(pl.String)` in `_categorical_value_counts_expr`), that chip ALSO produces the key `field:__null__`. The two distinct chips then collide on the same React key.
evidence: Backend: `_format_display_value(None) -> None` (src/haute/routes/_explore_service.py:119-120) and `_parse_categorical_value_counts` builds `ExploreDistinctValueCount(value=None, ...)`; the literal string "__null__" survives `.cast(pl.String).value_counts(...)` unchanged. Frontend: `profile.values.map((item) => (<span key={`${profile.field}:${item.value ?? "__null__"}`} ...>)` (line 370). When values = [{value: null, count: 3}, {value: "__null__", count: 1}] both yield key `field:__null__` -> React duplicate-key warning and unstable list reconciliation (one chip may be dropped/reused incorrectly across re-renders), even though both counts are legitimate distinct groups.

title: computeGini re-derives Gini that the backend already provides in result.metrics.gini, on a lossy downsampled curve
description: LorenzChart calls computeGini(curve, perfectCurve) to annotate the chart with a Gini value. But the backend already computes the canonical normalised Gini (_metrics.py:189 _gini, registered as 'gini' at _metrics.py:976) and ships it to the frontend in result.metrics, which SummaryTab.tsx:120 renders directly. The frontend therefore (a) duplicates a non-trivial metric the backend owns, and (b) computes it from result.lorenz_curve, which compute_lorenz_curve (_metrics.py:805-818) explicitly DOWNSAMPLES to at most n_points=200 unique indices via np.round(np.linspace(...)). Trapezoidal area over a downsampled monotone Lorenz curve under-estimates the true area, so the chart's 'Gini = X.XXXX' can disagree with the 'gini' value shown in the Summary tab of the same panel. The fix is to display result.metrics.gini (or a dedicated gini field) rather than recomputing.
evidence: Backend: _metrics.py:224 area = np.trapezoid(cum_loss/total_loss, cum_weight/total_weight); raw_gini = 1 - 2*area; normalised by perfect_gini -> registered 'gini' (_metrics.py:976). Frontend LiftTab.tsx:364 rawGini = 2*trapArea(curve) - 1; LiftTab.tsx:367 return rawGini/perfectGini — same ratio mathematically (numerator and denominator both sign-flipped vs backend) BUT trapArea runs over the downsampled `curve` (>=200-point cap, _metrics.py:807-810), whereas backend _gini runs over the full per-unique-key aggregated points. SummaryTab.tsx:120 Object.entries(result.metrics) renders 'gini' with fmt(v). Two 'Gini' numbers for one model, derivable from the same payload, can differ.
est_reduction: ~23 lines (delete computeGini at LiftTab.tsx:347-370 and the call/annotation wiring at 256/315-317), replacing with a prop carrying result.metrics.gini.
behavior_preservation: Behaviour changes intentionally only in that the annotation becomes exactly the canonical backend Gini (eliminating the downsample-induced discrepancy). If exact byte-for-byte annotation must be preserved, this is a consistency bug rather than a pure refactor; either way the duplicate client-side derivation should go.

title: DoubleLiftChart y-axis padding breaks for all-negative data: padded yMax falls below the true maximum, pushing the zero line and bars above the chart top
description: yMax = allVals.reduce(max) * 1.1 and yMin = Math.min(0, reduce(min) * 1.1). The *1.1 'headroom' multiplier assumes the extremes are non-negative. When all decile values are negative (possible for regression targets / signed residual-style averages), multiplying a negative maximum by 1.1 makes yMax MORE negative than the actual largest value, so the data point lies above the plotted top of the axis. Worse, zeroY = yScale(0) is then computed for a 0 that sits above yMax: (0 - yMin)/ySpan > 1, so zeroY < marginTop, i.e. the zero baseline and every downward bar (drawn from zeroY for d.value < 0, lines 142/144) render above the chart's top edge / get clipped. Standard pricing diagnostics (frequency/severity averages) are non-negative so this is an unusual-input edge, but the code claims to support negatives (it has a yMin<0 zero-line branch at line 132 and signed-bar logic at 141-144), so the padding logic is internally inconsistent with that support.
evidence: data = [{actual:-1,...},{actual:-2,...}]: allVals=[-1,-2]; yMax = max(-1,-2)*1.1 = -1.1; yMin = min(0, min(-1,-2)*1.1) = min(0,-2.2) = -2.2; ySpan = 1.1. For the largest value actual=-1 (>=0 is false) -> actualY = zeroY = yScale(0) = marginTop + chartH - ((0 - (-2.2))/1.1)*chartH = marginTop + chartH - 2*chartH = marginTop - chartH < marginTop. Bar top is a full chartH above the chart. Correct padding for the negative side would multiply the negative extreme outward (e.g. min*1.1 only when min<0, and pad the positive extreme by *1.1 only when max>0).
behavior_preservation: N/A (bug report)

title: Dead banding sub-condition in showColumnValuesTable is fully subsumed by !richNodeDetail
description: showColumnValuesTable = !step.expression && !step.calculation && !richNodeDetail && !(hasRichBandingDetail(step) && hasRenderableBandingRows(step.node_detail)). The trailing banding clause can never change the result: richNodeDetail = hasPrimaryNodeDetail(step), and hasPrimaryNodeDetail returns true whenever hasRichBandingDetail(step) is true (it ORs hasRichBandingDetail in directly). Both predicates read the same step.node_detail and hasRichBandingDetail is literally `detail?.detail_type === "banding"`. So when hasRichBandingDetail(step) is true, !richNodeDetail is already false and short-circuits the whole expression; when it is false, the sub-clause is vacuously true. The `&& !(hasRichBandingDetail(step) && hasRenderableBandingRows(...))` term is therefore dead. It is also the ONLY use of hasRenderableBandingRows in this file (import at line 15), so removing the dead term makes that import droppable.
evidence: StepCard.tsx:88 `const richNodeDetail = hasPrimaryNodeDetail(step)`; traceStoryView.ts:52-61 hasPrimaryNodeDetail ORs `hasRichBandingDetail(step)`; traceStoryView.ts:23-26 `hasRichBandingDetail` => `step?.node_detail?.detail_type === "banding"`. Thus hasRichBandingDetail(step) ⇒ richNodeDetail ⇒ the `!richNodeDetail` clause already gates out every case the banding sub-clause targets. Line 122 sub-clause never flips the boolean.
est_reduction: 1 line of condition + 1 import symbol (hasRenderableBandingRows)
behavior_preservation: Behavior-identical: the removed term is logically implied by the preceding !richNodeDetail clause for all inputs, so showColumnValuesTable evaluates to the same value in every case.

title: formatTraceValue emits a spurious 'full precision' title/aria-label for grouped non-integers (no precision actually hidden)
description: formatTraceValue compares display (formatValue = _formatValue(v,2), which uses v.toLocaleString(undefined, {maximumFractionDigits:2}) and therefore inserts thousands separators) against full = formatResultValueFull(v), which routes to formatResultValue(v) with no precision and returns bare String(v) for non-integers (traceFormatting.ts:38) — NO grouping separators. For any finite non-integer with magnitude >= 1000 whose fractional part already fits in 2 dp (e.g. 1234.5), display='1,234.5' but full='1234.5', so display !== full and the function attaches title=`${context}: 1234.5` and ariaLabel=`${context}: 1,234.5 (full precision 1234.5)` even though NO precision is hidden — the strings differ only by the comma. Screen-reader users hear a misleading '(full precision ...)' announcement and a tooltip appears with zero added information. Separately, when precision IS genuinely truncated (e.g. 1234.5678 -> display '1,234.57'), the 'full' value is rendered without grouping ('1234.5678'), inconsistent with the grouped formatting used everywhere else in the trace UI.
evidence: StepCard.tsx:22 `const formatValue = (v) => _formatValue(v, 2)`; formatValue.ts:28 non-integer path `v.toLocaleString(undefined, { maximumFractionDigits })` (grouped). StepCard.tsx:27 `const full = formatResultValueFull(value)`; traceFormatting.ts:45-47 -> formatResultValue(v) with precision undefined -> line 38 `return String(v)` (ungrouped). For v=1234.5: display='1,234.5', full='1234.5' => display!==full => StepCard.tsx:30-33 returns title+ariaLabel claiming full precision that does not exist.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Badge rendering uses a nested double-IIFE where a plain computed const would do
description: The conditional badge in the collapsed header is built with an outer IIFE that contains an inner IIFE computing `badge`, then renders it. Every other derived flag in this component (richNodeDetail, showSourceOrigin, calculationBlockText, showCalculationHero, showSecondaryDetail, showColumnValuesTable, etc.) is a top-level `const` computed before the JSX. Hoisting the badge value to a `const badge = ...` above the return (matching the existing style) and rendering `{badge ? … : null}` removes one layer of IIFE nesting and aligns with the file's established pattern.
evidence: StepCard.tsx:165 `{(() => { const badge = (() => { … })(); return badge ? (…) : null })()}` — two nested arrow IIFEs inside JSX, vs. the const-flag pattern used at lines 88-122.
est_reduction: ~3-4 lines of IIFE scaffolding
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: the computed badge value and rendered output are unchanged; only the boilerplate that computes/returns it moves out of the JSX.

title: isComputedPlaceholder is duplicated verbatim between StepCard and CalculationHero
description: `function isComputedPlaceholder(value: string | undefined): boolean { return value?.trim().toLowerCase() === "computed" }` is defined identically in StepCard.tsx (36-38) and CalculationHero.tsx (59-61). Both modules live in frontend/src/trace and both consume the same trace 'computed' placeholder sentinel. Extracting it to a shared trace util (e.g. alongside traceFormatting.ts) and importing it in both places removes the copy and keeps the placeholder semantics in one place.
evidence: StepCard.tsx:36-38 and CalculationHero.tsx:59-61 contain byte-identical implementations; grep for 'isComputedPlaceholder' returns exactly these two definitions.
est_reduction: ~3 lines (one duplicated definition)
behavior_preservation: Behavior-identical: same pure predicate referenced from a shared location; no call-site semantics change.

title: rewriteDownstreamEdgeJoinNode sets `selected: false` that is always overwritten by selectOnlyNode
description: rewriteDownstreamEdgeJoinNode is a file-private helper reached only via rewriteDownstreamSplitTargetNode, which is called only from insertEdgeJoinNode. Its three return statements all set `selected: false` (lines 269, 273, 277), but the caller wraps the entire mapped node array in selectOnlyNode([...nodes.map(rewriteDownstreamSplitTargetNode), newNode], newNodeId) (line 123). selectOnlyNode (flowElements.ts:95-100) unconditionally rewrites `selected: node.id === selectedNodeId` for every node, so the `selected` value produced inside rewriteDownstreamEdgeJoinNode is discarded for all three branches. The intermediate pass rewriteDownstreamInputsByParentContract preserves `selected` via spread, so it does not consume the value either. The writes are therefore dead.
evidence: insertEdgeJoinNode (line 121-129) -> selectOnlyNode([...nodes.map(node => rewriteDownstreamSplitTargetNode(node, targetEdge, newNodeId)), newNode], newNodeId). rewriteDownstreamSplitTargetNode (254-261) = rewriteDownstreamInputsByParentContract(rewriteDownstreamEdgeJoinNode(node, ...), ...). rewriteDownstreamEdgeJoinNode returns `{ ...node, selected: false }` at 269/273 and `{ ...node, selected: false, data: {...} }` at 277. selectOnlyNode (flowElements.ts:99): `selected: node.id === selectedNodeId` overrides all of them. Grep confirms these helpers have no other call sites.
est_reduction: 3 redundant property writes (remove `selected: false` from the three returns)
behavior_preservation: Exact. Final node.selected is determined solely by selectOnlyNode regardless of what rewriteDownstreamEdgeJoinNode sets, so removing the `selected: false` writes leaves output identical. The accompanying tests (edgeJoinGraph.test.ts) assert only config/edges, not interim selection.

title: EdgeJoinConnectedInput.label is computed for every connected input but never read anywhere
description: uniqueConnectedInputs builds an EdgeJoinConnectedInput { sourceId, label } for each unique incoming edge source, computing label via nodeLabel(edge.source, nodeMap). The resulting connectedInputs array is exposed on EdgeJoinAnalysis and passed into addRoleDiagnostics, but every consumer reads only .sourceId (addRoleDiagnostics line 321 does `new Set(connectedInputs.map((input) => input.sourceId))`). The EdgeJoinEditor destructure (EdgeJoinEditor.tsx:68-85) does not pull connectedInputs at all, and no test references it. Therefore the label field, the nodeLabel(...) lookup inside uniqueConnectedInputs, and the entire nodeMap parameter threaded into uniqueConnectedInputs exist solely to populate a value that is never consumed.
evidence: Grep for connectedInputs across frontend/src finds only edgeJoinValidation.ts; the sole read is `.sourceId` at line 321. Grep for EdgeJoinConnectedInput / `.label` shows no consumer of the label field. uniqueConnectedInputs (266-281) could be reduced to returning sourceIds (e.g. a Set/array of edge.source), dropping the nodeMap arg, the inputs.push({sourceId,label}) object construction, and the label type field on EdgeJoinConnectedInput (33-36).
est_reduction: ~10-14 lines (the label field, the EdgeJoinConnectedInput object shape, the nodeMap param + nodeLabel call in uniqueConnectedInputs, and the call-site nodeMap argument)
behavior_preservation: Diagnostics output is byte-for-byte identical because only sourceId is consumed; removing label and the lookup changes no produced diagnostic string and no editor rendering.

title: Same-name (on) join keys are never validated when base and join schemas are both known but share no columns
description: commonColumnOptions returns [] whenever baseColumns and joinColumns have an empty intersection, including the case where BOTH parent schemas are fully known but simply disjoint. addColumnDiagnostics (line 350) early-returns when columns.length === 0, so addColumnDiagnostics("Same-name", onKeys, commonColumns) emits nothing. A same-name join (on: ["k"]) requires k to exist in BOTH frames; when the two known schemas are disjoint, every on-key is by definition invalid, yet the frontend produces no diagnostic. The user only discovers the bad key when Polars fails at run time. By contrast leftKeys/rightKeys ARE checked against the individual (non-empty) baseColumns/joinColumns, so the paired path catches this but the same-name path does not. The empty-commonColumns early-return conflates 'columns unknown -> cannot validate' (legitimate skip) with 'columns known but disjoint -> every same-name key is invalid' (should be flagged).
evidence: commonColumnOptions (257-264): `if (baseColumns.length === 0 || joinColumns.length === 0) return []` then filters base by joinNames; for disjoint known sets this yields []. addColumnDiagnostics (344-350): `if (columns.length === 0) return`. Trace: baseColumns=[{a},{b}], joinColumns=[{c},{d}] (both known), on=["a"] -> commonColumns=[] -> addColumnDiagnostics returns immediately -> no "Same-name key a is not in the current upstream columns." emitted. The backend build_edge_join_kwargs (src/haute/_edge_join.py:157-212) does not validate keys against schema either, so this frontend guard is the only pre-run check.

title: Blank-only same/paired key config emits two overlapping diagnostics ('need join keys' and 'rows cannot be blank')
description: When config carries only blank key rows (e.g. on: [""], or leftOn: [""], rightOn: [""]), hasSameConfig/hasPairedConfig are true (length > 0) while hasSameValues/hasPairedValues are false (some(Boolean) on all-empty is false). Line 144 therefore fires 'Non-cross joins need join keys.' AND line 150's `[...onKeys, ...leftKeys, ...rightKeys].some((key) => key === "")` fires 'Join key rows cannot be blank.' for the same underlying state. The two messages are distinct strings so dedupe() (line 158) does not collapse them, surfacing two warnings for a single empty row. The in-app editor never persists a lone blank row (normalizeKeyRows trims it to []), but imported/decorator/API-sourced configs reach this code path with on:[""], so the redundant pair is user-visible for non-editor configs.
evidence: onKeys for on:[""] is [""] (readKeyList keeps empty strings, lines 240-251). hasSameConfig = onKeys.length>0 = true; hasSameValues = onKeys.some(Boolean) = false. Line 144 condition (how!==cross && !hasSameValues && !hasPairedValues) is true -> push #1. Line 150 condition (some key === "") is true -> push #2. dedupe keeps both because the strings differ.

title: CatalogTablePicker dropdown fetchers have no stale-response guard, letting a late getSchemas resolve repopulate the schema list for a catalog the user already left (and select an invalid catalog.schema.table)
description: refreshCatalogs/refreshSchemas/refreshTables each fire an unguarded promise and unconditionally call setCatalogs/setSchemas/setTables on resolution, with no request-generation check or AbortSignal. Because the catalog/schema/table selects also re-fetch on every onFocus and on every onChange, a slow in-flight request can resolve after the user has navigated to a different catalog/schema and overwrite the now-irrelevant option list. The user can then pick a stale option, producing a wrong fully-qualified table string. This is the exact stale-response race that the sibling component CacheFetchButton (same directory's component family) defends against with statusGenerationRef/activeResourceKeyRef guards; CatalogTablePicker omits all such guarding.
evidence: refreshSchemas(cat): getSchemas(cat).then((data) => { setSchemas(data.schemas || []); ... }) — no check that `cat` still === current `catalog`. Trace: (1) user picks catalog 'foo' -> onChange calls refreshSchemas('foo') [req B]; (2) user picks catalog 'baz' -> setCatalog('baz'), setSchemas([]), refreshSchemas('baz') [req D]; (3) req B (foo's schemas) resolves late -> setSchemas(foo schemas) while catalog='baz'. The schema <select> is disabled={!catalog} and catalog='baz' is truthy, so it is enabled and now shows foo's schemas. Selecting schema 'bar' fires onChange -> onSelect(`${catalog}.${dbSchema}.${tbl}`) building an invalid 'baz.bar.<table>'. The same pattern lets late getTables/getCatalogs overwrite their lists. Contrast CacheFetchButton.tsx:108-128 which guards every resolution with `if (activeResourceKeyRef.current !== requestKey || statusGenerationRef.current !== generation) return`.

title: updateCell commits non-finite and partially-parsed values that the paste path rejects
description: Direct cell edits go through updateCell, which uses parseFloat(val). parseFloat is lenient: it accepts trailing garbage ('1.2abc' -> 1.2) and returns non-finite values for overflow/literals ('1e400' -> Infinity, 'Infinity' -> Infinity, '-Infinity' -> -Infinity). Any of these are written straight into the entry value and propagated to onUpdateEntries (the rating config). The paste path for the SAME grid uses parsePastedNumber, which calls Number(trimmed) and guards with Number.isFinite, so it correctly rejects 'Infinity'/'1e400'/'1.2abc' with an error toast. Editing and pasting therefore disagree on what is a valid relativity, and the edit path can silently persist Infinity/-Infinity into the table.
evidence: Line 192-193: `const parsed = parseFloat(val); const numVal = val === "" ? safeDefault : (Number.isNaN(parsed) ? safeDefault : parsed)`. parseFloat('1e400') === Infinity and Number.isNaN(Infinity) === false, so numVal becomes Infinity and is pushed at line 204 `next.push({ ...sliceKey, [rowFactor]: row, [colFactor]: col, value: numVal })`. Contrast parsePastedNumber (line 13-18) which returns {kind:'invalid'} for the same inputs via `Number.isFinite(parsed)`. ControlledNumberCell.onBlur passes the raw local string to onCommit (ControlledNumberCell.tsx:18), so arbitrary text reaches updateCell. Downstream tableStats (ratingTableUtils.ts:98) filters only isNaN, not isFinite, so Infinity flows into min/max/avg and StatsFooter renders '.toFixed(3)' => 'Infinity'.

title: Label-based paste detection misroutes unlabelled numeric pastes when factor levels are numeric strings
description: handlePaste decides whether a pasted block is a labelled table (header row + row labels) vs a raw value matrix by checking whether the first row's cells match colLabels and whether first-column cells match rowLabels. Rating factor levels are frequently numeric-looking strings (age bands like '18'/'25', vehicle-age bands '1'/'3', NCD years). If colLabels/rowLabels are such numeric strings, a plain unlabelled numeric value matrix whose first row/column happen to contain those same numbers is misclassified as 'labelled', so values are re-keyed by label-match instead of by position. The user's intended top-left-anchored paste is then written to the wrong cells (or partially dropped), silently corrupting the table rather than failing loudly.
evidence: Line 163 `const labelledColumns = firstRow.slice(1).some(cell => colLabels.includes(cell.trim()))` and line 164 `const labelledRows = grid.slice(1).some(row => row[0] && rowLabels.includes(row[0].trim()))`. includes() does exact string compare, so when colLabels = ['18','25'] a pasted matrix like '18\t25\n0.8\t0.9' (first data row literally 18,25) sets labelledColumns true; if the first column also collides, labelledRows true, and the labelled branch (167-175) keys by `${rowLabel}\x1F${colLabel}` discarding the startRow/startCol anchor. The detection is purely value-based with no signal that the block is actually a header.

title: Slice-match predicate and lookup-with-default are duplicated across build/read/update paths
description: The same two pieces of logic are hand-rolled three times: (1) the slice-match predicate `Object.entries(sliceKey).every(([k,v]) => String(e[k]) === v)` appears in the lookup build (line 76), in applyCellUpdates (line 113) and (as a sub-clause) in updateCell.matchRow (line 195-196); (2) the 'read value with default' expression `lookup.get(`${row}\x1F${col}`) ?? safeDefault` is wrapped in valueFor (line 82) but then re-inlined verbatim in the cell render at line 284 instead of calling valueFor. Extracting a single `matchesSlice(e)` helper and using valueFor(row,col) at the render site would remove the repetition and keep the slice/default semantics defined in exactly one place.
est_reduction: ~6-10 lines and three divergence points collapsed to one helper each
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: matchesSlice(e) and valueFor(row,col) are already the exact expressions inlined at the duplicated sites; substituting them is behaviour-identical (same key construction `${...}\x1F${...}`, same `?? safeDefault`, same String() coercion).

title: Top-level TraceStep fields null_explanation / rename_info / expression_chain / taken_branch are never emitted by the backend and never read by any consumer
description: The TraceStep interface declares five optional TOP-LEVEL fields beyond what the backend wire contract carries: taken_branch (line 48), taken_branch_index (line 49), null_explanation (line 50), expression_chain (line 51), and rename_info (line 52). The backend never serialises these at the step level. The Pydantic response model TraceStepResponse (src/haute/schemas.py:314-326) carries only node_id/node_name/node_type/schema_diff/input_values/output_values/column_relevant/execution_ms/expression/calculation/node_detail/row_lineage_type. The enrichment pass (src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py) writes the real equivalents INTO step.calculation instead: calc_dict['taken_branch'] / ['taken_branch_index'] (lines 1525-1528), step.calculation['expression_chain'] (line 1587), and step.calculation['original_name'] + step.calculation['rename_chain'] (lines 1252-1256, 1282-1287). A grep of the whole Python source (src/haute/**/*.py) for 'rename_info' and 'null_explanation' returns zero matches. On the consumer side, four of the five fields are read NOWHERE: step.null_explanation, step.rename_info, top-level step.expression_chain, and top-level step.taken_branch have no reader in any .tsx/.ts file (components consume only calculation.expression_chain at CalculationHero.tsx:158 and calculation.taken_branch[_index]). Only step.taken_branch_index is genuinely read, as a fallback at StepCard.tsx:237 (step.calculation?.taken_branch_index ?? step.taken_branch_index), so it should be RETAINED. The four others are dead on both the wire and the consumer surface. Note rename_info is doubly mismatched: its declared shape is {original_name; chain} but the backend stores original_name + rename_chain (different key, different location) inside calculation, so neither the field nor its key names ever appear on the wire.
evidence: trace.ts:50 'null_explanation?: string | null' and :52 'rename_info?: {original_name: string; chain: string[]} | null'; backend schemas.py:314-326 TraceStepResponse has no such fields; _trace_enrichment.py:1252 step.calculation['original_name']=old_name, :1256 step.calculation['rename_chain']=chain, :1587 step.calculation['expression_chain']=enriched_chain, :1525-1528 calc_dict['taken_branch']; grep 'rename_info|null_explanation' over src/haute/**/*.py => no matches; grep '\.null_explanation|\.rename_info|step\.expression_chain|step\.taken_branch\b' over frontend/src .tsx/.ts => only references are the type decl and the guard parseTraceStep/parseTraceRenameInfo (guards.ts:813-814,828-833), which manufacture perpetual nulls; no component reads them.
est_reduction: ~4 interface members (lines 48,50,51,52) plus the coordinated removal of their never-consumed guard parsing
behavior_preservation: Removing taken_branch, null_explanation, top-level expression_chain, and rename_info from TraceStep is behaviour-preserving because no component reads them and the backend never emits them. KEEP taken_branch_index (read at StepCard.tsx:237). Because guards.ts:813-814/828-833 reference rename_info/null_explanation/expression_chain, removal must be coordinated with that file (a different bucket): the guard lines that construct these always-null fields would be deleted at the same time, with no runtime effect since the manufactured nulls are never consumed.

title: PdpBarChart top-padding is wrong-signed for all-negative categorical PDPs, pushing the zero baseline outside the plot
description: In PdpBarChart the y-axis top is computed as yMax = max(avg_prediction) * 1.1 and the bottom as yMin = Math.min(0, min(avg_prediction)). The *1.1 headroom only enlarges the visible range when the maximum is positive. When every categorical bar value is negative (e.g. a GLM / regression target whose predictions can go below zero — the codebase supports GLM models, see glm_coefficients/glm_relativities on TrainResult), max(avg_prediction) is negative, so yMax = negativeMax * 1.1 moves the top FURTHER from zero (more negative) instead of adding headroom. Then yMin = min(0, allNegative) = the most-negative value, and the computed zeroY = yScale(0) falls ABOVE marginTop (outside the plotting area). All bars are anchored at zeroY (barY = zeroY for negative values) and extend downward from a point above the chart, so they render partially outside the intended plot rectangle and the y grid/labels span an entirely-below-zero range. The bar-height geometry itself is self-consistent (verified: for v<0, zeroY + |v|/ySpan*chartH == yScale(v)), so this is purely a degraded/clipped visual layout, not a crash.
evidence: yVals = grid.map(p => p.avg_prediction); yMin = Math.min(0, yVals.reduce(min, Infinity)); yMax = yVals.reduce(max, -Infinity) * 1.1; ySpan = yMax - yMin || 1; zeroY = yScale(0) = marginTop + chartH - ((0 - yMin)/ySpan)*chartH. Example preds=[-5,-2]: yMin=min(0,-5)=-5, yMax=-2*1.1=-2.2, ySpan=2.8, zeroY = marginTop + chartH - (5/2.8)*chartH = marginTop - 0.786*chartH (above the top edge). Bars then start above the plot. The sibling numeric PdpLineChart pads symmetrically (yPad = (yMax-yMin)*0.1) and has no such issue.

title: Redundant single-child Fragment wrappers around the only <ChartSvg> in PdpLineChart and PdpBarChart
description: Both PdpLineChart (lines 194-242) and PdpBarChart (lines 277-341) wrap their single returned element <ChartSvg>...</ChartSvg> in a React Fragment <>...</>. The fragment contains exactly one child in each case (no sibling legend/label is rendered alongside, unlike AveChart which renders a ChartLegend next to the SVG). The wrapping fragment adds no value and the function can simply return the <ChartSvg> element directly.
evidence: PdpLineChart: `return ( <> <ChartSvg ...> ... </ChartSvg> </> )` — the fragment's only child is <ChartSvg>. PdpBarChart: identical pattern, fragment wraps only <ChartSvg>. Contrast AveChart in AveTab.tsx which legitimately uses a fragment because it returns <ChartSvg> plus a <ChartLegend>.
est_reduction: 4 lines (2 fragment open/close pairs)
behavior_preservation: Identical render output; a Fragment wrapping a single element produces the same DOM as returning that element directly.

title: Streaming chunk number input cannot be transiently cleared (empty string rejected on a controlled input)
description: The Chunk input is a controlled number input (value={streamingChunkSize}). Its onChange trims the raw value and, when raw === "", returns early WITHOUT calling setStreamingChunkSize. Because no state changes, the store value stays the same and the controlled input's value is forced back to the prior number on the next render. The net effect is that a user editing the field cannot delete all characters to type a fresh number from scratch (e.g. backspace to empty, then type) the way they would expect; they must select-all and overwrite. This is inconsistent with the sibling Rows input on line 198 (setRowLimit(Math.max(0, parseInt(e.target.value) || 0))), which gracefully treats an emptied field as 0. The existing test 'chunk input ignores non-numeric input' only covers "abc", not the empty-string clearing path, so this behavior is unverified.
evidence: onChange={(e) => { const raw = e.target.value.trim(); if (raw === "") return; const parsed = Number(raw); if (!Number.isFinite(parsed)) return; setStreamingChunkSize(parsed) }} with value={streamingChunkSize} (controlled). Empty input -> early return -> no setState -> controlled value reverts to streamingChunkSize.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

title: Steps field eagerly clamps an empty input to 1, preventing clear-and-retype (inconsistent with min/max draft handling)
description: Both Steps inputs are controlled (`value={steps}`) and their onChange is `onUpdate("steps", Math.max(1, parseInt(e.target.value) || 1))`. When the user clears the field to type a new value, `e.target.value` is "", so `parseInt("")` is NaN, `NaN || 1` is 1, and onUpdate immediately commits `steps = 1`. Because the input is controlled by that committed value, the field snaps back to "1" the instant it is emptied, so a user cannot delete the existing number and type a fresh one (e.g. clearing "21" to type "5" instantly becomes 1). This is the exact intermediate-edit problem the elaborate min/max draft state machine (activeRangeDraft + pendingConfigEcho) was built to solve, but Steps gets no draft handling at all, making the two number fields behave inconsistently. The backend already tolerates a missing/None `steps` (src/haute/_builders.py:859-861 defaults and clamps), so eager clamp-to-1 on every keystroke is unnecessary on the write path.
evidence: L217-219 (standalone) and L283-285 (range) both: value={steps}; onChange={(e) => onUpdate("steps", Math.max(1, parseInt(e.target.value) || 1))}. steps = configField(config, "steps", "") (L67) is controlled, so committing 1 on empty re-renders the field as "1".

title: Min/Max numeric draft handling is an over-engineered, fully-duplicated 4-field state machine
description: To preserve in-progress numeric text (e.g. "2.0", "-", "0.") while the parent echoes the parsed number back into config, the component maintains a 4-field ScenarioRangeDraftState ({config, committedText, draft, pendingConfigEcho}) per field, a derived selector activeRangeDraft() with 5 branches comparing object identity/committedText/parsed-number equality, plus two near-identical 11-line resync effects (L93-103 and L105-115) carrying eslint-disable for set-state-in-effect, and helper closures setMinDraft/setMaxDraft/updateRangeDraft/commitRangeNumber. The entire apparatus is duplicated verbatim for min and max (every piece of state, every effect, every closure differs only by the Min/Max prefix). This is a lot of bespoke machinery and identity-tracking for a two-field decimal editor. A single small helper hook (e.g. useNumericDraft(committedText, onCommit)) parameterised over the field, or a simpler uncontrolled-with-commit-on-blur pattern, would collapse the min and max copies into one reusable unit and remove the resync effects. NOTE: behavior is currently correct and is pinned by a rich test suite (negative-zero, "0." preservation, cross-node clearing, same-value echo), so any refactor must keep those behaviors; the duplication and identity-comparison complexity are the cleanup target, not a logic change.
evidence: ScenarioRangeDraftState type (L8-13), activeRangeDraft 5-branch selector (L30-46), two duplicated effects (L93-103 / L105-115) each with `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`, and parallel min/max state+closures (L71-91, L127-154). Grep confirms this draft pattern exists in no other editor — it is unique here, not a shared util.
est_reduction: ~40-60 lines (one of the two min/max copies plus one resync effect), depending on extraction approach
behavior_preservation: Must preserve all behaviors encoded in ScenarioExpanderEditor.test.tsx: invalid-draft persistence while editing the same node, '-'/'0.'/'2.0' intermediate text retention, clearing -> onUpdate(null), same-numeric-echo retention, and stale-draft clearing on node switch. Pure structural dedupe/extraction; no semantic change.

title: Identical steps-parse expression duplicated across the two Steps inputs
description: The expression `Math.max(1, parseInt(e.target.value) || 1)` appears verbatim on both the standalone Steps input (L218) and the range-grid Steps input (L284). Only one renders at a time (gated by `!columnName` vs `columnName`), so they are guaranteed to stay in lockstep; extracting a single `clampSteps(raw)` handler (or reusing the existing utils/configField.ts `safeParseInt`, which already supplies radix 10) removes the copy-paste and the missing-radix on the inline `parseInt`.
evidence: L218 and L284 are byte-identical: onChange={(e) => onUpdate("steps", Math.max(1, parseInt(e.target.value) || 1))}. safeParseInt exists at frontend/src/utils/configField.ts:26 but is unused by any editor.
est_reduction: ~1-2 lines plus a small clarity gain
behavior_preservation: Extract identical inline handler into one named function; output for every input (empty, negative, non-numeric, valid) is unchanged.

title: Artifact-load effect has no cancellation/staleness guard; out-of-order readJson resolutions can hide the metadata panel for the current artifact
