description: The `useEffect` that loads artifact metadata fires `readJson<ArtifactMeta>(artifactPath)` on every change of `artifactPath`/`sourceType` with no in-flight cancellation flag. If the user edits the Artifact Path quickly (A -> B), two POST requests to /api/pipeline/read-json race. Each `.then` writes `setMeta({ artifactPath, data })` tagged with its OWN captured path, and the render-time derivation `loadedMeta = sourceType === 'file' && meta?.artifactPath === artifactPath ? meta.data : null` (line 55) only displays meta whose tag matches the CURRENT path. When request A resolves AFTER request B (out-of-order completion), the last write leaves `meta.artifactPath === A` while the live `artifactPath === B`, so `loadedMeta` evaluates to null and the `ArtifactMetaPanel` (line 259) silently disappears for a path that loaded successfully; it only reappears if the component re-renders for another reason or the path is re-entered. The same staleness affects `loadError` (line 56). Notably the sibling `FileBrowser` in the same `_shared.tsx` (lines 179-205) guards exactly this hazard with a `let cancelled = false` cleanup, so the established codebase idiom is being violated here.
evidence: Lines 109-123: effect body calls readJson(...).then(data => setMeta({artifactPath, data})).catch(...) and returns no cleanup. Compare _shared.tsx:179-205 which captures `let cancelled = false`, checks `if (cancelled) return` in both then/catch, and returns `() => { cancelled = true }`. Derivation at line 55 only shows meta when meta.artifactPath === current artifactPath, so a stale last-writer wins -> panel hidden.

title: Clearing the run/version selection leaves a previously-mirrored optimiser_mode stale in config
description: The mode-mirror effect early-returns when `resolvedOptimiserMode` is neither 'online' nor 'ratebook' (line 97). In `run`/`registered` mode, `resolvedOptimiserMode` becomes '' when the selection is cleared (e.g. user reselects the 'Select a run...' placeholder so `run_id` -> '' -> `selectedRun` undefined -> resolvedOptimiserMode ''). Because the effect bails on '', a previously written `config.optimiser_mode` (e.g. 'ratebook', set while a ratebook run was selected) is left in place even though no run/version is now selected. The denormalised `optimiser_mode` is the field codegen relies on to decide ratebook wiring: `_resolve_ratebook_input` (src/haute/codegen.py:316-324) skips wiring for an MLflow source only when `optimiser_mode != 'ratebook'`; with the stale 'ratebook' value it instead proceeds to wire `ratebook_input` for a selection that no longer exists. The source-type TOGGLE handler resets `optimiser_mode` to '' (line 167), but plain de-selection within the same source type does not, so config and the live picker state diverge. Confidence is medium because the downstream failure surfaces only in combination with codegen on an otherwise-incomplete (no run selected) node.
evidence: Line 97: `if (resolvedOptimiserMode !== 'online' && resolvedOptimiserMode !== 'ratebook') return` -> no write when selection cleared. resolvedOptimiserMode (75-82) returns '' once selectedRun/selectedRegisteredVersion is undefined. Toggle handler (167) clears optimiser_mode but ExperimentRunPicker onChange (MlflowModelPicker.tsx:223-232) sets run_id='' without touching optimiser_mode. codegen.py:319 keys ratebook wiring off optimiser_mode !== 'ratebook'.

location: frontend/src/hooks/useJobPolling.ts:304-312 (interacts with reconcilePollers isCurrentJob at 118-125 and the resolved-poll callback at 180-242)
title: In-flight poll that resolves after unmount reschedules itself forever (post-unmount polling leak)
description: The unmount cleanup effect only clears the currently-stored timeout handles; it does NOT delete the per-node entries from pollerState.current, and it does not invalidate configRef.current. Because isCurrentJob() decides liveness purely from `stateRef.current[nodeId] === state` (still true after unmount) and `configRef.current.jobs[nodeId]` (still the last-rendered, non-empty jobs map), an in-flight poll that resolves AFTER unmount passes the isCurrentJob guard and calls schedulePoll(state), arming a brand-new setTimeout. That timer keeps re-polling and writing to the store indefinitely after the component is gone.
evidence: schedulePoll sets state.timeoutId = setTimeout(...) (line 180). When that callback is mid-`await pollFn(...)` (line 184) and the consumer unmounts, the cleanup at 306-310 runs `clearTimeout(state.timeoutId)` on the ALREADY-FIRED handle (no-op) and never deletes pollerState entries. The promise then resolves: line 191/214 `isCurrentJob(state)` -> `stateRef.current[nodeId] === state` is true (entry not deleted) and `configRef.current.jobs[nodeId]` is the stale last config (job still present), so it returns true -> line 215 `schedulePoll(state)` arms a new timeout -> next fire polls again -> infinite loop, plus onProgress/onComplete/onFail store writes after unmount. The existing 'clears all timeouts on unmount' test (useJobPolling.test.ts:590) uses mockResolvedValue so the poll resolves and schedules T2 BEFORE unmount, and cleanup clears the not-yet-fired T2 — it never exercises a poll still in flight across unmount, so the leak is untested.

title: Redundant `lastProgressPublishedAt === 0` disjunct in queueProgress throttle gate
description: The first-publish special-case `state.lastProgressPublishedAt === 0 ||` is fully subsumed by the adjacent `elapsed >= throttleMs` condition and can never independently change the branch outcome. It is provably dead within the boolean and can be removed.
evidence: Line 142 computes `elapsed = now - state.lastProgressPublishedAt`. When `lastProgressPublishedAt === 0`, `elapsed = Date.now() - 0`, i.e. current epoch milliseconds (~1.75e12), which is always >= throttleMs (a few seconds at most, e.g. VISIBLE_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_MS = 1000). Therefore whenever the `=== 0` disjunct is true, `elapsed >= throttleMs` is already true, and the branch (immediate publishProgress) is taken regardless. Dropping `state.lastProgressPublishedAt === 0 ||` leaves behavior identical.
est_reduction: 1 sub-expression (~0 net lines; simplifies the throttle gate to a single comparison)
behavior_preservation: Identical: in every case where the removed disjunct is true the remaining comparison is also true, so the same publish-immediately branch is taken.

title: matchCounts are mis-attributed to wrong breakpoint rows when boundaries are out of order or contain blank/invalid rows
description: BreakpointGrid renders `matchCounts[i]` against breakpoint row `i` in the array's original order, but the caller (BandingEditor) computes matchCounts from `breakpointsToRules(...)`, which SORTS boundaries ascending and FILTERS out blank/non-numeric rows (and may append an extra open-ended band). The two arrays therefore do not align index-for-index whenever the user's breakpoints are not already in strict ascending numeric order, or contain a blank/invalid intermediate row. The displayed per-band match count is then attached to the wrong band, silently giving the user incorrect feedback while editing.
evidence: BreakpointGrid.tsx:251-254 renders `{matchCounts[i] ?? "—"}` keyed by row index `i` (rows are shown in raw `breakpoints` order, never sorted). In BandingEditor.tsx:149-159, for `banding === "breakpoints"`: `const contRules = breakpointsToRules(bpRules, factor.rightClosed ?? true); return contRules.map(cont => previewRows.filter(...).length)`. bandingUtils.ts:233-296 `breakpointsToRules` does `bounded.sort((a,b) => a.boundary - b.boundary)` (line 252) and skips blanks/NaN (lines 243-249), producing rules in sorted, filtered order plus an optional appended open-ended rule (lines 287-293). Trace: breakpoints rows [{boundary:"30",label:"High"},{boundary:"10",label:"Low"}] -> contRules[0]=`<=10` (Low band), contRules[1]=`10<x<=30` (High band) -> matchCounts=[count(<=10), count(10..30)]. Grid row 0 ("High") shows matchCounts[0] = the Low-band count (wrong); row 1 ("Low") shows the High-band count (wrong). With a blank intermediate row [{"10","Low"},{"",""},{"20","Mid"}], contRules has length 2 so grid row 2 ("Mid") reads matchCounts[2]=undefined -> "—", and blank row 1 reads matchCounts[1]=Mid's count. The existing test (BreakpointGrid.test.tsx:291-306) only uses already-sorted numeric rows so it passes despite the gap.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: isHeaderRow (and sibling TSV helpers/style constants) duplicated verbatim with BandingRulesGrid
description: `isHeaderRow` is byte-for-byte identical to the copy in BandingRulesGrid.tsx, and several adjacent helpers/constants are also duplicated across the two banding grid files (the header-detection + paste-range machinery and shared style classes). There is no shared module in editors/shared exporting these. Extracting `isHeaderRow` (the cleanest standalone unit) and ideally the other shared TSV/header helpers into editors/shared/tableClipboard.ts (where parsePastedGrid/buildTsv already live) would remove the duplication and keep the two grids' paste semantics in sync.
evidence: BreakpointGrid.tsx:28-31 `function isHeaderRow(cols, expected) { if (cols.length < expected.length) return false; return expected.every((header, index) => cols[index]?.trim().toLowerCase() === header.toLowerCase()) }` is identical to BandingRulesGrid.tsx:37-40. Additional duplicated identifiers/constants confirmed across both files: `ACTION_BUTTON_CLASS` (BreakpointGrid:26 vs BandingRulesGrid:175), `BOXED_INPUT_CLASS`/`BOXED_LABEL_INPUT_CLASS` (BreakpointGrid:21-22 vs BandingRulesGrid:179-180), `dropRecognizedHeaderRow`/`applyPasted*Range` share the same structure. Grep over editors/shared for `isHeaderRow|ACTION_BUTTON_CLASS|BOXED_INPUT_CLASS` returns no matches, so none is centralized.
est_reduction: ~5-8 lines immediately for isHeaderRow; up to ~30-40 lines if the shared header/paste helpers are also consolidated
behavior_preservation: Pure extraction of identical logic/constants to a shared module; no behavioral change.

title: A `started` train response with a missing `job_id` is silently surfaced as a completed model instead of failing loudly
description: In handleTrain the dispatch is: `if (result.status === "started" && result.job_id) { startTrainJob(...) } else if (result.status === "error") { completeTrainJob(...) } else { completeTrainJob(...) }`. The `&& result.job_id` guard means a response with `status === "started"` but a falsy/absent `job_id` does NOT register an async job — it falls through to the generic `else` and is stored via `completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as TrainResult)` as though training had finished. `parseTrainResponse` (frontend/src/types/guards.ts:1088-1089) validates `status` against `["started","completed","error"]` but parses `job_id` with `optionalNullableString`, so a `started`-without-`job_id` payload is a *valid* parse result and this branch is reachable. The stored object has no metrics/model_path (training never ran), yet getModellingPreview (useNodeResultsStore.ts:1098-1105) and TrainingActionsAndResults (TrainingActionsAndResults.tsx:202) only special-case `status === "error"`, so a `"started"` result renders the green 'Model trained — results in preview panel below' badge. This masks a backend contract violation instead of failing loudly, contrary to CLAUDE.md ('code should be allowed to fail loudly ... far superior to a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice'). The correct behaviour is to throw when `status === "started"` and `job_id` is missing.
evidence: Line 140: `if (result.status === "started" && result.job_id)` → async path. Lines 146-149 `else { completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as unknown as TrainResult) }` catches `status==="completed"` AND `status==="started" && !job_id`. guards.ts:1089 `job_id: optionalNullableString(...)` allows null/absent. TrainingActionsAndResults.tsx:202 `trainResult && trainResult.status !== "error" && ...` → renders success badge for a `started` result that has no real output.

title: Duplicate `else if (status === "error")` and `else` branches in handleTrain have byte-identical bodies
description: The two trailing branches of the handleTrain dispatch are identical: `else if (result.status === "error") { useNodeResultsStore.getState().completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as unknown as TrainResult) }` and `else { useNodeResultsStore.getState().completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as unknown as TrainResult) }`. The only difference is the explanatory comment ('Immediate validation error' vs 'Synchronous completion'). Since both the error and the synchronous-completion cases call `completeTrainJob` with exactly the same arguments and no third (terminalStatus) argument, the `else if` predicate is dead — collapsing it into the single `else` is behaviour-preserving and removes a redundant branch. (Distinct from the known configHash="" staleness finding, which concerns store behaviour; this is purely the redundant control flow in the component.)
evidence: Lines 143-145 and 146-149 both execute `useNodeResultsStore.getState().completeTrainJob(nodeId, result as unknown as TrainResult)` with identical args. `parseTrainResponse` restricts `status` to started|completed|error, so the `else` already covers `completed`; merging the error branch into it changes nothing observable.
est_reduction: ~2 lines
behavior_preservation: Identical: both branches invoke completeTrainJob(nodeId, result) with the same arguments; merging removes a redundant predicate without changing any call or its arguments.

title: Switching utility files discards (does not flush) the pending debounced save, losing the last edit
description: loadFile starts with `clearTimeout(saveTimer.current)` and the comment says "Flush any pending save for the previous file", but clearTimeout CANCELS the scheduled save without ever calling updateUtilityFile. autoSave (line 65-88) only persists by firing the 500ms setTimeout; there is no synchronous flush path. So if a user types in file A and then selects file B from the dropdown within the debounce window, file A's most recent change is never written to the backend. The CodeMirror editor's blur handler flushes its own 150ms buffer and calls onChange -> autoSave(activeModule, val), which merely re-arms saveTimer; loadFile(f.module) then clears that timer too, so even the blur-flushed value is dropped. The comment is actively misleading (it claims a flush that does not happen).
evidence: loadFile: `clearTimeout(saveTimer.current)` (line 113) with comment "Flush any pending save" (line 112), but no updateUtilityFile call follows. autoSave persists only inside `saveTimer.current = setTimeout(... updateUtilityFile ...)` (line 67-71). Dropdown item: `onClick={() => { setDropdownOpen(false); if (!isActive) loadFile(f.module) }}` (line 220) -> loadFile -> clearTimeout cancels the in-flight debounce. Net effect: edits made <500ms before a file switch are silently lost.

title: Editor placeholder uses a JSX string-literal attribute, so backslash-n renders as literal "\n" instead of newlines
description:
The placeholder is written as a JSX double-quoted attribute: `placeholder="# Write reusable helper functions here

import polars as pl

def my_helper(df):
    return df"`. JSX string-literal attribute values (single/double quotes) are parsed like HTML attribute text and do NOT process backslash escape sequences, so the four `
` sequences are passed verbatim. CodeMirror's placeholder() then renders the literal characters `
` on a single line rather than line breaks, producing a garbled hint. Sibling editors deliberately use the JS-expression brace form so escapes are processed: ImportsPanel.tsx:35 `placeholder={"from utility.features import *
import numpy as np
..."}` and DataSourceEditor.tsx:99 `placeholder={"SELECT *
FROM ..."}`. This file should use `placeholder={"...
..."}` for the newlines to take effect.
evidence:
Line 266: `placeholder="# Write reusable helper functions here

import polars as pl

def my_helper(df):
    return df"` (no braces). Contrast ImportsPanel.tsx:35 and DataSourceEditor.tsx:99 which wrap the multi-line string in `{}`. The mock in UtilityPanel.test.tsx:12 forwards `placeholder` to a real textarea but no test asserts its content, so the defect is uncaught.

title: Create-file failures are silently swallowed when no file is active (errorMsg set but never rendered, and no toast)
description: On create failure, handleCreate sets only errorMsg (lines 151 and 153) and, unlike every other async handler in this component, does NOT call addToast. errorMsg is rendered exclusively inside the `activeModule ? (...)` branch (line 269-273). When the user creates the first utility file (activeModule === null) and the request fails, the component renders the `else` branch (line 275-291, the "No utility files yet."/"Select a file" view), so errorMsg is dropped on the floor and the user gets no feedback at all. The other handlers (loadFiles line 102, loadFile line 122, autoSave line 83, handleDelete line 169) all surface failures via addToast; handleCreate is the inconsistent outlier and the only failure path with no user-visible signal in the no-active-file case.
evidence: handleCreate catch (line 148-155) sets `setErrorMsg(...)` with no addToast. errorMsg is rendered only at line 269 `{errorMsg && (...)}` which lives inside `{activeModule ? (` (line 259); the no-file branch begins at line 275 `: (` and never references errorMsg. Creating the first file with a backend error therefore shows nothing. Compare addToast usage at lines 83, 102, 122, 169.

title: Version <select> has no synthetic <option> for a persisted version, so the UI silently shows "latest" while config holds a different version
description: In RegisteredModelPicker the Version dropdown is a controlled <select value={configField(config, "version", "latest")}> whose only options are a hard-coded <option value="latest"> plus selectedModelVersions.map(...). selectedModelVersions is `modelVersionsFor === selectedModel ? modelVersions : []` (line 35). On mount/remount, refreshVersions is only invoked via onFocus (line 86), so before the user focuses the dropdown modelVersions is [] and modelVersionsFor is "". Therefore, if config persists a numeric version (e.g. version: "3" — exactly what gets written when the user previously picked v3 from the loaded list), the select's value is "3" but no matching <option> exists. The browser renders the first option ("latest") as the visible selection while config.version remains "3". The user is shown "latest" but the model is actually pinned to v3 (config is not mutated, so the wrong-but-pinned value is what gets saved). React also logs a controlled-component value/option-mismatch warning. The model-name dropdown (lines 58-61) and the run dropdown (lines 237-243) both guard exactly this case by injecting a synthetic <option> for an unknown persisted value; the version dropdown is the only one of the three that omits it.
evidence: Line 35: selectedModelVersions = modelVersionsFor === selectedModel ? modelVersions : []. Lines 84-96: <select value={configField(config,"version","latest")} onFocus={() => refreshVersions(selectedModel)}> with options = <option value="latest"> + selectedModelVersions.map(...). Initial state (hook lines 71-72): modelVersions=[], modelVersionsFor="" => selectedModelVersions=[]. With config={ registered_model:'m', version:'3' } the only rendered option is value="latest" while value prop is "3" => mismatch. Contrast with the synthetic-option guard for model (lines 58-61: `selectedModel && !models.some(m=>m.name===selectedModel) && <option value={selectedModel}>`) and run (lines 237-243). Test file __tests__/MlflowModelPicker.test.tsx only renders the Version select with config={ registered_model:'my-model' } (no version), so the default 'latest' always matches and this gap is untested.

title: configField(config, "run_id", "") recomputed four times in the Run-select block
description: Inside ExperimentRunPicker the run <select> recomputes configField(config, "run_id", "") at the value prop (line 221) and three more times in the synthetic-option block (lines 237, 239, 240). A single `const runId = configField(config, "run_id", "")` (alongside the existing selectedModel-style locals at the top of the component) would remove the repetition and read more clearly. As a side benefit it would also remove the inconsistency at line 238 where the .some() callback compares against the raw `config.run_id` instead of the coalesced `runId`, making the guard use one consistent value.
evidence: Lines 221 (value={configField(config,"run_id","")}), 237 ({configField(config,"run_id","") && ...), 238 (!runs.some(r => r.run_id === config.run_id) — raw config.run_id), 239 (<option value={configField(config,"run_id","")}>), 240 ({configField(config,"run_name","") || configField(config,"run_id","")}). Same string accessor invoked 4x in ~20 lines.
est_reduction: ~4 repeated calls collapsed to 1 local; ~3 lines net
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor; identical render output. Coalescing the line-238 comparison to use the same `runId` only changes behavior for the impossible case where config.run_id is a non-string, which the wire contract (run_id: string) excludes.

title: detectGaps reports spurious/incorrect gaps when continuous rules overlap or nest (uses predecessor upper, not running-max upper)
description: detectGaps sorts intervals by lower bound only, then in the loop compares each interval against its immediate successor using `curr.upper` (the predecessor's own upper) rather than the maximum upper bound seen so far. When an earlier-sorted interval has a wider/larger upper than a later one (i.e. the intervals overlap or one is contained in another), the comparison uses the narrower interval's upper and fabricates a gap that does not exist, or reports the wrong gap bounds. Because detectGaps is invoked only for `factor.banding === "continuous"` (hand-authored rules in BandingEditor.tsx:199), where a user can freely author overlapping/nested ranges, this surfaces a false validation warning directly to the user.
evidence: Rules A: {op1:'>=',val1:'0',op2:'<=',val2:'100'} -> [0,100]; B: {op1:'>=',val1:'10',op2:'<=',val2:'20'} -> [10,20]; C: {op1:'>=',val1:'200'} -> [200,inf). After sort-by-lower order is A(0), B(10), C(200). Loop i=1 compares curr=B (upper=20) vs next=C (lower=200): `curr.upper(20) < next.lower(200)` -> pushes 'Gap between 20 and 200'. Actual coverage [0,100] U [10,20] U [200,inf) has its only gap at (100,200); the reported '20..200' is wrong. With B contained in A and C absent, a similar inner interval can even invent a gap where none should be reported at all. The bug is the use of `intervals[i].interval.upper` instead of a running max upper carried forward across the sorted list. BandingEditor.tsx:199-202 pushes these strings straight into user-facing warnings.

title: parseRuleInterval duplicates the op/val parsing logic verbatim for op1/op2
description: The op1/val1 block (lines 37-53) and the op2/val2 block (lines 55-71) are byte-for-byte identical except for the field names. They can be unified by extracting a small local helper that takes an (op, val) pair and mutates the lower/upper/inclusive accumulators (or returns a partial), then calling it for [rule.op1, rule.val1] and [rule.op2, rule.val2]. This removes ~17 lines of duplicated branching and makes the operator handling single-sourced (so e.g. adding a new operator only needs one edit).
evidence: Lines 38-53 and 56-71 differ only in `op1/val1` vs `op2/val2`; both branch identically on '>','>=','<','<=','=','=='. A helper `applyBound(op: string, val: string)` invoked twice yields the same result. Note: last-write-wins semantics across op1/op2 (current behavior) must be preserved by applying op1 then op2 in order.
est_reduction: ~17 lines
behavior_preservation: Behavior preserved if the helper is applied op1-then-op2 in the same order, keeping the existing last-write-wins overwrite semantics and the final `lower===null && upper===null -> null` check.

title: breakpointsToRules silently emits a degenerate empty band for duplicate numeric boundaries
description: breakpointsToRules does not deduplicate boundary values. If two breakpoints carry the same numeric boundary (e.g. boundary '10' entered twice), the sort keeps both, and the second iteration produces a rule whose interval is empty: with rightClosed it emits {op1:'>', val1:'10', op2:'<=', val2:'10'} -> (10,10] which matches nothing (and left-closed yields {op1:'>=', op2:'<', same value} -> [10,10) which also matches nothing). The resulting band can never be assigned, and no warning is produced, so a user with an accidental duplicate boundary gets a silently dead band.
evidence: breakpoints=[{boundary:'10',label:'A'},{boundary:'10',label:'B'},{boundary:'',label:'C'}], rightClosed=true. bounded=[{10,'A'},{10,'B'}] after sort. Iter1 (prev=null): rule '<=10' label A. Iter2 (prev=10): rule '>10 && <=10' label B -> matchesContinuousRule(v) is false for all v (needs v>10 AND v<=10). Then open-ended '>10' label C. Band B is unreachable; no validation surfaces this because detectGaps/validateRule are not run on the breakpoints->rules output.

kind: consistency / hand-rolled parse replaceable by shared idiom
title: row_limit parses with raw parseInt(v) (no radix) instead of the imported safeParseInt helper
description: The row-limit onChange uses `Math.max(0, parseInt(v) || 0)`. `parseInt` is called with no radix argument (a lint-flagged smell) and re-implements NaN-handling via `|| 0`, even though `safeParseInt(raw, fallback)` is already imported at the top of this very file (line 3) and is used a few lines above for the seed input (line 86: `safeParseInt(e.target.value, 42)`). Replacing with `Math.max(0, safeParseInt(v, 0))` removes the missing-radix smell and matches the established idiom. This is the same finding-class already catalogued for another editor (review/04-exhaustive/raw/frontend-b1.json:1508, the GLMFactorConfig `df` field), so it is a recognised cleanup pattern in this repo.
evidence: Line 181: `onUpdate("row_limit", v === "" ? null : Math.max(0, parseInt(v) || 0));` — note `parseInt` has no radix arg and `|| 0` re-rolls NaN-safety. Compare line 86 (seed): `safeParseInt(e.target.value, 42)`. `safeParseInt` is defined utils/configField.ts:26-29 as `parseInt(raw, 10)` with NaN fallback, and is already imported on line 3. Behaviour is identical for all values a `type=number` input can emit (parseInt and parseInt(.,10) differ only on `0x`/legacy-octal prefixes the input rejects).
est_reduction: ~1 line simplified; removes one missing-radix lint smell and one duplicated NaN-guard
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-preserving for all inputs a numeric input field can produce; both paths yield the same integer and the same 0 fallback.

kind: duplicated dtype list diverging from a shared definition
title: Monotonic-constraint 'numeric only' dtype filter hard-codes a 3-element list that diverges from the sibling STRING_TYPES set
description: The monotonic-constraints row filter decides 'numeric features only' by excluding `!['Utf8','Categorical','String'].includes(c.dtype)`. The sibling GLM editor in the same folder already centralises the categorical/string dtype check as `STRING_TYPES = new Set(['Utf8','String','Categorical','str','string','object','Enum'])` (GLMFactorConfig.tsx:43). The two lists disagree: a column whose dtype string is `str`, `string`, `object`, or `Enum` is treated as categorical by GLMFactorConfig but as a numeric feature here, so it would (incorrectly) get a +1/0/-1 monotonic-constraint control. The two notions of 'string-like dtype' should share one definition rather than maintaining a narrower inline copy. (Note: the narrow 3-element list does happen to match the backend CatBoost cat-feature detector at src/haute/modelling/_algorithms.py:599 which checks `pl.Utf8, pl.Categorical, pl.String`, so for the dtype strings polars actually emits today the practical divergence is small — hence lower confidence — but the duplicated, hand-maintained list is still a consistency hazard.)
evidence: Line 251: `.filter(c => c.name !== target && c.name !== weight && !exclude.includes(c.name) && !['Utf8','Categorical','String'].includes(c.dtype))`. Compare GLMFactorConfig.tsx:43 `const STRING_TYPES = new Set(["Utf8", "String", "Categorical", "str", "string", "object", "Enum"])` used at line 46 to classify a column as categorical. dtype strings reach the frontend via `str(df[c].dtype)` (executor.py:1135 / ColumnInfo.dtype) so the exact spelling set is backend-defined and could widen over time.
est_reduction: Replace inline 3-element array with the shared STRING_TYPES set (or a shared isNumericDtype helper); removes one duplicated dtype list
behavior_preservation: For the dtype strings polars currently emits the visible rows are unchanged; only widens the exclusion to the already-agreed categorical set, eliminating a future divergence.

kind: hand-rolled NaN-handling replaceable by shared safeParseFloat
title: validation_size / holdout_size onChange use parseFloat(...) || 0 instead of the NaN-safe safeParseFloat helper
description: The four numeric size inputs (validation_size and holdout_size, in both the random and group branches) parse with `parseFloat(e.target.value) || 0`. The codebase already provides `safeParseFloat(raw, fallback)` (utils/configField.ts:20) which the sibling GLMFactorConfig uses for exactly this purpose (GLMFactorConfig.tsx:301, `safeParseFloat(e.target.value, 1.0)`). Using `safeParseFloat(e.target.value, 0)` would be the consistent idiom. This is weaker than the row_limit item because `parseFloat(...) || 0` is also used in GLMRegularizationConfig.tsx:70, so the `|| 0` form is an existing (if non-canonical) pattern; behaviour is identical here since the fallback is 0 (the one value where `|| 0` and a NaN-guard coincide).
evidence: Lines 66, 76, 152, 162 all: `parseFloat(e.target.value) || 0`. configField.ts:20-23 defines `safeParseFloat`. GLMFactorConfig.tsx:4 imports and l.301 uses it. Behaviour identical because fallback is 0: `parseFloat('') || 0 === 0` and `safeParseFloat('',0) === 0`.
est_reduction: Swap 4 occurrences to safeParseFloat for cross-editor consistency; no logic change
behavior_preservation: Fully behaviour-preserving — fallback value of 0 makes `|| 0` and a NaN-guarded parse produce identical results for every input.

title: defaultExpandedStepIds re-walks the same source-name/dependency-column traversal already implemented by targetDependencyStepIds + directInputSourceStepIds
description: defaultExpandedStepIds performs the identical step walk used by the preserve helpers: find the target index, skip the target itself, skip steps after the target, then for each remaining step match sourceNodeNames first (else dependencyColumns) via stepCreatesOrModifiesColumn. targetDependencyStepIds (the dependency-column half) and directInputSourceStepIds (the source-name half) implement the same matching, and traceStoryPreserveStepIds unions them with the target. The id set produced by defaultExpandedStepIds is provably a subset of traceStoryPreserveStepIds (target: both add it; source-name match before target: preserve adds via directInputSourceStepIds, expand adds gated by shouldDefaultExpandStep; dependency-column match before target: preserve adds via targetDependencyStepIds, expand adds gated). So defaultExpandedStepIds == preserveStepIds restricted to {before-or-at target} and {shouldDefaultExpandStep == true}. The matching logic (sourceNodeNames/dependencyColumns computation, the self-skip, the per-column loop with early return) is duplicated across these functions and must be kept in agreement by hand.
evidence: Lines 215-224 (targetDependencyStepIds dependency-column loop) and 234-238 (directInputSourceStepIds source-name loop) are reproduced at 255-272 inside defaultExpandedStepIds, with the only additions being the shouldDefaultExpandStep(step, targetStep) gate (259, 266) and the explicit target add (247-249). All three call directInputSourceNodeNames(targetStep) and/or targetStepDependencyColumns(targetStep, column) on the same inputs (231/252, 212/253).
est_reduction: ~10-15 LOC if defaultExpandedStepIds is expressed by filtering the preserve set; marginal
behavior_preservation: NOT a drop-in pure extraction. directInputSourceStepIds (line 234) scans ALL steps with no index bound, whereas defaultExpandedStepIds only matches source names for steps with index <= targetIndex (257). A naive 'filter preserveStepIds by shouldDefaultExpandStep' would therefore need to also re-impose the index<=targetIndex constraint (re-deriving each step's index), which adds back complexity and makes the net reduction small. The collapse-duplication is real but the safe form is roughly LOC-neutral; flagged for the maintainer's judgement rather than as a clear win.

title: Button visual variant (danger/success/accent) is recomputed three times in inline style
description: The inline `style` object computes the same branch selector for `background`, `border`, and `color`. Each of the three lines re-evaluates `(building && cancelFetchFn) || hasStatusError` and then `cache?.cached`, producing an identical 3-way variant decision triplicated across the properties. The variant should be computed once (e.g. `const variant = (building && cancelFetchFn) || hasStatusError ? 'danger' : cache?.cached ? 'success' : 'accent'`) and the three CSS-var lookups derived from it, removing the duplicated boolean ladder and making the danger/success/accent intent explicit.
evidence: Lines 224-226: `background: (building && cancelFetchFn) || hasStatusError ? 'var(--danger-soft)' : cache?.cached ? 'var(--success-soft)' : 'var(--accent-soft)'`, then the same `(building && cancelFetchFn) || hasStatusError ? ... : cache?.cached ? ...` ladder again for `border`, then again for `color`. Three evaluations of the same two predicates.
est_reduction: ~4 lines; removes 2 redundant evaluations of the variant predicate
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: same CSS variables selected for the same state combinations; no change to rendered output.

location: frontend/src/components/CacheFetchButton.tsx:196-210 (interaction with doFetch at 160-189 and render at 244-262)
title: Clicking 'clear' (doDelete) during a non-cancellable refresh can be silently overwritten by the completing refresh
description: When `cancelFetchFn` is absent (the Databricks consumer), starting a refresh on an already-cached resource sets `building=true` but `doFetch` does not clear `cache`, so `cache?.cached` stays true and the cache-details row (line 244) — including the 'clear' delete button (line 255) — keeps rendering and is NOT disabled. A user can therefore click 'clear' mid-refresh. `doDelete` bumps `deleteGenerationRef` and `statusGenerationRef` but NOT `fetchGenerationRef`, so when the in-flight `startFetch` later resolves its guard `fetchGenerationRef.current !== generation` still passes and it runs `setCache(data)` (cached:true), silently re-showing a cache the user just deleted. The UI flips uncached -> cached without the user re-initiating, with no error surfaced. The backend ordering of delete-vs-build is itself ambiguous, so the displayed state may not match disk.
evidence: doFetch (160-189) sets building=true but never setCache(null); render block at 244 gates only on `cache?.cached`, and the clear <button> at 255 has no `disabled`/`externalDisabled` guard, so it is clickable while building. doDelete (199-200) increments deleteGenerationRef+statusGenerationRef only; the fetch resolution guard at 171 checks fetchGenerationRef, which doDelete leaves untouched, so the late fetch `.then` overwrites the delete result at 173.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: ActualVsPredictedScatter re-subsamples to 2000 points, but the backend already caps the array at 2000 — the >2000 branch is dead
description: ActualVsPredictedScatter contains a useMemo block that, when data.length > 2000, deterministically downsamples to 2000 points (lines 189-197), plus a footer that renders "Showing 2,000 of N points (sampled)" when data.length > 2000 (lines 274-276). However, the sole production data source for `result.actual_vs_predicted` is the backend `compute_actual_vs_predicted`, which is invoked with its default `max_points=2000` (src/haute/modelling/_training_job.py:1218) and already performs stratified decile subsampling so it returns at most 2000 entries. The only production render path is ModellingPreview.tsx:117, which passes `result` straight from the store. Therefore `data.length <= 2000` is always true at runtime: the useMemo always returns `data` unchanged, and the sampled footer string is never shown. The client-side `Math.floor(i * step)` linear resampling is also strictly worse than the backend's stratified-by-decile sampling (it would re-thin an already-stratified set with a naive stride), so even if it did fire it would degrade the distribution the backend deliberately preserved. The whole >2000 path is dead under the wire contract and adds an unnecessary useMemo + branch.
evidence: Frontend: line 190 `if (data.length <= 2000) return data` then lines 191-196 build a strided sample; line 274 `data.length > 2000 ? 'Showing 2,000 of ...' : '${...} points'`. Backend: _training_job.py:1218 `actual_vs_predicted = compute_actual_vs_predicted(y_true, y_pred, w)` (no max_points override) -> _metrics.py:686-691 default `max_points: int = 2000`; for n>2000 it samples `per_decile = max_points // 10` per decile (<=2000 total), for n<=2000 returns all rows. Type contract: useNodeResultsStore.ts:65 `actual_vs_predicted?: { actual; predicted; weight }[]`. Net: `data.length` <= 2000 always, so the subsample branch and the 'sampled' footer are unreachable.
est_reduction: ~12 lines (drop the useMemo subsample block; use `data` directly; collapse the footer to a single `${data.length.toLocaleString()} points` expression)
behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving under the production wire contract: the removed branch never executes because actual_vs_predicted is always <=2000 entries. Only a synthetic caller passing >2000 raw points would observe a difference, and there is no such caller.
behavior_preservation_note: If the team wants the component to stay defensively generic for >2000 inputs, the better fix is to keep a cap but not duplicate sampling logic; however given the backend guarantee, removal is the cleaner option.

title: Stale pageIndex not reconciled when report prop shrinks; Previous button needs multiple clicks
description: pageIndex is held in state but only clamped at render time via currentPageIndex = Math.min(pageIndex, pageCount - 1). The clamp never writes back to state. When the report prop changes to one with fewer pages (e.g. user explores a 200-column dataset, pages to page 3, then explores a 60-column dataset), the SchemaTableCard instance is NOT remounted (ExploreOverviewPane keys it by the static card.key 'schema', not by node/report id - see ExploreOverviewPane.tsx:101-103), so pageIndex stays 3 while pageCount drops to e.g. 2. Render shows the clamped last page, and Next is correctly disabled. But the Previous onClick does setPageIndex(current => Math.max(current - 1, 0)) operating on the raw stale value (3 -> 2), so currentPageIndex stays Math.min(2, 1) = 1 and the visible page does not change. The user must click Previous repeatedly (3 -> 2 -> 1) before raw pageIndex falls within range and the page actually moves. The Previous button is effectively dead for the first N-(pageCount-1) clicks.
evidence: Line 133 currentPageIndex = Math.min(pageIndex, pageCount - 1) is render-only; pageIndex state is never corrected. Line 196 onClick={() => setPageIndex((current) => Math.max(current - 1, 0))} decrements raw pageIndex, not currentPageIndex. ExploreOverviewPane.tsx:102 `<div key={card.key}>` keys by 'schema' so the component is not remounted on report change; no useEffect resets pageIndex on report identity change (entire component read, none present).

title: Search query and page index persist across dataset/node switches with no reset
description: query and pageIndex are component-local state that is never reset when the report prop changes, because the component is keyed by the static card key 'schema' (ExploreOverviewPane.tsx:101-103) rather than by node/report identity, and there is no useEffect keyed on report. If a user searches the schema of dataset A (e.g. query 'amount') and then switches the explored node to dataset B without clearing the box, dataset B's schema is silently filtered by A's stale query. The search input itself is only rendered when columnCount > 50 (line 169), so if B has <=50 columns the user sees a filtered/empty table ('(no matching columns)') with NO visible search box to discover or clear the active filter. pageIndex similarly carries over (mitigated only by the clamp).
evidence: useState('') for query (line 114) and useState(0) for pageIndex (line 115) are only reset by handleQueryChange (line 141-144) on user typing; nothing resets them when `report` changes. Filtering at line 117-131 uses normalisedQuery unconditionally. The controls block (line 169) gates on columnCount > SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE, so a small new report hides the search box while the stale query still filters visibleColumns, surfacing the '(no matching columns)' empty state at line 254-264 with no way to clear it.

title: Duplicated null-ratio bucketing across nullSeverity and nullPctStyle
description: nullSeverity and nullPctStyle independently compute the identical ratio (nullCount / rowCount) * 100 and branch on the exact same thresholds in the same order: rowCount === 0, pct > 50, pct === 0, else. They map the same four buckets to a severity string and to a style object respectively. SchemaRow (lines 72-74) then calls both PLUS formatNullPct, computing the same ratio a third time. A single classifier (e.g. classifyNullBucket(nullCount, rowCount) -> 'empty' | 'high' | 'none' | 'normal') consumed by both call sites would remove the duplicated threshold logic and keep severity and colour guaranteed in sync (today a future edit to one threshold can silently desync the colour from the data-null-severity attribute).
evidence: Lines 39-45 (nullSeverity) and 57-63 (nullPctStyle) have byte-for-byte equivalent control flow: `if (rowCount === 0) ...; const pct = (nullCount / rowCount) * 100; if (pct > 50) ...; if (pct === 0) ...; return <default>`. SchemaRow lines 72-74 invoke formatNullPct, nullPctStyle, nullSeverity in sequence on the same (column.null_count, rowCount).
est_reduction: ~10-14 lines and one of three redundant ratio computations per row
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: a shared bucket classifier reproduces the same severity strings and style objects for every input; no visible output changes.

title: Pagination/search gate keyed on report.column_count but slicing keyed on report.columns.length
description: The controls (search + pager) are gated on columnCount = report.column_count > SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE (lines 113, 169), but the actual data path - filteredColumns, pageCount, visibleColumns - is driven entirely by report.columns / report.columns.length (lines 118, 132, 135). The backend currently guarantees column_count === len(columns) (_explore_service.py:808-809 sets column_count=len(schema.names()) and columns=frame_stats.columns, one stat per schema name), so today they agree. But the component trusts two different fields for the same quantity: if report.columns.length > 50 while report.column_count <= 50 (any wire skew, partial payload, or future backend change where column_count is a declared/summary count), the table would render only visibleColumns.slice(0,50) and silently drop the remaining rows because the pager that would page to them is never rendered. The gate should be derived from the same array that is sliced (report.columns.length / filteredColumns.length).
evidence: Line 113 columnCount = report.column_count; line 169 `columnCount > SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE` gates the controls. Line 132 pageCount = Math.ceil(filteredColumns.length / SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE); line 135 visibleColumns = filteredColumns.slice(firstVisibleIndex, firstVisibleIndex + SCHEMA_PAGE_SIZE). filteredColumns derives from report.columns (line 118). The two source fields are distinct properties of ExploreCacheReport (api/types.ts:456-459).

title: Selection-reset effect round-trips feature names through join(",")/split(","), corrupting any feature whose name contains a comma
description: featureKey is built as featureItems.map(f => f.feature).join(",") (line 51), and the reset effect then reconstructs the feature-name list inside itself via featureKey.split(",") (line 60) to decide the default/fallback selection. If any feature name contains a comma, the split produces the wrong number of tokens and the wrong substrings. Consequences: (a) names.includes(selectedFeature) can never match the real (comma-containing) selected feature, so the effect believes the selection is invalid and overwrites it; (b) setSelectedFeature(names[0]) (line 63) sets the selection to a corrupted prefix substring that does not exist in aveData, so selectedData (line 72-75) resolves to null and the user is stuck on the 'Select a feature' empty state for that dataset. Feature names are user-supplied data-frame column names (CSV/parquet headers), which are not guaranteed comma-free. The full featureItems array is already in lexical scope inside the effect, so the join/split round-trip is both the source of the bug and unnecessary: names could be computed directly as featureItems.map(f => f.feature) (comma-safe), keeping featureKey solely as the primitive effect dependency. The same pattern exists in the sibling PdpTab, but this bucket is scoped to AveTab.
evidence: Line 51: const featureKey = featureItems.map(f => f.feature).join(","). Line 60 inside the effect: const names = featureKey.split(","). For a feature named e.g. "city, state", join yields "...,city, state,..." and split re-tokenises it into ["city"," state"], so names no longer equals the real feature set. Line 61: !names.includes(selectedFeature) is then true for the real name, and line 63 setSelectedFeature(names[0]) may assign a fragment like "city" that aveData.find (line 74) cannot match, leaving selectedData null (line 89 renders the empty state). featureItems is in scope at line 58, so the round-trip is avoidable.

title: AveChart x-axis label truncation collapses distinct categorical levels sharing a 9-char prefix into byte-identical labels with no disambiguation
description: truncLabel (line 149) shortens a label to maxLen via s.slice(0, maxLen - 1) + ellipsis, and the x-axis ticks call truncLabel(b.label, 10) (line 214), keeping only the first 9 characters before the ellipsis. Two distinct categorical bins whose labels share a 9-character prefix (e.g. "MERCEDES_BENZ_C200" vs "MERCEDES_BENZ_C220") therefore render the identical x-axis <text> ('MERCEDES_…'). There is no tooltip, title element, or other disambiguation on the bins/points, so a genuinely mis-calibrated bin (high avg_actual vs avg_predicted divergence) cannot be attributed to the correct level off the chart. This is the same defect class already catalogued for the backend static SVG renderer (render_ave_feature_svg / _render_dual_axis_chart in _charts.py), but it is a distinct, separately-rendered surface: the interactive in-app React chart, which has its own truncation width (10 vs the backend's 15) and no fallback hover text.
evidence: Line 149: const truncLabel = (s, maxLen) => s.length > maxLen ? s.slice(0, maxLen - 1) + "…" : s. Line 214: const label = truncLabel(b.label, 10) -> for any label longer than 10 chars only label.slice(0,9) + '…' is emitted. Distinct backend categorical levels (e.g. produced by _ave_categorical_bins in _metrics.py) that agree on their first 9 characters map to the same displayed string. The <text> at lines 218-228 carries no title/aria/tooltip, so no other element distinguishes the two bins.

title: Failed explore cancel leaves panel showing "Ready" instead of an error state
description: In handleCancel's catch branch, failExploreJob is called with only (nodeId, message) and no terminalStatus. failExploreJob (useNodeResultsStore.ts:1056-1086) then stores the cached explore result with terminalStatus: null (terminalStatus ?? null) and error: message. After the job is removed from exploreJobs, the component's status derivation `status = currentExploreJob?.progress ?? currentCachedResult?.terminalStatus ?? null` resolves to null, so statusMessage(null, false) returns "Ready". The subtitle then reads e.g. "pricing | Ready" for a node whose cancel actually errored, while the only error signal is a transient toast that disappears. This is inconsistent with the startup-failure path (line 141-147) which passes a terminalStatus of {status:"error"} and correctly renders "Error". The stored error string is also never surfaced anywhere in the panel (currentCachedResult.error is read by no JSX), so once the toast clears the user sees a benign "Ready" for a failed operation.
evidence: handleCancel catch: `failExploreJob(nodeId, message)` (no 3rd arg) -> store sets terminalStatus=null, error=message. Render: status = currentExploreJob?.progress(null, job removed) ?? currentCachedResult?.terminalStatus(null) ?? null => null. statusMessage(null,false) => "Ready". Compare success path line 179 `failExploreJob(nodeId, cancelled.message||..., cancelled)` which yields "Cancelled".

title: GPU-only params silently fabricate and then persist DEFAULT_PARAMS
description: When the incoming params contain only the GPU flag (params = { task_type: "GPU" }), displayParams is {} so effectiveParams falls back to DEFAULT_PARAMS. The textarea then shows iterations/learning_rate/depth/l2_leaf_reg/early_stopping_rounds that are NOT actually part of the saved config (misrepresentation of persisted state). Worse, because `draft` is seeded from those defaults, the next commit bakes them in: toggling the GPU checkbox off runs handleGpuToggle(false) -> current = JSON.parse(draft) = DEFAULT_PARAMS -> onUpdate("params", { ...DEFAULT_PARAMS }), silently writing 5 hyperparameters the user never chose. Likewise a blur commits { ...DEFAULT_PARAMS, task_type: "GPU" }. This state is reachable from any node/pipeline config authored outside this panel that sets params to just { task_type: GPU }.
evidence: L40 `const { task_type: _taskType, ...displayParams } = params` -> for params={task_type:'GPU'}, displayParams={}. L41 `effectiveParams = Object.keys(displayParams).length > 0 ? displayParams : DEFAULT_PARAMS` -> effectiveParams=DEFAULT_PARAMS. L42/46 draft and serialised = JSON.stringify(DEFAULT_PARAMS). L71 `current = JSON.parse(draft)` = DEFAULT_PARAMS. L72 disable branch `onUpdate('params', { ...current })` persists all 5 defaults. The DEFAULT_PARAMS fallback is meant for a genuinely empty config, but it also fires for GPU-only configs where the user has intentionally left hyperparameters unset.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Feature-column derivation duplicated three times
description: The expression `columns.filter(c => c.name !== target && c.name !== weight).map(c => c.name)` is written twice in this component (the Deselect-all onClick at L117-120 and the render IIFE at L131-133), and the equivalent filter `columns.filter(c => c.name !== target && c.name !== weight && !exclude.includes(c.name))` is also computed by the parent ModellingConfig (L118) to produce featureCount. The render IIFE additionally rebuilds `new Set(staleExcludes)` (already available as a memoised concept) each render. Hoisting a single `const featureCols = useMemo(() => columns.filter(...).map(c => c.name), [columns, target, weight])` and reusing it removes the duplication and keeps the include/exclude list and the count in sync from one definition.
evidence: L117-120 (Deselect all): `columns.filter(c => c.name !== target && c.name !== weight).map(c => c.name)`. L131-133 (render): same expression assigned to `featureCols`. Parent L118 computes featureCount with the same predicate plus `!exclude.includes`.
behavior_preservation: Pure extraction of an identical expression into a memo; rendered output and onUpdate payloads are unchanged.

title: Excluded-count in summary counts stale entries, disagreeing with the rendered list
description: The collapsed/expanded summary shows `{featureCount} of {columns.length}, {exclude.length} excluded`. featureCount (from the parent) only subtracts excludes that actually exist in columns, but `exclude.length` includes stale entries (excludes with no matching upstream column). When the exclude list contains a stale name, the header reports e.g. '2 excluded' while only one real column is excluded and the stale one is rendered separately under a 'not found' row with its own 'Remove all stale' control. The 'excluded' figure should count only real (non-stale) excludes to match what the list and featureCount represent.
evidence: L101 renders `${exclude.length} excluded`. Parent L118: featureCount = columns.filter(... && !exclude.includes(c.name)).length, so a stale exclude never reduces featureCount, yet it still increments exclude.length. With exclude=['age','ghost'] and only 'age' in columns: featureCount drops by 1 but the label says '2 excluded'. staleExcludes (L82-85) already isolates the stale set, so exclude.length - staleExcludes.length is the real excluded count.

title: Candidate Curve chart suppressed when candidates have finite objective but non-finite decision_score (objective dashed line never shown)
description: The entire 'Candidate Curve' SVG section is gated by `points.length > 0`. `points` is derived from `optimiserChartPath(...).points`, which contains ONLY candidates whose `decision_score` is finite (optimiserApplyHelpers.ts:154-164 builds `points` from `scoreCandidates`, i.e. `isFiniteNumber(point.scoreValue)`). However `optimiserChartPath` independently computes a non-empty `objectivePath` whenever any candidate has a finite `objective` (helpers:157-167). So when every candidate has a finite `objective` but no candidate has a finite `decision_score` (decision_score emitted as a NaN/Inf sentinel via the `__haute_type__: non_finite_float` wire encoding that formatValue/formatJsonSpecialValue explicitly supports), `objectivePath` is a valid path string but `points.length === 0`, and the whole chart block (including the objective dashed line, axes, and legend) is hidden even though there is renderable objective data. The gate should also consider the objective curve, e.g. `(points.length > 0 || objectivePath) && (...)`.
evidence: OptimiserApplyDetail.tsx:40 `const { points, objectivePath, scorePath } = optimiserChartPath(displayCandidates)`; line 97 `{points.length > 0 && (` wraps the <TraceDetailSection title="Candidate Curve">. helpers:128 keeps a candidate if `isFiniteNumber(objective) || isFiniteNumber(decision_score)`; helpers:160-164 `points = scoreCandidates.map(...)` where scoreCandidates filters on finite scoreValue only; helpers:165-167 `objectivePath` is built from objectiveCandidates (finite objective) independently. Thus objectivePath can be non-empty while points is empty, and line 97 still suppresses the section.

title: Selected-scenario score equation silently drops non-finite lambda terms, so displayed addends need not equal displayed score
description: The selected-scenario callout renders a literal equation `objective <objective> + lambda <name> <value> ... = score <decision_score>`. The addends come from `selectedLambdaEntries = finiteRecordEntries(selected?.lambda_terms)`, which filters out any lambda term that is not a finite number (optimiserApplyHelpers.ts:18-21). The right-hand side `selected.decision_score` is rendered verbatim. If `lambda_terms` contains a non-finite term (NaN/Inf sentinel, which the formatValue layer explicitly models), that term is omitted from the shown sum while still being reflected in the backend `decision_score`, so the rendered equation does not visually add up (objective + shown_terms != shown_score). The plus-separated layout presents this as an arithmetic identity, so the silent omission is misleading rather than merely incomplete. Showing the term (e.g. as NaN/Infinity, consistent with formatValue's sentinel handling) would keep the equation faithful.
evidence: Line 41 `const selectedLambdaEntries = finiteRecordEntries(selected?.lambda_terms)`; helpers:18-21 `finiteRecordEntries` keeps only entries where `isFiniteNumber(entry[1])`. Lines 80-92 render `{objectiveLabel}{selected.objective}` then `selectedLambdaEntries.map(([name,value]) => ...'+ lambda name value')` then `=score {selected.decision_score}` — the LHS omits any non-finite lambda term while the RHS shows the full decision_score.

title: Input-port node created before child-membership filter -> orphan port nodes (asymmetric with output-port handling)
description: In handleDrillIntoSubmodel, the input-port construction creates a SUBMODEL_PORT node for every parent source (line 120) and only afterwards filters which child edges to draw with `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue` (line 127). The output-port construction does the opposite: it applies the membership filter during grouping (line 146 `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue`) and additionally requires `e.sourceHandle` (line 141), so a target with no valid in-submodel children never enters `outputsByTarget` and no orphan output port is created. Because of this asymmetry, any parent edge that targets the submodel node but resolves to a childId not present in the submodel (e.g. `targetHandle` missing -> childId becomes the sentinel `"__unconnected__"`, line 111; or a stale `in__<id>` handle after edit/dissolve/re-create cycles) still produces an input port node (`port_in__<srcId>`) with zero connecting edges. That orphan node is passed to getLayoutedElements and rendered with no edges. There is no later pruning of edge-less port nodes.
evidence: Input branch: inputsBySource groups e.source -> childIds (including "__unconnected__" sentinel). For each srcId it unconditionally `newNodes.push(validateReactFlowNode({id: port_in__<srcId>, ...}))` (120-125), THEN loops children with `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue` (126-127). So a source whose only target child is "__unconnected__" (or any non-member id) yields a port node but no edge. Output branch filters first (146 `if (!childIds.has(childId)) continue` before adding to outputsByTarget), so no equivalent orphan output port is ever created. Symmetric fix would skip creating the input port when none of its targetChildIds are in childIds.

title: Duplicated submodel API request-payload construction in handleCreateSubmodel and handleDissolveSubmodel
description: handleCreateSubmodel and handleDissolveSubmodel build an identical graph object (`{ nodes: graphRef.current.nodes, edges: graphRef.current.edges, submodels: submodelsRef.current }`) and pass the same four contextual ref fields (preamble: preambleRef.current, source_file: sourceFileRef.current, pipeline_name: pipelineNameRef.current, pipeline_description: descriptionRef.current). The only differing field is the operation-specific key (name+node_ids vs submodel_name). The shared portion could be produced by one small helper (e.g. `buildSubmodelContext()`), removing the copy-paste and the risk of the two call sites drifting (e.g. one forgetting to include submodels or pipeline_description).
est_reduction: ~8 lines / 1 small helper
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: helper returns the same object literals; request payloads to createSubmodel/dissolveSubmodel are byte-identical, so no behavioral change.

title: GPU VRAM estimate scaled by wrong denominator (safe_row_limit instead of total_rows), overstating VRAM whenever RAM downsampling applies
description: The reactive `adjusted` memo rescales the backend's `gpu_vram_estimated_mb` to the user's effective GPU row count, but uses `originalRows = safe_row_limit ?? sourceRows` as the baseline the backend estimate was computed at. The backend actually computes that estimate at `total_rows` (full source rows), NOT at `safe_row_limit`. So whenever `was_downsampled` is true (i.e. `safe_row_limit < total_rows`), the displayed GPU VRAM is inflated by a factor of `sourceRows / safe_row_limit`. This also feeds the warning banner at lines 170-177 ("GPU training needs ~X but GPU has Y. Training will fall back to CPU automatically."), so a spurious CPU-fallback warning can be shown to the user even when the GPU could actually fit the workload.
evidence: Backend: src/haute/routes/modelling.py:196 sets `effective_rows = ram_est.total_rows or 0` and line 203 calls `_check_gpu_vram(effective_rows, ...)`, whose result populates `gpu_vram_estimated_mb` (line 218). So the baseline row count for the estimate is `total_rows == sourceRows`. Frontend TrainingActionsAndResults.tsx: line 76 `gpuRows = hasUserLimit ? Math.min(rowLimit, sourceRows) : sourceRows`; line 77 `originalRows = ramEstimate.safe_row_limit ?? sourceRows`; line 79 `gpuVramMb = gpuVramMb * gpuRows / originalRows`. Case: total_rows=100000, safe_row_limit=50000 (was_downsampled), no user rowLimit -> gpuRows=100000, originalRows=50000, gpuRows!==originalRows so it scales B*100000/50000 = 2*B, doubling the estimate the backend already computed for 100000 rows. With a user limit L: scales B*min(L,source)/safe_row_limit instead of the correct B*min(L,source)/sourceRows, still overstated by sourceRows/safe_row_limit. The correct denominator is `total_rows` (sourceRows). Not covered by TrainingActionsAndResults.test.tsx (no test sets gpu_vram_estimated_mb together with safe_row_limit).

title: CANONICAL_LINKS has an unreachable 'quasibinomial' entry — no such family exists in FAMILIES
description: `CANONICAL_LINKS` maps `quasibinomial -> logit`, but `quasibinomial` is not present in the `FAMILIES` array (lines 7-15), which is the only source of selectable family values. `family` is read via `configField(config, "family", "poisson")` and is only ever set by the family buttons (line 126 `family: f.value`), so it can never take the value `"quasibinomial"`. The lookup `CANONICAL_LINKS[family]` therefore never reads this key, making it dead data. The design doc (docs/GLM_INTEGRATION_DESIGN.md:120) lists quasibinomial as an intended family, but the UI never offers it (line 586 of the doc's mock and the FAMILIES array both omit it), so the entry is a leftover.
evidence: FAMILIES values (lines 8-14): poisson, gamma, tweedie, gaussian, binomial, quasipoisson, negbinomial — no quasibinomial. CANONICAL_LINKS (lines 18-25) includes `quasibinomial: "logit"` (line 24). Grep for 'quasibinomial' across the repo returns only this file and the design doc; it is never referenced in backend code. Since `family` can only equal a FAMILIES value, `CANONICAL_LINKS["quasibinomial"]` is unreachable.
est_reduction: 1 line
behavior_preservation: Removing the unreachable map entry changes no behaviour: the key is never looked up because no family value equals 'quasibinomial'. All existing GLMComponents.test.tsx assertions (which only exercise the 7 real families) remain green.

title: Flat-lambda branch of frontierLambdaEntries uses frontierPointNumber where requiredPointNumber is the exact parallel
description: In the fallback (flat lambda_*) branch of frontierLambdaEntries, each value is read via frontierPointNumber(point, key) with no nestedKey/nestedName/alternateFlatKey arguments. With only flatKey supplied, frontierPointNumber degenerates to exactly optionalPointNumber(point[flatKey]) followed by a throw on null - which is precisely what requiredPointNumber(point[key], key) does. The sibling branch (the point.lambdas object case, line 73) already uses requiredPointNumber. Using requiredPointNumber(point[key], key) in the flat branch would make the two branches symmetric and avoid routing through the multi-key resolver whose nested/alternate machinery is unreachable here.
evidence: Line 79: .map((key) => [key.replace(/^lambda_/, ""), frontierPointNumber(point, key)]). frontierPointNumber(point, key) -> optionalPointNumber(point[key], key); if null, no nestedKey/alternateFlatKey so it throws 'missing numeric '+key. requiredPointNumber(value, field) -> optionalPointNumber(value, field); if null throws 'missing numeric '+field. Both throw on null/non-finite and return the finite number otherwise. The object branch at line 73 already calls requiredPointNumber(value, `lambdas.${name}`).
est_reduction: ~0 LOC (clarity/symmetry; removes an unreachable resolver path for this call site)
behavior_preservation: Identical: both helpers return the finite number when present and throw when the value is null/missing/non-finite. Only the thrown message field-prefix style differs cosmetically; values rendered are unchanged.

title: buildExecutionFailureMessage drops UI options when delegating to buildExecutionDiagnostic, silently suppressing the memory diagnostic when metrics.status is a non-memory terminal reason
description: buildExecutionFailureMessage decides a failure is memory-limited via isMemoryLimitedFailure(metrics, resolvedOptions), which considers options.status / options.terminalReason / options.errorCode in addition to metrics.terminal_reason. But when it then builds the human message it calls buildExecutionDiagnostic(metrics) WITHOUT forwarding resolvedOptions. Inside, shouldShowMemoryPressureDiagnostic(metrics, {}) re-derives the memory signal using only metrics.* and, crucially, suppresses the diagnostic whenever metrics.status (or metrics.terminal_reason) is a non-memory terminal reason. So if the memory signal arrived via the explicit options.status='memory_limited' (e.g. job-level terminal reason) while the embedded metrics.status is 'error'/'contract_error'/'timed_out'/'cancelled'/'superseded', the outer guard passes (memory) but the inner re-check fails (non-memory), buildExecutionDiagnostic returns null, and the function falls back to the bare base message — dropping the memory-pressure detail the caller intended to surface.
evidence: Line 199 guard: isMemoryLimitedFailure(metrics, resolvedOptions) — true when resolvedOptions.status='memory_limited'. Line 203: buildExecutionDiagnostic(metrics) — options NOT passed. buildExecutionDiagnostic -> shouldShowMemoryPressureDiagnostic(metrics, {}) (line 174). With options={}, isMemoryLimitedFailure(metrics,{}) checks only metrics.terminal_reason; then lines 162-163 isNonMemoryTerminalReason(metrics.terminal_reason)/isNonMemoryTerminalReason(metrics.status) return true if metrics.status is e.g. 'error' -> returns false -> diagnostic null -> line 204 returns baseMessage?.trim()||prefix. The existing test at executionDiagnostics.test.ts:111 only survives because the fixture default metrics.status='running' (non-terminal); the divergent metrics.status='error' case is untested and regresses to the generic message.

title: setSources can leave activeSource pointing at a non-existent 'live' source, breaking the invariant removeSource enforces
description: setSources resets activeSource to the literal 'live' whenever the incoming list does not contain the current activeSource (line 166). This assumes 'live' is always a member of the new list, but setSources accepts an arbitrary array and does not guarantee/insert 'live'. Calling setSources with a list that omits 'live' (e.g. setSources(['foo'])) leaves activeSource='live' referencing a source that is not in sources. removeSource deliberately hard-blocks removing 'live' (line 177) to preserve exactly this invariant, so the two setters are asymmetric: the 'live-always-present' assumption baked into the fallback is enforced by removeSource but silently violable via setSources.
evidence: Line 166: activeSource: sources.includes(s.activeSource) ? s.activeSource : 'live'. If sources=['foo'] and current activeSource='bar', result is activeSource='live' while sources has no 'live'. Contrast removeSource line 177: if (name==='live') return s (cannot remove live). The fallback target 'live' is never validated against the new sources array.

title: _mlflowFetching store field is write-only redundant state; concurrency is actually gated by the module-level _mlflowFetchingGuard
description: The store exposes a boolean _mlflowFetching that is written on fetch start (set true, line 104) and in finally (set false, line 156), but it is never read anywhere for control flow. The actual re-entrancy guard for fetchMlflow is the module-level variable _mlflowFetchingGuard (lines 19/101/103/155). A grep shows _mlflowFetching is referenced only inside test files for assertions, never by any .tsx component nor by the gating logic. It duplicates the information already held by _mlflowFetchingGuard, adding two set() calls (extra re-renders for any subscriber) and store surface for no behavioural benefit.
evidence: Gate uses the module var: line 101 if (_mlflowFetchingGuard) return; line 103 _mlflowFetchingGuard=true; line 155 _mlflowFetchingGuard=false. _mlflowFetching is only set (lines 104,156), never read for logic. Grep of frontend/src/**/*.tsx for _mlflowFetching returns only App.*.test.tsx and the store test — zero production consumers.
est_reduction: ~3 lines + 2 set() calls + interface field; one fewer store field to reason about
behavior_preservation: Removing _mlflowFetching and its two set() writes preserves behaviour because the field gates nothing; only the test assertions referencing it would need to switch to observing mlflow.status. No component reads it.

title: Ctrl+Shift+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z redo is unreachable (contradictory key+shift check) — breaks keyboard redo, the only redo shortcut on macOS
description: The redo branch requires `mod && e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey && !isTyping`. In every real browser, holding Shift changes the printable key value, so pressing Shift+Z yields `e.key === "Z"` (uppercase), never `"z"`. Therefore the condition `e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey` can never be simultaneously true: when `shiftKey` is true the key is `"Z"`. The standard redo accelerator Ctrl+Shift+Z (Windows/Linux) and Cmd+Shift+Z (macOS) is dead. On macOS there is no Ctrl+Y fallback (line 60 only helps Windows users), so keyboard redo is completely non-functional for Mac users. The undo branch at line 49 (`e.key === "z" && !e.shiftKey`) works because Ctrl alone does not alter the character.
evidence: Line 49 undo: `if (mod && e.key === "z" && !e.shiftKey && !isTyping)`. Line 54 redo: `if (mod && e.key === "z" && e.shiftKey && !isTyping)`. Browser semantics: Shift+Z => KeyboardEvent.key === "Z". So line 54 is unreachable in real browsers; Cmd+Shift+Z on Mac matches NO handler (lines 49/54/60 all fail) => nothing happens, no preventDefault. The unit test (useKeyboardShortcuts.test.ts:67-70) fires `new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'z', shiftKey: true })` — an artificial combination browsers never emit — so it passes while masking the real-browser breakage.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: All letter-key shortcuts silently break when CapsLock is on (no e.key case normalization)
description: Every letter shortcut compares the raw `e.key` against a lowercase literal: Ctrl+S (`"s"`), Ctrl+Z (`"z"`), Ctrl+Y (`"y"`), Ctrl+C (`"c"`), Ctrl+V (`"v"`), Ctrl+A (`"a"`), Ctrl+K (`"k"`), Ctrl+G (`"g"`). When CapsLock is active, the browser reports the uppercase key value (e.g. `e.key === "S"`), so none of these comparisons match and every letter shortcut — including save, undo, copy, paste, select-all — silently stops working with no feedback. The handler never normalizes case (no `e.key.toLowerCase()`), so the behaviour depends on the user's CapsLock state. Shares a root cause with the Ctrl+Shift+Z bug: normalizing the key once (`const key = e.key.toLowerCase()`) fixes both.
evidence: Line 42 `e.key === "s"`, line 49/54 `"z"`, line 60 `"y"`, line 67 `"c"`, line 81 `"v"`, line 122 `"a"`, line 136 `"k"`, line 157 `"g"`. No `toLowerCase()` anywhere in the file. CapsLock on => `e.key` is uppercase for letters => all these strict-equality checks fail. No test exercises uppercase keys (grep for `toLowerCase|getModifierState|key: "[A-Z]"` returns nothing in hook and test).
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Paste generates colliding edge ids for parallel edges (id derived only from node ids, ignoring handles)
description: When pasting copied nodes, each new edge id is built solely from the remapped source/target node ids: `id: `e-${newSource}-${newTarget}``. The copied edges spread `...ed` (retaining distinct `sourceHandle`/`targetHandle`), so a selection containing two parallel edges between the same node pair (e.g. an edgeJoin with `role-left`/`role-right` target handles, both fed from copies of the same upstream node) produces two new edges with identical ids. React Flow requires unique edge ids; duplicate ids cause one edge to be dropped or render incorrectly. The id should incorporate the handles (as the rest of the edge layer keys on sourceHandle/targetHandle — see useEdgeHandlers.ts:142-143, edgeJoinCanonicalTargetHandle).
evidence: Line 113: `return [{ ...ed, id: `e-${newSource}-${newTarget}`, source: newSource, target: newTarget }]`. Two copied edges with same source/target node but different targetHandle (legal per useEdgeHandlers role handles) => same `newSource`/`newTarget` => identical generated id. Contrast: edge creation elsewhere preserves sourceHandle/targetHandle (useEdgeHandlers.ts:181-201) precisely because the pair is not unique.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: useUIStore() subscribed without a selector forces App to re-render on every UI-store mutation
description: The hook calls `const { setShortcutsOpen, setSubmodelDialog, setNodeSearchOpen } = useUIStore()` with no selector, subscribing the consuming component (App, the top-level component) to the entire UI store. Any UI-store change (hoveredNodeId, paletteOpen, nodePanelWidth, explorePanes, etc.) re-renders App even though this hook only ever needs three referentially-stable setters. The file is inconsistent with itself one line up — line 32 uses a selector (`useToastStore((s) => s.addToast)`). Because the setters are stable Zustand actions, a selector (or `useUIStore.getState()` inline, mirroring how the hook already reads `useUIStore.getState().nodeSearchOpen` at line 136) avoids the spurious subscription with no behavior change.
evidence: Line 33: `const { setShortcutsOpen, setSubmodelDialog, setNodeSearchOpen } = useUIStore()`. Store (useUIStore.ts:62) defines actions once in `create((set) => ({...}))` so they are stable; the no-selector subscription only adds re-renders. Line 32 already demonstrates the selector idiom; line 136 already uses `useUIStore.getState()` for one-off reads.
est_reduction: ~1 line changed; removes whole-store subscription on the top-level App component
behavior_preservation: Setters are stable store actions; reading them via a selector or getState yields identical references and identical handler behavior, only reducing re-render frequency.

title: Error path sets columns to [] without updating prevColumnFingerprint, can wedge state empty against a later equal-schema cache
description: The fetch .catch handler does `if (!cachedColumnsRef.current) setDataInputColumns([])` but never updates `prevColumnFingerprint.current`. Every OTHER place that calls setDataInputColumns first writes the new fingerprint into prevColumnFingerprint (lines 102, 111, 118, 127, 132, 156). After a no-cache error with a NON-empty `fallbackColumns`, state becomes [] while prevColumnFingerprint still holds fp(fallback). If the store cache is later populated externally with columns whose fingerprint equals that stale prev (e.g. the same schema as the fallback), the sync effect (lines 100-105) compares fp(cache) === prev and SKIPS the update, leaving the hook permanently returning [] even though valid cached columns now exist. The invariant 'prevColumnFingerprint mirrors the currently displayed columns' is silently broken only on this branch.
evidence: Line 166 `if (!cachedColumnsRef.current) setDataInputColumns([])` with no accompanying `prevColumnFingerprint.current = columnFingerprint([])` (which would be the EMPTY_COLUMNS_FINGERPRINT "0:"). Contrast every successful update which pairs the setState with a prev write (e.g. lines 155-157). Reachability: requires `enabled` true with a non-empty `fallbackColumns` (so initial prev = fp(fallback), not "0:"), then a rejected fetch with no cache, then an external cache populate matching the fallback schema. The current sole caller (OptimiserConfig.tsx:277-280) only enables the hook when `fallbackDataInputColumns` is empty, so it avoids the trigger today, but the hook is a reusable public API and the missing fingerprint write is a genuine state-sync defect.

title: readV2 silently downgrades an unknown column `type` to "str", defeating the backend's B1 loud-fail guardrail on editor round-trip
description: readV2 coerces any column `type` that is not one of int|float|str|bool|date to "str" (the `ALLOWED_TYPES.has(...) ? cc.type : "str"` branch). The backend mirror `_api_input_schema.py` deliberately does the OPPOSITE: guardrail B1 (validate_v2_schema, lines 368-376) raises ApiInputSchemaError on an unknown type precisely because — per its own comment — 'Today's silent downgrade to str (in _json_shred.py) loses information; loud-fail ... forces the user to correct typos.' Because the editor reads via readV2 (ApiInputEditor.tsx:171,287-291) and persists via writeV2 (volatileSchema at :408 + save), a config that arrived with e.g. `type:"decimal"` is silently rewritten to `type:"str"`, which then PASSES B1. So any config opened+saved in the editor bypasses the very guardrail the backend added, with no user-visible signal (the type <select> at ApiInputEditor.tsx:717-729 just shows the already-coerced "str"). This contradicts CLAUDE.md's 'fail loudly' directive and the module's own claim that the strict serialiser only DROPS unknown keys (it also mutates a declared type here).
evidence: apiInputSchema.ts:113-117 `typeof cc.type === "string" && ALLOWED_TYPES.has(cc.type as ColumnType) ? cc.type : "str"` vs _api_input_schema.py:369-376 `if not isinstance(ctype, str) or ctype not in _ALLOWED_COLUMN_TYPES: raise ApiInputSchemaError(...)`. The backend comment at lines 281-285 names the silent str-downgrade as the defect B1 exists to prevent; readV2 reintroduces it at the editor read layer. writeV2 (:170-177) emits the coerced `type` verbatim, so the mutation reaches disk.

title: The 4-column contribution-ladder grid-template class string is duplicated verbatim four times
description: The Tailwind grid-template `grid-cols-[minmax(0,1.2fr)_minmax(0,0.8fr)_minmax(4.5rem,auto)_minmax(4.5rem,auto)] gap-2 ... text-[10px]` appears character-for-character at the header row (102), the Base row (109), every contribution row (123), and the Prediction footer (147). Any column-width tweak must be hand-applied to all four occurrences or the ladder rows visually de-align. Hoisting the shared grid class to a single `const ladderRowClass = "..."` (or a tiny wrapper) collapses the duplication and makes the alignment invariant structural. (Minor related duplication: the omitted-count fallback `explanation.omitted_count ?? 0` is precomputed into `omittedContributionCount` at line 52 for the ladder but re-inlined at line 187 for the non-ladder Contributions section.)
evidence: Grep for `grid-cols-[minmax(0,1.2fr)` returns 4 occurrences, all in ModelScoreDetail.tsx (lines 102, 109, 123, 147), each carrying the identical 4-track template differing only in trailing modifiers (font-semibold / data-testid / border-t).
est_reduction: ~6-10 LOC plus removal of a 4-way hand-sync hazard
