behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: extracting the shared class substring to a constant and concatenating per-row modifiers produces byte-identical className output and identical DOM.

title: Pointless local aliases `labelStyle = traceDetailLabelStyle` and `modelDetail = detail`
description: `const labelStyle = traceDetailLabelStyle` (line 23) merely re-binds the module-level constant defined 5 lines above (line 18); `const modelDetail = detail` (line 24) is a no-op rename of the destructured prop. Both add an indirection layer with no behavioural or readability benefit — references could use `traceDetailLabelStyle` / `detail` directly, or `labelStyle` could simply BE the module constant's name. Trivial, but it is needless aliasing in an otherwise tightly-written component.
evidence: Line 18 `const traceDetailLabelStyle = { ... }`; line 23 `const labelStyle = traceDetailLabelStyle`; line 24 `const modelDetail = detail`. `modelDetail` is then threaded through modelScorePrediction(modelDetail), modelScoreFeatureColumns(modelDetail), etc., where `detail` would read identically.
est_reduction: 2 LOC
behavior_preservation: Identical: aliases are referentially equal to their targets; inlining changes no runtime value.

title: Histogram block dereferences edges[0]/edges[last] without a guard, unlike counts
description: The scenario-value histogram IIFE guards counts (`if (!counts || counts.length === 0) return null`) but never guards `edges`. It then reads `eMin = edges[0]` and `eMax = edges[edges.length - 1]` and renders `eMin.toFixed(2)` (line 136) and `eMax.toFixed(2)` (line 140) unconditionally. If a payload ever has non-empty `counts` but empty/short `edges`, both `eMin` and `eMax` are `undefined` and `undefined.toFixed(2)` throws a TypeError, crashing the whole SummaryTab render (an uncaught error in render, not a localized fallback).
evidence: Line 114 guards only counts: `if (!counts || counts.length === 0) return null`. Lines 119-120: `const eMin = edges[0], eMax = edges[edges.length - 1]`. The Pydantic wire schema `OptimiserScenarioValueHistogram` (src/haute/schemas.py:1135-1137) declares `counts: list[int] = Field(default_factory=list)` and `edges: list[float] = Field(default_factory=list)` — both default to empty independently, and the frontend type marks `edges: number[]` as required without enforcing the implicit N+1 length relationship to `counts`. The producing code (`_compute_scenario_value_stats`, _optimiser_service.py:1315) emits counts(20)/edges(21) together, so the mismatch is not reachable via current backend output; this is a latent robustness gap / contract-trust asymmetry rather than a live crash. The `oneX` computation (line 120) already degrades safely to null for empty edges, but the axis labels do not.

title: Constraint-met derivation duplicated verbatim with DetailCard
description: The three-line derivation `const thresholdType = Object.keys(spec)[0]; const thresholdVal = spec[thresholdType] ?? 0; const met = isConstraintMet(thresholdType, 0, value, thresholdVal)` is identical in SummaryTab.tsx:61-63 and DetailCard.tsx:141-143. The repo already factors constraint logic into optimiserHelpers (`isConstraintMet`); the surrounding spec-key extraction belongs there too. Extracting a single helper (e.g. `constraintStatus(spec, value): boolean`) into optimiserHelpers.ts and calling it from both components removes the duplication and keeps the single-bound-key assumption (`Object.keys(spec)[0]`) in one place, consistent with CLAUDE.md's directive to share existing functionality.
evidence: Grep shows the same pattern at SummaryTab.tsx:61 (`const thresholdType = Object.keys(spec)[0]`), :62 (`const thresholdVal = spec[thresholdType] ?? 0`), :63 (`const met = isConstraintMet(...)`) and at DetailCard.tsx:141-143. Both feed `isConstraintMet` from optimiserHelpers.ts, which already centralises the comparison but not the spec-key extraction.
est_reduction: ~3 duplicated lines folded into one shared helper (~6 lines net across the two call sites)
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: the extracted helper performs the exact same key lookup, default, and isConstraintMet call; identical boolean output for all inputs. No behavioural change.

title: Best-iteration reference line treats best_iteration as an array index, misplacing it when loss_history is truncated
description: `bestX` is computed as `xScale(Math.min(Math.max(bestIteration, 0), lossHistory.length - 1))`, but `xScale(i) = marginLeft + (i / (length-1)) * chartW` interprets its argument as a 0-based ARRAY INDEX into `lossHistory`, whereas `result.best_iteration` is the model's actual ITERATION NUMBER. These coincide only when `loss_history` starts at iteration 0 and is 1:1 with its index. The backend (`_train_service.py` `_bounded_loss_history`, default `HAUTE_TRAIN_LOSS_HISTORY_LIMIT=200`) keeps only the last 200 rows (`history[-200:]`) for runs longer than 200 iterations, so the window slides and `lossHistory[0].iteration` is non-zero (e.g. iterations 700..899 for a 900-iteration run). In that case a `best_iteration` of, say, 750 is clamped to `min(750, 199)=199` and the dashed best line is drawn at the far RIGHT edge while the x-axis labels (which correctly render `lossHistory[idx].iteration`) and the legend (`Best iteration (750)`) point elsewhere — a misleading model-diagnostic. The correct placement is to find the array index `j` with `lossHistory[j].iteration === bestIteration` and use `xScale(j)` (and hide the line when no such row is in the visible window).
evidence: Line 76: `const xScale = (i: number) => marginLeft + (i / (lossHistory.length - 1)) * chartW` (i is an index). Line 122-124 x labels use real iterations: `const iter = lossHistory[idx]?.iteration ?? idx`. Line 100: `xScale(Math.min(Math.max(bestIteration, 0), lossHistory.length - 1))` passes an iteration number into the index-based scale. Backend truncation: `_train_service.py` `history = history[-_MAX_TRAIN_LOSS_HISTORY:]` with `_MAX_TRAIN_LOSS_HISTORY = 200`, so index != iteration after truncation; `best_iteration` (schemas.py:840) is the unbounded model best.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: optimiserScoreFormulaText drops constraint/lambda names, producing an ambiguous tooltip for multi-constraint optimisers
description: The function destructures `lambdaTerms.map(([, value]) => formatSignedValue(value))`, discarding the constraint name (the key). For a candidate with multiple lambda terms the rendered tooltip becomes e.g. `score = objective +0.50 +1.20` with no indication of which constraint each penalty belongs to, and adjacent signed numbers are joined only by a space. It is used as the `title=` of the score cell in OptimiserApplyDetail.tsx:179. The sibling inline view (OptimiserApplyDetail.tsx:82-90) shows `lambda <name> <value>`, so the information exists; the tooltip just loses it. Including the name (e.g. `score = objective + lambda <name> <value> ...`) would make the per-row tooltip unambiguous. Low severity because it is a hover tooltip, not data; flagged as information-loss rather than pure style.
evidence: Lines 71-74: `const terms = lambdaTerms.map(([, value]) => formatSignedValue(value)).join(" "); return ` + "`score = ${objectiveLabel} ${terms}`" + `. The `name` from `finiteRecordEntries` (which returns `[string, number]` pairs) is thrown away. Consumer: OptimiserApplyDetail.tsx:179 `<span ... title={optimiserScoreFormulaText(candidate, objectiveLabel)}>`.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Stale-response race: out-of-order getRuns/getModelVersions can overwrite current data
description: refreshRuns and refreshVersions fire an un-cancellable fetch and unconditionally apply the result in .then. The fetch guard (fetchedRunsFor / fetchedVersionsFor) only prevents duplicate in-flight fetches for the SAME key; it does not discard a response for a stale key. When the user switches experiments, MlflowModelPicker (ExperimentRunPicker onChange, MlflowModelPicker.tsx:182-184) calls setRuns([]), resetRunsGuard(), then refreshRuns(newExpId). If the previous getRuns(oldExpId) is still in flight, its .then runs setRuns(oldData) whenever it resolves and can land AFTER the new experiment's data, leaving the dropdown showing runs from the wrong experiment. Same pattern for refreshVersions on a fast model switch. getRuns/getModelVersions already accept an AbortSignal (api/client.ts:1032,1047) but the hook never passes one nor tracks a request id, so there is no last-write-wins protection.
evidence: refreshRuns: fetchedRunsFor.current = expId; getRuns(expId, runTag).then(data => setRuns(...)). No signal, no per-call sequence check. resetRunsGuard() clears the guard so a slow prior request's .then is no longer even gated. Consumer switches exp -> two getRuns promises in flight -> whichever resolves last wins, not whichever was requested last.

title: Mount effect that resets fetch-guard refs is a no-op
description: The useEffect with [] dependency reassigns fetchedExperiments/fetchedModels/fetchedRunsFor/fetchedVersionsFor to false/"" on mount. But these refs are created with useRef(false)/useRef(""), which already initializes them to exactly those values, and React creates fresh ref objects for every new component instance (i.e. after any unmount+remount). At the first render of every mount the refs already hold their initial values, so the effect writes the values they already have. The comment 'Reset all fetch guards on mount so data is re-fetched after remount' describes behavior that remount provides for free; the effect adds nothing.
evidence: const fetchedExperiments = useRef(false) ... useEffect(() => { fetchedExperiments.current = false; fetchedModels.current = false; fetchedRunsFor.current = ""; fetchedVersionsFor.current = "" }, []). On remount React calls useRef(false) again -> new ref initialized to false; the effect sets it to false again.
est_reduction: ~7 lines
behavior_preservation: Removing the effect leaves identical runtime behavior: refs are already false/empty at first render of every mount.

title: Unreachable NaN guard in updateCell push branch
description: updateCell computes num = val === "" ? safeDefault : (Number.isNaN(parsed) ? safeDefault : parsed). safeDefault comes from resolveDefault(), which is guaranteed non-NaN (returns 1 on NaN). parsed is only used when it is not NaN. So num is always a finite number. The new-entry push then writes value: Number.isNaN(num) ? 0 : num, but Number.isNaN(num) can never be true, so the ': num' branch is the only reachable one and the '0' fallback is dead.
evidence: Line 67: const num = val === "" ? safeDefault : (Number.isNaN(parsed) ? safeDefault : parsed). Line 70: next.push({ [factor]: level, value: Number.isNaN(num) ? 0 : num }). num cannot be NaN -> fallback 0 unreachable; the map branch (line 68) correctly uses num directly without the guard, confirming intent.
est_reduction: 1 expression simplified to `value: num`
behavior_preservation: value: num is identical because num is never NaN; matches the sibling map branch which already uses num unguarded.

title: Hook re-declares MLflow wire types instead of reusing api/types.ts, and drifts from them
description: Experiment/Run/RegisteredModel/ModelVersion are redefined locally and re-exported, duplicating the canonical MlflowExperiment/MlflowRun/MlflowModel/MlflowModelVersion in api/types.ts. The fetch functions (getRuns etc.) return the canonical types; the hook stores them into state typed as the local copies. The local copies have drifted: local Run omits status and start_time (present on MlflowRun), and local ModelVersion omits creation_timestamp (present on MlflowModelVersion). Reusing the api types (or `export type Run = MlflowRun`) removes the duplication and the drift risk where a wire-contract field added to api/types.ts silently fails to surface through this hook.
evidence: useMlflowBrowser.ts defines export type Run = { run_id; run_name; metrics; params?; artifacts } whereas api/types.ts:816 MlflowRun additionally has status?, start_time?. getRuns returns Promise<MlflowRun[]> but the hook holds it as Run[]; consumers (MlflowModelPicker.tsx:3) import Run from the hook, so the narrower shape propagates.
est_reduction: ~16 lines of type declarations replaced by re-exports/aliases
behavior_preservation: Aliasing local names to the api types (or importing them) preserves all current usage while widening to the true wire shape; no runtime change.

title: Relativity bar colors a neutral 1.0 value as danger (red), inconsistent with heatmap semantics
description: The relativity bar uses background: val >= 1 ? danger-rgb : chart-below-rgb. A value of exactly 1.0 (a neutral relativity, i.e. no effect) is rendered with the 'danger' (above-1) color. The rest of the rating UI's heatmap (ratingTableUtils.relativityColor/relativityTextColor) treats values within ±0.005 of 1.0 as neutral/transparent and only colors dev > 0.005 as danger. So a neutral factor level is shown red here, conflicting with the established convention and over-emphasizing no-op relativities.
evidence: OneWayEditor.tsx:155 background: val >= 1 ? 'rgba(var(--danger-rgb), .35)' : 'rgba(var(--chart-below-rgb), .35)'. Contrast ratingTableUtils.ts:84-86 relativityColor where dev>0.005 => danger, dev<-0.005 => below, else transparent. val===1 falls into '>=1' => danger.

title: CI whiskers can overflow the bar container because maxDev ignores confidence-interval bounds
description: The horizontal scale `maxDev` is derived ONLY from each term's point deviation `|relativity - 1|` (with a 0.1 floor). The confidence-interval whiskers are then positioned/sized against this same `maxDev`. Because a relativity's CI is frequently WIDER than the largest point-deviation across the displayed terms, `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` routinely fall outside the `[1 - maxDev, 1 + maxDev]` range, producing a whisker with negative `left` (overflowing left, past the feature-name column) and/or `width` > 100% (extending past the right edge). The bar container (line 91, `className="flex-1 h-4 relative"`) has no `overflow: hidden`, so the overflow is visible and the whisker is clipped/misplaced, misrepresenting the displayed uncertainty.
evidence: Line 45: `const maxDev = Math.max(rows.map(r => Math.abs(r.relativity - 1)).reduce((a,b)=>Math.max(a,b), -Infinity), 0.1)` — only point deviations feed maxDev. Lines 116-117 scale the whisker against maxDev: `left: ${50 + ((row.ci_lower - 1) / maxDev) * 50}%` and `width: ${((row.ci_upper - row.ci_lower) / maxDev) * 50}%`. Worked example: a single term with relativity=1.05 (dev 0.05 → maxDev floored to 0.1) and CI [0.7, 1.5] yields whisker left = 50 + ((0.7-1)/0.1)*50 = -100% and width = ((1.5-0.7)/0.1)*50 = 400%. The point bar itself never overflows (pct = (|dev|/maxDev)*50 ≤ 50 since maxDev ≥ |dev|), so the defect is whisker-specific. Container at line 91 has no overflow clipping.

title: Unreachable defensive branch coerces non-numeric relativity to dev=0, inconsistent with the rest of the component
description: `const dev = typeof row.relativity === 'number' ? row.relativity - 1 : 0` defends against `relativity` not being a number, but the wire contract guarantees it always is: the TrainResult type declares `glm_relativities: { feature: string; relativity: number; ... }[]` (relativity is a required `number`), and the backend runs `_assert_json_finite(response)` over the whole train response (routes/_train_service.py:1147 and routes/modelling.py:78), which RAISES on any non-finite numeric rather than emitting a sentinel. So `row.relativity` is always a finite number when rows are populated, making the `: 0` branch unreachable. The branch is also internally inconsistent: the very same `row.relativity` is used WITHOUT this guard in the sort comparator (lines 30-31, `b.relativity - a.relativity` / `Math.abs(b.relativity - 1)`), which correctly assumes it is always a number. Worse, were the impossible case to occur, this branch would silently place the bar exactly on the baseline (dev=0) instead of failing loudly, contrary to the project's no-silent-fallback guidance.
evidence: Type at frontend/src/stores/useNodeResultsStore.ts:73 `glm_relativities?: { feature: string; relativity: number; ci_lower?: number; ci_upper?: number }[]`. Backend finiteness gate: src/haute/routes/_train_service.py:338-341 raises `ValueError("non-finite numeric value at {path}")`. The dead branch (line 75) contradicts the unguarded numeric use at lines 30-31 of the same prop.
est_reduction: ~1 line simplified (drop the ternary, use `const dev = row.relativity - 1`)
behavior_preservation: Behavior is identical for all inputs permitted by the wire contract (finite numeric relativity); only the unreachable non-number path changes, and removing it aligns with fail-loud policy.

title: handleSort default-direction ternary has two identical branches (no-op conditional, intended numeric-desc default lost)
description: When switching the active sort to a NEW column, the code computes the new sort direction with `setSortDir(key === "feature" ? "asc" : "asc")`. Both arms of the ternary evaluate to the literal `"asc"`, so the condition `key === "feature"` is computed and then discarded — it has zero effect on the result. The shape of the expression (a ternary keyed on whether the column is the text column `feature` vs the numeric columns coefficient/std_error/z_value/p_value) strongly indicates the author intended numeric statistic columns to default to descending order (largest-magnitude / most-significant first, the conventional default for a coefficients table), while the text `feature` column defaults to ascending. As written that intent is silently dropped: every freshly selected column always starts ascending, so e.g. clicking the `Estimate` or `z` header first shows the smallest values at the top rather than the largest. There is no incorrect state — just a dead conditional plus a missing feature.
evidence: Line 63-70 handleSort: `if (sortKey === key) { setSortDir(d => d === "asc" ? "desc" : "asc") } else { setSortKey(key); setSortDir(key === "feature" ? "asc" : "asc") }`. The else-branch ternary returns "asc" for both true and false, so `key === "feature"` is evaluated and thrown away. Contrast with the numeric vs string handling that exists in the `sorted` comparator (localeCompare for strings, numeric subtraction otherwise), confirming the two column families are meant to behave differently.
est_reduction: Collapse to `setSortDir("asc")` (or implement the intended `key === "feature" ? "asc" : "desc"`); removes a dead conditional (~1 line of pointless branching).
behavior_preservation: Replacing the ternary with the constant `"asc"` is exactly behavior-preserving (both arms already return "asc"). If instead the intended numeric-desc default is restored, behavior changes only in the initial sort direction when a numeric column is first selected — no data/values change, only ordering of an already-sortable table.

title: Duplicating a node copies the original's cached preview/result fields (_columns, _availableColumns, _schemaWarnings, _status, _traceValue) into the duplicate, violating the clearCachedResultShape invariant
description: handleDuplicateNode builds the new node's data with a shallow spread `data: { ...original.data, label: ... }`. This carries over ALL runtime/cached fields the original accumulated from its last preview/run: `_columns`, `_availableColumns`, `_schemaWarnings`, `_status`, `_traceValue`, `_traceActive`, etc. (defined on HauteNodeData in types/node.ts). The duplicate has a brand-new id with NO cached result in useNodeResultsStore, yet its `data` advertises the original's columns and an `_status: "ok"`. Downstream this is user-visible: ColumnsTab is fed `availableColumns`/`columns` derived from these `_*` fields, so the freshly duplicated (never-run) node shows the original's schema and lets the user edit `selected_columns` against stale columns; the node also renders as already-succeeded. The codebase already encodes the opposite invariant: NodePanel.handleConfigUpdate wraps every config write in `clearCachedResultShape()` (NodePanel.tsx:567-573, deleting _columns/_availableColumns/_schemaWarnings) precisely because a node whose identity/config changed must not keep stale cached schema. handleCreateInstance (same file, lines 94-105) constructs `data` from scratch with no `_*` fields, so duplicate is the inconsistent outlier. Secondary: the shallow spread also makes `newNode.data.config` the SAME object reference as `original.data.config`; the normal edit path replaces config immutably so this is currently latent, but any in-place config mutation would corrupt both nodes.
evidence: Lines 75-81: `const newNode: Node = { ...original, id: newId, position: {...}, selected: true, data: { ...original.data, label: `${original.data.label} copy` } }`. `original.data` includes _columns/_availableColumns/_schemaWarnings/_status (HauteNodeData). No call to clearCachedResultShape or stripping of `_*` keys. Compare NodePanel.tsx:616 `onUpdateNode(id, clearCachedResultShape({ ...currentNode.data, config: newConfig }))` and useNodeHandlers handleCreateInstance which sets `data: { label, description, nodeType, config }` only.

title: Stale (ghost) entries in selected_columns inflate the toggle count, causing 'select one column' to silently revert to all-selected and pull in unrelated real columns
description: When selected_columns contains names that are no longer in the current schema (the component's own first-class 'stale ghost rows' feature, rendered with the '(not found)' suffix), those stale names still live inside `selectedColumns`. In toggleColumn's add-branch, `const next = [...selectedColumns, col]` includes the stale entries, and the all-selected revert guard `if (next.length >= allColumns.length)` compares this inflated length against `allColumns.length` (which EXCLUDES stale columns). The stale entries can push `next.length` to `>= allColumns.length` before the user has actually selected every real column, so toggling a single real column ON silently flips the node back to empty (= keep all columns), thereby selecting other real columns the user never checked and dropping the explicit list. Example: allColumns=[a,b,c], selected_columns=["a","stale1"]; user checks `b` -> next=["a","stale1","b"], length 3 >= 3 -> onUpdate('selected_columns', []) -> a,b,AND c are now kept. Column `c` was never selected by the user. The length comparison should be against the count of REAL selected columns (filtered through allColumnNames), not the raw array that includes ghosts.
evidence: Lines 57-64: `const next = [...selectedColumns, col]; if (next.length >= allColumns.length) { onUpdate('selected_columns', []) } else { onUpdate('selected_columns', next) }`. `selectedColumns` may contain stale names (staleColumns is built at lines 28-33 from exactly `selectedColumns.filter(name => !allColumnNames.has(name))`), so `next.length` over-counts relative to `allColumns.length` which is derived from availableColumns/columns with no stale entries.

title: selectedCount counts stale ghost columns, so the 'N / total' badge can read e.g. '3 / 3' when only 1 real column is actually selected
description: selectedCount uses `selectedColumns.length` in the explicit (non-all) case, but selectedColumns can include stale names not present in allColumns. The denominator of the badge is `allColumns.length`, which excludes stale entries. The result is a count that double-misleads: the numerator is inflated by ghost columns while the denominator excludes them, so the badge can display the count of selected as equal to or greater than the real total. Example: allColumns=[a,b,c], selected_columns=["a","stale1","stale2"] -> isAllSelected=false, selectedCount=3, badge shows '3 / 3', implying every output column is selected, when in fact only `a` is a real selected output column and b,c are deselected. The count should be the number of selectedColumns that are also in allColumnNames (real, kept columns).
evidence: Line 77: `const selectedCount = isAllSelected ? allColumns.length : selectedColumns.length`. Badge lines 93-95: `{selectedCount} / {allColumns.length}`. staleColumns (lines 28-33) proves selectedColumns can contain names absent from allColumnNames; those are counted by selectedColumns.length but not by allColumns.length.

title: showCode visibility derived from config only at mount; goes stale across node switches
description: `const defaultCode = configField(config, "code", "")` then `const [showCode, setShowCode] = useState(!!defaultCode)`. The `useState` initializer runs exactly once per component instance, so `showCode` reflects the code-presence of whichever MODEL_SCORE node was selected when ModelScoreEditor first mounted. NodePanel is rendered without a per-node `key` (App.tsx:686) and `renderEditor()` returns the editor without a `key` either (NodePanel.tsx:1036, which calls ModelScoreEditor at NodePanel.tsx:801), so switching from one MODEL_SCORE node to another does NOT remount ModelScoreEditor — only the `config` prop changes. There is also no effect that re-derives `showCode` from the new config, and `nodeId` is not even passed to this editor (NodePanel.tsx:801 omits it), so it cannot reset on node switch the way the codebase's own RatingStepEditor does (RatingStepEditor.tsx:287-290 resets its visible section on `[nodeId]`). Result: select node A that has post-processing code (panel mounts with showCode=true, editor expanded); without closing the panel, select node B that has no code -> the empty Post-processing Code editor stays expanded for node B. Reverse direction (node B with no code -> node A with code) leaves the panel collapsed, hiding node A's existing post-processing code from view even though that code is still active in the pipeline, so the user may not realize node A has post-processing logic. The underlying code TEXT does not corrupt (CodeMirrorEditor re-syncs `defaultValue` via its effect at CodeMirrorEditor.tsx:322-340), so this is a stale-visibility defect, not data loss.
evidence: ModelScoreEditor.tsx:33 `const [showCode, setShowCode] = useState(!!defaultCode)` (mount-only init, no `[config]`/`[nodeId]` resync effect; nodeId not a prop) | App.tsx:686 `<NodePanel node={panelNode} ...>` (no key) | NodePanel.tsx:1036 `) : renderEditor()}` (no key) | NodePanel.tsx:801 `<ModelScoreEditor config={config} ... />` (no nodeId) | contrast RatingStepEditor.tsx:287-290 `useEffect(() => { setActiveSectionState(...) }, [nodeId])` establishes the reset-on-node-switch convention this editor violates.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

title: ModellingPreview passes config={{}} to SummaryTab, silently dropping the user's MLflow experiment_name and model_name on export
description: ModellingPreview renders <SummaryTab ... config={{}} />. SummaryTab forwards `config` into MlflowExportSection, which derives the MLflow request fields via configField(config, "mlflow_experiment", "") and configField(config, "model_name", ""). Because an empty object is passed, both lookups return "" → coerced to null, so when the user clicks "Log to MLflow" from the modelling result panel, the experiment name and model name they configured on the Modelling node are silently discarded and the run is logged under a default/unnamed experiment. These two keys are real persisted config: SplitAndMetricsConfig.tsx (lines 215-227) writes `mlflow_experiment` and `model_name` onto the modelling node's config via onUpdate. ModellingPreview has `nodeId` in scope and the node config is reachable from the graph store (the codebase reads node config by id elsewhere, e.g. App.tsx:634 `nodeData(activeNode).config ?? {}`), so the real config is available — the hardcoded `{}` is an oversight, not a necessity. This is the only place the modelling flow surfaces the MLflow export (ModellingConfig does not render MlflowExportSection), so there is no other path that supplies the correct names.
evidence: ModellingPreview.tsx:111 `<SummaryTab result={result} jobId={data.jobId} mlflowBackend={mlflowBackend} config={{}} />` → SummaryTab.tsx:194 `<MlflowExportSection trainJobId={jobId} mlflowBackend={mlflowBackend} config={config} />` → MlflowExportSection.tsx:40-41 `experiment_name: configField(config, "mlflow_experiment", "") || null, model_name: configField(config, "model_name", "") || null`. configField.ts:14-16 returns fallback when key absent, so with config={} both resolve to "" then null. The keys originate from SplitAndMetricsConfig.tsx:215-227 (`onUpdate("mlflow_experiment", ...)`, `onUpdate("model_name", ...)`). The export button is reachable whenever MLflow is connected (ModellingPreview.tsx:62 sets mlflowBackend.installed=true on status==="connected"; SummaryTab.tsx:189 gates on `mlflowBackend?.installed && jobId`).

title: ContextMenu auto-focus runs only on mount; reopening on a different node without unmount leaves stale focusIndex and no focused item
description: The 'Auto-focus first item' effect has an empty dependency array, so it runs exactly once when the ContextMenu instance mounts. ContextMenu is rendered without a `key` (App.tsx:717) and onNodeContextMenu calls setContextMenu({...}) for the new node directly (useEdgeHandlers.ts:370) without first setting it to null. In the common mouse path this is harmless because right-clicking elsewhere fires a `mousedown` (handled at lines 56-64) that closes/unmounts the menu before the `contextmenu` event reopens it, so a fresh mount re-focuses. However, opening the menu via the keyboard context-menu key (Menu/Shift+F10) on a different node while a menu is already open produces no preceding mousedown: the same instance is reused, the mount-only auto-focus effect does not re-run, and `focusIndex` retains its prior value. If the new node's `items` list is shorter (e.g. previous node had 'Dissolve Submodel'/5 items with focusIndex pointing high, new node is a singleton with fewer items), `tabIndex={i === focusIndex ? 0 : -1}` leaves no button with tabIndex 0 until the user presses an arrow key (the Arrow handlers self-correct via `% items.length`). Net effect: focus is not placed on the menu and roving tabindex is momentarily inconsistent on keyboard-triggered reopen.
evidence: ContextMenu.tsx:67-69 `useEffect(() => { buttonRefs.current[0]?.focus() }, [])` (empty deps). Reuse without remount: App.tsx:717 renders <ContextMenu .../> with no key; useEdgeHandlers.ts:370 `setContextMenu({ x, y, nodeId: node.id, ... })` with no intervening null. focusIndex (line 34) persists across prop changes; tabIndex roving at line 118 `tabIndex={i === focusIndex ? 0 : -1}` yields no tabbable item when focusIndex >= items.length. Arrow handlers (lines 77, 87) recover via modulo on next keypress.

title: Modal focus effect re-runs on every parent re-render (unstable onClose/extraCloseKeys deps), yanking focus out of the modal and corrupting focus restoration
description: The mount/focus effect depends on [onClose, extraCloseKeys]. All three call sites in App.tsx pass a fresh arrow for onClose (App.tsx:733 KeyboardShortcuts, :738 SubmodelDialog, :749 RenameDialog), and KeyboardShortcuts additionally passes a fresh extraCloseKeys={["?"]} array literal (KeyboardShortcuts.tsx:21). Because App subscribes to frequently-changing store slices (notably hoveredNodeId at App.tsx:156, which updates on every node hover, plus syncBanner/dirty/etc.), App re-renders continuously while a modal is open. Each re-render gives ModalShell new dep references, so the effect's cleanup+setup fire every time: the cleanup runs `previousFocusRef.current.focus()` (pulls focus back to the pre-modal background element), then the setup overwrites `previousFocusRef.current = document.activeElement` and calls `containerRef.current?.focus()` (yanks focus to the modal container). Net effect: while the user hovers nodes in the background graph, the open modal repeatedly steals focus back to its container, so the user cannot keep keyboard focus on an inner control (e.g. Tab-navigating the shortcuts list or typing in RenameDialog's textarea is interrupted), and the saved restore target is repeatedly reset.
evidence: ModalShell.tsx:36 `previousFocusRef.current = document.activeElement`; :37 `containerRef.current?.focus()`; :91-97 cleanup removes listener and `if (previousFocusRef.current instanceof HTMLElement) previousFocusRef.current.focus()`; :98 deps `[onClose, extraCloseKeys]`. App.tsx:733 `onClose={() => setShortcutsOpen(false)}` (new fn each render); KeyboardShortcuts.tsx:21 `extraCloseKeys={["?"]}` (new array each render); App.tsx:156 `const hoveredNodeId = useUIStore((s) => s.hoveredNodeId)` makes App re-render on every hover. No test exercises a parent re-render with changed props (ModalShell.test.tsx / focusTrap / shell-merge all render directly with stable vi.fn() onClose and no extraCloseKeys), so this is uncovered.

title: Min/max numeric labels rendered in a non-uniformly scaled viewBox (preserveAspectRatio="none") are horizontally stretched/illegible
description: The main (range>0) SVG uses viewBox="0 0 100 {height}" with preserveAspectRatio="none", so the 100-unit-wide user space is stretched to the full rendered pixel width while the height axis maps 1:1 (height px). For any realistic panel width (hundreds of px vs height 50), the horizontal scale is ~3-6x and the vertical scale ~1x. The <text> min/max labels at lines 107-112 are drawn with fontSize={2.5} in user units, so each glyph is rendered ~2.5px tall but horizontally smeared 3-6x, producing distorted, hard-to-read numbers. The range===0 branch (lines 25-53) instead renders in pixel coordinates (no viewBox) with a sensible fontSize={9}, confirming the main branch's tiny stretched text is unintended rather than a deliberate convention.
evidence: Line 70 `viewBox={\`0 0 100 ${height}\`} preserveAspectRatio="none"`; lines 107-112 `<text ... fontSize={2.5} ...>{formatNum(min)}</text>` and `{formatNum(max)}`. Contrast line 35 (no-range branch) `<text x="0" y={height} fontSize={9} ...>`. Non-uniform preserveAspectRatio="none" scaling distorts text aspect ratio so labels are unreadable at typical widths.

title: range===0 branch renders every boundary as an identical overlapping line at x=50% (no dedup, no off-range filter)
description: In the all-values-equal branch, boundaries.map renders one <line> per boundary but hard-codes x1/x2 to "50%" for all of them, so N boundaries produce N identical lines stacked exactly on top of each other — visually indistinguishable from a single line, and the extra DOM nodes are pure waste. It also omits the off-range filtering the main branch applies (lines 90-91 `if (xPct < 0 || xPct > 100) return null`), so boundaries that don't actually fall on the single value still draw a centre line, which is arguably misleading. At most one centre marker is meaningful here.
evidence: Lines 38-52: `boundaries.map((_b, i) => { ... <line key={i} x1="50%" ... x2="50%" ... /> })` — `_b` (the boundary value) is unused, so all lines are positionally identical regardless of value; compare the main branch which positions each line by value and filters out-of-range ones (lines 89-91).
est_reduction: ~8 lines / collapse N identical lines to a single conditional marker
behavior_preservation: Rendering one centre line (or none when no boundary equals the value) instead of N overlapping identical lines is visually equivalent; the only observable change is the count of <line> nodes, which BandingHistogram.test.tsx asserts only for range>0 cases (the single/same-value tests check svg presence and, for negatives, range>0).

title: interactiveRows without checkbox makes rows look clickable but do nothing
description: The row's cursor/hover affordance is gated on `interactiveRows` alone (line 74: `className={interactiveRows ? "cursor-pointer hover-bg" : undefined}`), but the actual click handler is gated on `interactiveRows && checkbox` (line 76: `onClick={interactiveRows && checkbox ? () => checkbox.onToggle(col.name) : undefined}`). When a caller passes `interactiveRows` without a `checkbox` (which the public prop types permit — both are independent optional props), every row renders with a pointer cursor and hover highlight yet clicking does nothing. The affordance and the behaviour disagree. The two conditions should share the same gate (e.g. derive `const rowInteractive = interactiveRows && !!checkbox` and use it for both the className and onClick), or the cursor/hover styling should also require `checkbox`.
evidence: Line 74 keys pointer+hover on `interactiveRows`; line 76 keys onClick on `interactiveRows && checkbox`. With `interactiveRows` true and `checkbox` undefined => `cursor-pointer hover-bg` applied but `onClick` is undefined => dead affordance.

title: Needless `const row = (...); return row` indirection inside columns.map
description: The map callback builds the entire <tr> JSX into a local `const row` (line 71) spanning ~33 lines and then simply `return row` (line 105) with nothing in between. The intermediate binding adds no value (no reuse, no conditional, no transformation) and only widens the closure body. Returning the JSX expression directly removes the indirection and the extra indentation level, improving readability of an already-dense render.
evidence: Lines 71 (`const row = (`) and 103-105 (`)` ... `return row`) bracket a single JSX expression with no statements between the assignment and the return.
est_reduction: ~2 lines + one indentation level
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: returning the same JSX expression directly is identical output; React key and props unchanged.

title: nameSuffix callback invoked twice per row
description: Inside each row, `nameSuffix?.(col.name)` is called once as the `&&` guard (line 91) and `nameSuffix(col.name)` is called a second time to render the value (line 93). For a caller whose `nameSuffix` does non-trivial work (e.g. ColumnsTab passes `(name) => !allColumnNames.has(name) ? "(not found)" : null`, a Set lookup per call), this doubles the work and risks subtle inconsistency if the callback were ever non-pure. Computing it once into a local (`const suffix = nameSuffix?.(col.name)`) and rendering `{suffix && {suffix}}` evaluates it a single time.
evidence: Line 91 `{nameSuffix?.(col.name) && (` ... line 93 `{nameSuffix(col.name)}` — two invocations of the same callback with the same argument per rendered row.
est_reduction: 1 redundant call per row; ~1 line net
behavior_preservation: Output identical for pure callbacks (all current callers are pure); single evaluation is strictly less work.

title: Stale importanceType ('loss'/'shap') hides valid prediction importances after result changes
description: FeaturesTab keeps the selected importance type in component state (`importanceType`, line 19) with no effect or key to reset it when the underlying `result` changes. If a user selects 'Loss' or 'SHAP', and the component then re-renders with a new `result` whose `feature_importance_loss`/`shap_summary` is absent (e.g. switching the panel to a different model node, or re-training without SHAP/loss importance), the corresponding switcher button is dropped from `types` (lines 23-24) but `importanceType` remains 'loss'/'shap'. `items` (lines 28-36) then evaluates `result.feature_importance_loss || []` (or the shap branch) to `[]`, so the component renders the 'No feature importance data available' empty state (line 38) even though `result.feature_importance` (Prediction) is fully populated. The user sees a false 'no data' message and the only visible type button is 'Prediction', whose own selection is silently ignored.
evidence: Line 19: `useState<'prediction'|'loss'|'shap'>('prediction')` is never reset. Lines 23-24 build the `loss`/`shap` buttons only when `result.feature_importance_loss?.length` / `result.shap_summary?.length` are truthy, so those buttons vanish for a new result lacking them. Lines 32-35: `if (importanceType === 'loss') return result.feature_importance_loss || []` returns `[]` for the new result while `importanceType` is still 'loss'. Line 38 then returns the empty state. ModellingPreview.tsx:118 renders `<FeaturesTab result={result} />` with no `key` tied to node/result, so the same instance (and its stale state) persists across result changes; the file has no `useEffect` (confirmed via grep) to clamp `importanceType` back into the available `types`.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Fallback `rating_step` trace detail is mislabeled as "Rate Table Lookup" and renders empty (wrong field names read)
description: The second branch handles `detailType === "rate_table_lookup" || detailType === "rating_step"` and reads `detail.lookup_keys`, `detail.matched_row`, and `detail.default_used`. Those field names belong to the `rate_table_lookup` shape only. A `rating_step` detail produced by the backend fallback path emits `matched_key`, `matched` (a boolean), and `rate_value` — and crucially has NO `tables` array and NO `combined_outputs`. Such a detail fails the rich guard on line 37 (which requires `Array.isArray(detail.tables) || Array.isArray(detail.combined_outputs)`) and therefore falls into this `rate_table_lookup` branch. Because `lookup_keys` and `matched_row` are undefined for that shape, the panel renders with the wrong title ("Rate Table Lookup") and shows no key chips and no matched-row chip, silently dropping the `matched_key`/`rate_value`/`matched` information the user expects to see for a rating step.
evidence: Backend src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py lines 272-277 returns `{ "detail_type": "rating_step", "matched_key": ..., "rate_value": ..., "matched": ... }` with no `tables`/`combined_outputs`. In NodeDetailBlock.tsx, line 37 guard is false for this (no array fields), so line 41 `|| detailType === "rating_step"` matches; line 42 reads `detail.lookup_keys` (undefined for this shape) -> the `keys &&` block on line 47 is skipped; line 43 reads `detail.matched_row` (undefined; backend emits `matched`) -> line 54 `matched != null` is false. Net result: `<TraceDetailPanel title="Rate Table Lookup">` with empty body. Distinct shapes are confirmed by frontend/src/panels/trace/traceStoryView.ts:52-60 (treats `rate_table_lookup` as primary but routes generic `rating_step` via `hasRichRatingStepDetail`) and by the `rate_table_lookup` fixtures in TracePanel.enhanced.test.tsx:476-478 which carry `lookup_keys`/`matched_row`. The intended fix is to remove `|| detailType === "rating_step"` from line 41 so fallback rating_step details fall through to the generic JSON renderer (or are given a dedicated rating-step fallback panel reading `matched_key`/`rate_value`/`matched`).

title: clusterSnap docstring example contradicts the code's even-length median selection
description: clusterSnap snaps each cluster to cluster[Math.floor(cluster.length / 2)], i.e. the UPPER-middle element for even-length clusters. The docstring's own worked example claims the cluster [250,253] snaps to 250, but for a 2-element cluster Math.floor(2/2) = 1, so cluster[1] = 253 is selected — the function snaps to 253, not 250. The odd-length example ([100,103,108]->103) is correct and is pinned by tests, but the even-length behavior is undocumented/misdocumented and untested. The actual code path always picks the larger of the two middle values, which is a deterministic but asymmetric 'representative', not the arithmetic median the comment implies. Functionally the snap is still consistent (all cluster members receive the same value, so visual alignment holds), so this is a comment-correctness/spec defect rather than a runtime mis-render, but a maintainer relying on the documented example would compute the wrong expected output (e.g. when adding a regression test).
evidence: Line 38: `const median = cluster[Math.floor(cluster.length / 2)]`. For cluster = [250,253]: cluster.length = 2 -> Math.floor(1) = 1 -> cluster[1] = 253. Docstring lines 25-26 assert `[250,253]→250`. No test in frontend/src/__tests__/utils/layout.test.ts or frontend/src/utils/__tests__/layout.test.ts exercises an even-length cluster, so the discrepancy is unguarded.

title: No-op ternary `color: isUsed ? accentColor : accentColor`
description: Inside the chip button's inline `style` object, the `color` property is computed as `isUsed ? accentColor : accentColor`. Both branches of the ternary yield the identical value (`accentColor`), so the conditional is dead code. It can be simplified to `color: accentColor`. The distinction between used and unused chips is already carried entirely by `background`, `border`, `opacity`, and `cursor` on the surrounding lines, so the text colour is intentionally constant — the ternary just obscures that.
evidence: style={{ background: isUsed ? withAlpha(accentColor,0.08) : withAlpha(accentColor,0.12), border: `1px solid ${isUsed ? withAlpha(accentColor,0.2) : withAlpha(accentColor,0.35)}`, color: isUsed ? accentColor : accentColor, opacity: isUsed ? 0.5 : 1, cursor: isUsed ? "default" : "pointer" }} — the `color` line evaluates to `accentColor` regardless of `isUsed`.
est_reduction: 1 line simplified (ternary -> plain value)
behavior_preservation: Identical rendered output: both branches already produce `accentColor`. No test asserts the colour value (CategoricalValuePicker.test.tsx only checks opacity and onAddValue behaviour), so replacing with `color: accentColor` is purely cosmetic in the source.

title: `onClick` re-checks `isUsed` though the button is already `disabled={isUsed}`
description: The chip button sets `disabled={isUsed}` (line 65) and its `onClick` handler additionally wraps the call as `if (!isUsed) onAddValue(v.value)` (lines 66-68). A button rendered with the DOM `disabled` attribute does not fire React's synthetic `onClick`, so the inner `if (!isUsed)` guard is unreachable in practice and duplicates the `disabled` gate. The handler could be `onClick={() => onAddValue(v.value)}`. (The existing test 'clicking used value does NOT call onAddValue' passes because of `disabled`, not because of the guard.)
evidence: <button disabled={isUsed} onClick={() => { if (!isUsed) onAddValue(v.value) }}> — `disabled` already prevents the click; the `if (!isUsed)` branch can never be reached with `isUsed === true`.
est_reduction: Collapses a 3-line guarded handler into a 1-line direct call
behavior_preservation: Behaviour is preserved: with `disabled={isUsed}` the synthetic onClick never fires for used chips, so dropping the redundant `if (!isUsed)` cannot change observable behaviour. Lower confidence than the color finding because some prefer keeping the guard as defense-in-depth against future removal of the `disabled` attribute.

title: formatTraceValue, formatCalculation and formatSchemaSummary (plus escapeRegExp/DATE_RE) are exported-but-only-tested dead code
description: Of the public surface of formatTrace.ts, only formatExpression has a production consumer. formatTraceValue, formatCalculation and formatSchemaSummary are never imported by any non-test module; their only callers are formatTrace.test.ts. escapeRegExp is used solely by the dead formatCalculation, and the DATE_RE regex is used solely by the dead formatTraceValue, so they are dead transitively. StepCard.tsx — the only production importer of this module — imports just formatExpression and defines its OWN local formatTraceValue (StepCard.tsx:24) backed by formatValue (which, unlike this module's formatTraceValue, correctly decodes the non-finite-float wire sentinel). The exported functions therefore have no behavioural reach: they cannot render anything to a user and exist only to satisfy their own unit tests. Removing them (keeping formatExpression) deletes ~50 LOC of source plus the corresponding tests, and eliminates a latent correctness trap: this module's formatTraceValue JSON.stringifies an object value, so it would emit raw `{"__haute_type__":"non_finite_float","value":"nan"}` for a NaN/Inf cell instead of "NaN" — a bug that is masked precisely because the function is unreachable.
evidence: Grep across frontend/ for `formatTrace`: the only source import is StepCard.tsx:9 `import { formatExpression } from "../utils/formatTrace"`; every other reference to formatTraceValue/formatCalculation/formatSchemaSummary is in frontend/src/utils/__tests__/formatTrace.test.ts. StepCard.tsx:24 defines a local `function formatTraceValue(...)` shadowing any intent to use the exported one. escapeRegExp (formatTrace.ts:62) is referenced only at formatTrace.ts:51 inside formatCalculation; DATE_RE (formatTrace.ts:3) only at formatTrace.ts:19 inside the exported formatTraceValue.
est_reduction: ~50 LOC of source (3 functions + escapeRegExp + DATE_RE) plus their dedicated unit tests; file collapses to just formatExpression.
behavior_preservation: No runtime behaviour changes: none of the removed symbols is reachable from any rendered component or hook (only formatExpression is consumed in production). Deleting them and their tests leaves all production output identical.

title: Pluralisation ternary in the multi-output banding summary chip is unreachable (always renders "s")
description: The summary chip `{rows.length} banded output{rows.length === 1 ? "" : "s"}` is rendered only inside the guard `showBandingSummary && !singleRow && rows.length > 0`. `singleRow` is defined as `rows.length === 1 ? rows[0] : null` (line 28), so `!singleRow` is true exactly when `rows.length !== 1`. Combined with `rows.length > 0`, entering this branch requires `rows.length >= 2`. Therefore the inner `rows.length === 1` test is always false and the singular form `""` can never be produced — the chip always reads "N banded outputs". The ternary is dead: the singular arm is unreachable. It can be simplified to a constant `s` (or the condition removed), which also documents the invariant that this chip is the >=2 case.
evidence: BandingDetail.tsx:28 `const singleRow = rows.length === 1 ? rows[0] : null`; BandingDetail.tsx:42 branch guard `showBandingSummary && !singleRow && rows.length > 0`. `!singleRow` ⇔ `rows.length !== 1`; with `rows.length > 0` this forces `rows.length >= 2`, so `rows.length === 1` at line 43 is constant-false.
est_reduction: 1 dead sub-expression (the `rows.length === 1 ? "" : "s"` ternary reduces to literal "s").
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-identical: in every input that reaches this branch rows.length is >=2, so the ternary already evaluates to "s"; replacing it with the literal yields the same rendered text in all cases.

title: LossChart y-range poisoned by NaN/Infinity loss values (no finite-value guard)
description: LossChart gathers y-values into allVals using only a `!= null` filter (lines 30-31), so NaN/Infinity values flow in. yMin/yMax are then computed with Math.min/Math.max (lines 33-34); any NaN poisons both to NaN, making yRange and yScale(v) return NaN for EVERY point. The whole chart breaks (train/eval paths and the best-iteration line render with NaN coordinates -> invalid/empty SVG), not just the single bad point. The backend demonstrably emits NaN/Infinity in loss_history: the sibling LossTab tests feed `eval_rmse: Number.NaN` and `train_rmse: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` (frontend/src/panels/modelling/__tests__/LossTab.test.tsx:26,44-45). The sibling LossTab.tsx (doc-comment line 4 claims LossChart is 'same logic') guards every value with `isFiniteNumber` (LossTab.tsx:29-30,61-62) and renders an empty-state when no finite points remain (LossTab.tsx:46-49,64-66); LossChart has none of these guards.
evidence: LossChart.tsx:30-31 push when `entry[trainKey] != null` (NaN passes) -> :33-34 `yMin=allVals.reduce(Math.min,Infinity)` becomes NaN -> :35 `yRange = NaN || 1` = NaN -> :38 `yScale(v) = py+chartH-((v-yMin)/yRange)*chartH` = NaN for all v. Contrast LossTab.tsx:61-62 `if (isFiniteNumber(entry[trainKey])) allVals.push(...)`.

title: LossChart.makePath emits 'NaN' path coordinates for non-finite loss points
description: makePath filters points with `e[key] != null` (line 42), so a NaN/Infinity value produces a path segment like `L12.3,NaN`. Even setting aside the y-range poisoning above, an individual non-finite point yields an invalid SVG path `d` string. The sibling LossTab.makePath guards with `isFiniteNumber(e[key])` and skips such points entirely (LossTab.tsx:83), producing a clean broken-line path. LossChart should do the same.
evidence: LossChart.tsx:42 `e[key] != null ? \`L${xScale(i)},${yScale(e[key])}\` : null` with yScale(NaN)=NaN -> 'L..,NaN'. LossTab.tsx:83 `if (!isFiniteNumber(e[key])) return null`.

title: LossChart best-iteration line: no lower clamp and no NaN guard on bestIteration
description: bestX = bestIteration != null ? xScale(Math.min(bestIteration, lossHistory.length - 1)) : null. Two defects vs the hardened sibling: (1) no lower clamp -> a negative bestIteration yields a negative x and the dashed line is drawn off-canvas to the left; (2) `!= null` lets NaN through (NaN is not null) -> Math.min(NaN, n)=NaN -> xScale(NaN)=NaN -> a <line> with x1/x2=NaN is rendered, and the legend gains a spurious 'Best iter' entry. LossTab.tsx:100 uses `isFiniteNumber(bestIteration) ? xScale(Math.min(Math.max(bestIteration, 0), lossHistory.length - 1)) : null`, which clamps to [0, length-1] and rejects NaN. best_iteration is typed `number | null` (useNodeResultsStore.ts:56) and originates from the backend, so a NaN/negative value is a realistic wire input.
evidence: LossChart.tsx:49 lacks Math.max(_,0) and isFiniteNumber present in LossTab.tsx:100. NaN != null === true, so Number.NaN flows into xScale.

title: FeatureImportance maxVal uses items[0].importance, wrong for negative/zero importances
description: maxVal is taken as `items[0]?.importance || 1` on the assumption that the first (descending-sorted) feature is the largest by magnitude. Bar width is then `(Math.abs(fi.importance) / Math.abs(maxVal)) * 100%` (line 60), which uses absolute values. The backend sorts feature_importance / feature_importance_loss by RAW value descending, not by absolute value (src/haute/modelling/_algorithms.py:620-624 and 639-643 `sorted(..., key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)`), and CatBoost LossFunctionChange importances can be negative (no abs/clip applied; _result_types.py:19). Consequences on the 'Loss' tab: (a) a feature with a large NEGATIVE importance sorts LAST, so its |importance| can exceed |items[0].importance|, yielding a bar width > 100% (overflow); (b) if items[0].importance is itself negative, Math.abs(maxVal) is a small positive denominator and ALL bars are massively over-scaled; (c) if items[0].importance === 0, `0 || 1` forces maxVal=1, mis-scaling every bar. The hardened sibling FeaturesTab.tsx computes `maxVal = items.map(i => Math.abs(i.importance)).reduce((a,b)=>Math.max(a,b), -Infinity)` (FeaturesTab.tsx:46) and guards the denominator with `maxVal > 0 ? ... : '0%'` (FeaturesTab.tsx:91). Existing FeatureImportance tests only use positive descending importances, so this is uncovered.
evidence: FeatureImportance.tsx:28 `const maxVal = items[0]?.importance || 1` -> :60 `width: ${(Math.abs(fi.importance)/Math.abs(maxVal))*100}%`. Backend _algorithms.py:620-624 sorts by raw value desc; LossFunctionChange may be negative; _result_types.py:19 stores it unmodified. Correct pattern in FeaturesTab.tsx:46,91.

title: LossChart and LossTab duplicate loss-curve logic that has already diverged (stale 'same logic' claim)
description: LossChart.tsx and LossTab.tsx independently re-implement the same loss-curve pipeline: filter iteration keys, find train_/eval_ keys, gather y-values, compute yMin/yMax/yRange, xScale/yScale, makePath, and the best-iteration clamp. The LossChart doc-comment is not the source of this note, but LossTab.tsx:4 explicitly says 'Same logic as LossChart.tsx'. They have already drifted apart on finite-value handling and best-iteration clamping (see the bug findings above), which is exactly the failure mode of copy-paste duplication. Extracting the shared scaling/path helpers (e.g. a `useLossCurveGeometry(lossHistory, bestIteration)` hook returning { trainKey, evalKey, makePath, bestX, isEmpty }) into one module would remove the divergence and let both the sidebar and full-size charts share one hardened implementation.
evidence: LossChart.tsx:18-49 mirrors LossTab.tsx:38-100 (key discovery, allVals reduce for yMin/yMax, xScale/yScale closures, makePath, bestX). LossTab.tsx:4 'Same logic as LossChart.tsx'.
est_reduction: ~30-40 lines of duplicated scaling/path logic consolidated into one shared helper
behavior_preservation: Behavior-changing if unified on the hardened LossTab version (fixes the NaN/clamp bugs); if pure consolidation is desired, the shared helper must reproduce each chart's current sizing/margins and empty-state, leaving rendered output identical for finite data.

title: JSON Preview interpolates column names without escaping, producing invalid JSON for names containing quotes/backslashes/newlines
description: The "JSON Preview" block builds a JSON-looking string by raw template-interpolating each selected field name: `fields.map((f) => `  "${f}": ...`).join(",\n")`. Field names are upstream Polars column names, which can legitimately contain double-quotes, backslashes, or newlines (Polars permits arbitrary column-name strings). For such a column the rendered preview is not valid JSON (e.g. a column named `a"b` renders as `  "a"b": ...`), so the panel labelled 'JSON Preview' would misrepresent the actual response shape. The correct idiom is to serialize the key via `JSON.stringify(f)` (which yields a properly-escaped, quoted key) instead of wrapping in literal quotes. Impact is display-only — the string lives inside a `<pre>` and is never parsed or sent over the wire — so there is no runtime/security consequence, only a misleading preview for unusual column names.

title: `abortRef` is write-only — assigned but never read
description: The hook declares `const abortRef = useRef<AbortController | null>(null)` (line 15) and assigns it inside the mount effect (`abortRef.current = controller`, line 39), but the ref is never read anywhere. The effect's cleanup aborts the *local* `controller` variable (`return () => { controller.abort() }`), not `abortRef.current`. The manual `fetchForPath` call path never consults `abortRef` either. The ref therefore serves no purpose and gives the misleading impression that in-flight requests are tracked/cancellable across calls when they are not.
evidence: Line 15 declares ref; line 38 creates `const controller = new AbortController()`; line 39 `abortRef.current = controller`; line 42 calls `fetchForPath(initialPath, controller.signal)`; cleanup (line 44-46) calls `controller.abort()` using the closure variable, not `abortRef.current`. Grep for `abortRef` in the file returns only the declaration (15) and the assignment (39) — zero reads.
est_reduction: 2 lines (the ref declaration + the assignment), plus removes a false signal that request cancellation is centrally tracked.
behavior_preservation: Removing the unused ref does not change any observable behavior: cleanup already aborts via the local `controller`, and no code reads `abortRef.current`.

title: Manual `fetchForPath` call has no abort signal → stale schema can overwrite newer result on rapid file switch
description: `fetchForPath(path, signal?)` only guards its `.then`/`.catch` with `signal?.aborted`. The auto-fetch effect passes a real signal (so it is cancellable), but consumers call it manually WITHOUT a signal: `ApiInputEditor` does `onUpdate('path', path); fetchForPath(path)` on file select. Because `signal` is undefined, that promise's `.then` runs unconditionally and calls `setSchema(data)` whenever it resolves. If the user selects file A (manual fetch A, unabortable) and quickly selects file B, the path-change effect aborts only its own controller for the *previous* path; the manual fetch A is never aborted, so a late-resolving A response can call `setSchema(dataA)` after B's result, leaving the panel showing A's schema while config.path is B. Additionally, on every select the same path is fetched twice (once manually, once by the effect that fires when `initialPath` changes), wasting a network round-trip.
evidence: useSchemaFetch.ts:21 `if (signal?.aborted) return` then `setSchema(data)`; ApiInputEditor.tsx:154 `useSchemaFetch(currentPath)` where `currentPath = config.path`; ApiInputEditor.tsx:374-376 `onUpdate('path', path); fetchForPath(path)` — manual call passes no signal. The effect (useSchemaFetch.ts:35-47) re-runs when `initialPath` changes (config.path just changed), starting a second fetch for the same path. The manual fetch is not stored/abortable (abortRef is unused), so it cannot be cancelled when the path changes again.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: sanitizeName omits the keyword-prefix step, diverging from backend _sanitize_func_name for Python-keyword labels (e.g. "class" -> frontend "class" vs backend "node_class")
description: The frontend sanitizeName() is explicitly documented to stay in sync with the backend src/haute/_graph_utils.py::_sanitize_func_name (see the file's own docstring and the comment block at NodePanel.tsx:699-708). The backend performs FOUR final guards: (1) prefix node_ if the result starts with a digit, (2) prefix node_ if the result is a Python keyword via keyword.iskeyword(name), then (3) fall back to unnamed_node. The frontend implements only guards (1) and (3) and SKIPS the keyword guard entirely. There is no keyword check anywhere in frontend/src (grep for iskeyword/keyword finds only CodeMirror syntax-highlight tokens). Consequently, for any node whose label sanitises to a reserved Python keyword (class, return, import, for, if, def, lambda, while, with, yield, global, None, True, False, and, or, not, in, is, etc.), the two implementations disagree: backend produces e.g. "node_class" but frontend produces "class". sanitizeName feeds load-bearing identifiers in NodePanel.tsx: upstream input varNames for wiring (lines 244, 254, 360, 636), and the api_input cache configPath `config/quote_input/${sanitizeName(label)}.json` (line 708). The backend writes/reads these under the keyword-prefixed name. The mismatch reproduces exactly the class of bug the NodePanel.tsx:699-708 comment says was fixed: the frontend computes a name the backend never wrote, so the api_input cache-status GET resolves to the wrong path -> silent cached=false / unresponsive cache button; and editor-displayed input variable names disagree with the names in generated code. The keyword guard is necessary precisely because str.isidentifier() returns True for keywords (so the identifier-validity invariant alone does not catch them) - the backend's own test_parser_sanitize_contracts.py::test_round_trip_stability_on_ascii deliberately includes "class" in its candidate list.
evidence: Backend _graph_utils.py:121-125: `if name and name[0].isdigit(): name = f"node_{name}"` then `if keyword.iskeyword(name): name = f"node_{name}"` then `return name or "unnamed_node"`. Frontend sanitizeName.ts:36-37: `if (name && /^[0-9]/.test(name)) name = \`node_${name}\`` then `return name || "unnamed_node"` -- the keyword branch is absent. So sanitizeName("class") === "class" while _sanitize_func_name("class") === "node_class". NodePanel.tsx:708 builds `config/quote_input/${sanitizeName(node.data.label)}.json`, and codegen.py:546/_save_pipeline.py:229 build the backend-side names via _sanitize_func_name -> the two paths/idents differ for keyword labels.

title: Unused `_ratio` parameter in isConstraintMet is dead in all production callers
description: isConstraintMet(thresholdType, _ratio, absValue, thresholdVal) never reads `_ratio`; its body only branches on thresholdType and compares absValue against thresholdVal. Both production call sites pass the literal `0` for the ratio argument (SummaryTab.tsx:63 and DetailCard.tsx:143). The parameter exists purely as a placeholder in the signature. Since neither caller derives anything from a ratio, the second positional argument is dead weight that forces callers to thread a meaningless `0` and slightly obscures the constraint-evaluation contract. The underscore prefix indicates the author already recognises it is unused. Removing it (and updating the two callers + the test) would simplify the signature with zero behaviour change.
evidence: optimiserHelpers.ts body: `if (thresholdType === "min") return absValue >= thresholdVal; if (thresholdType === "max") return absValue <= thresholdVal; return false` — `_ratio` is never referenced. Callers: SummaryTab.tsx:63 `isConstraintMet(thresholdType, 0, value, thresholdVal)`; DetailCard.tsx:143 `isConstraintMet(thresholdType, 0, value, thresholdVal)`. No call site passes a non-zero ratio in production (only the unit test passes varying ratios, and those values cannot change the result).
est_reduction: ~1 parameter removed from signature + 2 call-site arg removals + 1 test signature tidy
behavior_preservation: Fully behaviour-preserving: the parameter is never read, so removing it and dropping the `0` arg at both call sites yields identical output for every input.

title: Write-only instance attribute `self._contract_categorical_levels` is never read anywhere
description: `self._contract_categorical_levels` is initialised in `__init__` (line 369) and reassigned in `run()` (line 426: `self._contract_categorical_levels = dict(prepared.categorical_levels)`), but it is never read in production code or tests. A repo-wide search for the name returns only those two write sites. Its two sibling snapshot attributes set on the adjacent lines are genuinely consumed (`_contract_feature_dtypes` at line 1473 in `_feature_dtypes_for_contract`, `_contract_target_dtype` at line 1477 in `_target_dtype_for_contract`), but the categorical-levels snapshot has no reader: the categorical domains that actually reach the artifact/signature writers flow through a different path entirely — `prepared.categorical_levels` is passed straight into `_save_artifacts` (line 509), and `_log_to_mlflow`/`_save_artifacts` recompute via `_categorical_levels_for_contract`. The docstring at lines 365-370 justifies the snapshot trio generically, but the categorical-levels member is swept along unused. The `dict(...)` copy at line 426 is therefore wasted work and the attribute is misleading state.
evidence: Grep for `_contract_categorical_levels` across the whole repo (src + tests) yields exactly two hits, both assignments (line 369 init, line 426 in run); zero reads. Contrast `_contract_feature_dtypes` (read at line 1473) and `_contract_target_dtype` (read at line 1477). The live categorical-levels value used downstream comes from `prepared.categorical_levels` (run() line 509 -> _save_artifacts) and `_categorical_levels_for_contract`, never from `self._contract_categorical_levels`.
est_reduction: ~2 lines (remove the line 369 declaration and the line 426 assignment)
behavior_preservation: No behavioural change: the attribute has no readers, so deleting both writes cannot affect any artifact, signature, contract, or test output. Pure dead-state removal.

title: Split parquet leaks if the bare `os.unlink(data_path)` at line 821 raises after the split file was written
description: `_split_data` writes the split parquet to `split_path` (lines 789-807) and then, on success, removes the prepared input with a bare `os.unlink(data_path)` (line 821) — bypassing the loud-but-safe `_remove_temp_parquet` helper used everywhere else in this module. If that `os.unlink` raises an `OSError` (e.g. a transient Windows file lock, EBUSY, or a permission/network-FS hiccup on the temp dir), the exception propagates out of `_split_data` BEFORE it can `return _SplitResult(...)`. Because `_SplitResult` was never returned, `run()`'s `split_result` stays `None`, so the `finally` -> `_cleanup_owned_temp_parquets(prepared, split_result)` only considers `prepared` and never sees `split_path`. The freshly written split parquet (potentially multi-GB) is therefore orphaned in the OS temp dir — exactly the failure mode the remediation-4b.6 cleanup net (run() lines 550-558) was built to prevent. The same bare-unlink pattern at `_prepare_data` line 707 has the analogous shape, though there `data_path` is still tracked by `prepared` so the leak is narrower. The dedicated cleanup test suite (tests/test_training_temp_cleanup.py) exercises cancellation and metrics/validation failures but has no case where the inline `os.unlink` itself fails, so this window is untested.
evidence: _split_data: split_path created (789-794) and written via bounded_sink (803); on the failure branch only split_path is removed (812-814); on success line 821 does `os.unlink(data_path)` then line 824 `return _SplitResult(... owns_tmp=True)`. If line 821 throws, the function raises pre-return, so run() (474-478) gets no split_result; the finally at 558 calls _cleanup_owned_temp_parquets(prepared, None) which builds candidates only from prepared (573-576) — split_path is never a candidate and leaks. Every other temp deletion in the module routes through _remove_temp_parquet (which swallows OSError to a warning), but lines 707 and 821 use a raw os.unlink.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: `asdict(self.split_config) if self.split_config else {}` — the `else {}` branch is unreachable and contradicts the unconditional `self.split_config.<attr>` access 17 lines below in the same call
description: In `_log_to_mlflow`, the `metadata = ModelCardMetadata(...)` construction guards the split_config field with `split_config=asdict(self.split_config) if self.split_config else {}`. `self.split_config` is assigned unconditionally in `__init__` (lines 358-363): it is always a `SplitConfig` — a passed `SplitConfig`, a `SplitConfig(**split)` built from a dict, or `SplitConfig()` — and is never `None`. `SplitConfig` is a plain `@dataclass` (src/haute/modelling/_split.py:12-13) with no `__bool__` or `__len__`, so any instance is always truthy. The `else {}` branch is therefore dead. Worse, it is internally inconsistent: the very same `log_experiment(...)` call dereferences `self.split_config` WITHOUT any guard at lines 1568-1570 (`self.split_config.strategy`, `self.split_config.validation_size`, `self.split_config.holdout_size`). If `self.split_config` could ever be falsy/None (the premise of the line-1551 guard), those three accesses would raise `AttributeError` first — proving the guard is both unnecessary and contradictory. The simplification is to drop the guard: `split_config=asdict(self.split_config)`.
evidence: __init__ lines 358-363: `if isinstance(split, SplitConfig): self.split_config = split / elif isinstance(split, dict): self.split_config = SplitConfig(**split) / else: self.split_config = SplitConfig()` — every branch sets a SplitConfig, none sets None. _split.py:12-13 shows `@dataclass\nclass SplitConfig:` with no __bool__/__len__ override (grep found none) ⇒ always truthy. Same method, line 1551 guards it, while lines 1568-1570 inside the immediately-following `log_experiment(...)` call read `self.split_config.strategy / .validation_size / .holdout_size` unconditionally. The guarded and unguarded usages cannot both be correct; the unguarded ones are correct, so the guard is dead.
est_reduction: -0 to -1 LOC (replace `asdict(self.split_config) if self.split_config else {}` with `asdict(self.split_config)`); removes one dead branch and the false implication that split_config can be None.
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-identical for all reachable states: self.split_config is always a truthy SplitConfig, so the expression already always evaluates to `asdict(self.split_config)`. No call path can make the `else {}` fire (run() is the only caller of _log_to_mlflow and it uses the same self instance whose __init__ guaranteed a SplitConfig).

title: `model_path=result.model_path or None` — `result.model_path` is always a non-empty string on the only call path, so the `or None` fallback never fires
description: In `_log_to_mlflow`, `log_experiment(...)` is called with `model_path=result.model_path or None`. `_log_to_mlflow` is invoked only from `run()` (line 545), and the `TrainResult` it receives is built at lines 512-540 with `model_path=str(model_path)`, where `model_path` is the `Path` returned by `_save_artifacts` (always `output_dir / f"{self.name}{ext}"`, a non-empty path). `str(Path(...))` is therefore always a non-empty string, which is truthy, so `result.model_path or None` always evaluates to `result.model_path`. The `or None` fallback is dead. (`TrainResult.model_path` is even typed `str`, not `str | None`, at line 174, reinforcing that None is not an expected value.) This is lower-confidence than the split_config finding because `TrainResult` is a public dataclass that an external caller could in principle construct with `model_path=""` before calling `_log_to_mlflow` directly; on the actual in-tree call path the branch is unreachable.
evidence: run() line 505-510 binds `model_path = self._save_artifacts(...)` (a Path); _save_artifacts returns `output_dir / f"{self.name}{ext}"` (line 1324/1360). TrainResult constructed at 512 with `model_path=str(model_path)` ⇒ non-empty str. TrainResult.model_path annotated `str` (line 174). _log_to_mlflow is reached only via run() line 545 with that same result, so `result.model_path` is always a truthy non-empty string and `... or None` never yields None.
est_reduction: -0 LOC (replace `result.model_path or None` with `result.model_path`); removes a dead fallback.
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-identical on the in-tree call path (result.model_path is always a non-empty string). Only a direct external caller passing model_path="" would observe a difference, which the production pipeline never does.

title: _ave_categorical_bins sentinel '__MISSING__' collides with a real category of that name
description: In _ave_categorical_bins the null-handling uses a string sentinel: `col.cast(pl.Utf8).fill_null("__MISSING__")` (line 567), and a group whose category equals `"__MISSING__"` is later relabeled to "Missing" (line 590). If the categorical feature contains a genuine category whose string value is literally `"__MISSING__"`, those real rows are merged into the same group as the true nulls and then presented under the label "Missing". This silently conflates two distinct populations (real value vs. missing) in the Actual-vs-Expected diagnostic, producing a misleading AvE row. The collision is a stringly-typed sentinel rather than an out-of-band null marker, so it is data-dependent and not guarded against. Note _ave_numeric_bins is NOT affected (its "Missing" label is for NaN-masked numeric rows, which cannot collide with a numeric value).
evidence: Line 567: `"cat": col.cast(pl.Utf8).fill_null("__MISSING__")`. Group-by at lines 573-581 keys on this column, so a row with the real string `"__MISSING__"` shares the null group's key. Line 590: `label = "Missing" if row["cat"] == "__MISSING__" else row["cat"]` — both the genuine-null group and any real `"__MISSING__"` category render as "Missing". The two populations are summed together in `exposure`/`sum_actual`/`sum_predicted` and cannot be distinguished downstream.

title: render_horizontal_bars_svg scales the axis by abs(value) but orders/selects bars by raw signed value, so a single large-magnitude negative inflates the scale while being sorted last or dropped
description: The function sorts items by RAW value descending and truncates to max_items: `items = sorted(data, key=lambda d: d.get(value_key, 0), reverse=True)[:max_items]` (line 446). The axis scale is then computed from the ABSOLUTE value: `max_val = max(abs(d[value_key]) for d in items)` (line 455), and each bar width is `plot_w * abs(item[value_key]) / max_val` (lines 473-474), while the printed value label uses the SIGNED value `{item[value_key]:.4f}` (line 489). These two sort/scale conventions disagree for mixed-sign data: a feature with a large negative value (e.g. -50) is the LEAST important by raw-descending sort (placed at the bottom, or dropped entirely when there are more than max_items rows), yet it sets max_val=50, shrinking every positive bar toward zero and making them visually near-invisible. The chart thus draws bar magnitudes (abs) and bar ordering (signed) that tell contradictory stories about 'importance'. Reachable via diag.feature_importance_loss (CatBoost LossFunctionChange), which the caller _model_card.py:201-205 routes through this function and which can legitimately be negative when a feature's removal would reduce loss (importance/mean_abs_shap are always >=0, so those two callers are unaffected).
evidence: Confirmed with synthetic data: render_horizontal_bars_svg([{feature:'strong_negative',v:-100},{feature:'tiny_pos_1',v:0.3},{feature:'tiny_pos_2',v:0.2}], max_items=2) renders only ['tiny_pos_1','tiny_pos_2'] — 'strong_negative' (|v|=100, the largest magnitude) is dropped because raw-descending sort places it last, yet had it been kept it would set max_val=100 and crush the others. With max_items not limiting, top->bottom order for v=[0.5,-0.9,0.1] is ['A','C','B'] even though B has the biggest |v|. Upstream producer (_algorithms.py:639-644 feature_importance_typed) also sorts by raw value desc, so the chart's ordering is consistent with the system, but the abs-based scale at line 455 is the lone inconsistency. tests/test_charts.py::test_negative_values only asserts well-formed XML, not scale/ordering, so this is uncovered.

title: _render_dual_axis_chart computes a truncated `display` label for every x tick but the non-rotated branch ignores it and emits the full untruncated label, so long non-rotated x-labels render at full length (overlap/overflow) while `display` is dead on that path
description: At line 210 the loop unconditionally computes `display = _truncate_label(str(label), 15)`. The rotated branch (lines 213-218) renders `_escape(display)` (truncated), but the non-rotated branch (lines 220-224) renders `_escape(str(label))` — the FULL, untruncated label. Consequently the `display` computation is wasted work on the common non-rotated path (a small per-tick allocation), and, more importantly, the two branches apply inconsistent truncation policy: rotated labels are capped at 15 chars while non-rotated labels are emitted verbatim. A caller that passes long labels with rotate_labels=False (e.g. render_double_lift_svg, which is hard-wired to the non-rotated path) renders the full string centered under each point, so long labels overlap their neighbours and overflow the plot width, whereas the same labels under rotation would have been truncated. This is distinct from the known AvE-label-truncation finding (which concerns rotated labels with a shared 15-char prefix colliding AFTER truncation); here the defect is the non-rotated branch never truncating at all and `display` being unused on that branch.
evidence: Confirmed: render_double_lift_svg([{decile:'VERY_LONG_DECILE_LABEL_0123456789',...},{decile:'B',...}]) (always non-rotated) emits the full 'VERY_LONG_DECILE_LABEL_0123456789' in the SVG and never the truncated form 'VERY_LONG_DECIL…'. The same chart with rotate_labels=True emits the truncated '…' form and not the full label. So `display` at line 210 is computed-but-unused whenever rotate_labels is False, and non-rotated long labels are not length-bounded.
behavior_preservation: Either hoist the `display` computation into the rotated branch only (eliminating dead work on the non-rotated path) or use `_escape(display)` in BOTH branches so non-rotated long labels are truncated consistently (a behaviour change that bounds label width). The truncation width (15) and rotation decision are otherwise unchanged.
est_reduction: ~1 line of dead computation removed from the hot non-rotated path; resolves the truncate-policy asymmetry between the two branches
