title: early_stopping_rounds default block collapses to a single assignment (pop + guard are no-ops)
description: Inside CatBoostAlgorithm.fit, the block `if eval_pool is not None and "early_stopping_rounds" not in model_params:` is only entered when the key is ABSENT from model_params. It then does `early_stop = model_params.pop("early_stopping_rounds", 50)` — but since the key is guaranteed absent (that is the branch condition), `.pop` unconditionally returns the default 50; it never pops anything. The subsequent guard `if early_stop and early_stop > 0:` is therefore `if 50 and 50 > 0`, which is always True. The whole 3-line body is exactly equivalent to `model_params["early_stopping_rounds"] = 50`. The pop, the local, and the conditional are dead complexity that imply a configurability (e.g. honouring/clearing a user-supplied value) that the outer guard has already excluded.
evidence: Line 513 guard: `"early_stopping_rounds" not in model_params` -> key absent. Line 514: `model_params.pop("early_stopping_rounds", 50)` on an absent key returns 50 (default) and removes nothing. Line 515: `if early_stop and early_stop > 0` with early_stop==50 is always True. Line 516 then sets it to 50. Test tests/test_algorithms_coverage.py:475 `test_early_stopping_rounds_default` asserts only the net effect `captured_params.get("early_stopping_rounds") == 50`, so collapsing to one assignment preserves behaviour.
est_reduction: 3 lines -> 1 line (drop the pop, the local, and the always-true conditional).
behavior_preservation: Net effect is identical: when an eval pool is present and the user did not set early_stopping_rounds, the param becomes 50. The replaced internals are provably unreachable/constant (key absent by the guard; 50 is truthy/positive), so no input changes the outcome. The existing default test continues to pass.

title: feature_importance and feature_importance_typed are byte-identical except the get_feature_importance call
description: CatBoostAlgorithm.feature_importance (617-625) and feature_importance_typed (627-644) share the same body: read `model.feature_names_`, `zip(names, importances)`, `sorted(..., key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)`, then `[{"feature": name, "importance": float(imp)} for name, imp in pairs]`. The only difference is the importances source: `model.get_feature_importance()` vs `model.get_feature_importance(data=pool, type=type_name)`. The sort+projection tail can be factored into one private helper (e.g. `_rank_importances(names, importances)`) called by both, removing the duplicated ranking/formatting logic.
evidence: Lines 618-625 and 637-644 differ only at line 619 (`model.get_feature_importance()`) vs line 638 (`model.get_feature_importance(data=pool, type=type_name)`); the `names = model.feature_names_`, the `sorted(zip(...), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)` and the return comprehension are textually identical.
est_reduction: ~8 duplicated lines reduced to a shared 3-line helper (net ~5 lines).
behavior_preservation: Both methods keep their exact public signatures and call the same CatBoost API with the same arguments; only the shared post-processing (sort by importance desc, project to {feature, importance:float}) is centralised, producing byte-identical output lists.

title: GPU loss-history 'iteration' is 0-based int while CPU callback writes 1-based float, mis-aligning the loss-curve x-axis between paths
description: The CPU progress callback (_CatBoostProgressCallback.after_iteration) records `history_entry = {"iteration": float(it)}` with `it = info.iteration + 1` — i.e. 1-based and float. The GPU reconstruction branch in CatBoostAlgorithm.fit (lines 567-581) instead appends `{"iteration": i}` where `i` is the 0-based enumerate index and an int. The two paths therefore emit different `iteration` conventions for the same logical training. render_loss_curve_svg (src/haute/modelling/_charts.py:310/369/378) uses this `iteration` field directly as the x-coordinate (`x_pos(iterations[i])`), and the best-iteration marker is positioned with `x_pos(best_iteration)` (line 386-387) where best_iteration comes from CatBoost's 0-based `best_iteration_`. Consequently the marker is consistent with the curve on GPU (both 0-based) but off-by-one on CPU (curve 1-based, marker 0-based), and the same model trained on CPU vs GPU renders its x-axis shifted by one. The divergence is a contract mismatch between two in-scope code paths writing the same loss_history schema.
evidence: Line 190-194: `it = info.iteration + 1` then `history_entry = {"iteration": float(it)}` (1-based, float). Lines 573-575/579-581: `if i >= len(loss_history): loss_history.append({"iteration": i})` with `for i, v in enumerate(values)` (0-based, int). _charts.py:386 `clamped = min(best_iteration, x_max); bx = x_pos(clamped)` plots best_iteration on the same axis as `iterations` (line 310 `d.get("iteration", i)`), so a 1-based curve + 0-based marker (CPU) is misaligned by one.

location: src/haute/modelling/_mlflow_log.py:376-381 (register_model call in log_experiment); contrast _log_model_with_signature at 457-462 (catboost.log_model artifact_path="model") and 471-476 (pyfunc.log_model artifact_path="model" + log_artifact at run root)
title: Databricks model registration uses the source filename basename, not the artifact_path the model was actually logged under — registration fails for CatBoost models
description: log_experiment registers the model with source URI f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/{Path(model_path).name}" (e.g. runs:/<id>/model.cbm). But the model is logged by _log_model_with_signature via mlflow.catboost.log_model(cb_model=..., artifact_path="model", ...), which writes an MLflow model *directory* at artifact path 'model' (containing MLmodel + the serialized CatBoost file) and never logs a top-level 'model.cbm' artifact (the CatBoost branch returns at line 462 without any log_artifact). The correct registration source for that logged model is runs:/<id>/model, not runs:/<id>/model.cbm. On Databricks (the only branch where register_model runs: line 376 gates on backend=="databricks"), mlflow.register_model("runs:/<id>/model.cbm", ...) resolves a non-existent artifact path and fails. The non-CatBoost branch (.rsglm/pyfunc) does log the raw file at the run root via mlflow.log_artifact(str(model_file)) (line 476), so runs:/<id>/<name>.rsglm exists as a bare artifact — but that is the raw model file, not the logged pyfunc model at runs:/<id>/model, so registering it as a UC model is still the wrong source. Both flavors should register runs:/<id>/model.
evidence: Line 379: f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/{Path(model_path).name}" -> for model_path ending in 'model.cbm' this is runs:/<id>/model.cbm. Lines 457-462 (CatBoost branch): mlflow.catboost.log_model(cb_model=cat_model, artifact_path="model", signature=signature); return — no log_artifact, so the only model artifact is the directory 'model/' (flavor format), and there is NO 'model.cbm' file artifact at the run root. Therefore the registration source path 'model.cbm' does not exist among the run's artifacts and register_model raises. tests/test_mlflow_log.py:514-517 enshrines the wrong URI by asserting register_model is called with "runs:/abc123/model.cbm" while mlflow.catboost.log_model is mocked away, so the mismatch is never exercised end-to-end. The fix is to register f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/model" (the artifact_path both log_model calls use).
behavior_preservation: n/a (correctness fix changes the registration URI to runs:/<id>/model; the existing test assertion at tests/test_mlflow_log.py:514-517 would need updating to the correct path).

title: Temp JSON file leaks when json.dump raises — cleanup try/finally wraps only log_artifact, not the dump that created the file
description: _log_json_artifact opens tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(..., delete=False) and calls json.dump(data, f, indent=2) inside the with-block. The os.unlink(f.name) cleanup lives in a separate try/finally that begins AFTER the with-block and only guards the mlflow.log_artifact call. If json.dump raises inside the with-block (data is typed Any; a non-JSON-serializable value such as a numpy np.int64 / np.float32 / np.ndarray embedded in a diagnostic dict raises TypeError), the file has already been created on disk and is closed by the with-exit, but the unlink is never reached — the temp file is orphaned in the OS temp directory. The created file is also not removed on the exception path the way log_artifact failures are. In normal operation the diagnostic producers cast to native float() (e.g. _algorithms.py feature_importance/shap_summary), so this is primarily a defense-in-depth/cleanup-contract gap rather than a guaranteed production leak, but the helper's own try/finally clearly intends to always clean up and fails to do so for the write step.
evidence: Lines 140-150: `with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w", suffix=".json", prefix=f"{prefix}_", delete=False) as f: json.dump(data, f, indent=2)` then `try: mlflow.log_artifact(f.name, artifact_dir) finally: os.unlink(f.name)`. Because delete=False, the file persists after the with-block; the only unlink is in the finally attached to log_artifact. A TypeError from json.dump (json.dump(np.int64(5), f) raises 'Object of type int64 is not JSON serializable') propagates out before reaching the try/finally, leaking f.name. A correct shape wraps the NamedTemporaryFile usage (write + log) in a single try whose finally unlinks, or writes to a directory cleaned via try/finally around the whole body.
behavior_preservation: n/a (correctness/cleanup fix; on the success path behavior is unchanged).

title: Unreachable `list(invalid_series or [])` fallback in validate_categorical_value_domains is dead and would itself raise if reached
description: After `examples = streaming_collect(lazy.select(invalid_example_exprs), ...)`, the loop does `invalid_series = examples[column][0]`. Every expr in `invalid_example_exprs` ends in `.implode()`, so each output column has dtype List(String); indexing `[0]` into a List-typed Series ALWAYS returns an inner `polars.Series`, which always exposes `.to_list()`. Therefore `hasattr(invalid_series, 'to_list')` is invariably True and the `else list(invalid_series or [])` branch is never taken. Worse, the fallback is not even a valid safety net: if it ever did run on a non-empty Series, `invalid_series or []` raises `TypeError: the truth value of a Series is ambiguous` (verified: bool() on a polars Series of any length raises). `implode()` also never yields a null/None element (an all-valid or empty frame produces an empty inner Series, not None — verified), so the `or []` None-guard is doubly dead. This is exactly the kind of incorrect, hard-to-notice fallback CLAUDE.md forbids; the branch should be removed and replaced with a direct `invalid_series.to_list()`.
evidence: Empirically: for an empty input frame, `lazy.select(value_expr.filter(invalid).unique().head(10).implode())` yields shape (1,1) with `examples[column][0]` == an empty `pl.Series` (has `.to_list()` -> []); for invalid rows it's a non-empty `pl.Series`. `bool(pl.Series(['east']) or [])` -> TypeError 'truth value of a Series is ambiguous'. Thus the else-branch is unreachable, and unsound if reached.
est_reduction: ~4 lines collapse to 1 (`invalid_values = examples[column][0].to_list()`)
behavior_preservation: Behaviour identical for every reachable input (the else branch can never execute on the polars data path); removing it only deletes an unreachable, unsound fallback.

title: `truncated` flag is a false positive when exactly max_examples distinct invalid values exist
description: The error context computes `truncated=len(invalid_values) >= max_examples`. But `invalid_values` is produced by `.head(max_examples)`, so `len(invalid_values)` can never exceed `max_examples`; the comparison is true precisely when `len == max_examples`. That condition is reached both when the invalid set was genuinely larger than `max_examples` (truly truncated) AND when there were exactly `max_examples` distinct invalid values with none dropped. In the latter case `truncated=True` is wrong and would mislead an operator/log consumer into believing more invalid levels exist than were reported. The standard fix is to materialise `max_examples + 1` examples and report `truncated = len(examples) > max_examples` (then trim for display).
evidence: Line 456-461 builds `... .head(max_examples) .implode()`. Line 469-473 yields at most `max_examples` items. Line 481 sets `truncated=len(invalid_values) >= max_examples`, so a column with exactly `max_examples` distinct out-of-domain values reports `truncated=True` despite the list being complete.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: max_examples <= 0 silently disables the categorical-domain check (no-op validator)
description: `validate_categorical_value_domains` caps examples with `.head(max_examples)`. If a caller passes `max_examples=0`, `.head(0)` returns an empty Series for every column, so `invalid_values` is always `[]`, `if invalid_values:` is never true, and the function returns without raising even when the frame contains values outside the declared domain — a safety check silently becomes a no-op. A negative `max_examples` is worse: polars `.head(-k)` drops the LAST k rows (verified: `Series.head(-1)` returns all-but-last), so the validator under-reports invalid values and the `truncated` flag becomes meaningless. No current in-tree caller passes a non-default value (`_validate_runtime_categorical_values` and `_assert_runtime_contract_matches` omit it), so this is latent rather than active, but given the module's fail-loud mandate the function should reject `max_examples <= 0` instead of degrading into a silent pass.
evidence: Param default is `max_examples: int = 10`. `Series('x',['a','b','c','d']).head(0).to_list()` == [] and `.head(-1).to_list()` == ['a','b','c'] (verified). With max_examples=0 the per-column `.head(0)` yields empty implode -> invalid_values==[] -> no raise even for out-of-domain data.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: `ordered` list in normalise_categorical_levels is redundant with `seen`
description: Inside the per-column loop, both a `seen` set and an `ordered` list are maintained. Duplicate detection uses `seen` (line 363); the emptiness guard uses `if not ordered` (line 373); the final output is `sorted(level for level in ordered if level is not None)` plus an appended `None` (lines 380-384). Because the output is fully re-sorted, `ordered`'s insertion order is never used — every consumer of `ordered` could read `seen` instead (`if not seen` is equivalent since seen and ordered always have identical membership and are empty together). `ordered` (and its `.append` on every iteration) is therefore pure overhead and can be deleted, deriving the result solely from `seen`.
evidence: Lines 352/372 build `ordered`; line 373 `if not ordered`; line 381 `sorted(level for level in ordered if level is not None)`. `seen` (lines 353/363/371/383) already holds the exact same elements, and the final list is produced by `sorted(...)`, discarding any order `ordered` preserved.
est_reduction: ~3 lines (drop the `ordered` list and its append; use `seen` for the emptiness check and the sorted comprehension)
behavior_preservation: Identical output: duplicates already rejected before insertion so seen==set(ordered); sorted() makes insertion order irrelevant; `not seen` <=> `not ordered`.

title: include_main all-or-nothing guard still causes duplicate-main-effect singularity on partial factor overlap
description: The guard sets include_main=False only when ALL interaction factors are already in the main `terms` dict, and otherwise forwards include_main (default True). But RustyStats' include_main=True adds main effects for EVERY factor in the interaction. When an interaction mixes factors that ARE already standalone main terms with factors that are NOT (a partial overlap), include_main=True re-adds the main effect for the already-present factor, producing exactly the duplicated main effect / perfect-collinearity / singular-matrix error the docstring (lines 69-74, 89-90) claims to prevent. The guard's premise ('set include_main=True when at least one factor is NOT in terms') is incomplete: a single missing factor flips the whole interaction to include_main=True even though the other, present, factors must NOT get their main effects re-added. RustyStats exposes include_main only as one boolean for the whole interaction, so the present design cannot add only the missing main effects — the partial-overlap case is structurally mishandled.
evidence: terms={'age': {...}} (age is a standalone main term); config=[{'factors':['age','region'],'include_main':True}] with 'region' not in terms. Loop (82-87) builds rs_int={'age':{...copy...},'region':{'type':'categorical'}}. all_in_terms = all(f in terms for f in ['age','region']) = False (region missing). else-branch (95): rs_int['include_main']=interaction.get('include_main',True)=True. RustyStats then ADDS main effects for both age and region; age already exists as a standalone term => duplicate main effect for age => singular matrix at fit. This exact config is constructed in tests/test_rustystats_algorithm.py:92-98 (test_include_main_when_factor_not_in_terms), which asserts only result[0]['include_main'] is True and never attempts a fit, so the singularity is unexercised.

title: Primary coefficients_table path emits partial rows (missing required stat keys) when coef_table() column names are not in key_map, contradicting the strict fallback contract
description: GLMInferenceUnavailableError's docstring and the fallback path (lines 351-390) enforce that every emitted coefficient row carries ALL six normalized fields (feature, coefficient, std_error, z_value, p_value, significance) — the frontend's GlmCoefficientRow declares all six as REQUIRED (frontend/src/api/types.ts:317-324). But the PRIMARY path does no such validation: it maps each raw column with `key_map.get(k, k.lower().replace(' ','_'))` and returns whatever results. If RustyStats names any column outside the hard-coded key_map (e.g. the significance column as 'Signif.' with a trailing dot, a blank ' ' header as R uses for stars, or a renamed z column), that field is emitted under a non-canonical snake_cased key and the canonical key is silently absent. The two emission paths thus enforce opposite contracts: the fallback raises rather than ship a partial row, while the primary path ships partial rows. Because _training_job.py:1237-1241 records coefficients_table() output verbatim into glm_coefficients and the row is shipped to the UI, a future/changed RustyStats column header degrades to a malformed payload instead of the loud GLMInferenceUnavailableError the design intends.
evidence: Lines 331-338: `coef_df = model.coef_table(); raw = coef_df.to_dicts(); return [{key_map.get(k, k.lower().replace(' ','_')): v for k,v in row.items()} for row in raw]`. key_map (319-329) hard-codes exact strings ('Signif' -> 'significance', 'Pr(>|z|)' -> 'p_value', 'z'/'z value'/'z.value' -> 'z_value'). Any unlisted header H yields key H.lower().replace(' ','_') (e.g. 'Signif.' -> 'signif.'), so 'significance' never appears. No post-normalization check verifies the six required keys exist on each row before returning. Contrast: the fallback (367-375) explicitly raises GLMInferenceUnavailableError rather than ship rows missing a stat. Frontend GlmCoefficientRow (types.ts:317-324) lists all six as non-optional.

title: set(cat_features) rebuilt once per feature inside the list-comprehension filter
description: `continuous = [f for f in features if f not in set(cat_features)]` places set(cat_features) in the comprehension's filter predicate, which CPython re-evaluates for every element of `features` — rebuilding the set O(len(features)) times instead of once. Hoisting the set out of the comprehension (compute `cat_set = set(cat_features)` once, then `[f for f in features if f not in cat_set]`) preserves behaviour exactly and makes the membership test O(1) against a single set. The codebase already uses this hoisted idiom elsewhere (e.g. _auto_terms line 48 `cat_set = set(cat_features)`, _algorithms.py:276).
evidence: Line 481: `continuous = [f for f in features if f not in set(cat_features)]`. The expression `set(cat_features)` is part of the `if` clause, so it is constructed afresh on each iteration of `f in features`; the result is identical every time. Compare _auto_terms (line 48-49) which correctly binds `cat_set = set(cat_features)` once before the loop.
est_reduction: 0 net LOC (1 line hoisted into 1 binding + 1 use); removes a per-element set rebuild — micro-perf + consistency with the established cat_set idiom
behavior_preservation: Identical output: f not in set(cat_features) and f not in cat_set are equivalent for every f; only the number of times the set is built changes. No ordering, dtype, or value change.

title: Temporal mask ignores holdout_size when validation_size==0: holdout swallows ALL post-cutoff rows
description: In _temporal_mask the post-cutoff data is split between validation and holdout using holdout_frac = holdout_size / (validation_size + holdout_size). When validation_size == 0 (a valid, explicit request meaning 'no validation set'), this fraction collapses to holdout_size/holdout_size = 1.0, so EVERY post-cutoff row is assigned to holdout regardless of the requested holdout_size. The requested holdout fraction is silently discarded. The subsequent reclassification block (lines 316-318, 'if validation_size == 0: VALIDATION -> TRAIN') cannot help because there are no VALIDATION rows left to convert. This contradicts the documented semantics of holdout_size (a fraction of the dataset, honoured exactly by the sibling _random_mask) and produces a holdout set far larger than requested with no error or warning. The realised holdout fraction equals the entire post-cutoff portion of the data, which is driven by cutoff_date, not by holdout_size at all.
evidence: Executed with venv polars: df of 20 rows, 14 dated 2024-01-01 (pre-cutoff) and 6 dated 2024-08-* (post-cutoff), SplitConfig(strategy='temporal', cutoff_date='2024-06-01', validation_size=0.0, holdout_size=0.1). Result: TRAIN=14, VALIDATION=0, HOLDOUT=6 — i.e. ALL 6 post-cutoff rows (30% of the dataset) became holdout despite holdout_size=0.1 requesting ~2 rows. By direct contrast the SAME config with strategy='random' on 20 rows yields TRAIN=18, VALIDATION=0, HOLDOUT=2, correctly honouring holdout_size=0.1. Code trace: total = validation_size + holdout_size = 0.0 + 0.1 = 0.1; holdout_frac = 0.1/0.1 = 1.0 (line 302); n_holdout = int(len(sorted_non_train) * 1.0) = 6 (line 312); partition[sorted_non_train[-6:]] = HOLDOUT (line 314) marks every post-cutoff row. Reproduced identically with real Date dtype (not just Utf8). validation_size=0 is permitted by __post_init__ (0 <= validation_size) and flows unguarded from user dicts via _train_config.py / _train_service.py SplitConfig(**split).

title: Group mask validation fallback is a no-op when no TRAIN group exists, leaving both validation AND train empty
description: The 'ensure at least one validation group' fallback (lines 352-358) only fires when no group landed in VALIDATION, and it tries to flip the first group that is currently labelled PARTITION_TRAIN into VALIDATION. But when holdout_size is large relative to the (few) groups, it is possible for EVERY unique group to hash below holdout_size and be assigned PARTITION_HOLDOUT — so there is no TRAIN group for the loop to convert. The loop iterates, finds no group with value PARTITION_TRAIN, and breaks out having changed nothing. The result is that validation_size > 0 was requested but the validation partition is silently empty, AND the train partition is also empty (every row is holdout). Training then proceeds on zero rows with no error. The known catalog finding #51 explicitly assumes 'the only correction triggers solely on no_validation' and that it succeeds when it fires; this is the distinct failure mode where the correction fires but is ineffective because its precondition (an available TRAIN group) is not guaranteed.
evidence: Executed with venv polars: df = {'g': ['A','A','B','B','B']} (2 groups), SplitConfig(strategy='group', validation_size=0.2, holdout_size=0.6, seed=2). md5 hash fractions: frac(2,'A')=0.025, frac(2,'B')=0.037, both < holdout_size=0.6, so both groups -> PARTITION_HOLDOUT at lines 344-345. no_validation is True (line 352), validation_size>0 and len(unique_groups)=2>1, so the fallback enters the loop (lines 355-358), but neither A nor B is PARTITION_TRAIN, so nothing is flipped and it breaks. Final mask = [2,2,2,2,2]: TRAIN=0, VALIDATION=0, HOLDOUT=5 — validation requested (0.2) is empty and train is empty. Downstream _training_job._split_data counts n_train/n_validation from this mask and would attempt to train on an empty train partition.

title: _html_table zips body cells against `align` (not the row), silently dropping cells when align is shorter than a row
description: The body-cell loop is `for cell, a in zip(row, align):` (line 50). `zip` stops at the shorter of `row`/`align`, so the number of emitted `<td>` cells is capped at `len(align)`, NOT `len(row)`. If a caller ever passes a row with more cells than the supplied `align` list (or an `align` shorter than the header/row width), the trailing cell value is silently discarded — a column of data vanishes from the rendered table with no error. This is the opposite of the project's stated 'fail loudly' preference: a malformed alignment list produces a silently truncated table rather than an exception. The header loop has the same shape (`zip(headers, align)`, line 44), so a too-short `align` would also drop header columns silently. The correct contract is for cell count to be governed by the row width (e.g. iterate the row and default missing alignments to 'left'), or to assert `len(align) == len(headers)`.
evidence: Line 41 sets `align = ['left'] * len(headers)` ONLY when align is None. Lines 44/50 use `zip(headers, align)` and `zip(row, align)`. With e.g. row=['a','b','c','d'] and align=['left','right','left'], zip yields 3 pairs → only 3 `<td>` emitted; cell 'd' is dropped with no warning. All in-file callers (lines 101,108,116,141-145,172,237) currently pass align/rows consistent with headers, so the path is latent and not exercised by existing tests (tests/test_model_card.py only checks 2-column tables). `_html_table` is private (only used in this file), so the defect is a latent robustness/silent-failure hazard, not an active production bug.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Conflicting top-level var_power vs variance_power is silently resolved (var_power wins) instead of failing loud
description: build_training_job_kwargs only raises on a conflict between config['variance_power'] and an EXPLICIT params['var_power'] entry (guarded by params_has_explicit_var_power, which reads the ORIGINAL config['params'] dict). It does not detect the case where a GLM config carries BOTH a top-level 'var_power' alias and a top-level 'variance_power' with different values. In that case the top-level var_power silently overrides the user's variance_power with no error, contradicting the module's explicit 'Keep one Tweedie variance-power source' contract and the project's fail-loudly guideline.
evidence: Take config = {algorithm:'glm', family:'tweedie', var_power: 1.8, variance_power: 1.3} (no 'params' key). (1) build_train_params: algorithm=='glm' loops GLM_CONFIG_KEYS which includes 'var_power'; 'var_power' in config and not in params -> params['var_power']=1.8. The subsequent `config.get('variance_power') is not None and 'var_power' not in params` check at L67 is now False because var_power is in params, so it is skipped. (2) Back in build_training_job_kwargs: raw_params = config.get('params') or {} == {}, so params_has_explicit_var_power = {}.get('var_power') is None -> False. variance_power initial = config.get('variance_power') = 1.3. (3) L114 enters (glm and params.get('var_power')==1.8 not None). L115 condition: config.get('variance_power')=1.3 is not None AND params_has_explicit_var_power(False) -> overall False -> NO raise. L124: variance_power = params['var_power'] = 1.8. Result: the user-supplied variance_power=1.3 is silently discarded in favour of the var_power=1.8 alias, with no conflict error. The existing conflict test (test_glm_conflicting_variance_power_alias_fails_loudly) only covers the variance_power-vs-params['var_power'] path, not variance_power-vs-top-level-var_power.

title: Dead `reason == "cancelled"` branch in _coerce_stopped_terminal_reason; ternary always returns "superseded"
evidence: haute/routes/_job_lifecycle.py:34-42 defines TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS with "cancelled" as a key (line 38: "cancelled": CANCELLED_STATUS). _optimiser_service.py:383 `if reason in TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS:` therefore catches reason=="cancelled" first, making the `reason == "cancelled"` test on line 385 statically False on every path that reaches it. Contrast haute/routes/_background_jobs.py:231-242 (_coerce_worker_terminal_reason) which is the same shape written without the dead branch (just `return "error"`). Sole caller: _optimiser_service.py:2772 `terminal_reason = _coerce_stopped_terminal_reason(exc.terminal_reason)`.
est_reduction: 1 line simplified (replace ternary with `return "superseded"`); removes a misleading dead conditional
behavior_preservation: Identical: line 385 already evaluates to "superseded" on every reachable path because "cancelled" is always handled by the preceding `if reason in TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` branch. Replacing the ternary with `return "superseded"` is behaviour-preserving for all inputs.

title: _optimiser_setup_target_chunk_bytes and _auto_range_target_chunk_bytes are structurally identical clamp logic differing only in profile and three constants
description: Both functions implement the exact same computation: take `execution_budget_for_profile(<profile>).memory_limit_bytes`, integer-divide by a budget divisor (floored at 1), then clamp the result between a MIN and MAX byte bound via `min(MAX, max(MIN, budget_scaled))`. They differ only in (a) the ExecutionProfile passed (OPTIMISER_SETUP vs AUTO_RANGE) and (b) the three module constants used for divisor/min/max — and those constants are themselves defined to identical values (DIVISOR=16, MIN=16*1024*1024, MAX=512*1024*1024 in both the _DEFAULT_OPTIMISER_SETUP_* and _DEFAULT_AUTO_RANGE_* families, lines 128-133). The two bodies can be collapsed into a single helper such as `_target_chunk_bytes(profile, *, min_bytes, max_bytes, divisor)` (or a single helper taking just the profile, since the constants coincide), with the two named wrappers calling it. This removes a near-verbatim copy of a non-trivial clamp.
evidence: Line 437-446: `budget = execution_budget_for_profile(ExecutionProfile.OPTIMISER_SETUP); budget_scaled = max(1, budget.memory_limit_bytes // _DEFAULT_OPTIMISER_SETUP_TARGET_CHUNK_BUDGET_DIVISOR); return min(_DEFAULT_OPTIMISER_SETUP_TARGET_CHUNK_MAX_BYTES, max(_DEFAULT_OPTIMISER_SETUP_TARGET_CHUNK_MIN_BYTES, budget_scaled))`. Line 516-525 is byte-for-byte the same with AUTO_RANGE substituted. Constants at lines 128-133 confirm the MIN/MAX/DIVISOR values are equal across both families.
est_reduction: ~8-10 LOC (one 8-line body removed; replaced by a shared helper + two thin call sites)
behavior_preservation: Extract the shared clamp into one parameterised helper and have both functions delegate. Output is identical for every profile because the arithmetic is unchanged; the only inputs are the profile-specific budget and the (currently equal) constants, all preserved.

title: _resolve_online_auto_range_data_input_id is a pure single-call pass-through to _resolve_optimiser_data_input_id
description: The function body is exactly `return _resolve_optimiser_data_input_id(graph, node_id, config)` with the same `(graph, node_id, config)` signature and no added logic, error handling, or transformation. It has a single call site (_build_streaming_auto_range_plan at line 868). The wrapper provides only an alternate name; callers could invoke `_resolve_optimiser_data_input_id` directly, removing one layer of indirection. (Low severity — the docstring documents intent, so this is a judgement call rather than a defect.)
evidence: Definition at 762-768 returns `_resolve_optimiser_data_input_id(graph, node_id, config)` verbatim. Only reference found by grep across src/ is the definition (762) and one call (868) inside _build_streaming_auto_range_plan.
est_reduction: ~7 LOC (delete wrapper, inline the single call)
behavior_preservation: Identical: the wrapper performs no work beyond delegation, so replacing the one call site with a direct call to _resolve_optimiser_data_input_id is behaviour-preserving (same exceptions, same return).

title: Dead `if n else 0.0` ternary fallbacks in _compute_scenario_value_stats are unreachable (n is always >= 1 by the time they run)
description: In `_compute_scenario_value_stats`, `n = len(col)` and the function returns early at line 1290-1291 with `if n == 0: return None, None`. Therefore by lines 1310-1311 `n` is always >= 1 and always truthy. The two trailing `... if n else 0.0` conditional expressions for `pct_increase` and `pct_decrease` can never evaluate the `else 0.0` arm: the division `(col > 1.0).sum() / n` always executes. The `if n else 0.0` guard is dead code that falsely suggests a zero-length path is reachable here (it is not — that path is handled above), and it duplicates a guard that already exists earlier.
evidence: Line 1289 `n = len(col)`. Lines 1290-1291 `if n == 0:\n    return None, None` — every n==0 case returns before reaching the stats dict. `n` is an int in [1, +inf) at line 1300+, so `bool(n)` is unconditionally True at lines 1310-1311, making `else 0.0` unreachable. (The sibling `std` key on line 1302 uses the live `if n == 1` discriminator; only the two `if n` guards are vestigial.)
est_reduction: Replace `float((col > 1.0).sum() / n) if n else 0.0` with `float((col > 1.0).sum() / n)` (and likewise for pct_decrease): removes 2 dead conditional arms, no behaviour change.
behavior_preservation: Output is byte-identical for all reachable inputs (n >= 1). The removed `else 0.0` branch is provably never taken because the n==0 case returns at line 1291 before this dict is built.

title: Orphan apply/factor artifact-cleanup branches in _finalize_solve_result are unreachable
description: After a successful terminal transition, both post-transition cleanup branches are guarded by `updated_job.get("artifact_handles") is not artifact_handles`. This identity comparison can never be True on the only path where it is evaluated (updated_job is not None), so neither cleanup branch can ever run. The branches are dead code.
evidence: JobLifecycle.transition (src/haute/routes/_job_lifecycle.py:136-168) returns a non-None job ONLY via _store_merged_job_locked, which builds `merged = {**old, **fields}` (src/haute/routes/_job_store.py:252) where `fields` is our `completion_fields` containing the `artifact_handles` key (line 2266). `**fields` copies the reference, so `merged["artifact_handles"] is artifact_handles` is True. _prepare_heavy_object_policy_locked only touches _HEAVY_OBJECT_KEYS=(solver, solve_result, quote_grid, factors_df, ratebook_factor_contexts) (_job_store.py:31) and never `artifact_handles`. The only None returns from transition are the explicit `return None` paths (lines 150,153,155), and because every call here passes `to="completed"`, line 152 (`if ... or to == "completed": return None`) forces None whenever old_status != "running". Therefore: updated_job is None => the earlier block (lines 2285-2299) handles cleanup and returns; updated_job is not None => updated_job.get('artifact_handles') IS artifact_handles, so `is not artifact_handles` at lines 2302 and 2311 is always False. The bodies at 2304-2308 and 2313-2317 are unreachable.
est_reduction: ~16 lines (two if-blocks)
behavior_preservation: Removing both branches preserves behaviour exactly: they never execute. The genuine orphan-cleanup case (transition skipped) is fully handled by the `if updated_job is None:` block at lines 2285-2299.

title: Factor-table display ordering silently breaks for integer-valued float banding assignments
description: In _serialise_ratebook_factor_table_rows the configured display order (level_positions) is keyed by the RAW str() of banding-rule output values, but each emitted row is placed using its CANONICAL key (normalise_rating_key). When a banding rule's assignment/label is a JSON float with an integer value (e.g. 25.0), the canonical key is "25" while the display-order label is "25.0", so the level never matches its configured position and is silently demoted to the insertion-order fallback bucket. The serialised factor table is then ordered incorrectly relative to the configured banding rule order.
evidence: _ratebook_factor_level_order builds the order list by feeding raw rule values to _append_unique_factor_level (lines 1818-1819), which stores `str(value)` with NO canonicalisation (lines 1764-1771): a float 25.0 becomes "25.0". In _serialise_ratebook_factor_table_rows, `configured_level_order = _ratebook_factor_table_level_order(...)` and `level_positions = {level: index ...}` (lines 2046-2047) are therefore keyed by "25.0". But the row sort key uses the canonical key: `level_key = _canonical_ratebook_table_level(...)` (line 2051) and `sort_key = (0, level_positions[level_key]) if level_key in level_positions else (1, original_index)` (lines 2062-2063). normalise_rating_key(25.0) collapses integer-valued floats to "25" (src/haute/_rating.py:340-341), so `level_key == "25"` is not in level_positions (which has "25.0"), and the level falls into bucket (1, original_index) instead of its configured position. For composite tables the order labels are built via product()+join of raw values (line 1841), so any single integer-valued-float component breaks the composite ordering the same way.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Two orphaned auto-range helper methods (_build_streaming_auto_range_chain_functions, _streaming_scenario_steps) are never called by any code, test, or dispatch
description: Both `OptimiserService._build_streaming_auto_range_chain_functions` (lines 3951-3978) and `OptimiserService._streaming_scenario_steps` (lines 3980-3992) are fully defined but have no callers anywhere in the repository. They are leftovers from an earlier chain-based streaming auto-range design that was superseded by the chunk-plan approach: the live streaming job `_run_streaming_frontier_auto_range_job` builds its chunk iterator inline via `iter_chunked_frames(ChunkRunnerRequest(..., plan=streaming_plan.chunk_plan, ...))` (lines 3746-3769) and never calls `build_linear_execution_chain_functions` nor reads scenario steps. `_build_streaming_auto_range_chain_functions` is the SOLE caller of the module-level import `build_linear_execution_chain_functions` (the only other references are in review tooling/JSON), so removing the method also removes that import's only use. Carrying these methods adds maintenance surface (e.g. `_streaming_scenario_steps`'s `int(raw_steps)` would raise TypeError/ValueError on a non-numeric `steps` config and its `<1` guard, all untested and unreachable) and obscures the actual streaming control flow.
evidence: Grep across all of src/ and tests/ for `_build_streaming_auto_range_chain_functions` and `_streaming_scenario_steps` returns only their own `def` lines (3951, 3981) plus matches inside review/*.json tooling artifacts; no call site, no `getattr(self, ...)` dynamic dispatch exists in _optimiser_service.py, and optimiser.py / frontend contain no references. Grep for `build_linear_execution_chain_functions` shows it is invoked only at line 3967 (inside the dead method) besides its import at line 75 and its definition in src/haute/execution.py:720. The live streaming path at lines 3746-3769 uses `iter_chunked_frames`/`ChunkPlan` instead, confirming the chain-functions/steps helpers are superseded and unreachable.
est_reduction: ~42 LOC (both methods) plus the now-unused `build_linear_execution_chain_functions` import (1 line); a small further trim is possible if that executor export becomes unused elsewhere.
behavior_preservation: Deleting both methods is fully behavior-preserving: no runtime code path, test, or dynamic dispatch reaches them, so no observable behavior changes. The import of build_linear_execution_chain_functions can be dropped in the same change since line 3967 is its only consumer.

title: Constraint named identically to objective/quote_id/scenario_value/scenario_index produces a duplicate-column projection and surfaces a confusing low-level Polars DuplicateError instead of a clear config error
description: In _validate_and_project the required-column existence check is built as a SET (required_cols = {objective, qid_col, mult_col, step_col} plus constraints), so a constraint whose name collides with the objective (or quote_id/scenario_value/scenario_index) does NOT trip _missing_columns_detail. But the projection column list is built as a LIST: solver_cols = [qid_col, step_col, mult_col, objective] + [c for c in constraint_cols if c in available_cols] (4465-4467). When a constraint equals one of those four reserved names, solver_cols contains the same name twice. source_lf.select(solver_cols) (4479) is lazy and returns without error, deferring the failure to collection time. The collection happens inside _build_grid via bounded_sink(scored_lf, tmp_path, ...) (4731), where Polars raises a DuplicateError. That error is not HTTPException/memory/bounded, so it is caught by _build_grid's `except Exception` (4786) and re-raised as HTTPException(400, detail=f"Grid construction failed: {exc}"). Net effect: a misconfiguration (constraint name colliding with a reserved column) is reported as a 400 carrying an opaque Polars internal message ('Grid construction failed: ...projections contained duplicate output name ...') at grid-build time, rather than a clear 400 at validate time naming the offending constraint. _validate_config (4085-4117) does not guard against this, and no test pins it.
evidence: 4418 required_cols is a set so {objective, 'income'} collapses when a constraint is named 'income'==objective; 4421 _missing_columns_detail passes. 4465-4467 builds solver_cols as a list -> [qid, step, mult, 'income', 'income']. Verified in the project venv: pl.LazyFrame(...).select(['a','b','a']) returns a LazyFrame, then .collect()/sink raises DuplicateError('projections contained duplicate output name ...'). bounded_sink at 4731 triggers that collect inside _build_grid; _build_grid except Exception (4786-4795) -> HTTPException(400, 'Grid construction failed: <DuplicateError text>'). cast_map at 4468-4474 is a dict so it does not surface the duplicate; only the solver_cols list does. tests/test_optimiser_routes.py has no test for a constraint name colliding with objective (grep for 'duplicate output name'/'collides' -> none).
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

est_reduction: ~1 line / removes a misleading always-true filter
behavior_preservation: The upstream missing-columns guard (4418-4429) adds every constraint to required_cols and raises 400 if any required column is absent from available_cols, so by line 4465 every element of constraint_cols is guaranteed to be in available_cols. Therefore `[c for c in constraint_cols if c in available_cols]` is identically equal to `constraint_cols`; replacing it with `list(constraint_cols)` (or just `constraint_cols`) cannot change which columns are projected.
title: `if c in available_cols` filter in solver_cols is always true given the preceding missing-columns guard (dead/misleading conditional)
description: solver_cols = [qid_col, step_col, mult_col, objective] + [c for c in constraint_cols if c in available_cols]. The comprehension's `if c in available_cols` condition can never be False here: _missing_columns_detail at 4421 was computed over required_cols which includes all constraints (added at 4419-4420), and a missing constraint would have raised HTTPException(400) at 4429 before reaching this line. The filter therefore adds confusing dead logic implying constraints might be absent (they cannot be at this point). Note _extract_factors (4670-4671) and _validate_and_project_auto_range (4600-4601) project constraints WITHOUT this filter, so the filter is also inconsistent with siblings. Removing it (use constraint_cols directly) simplifies and de-confuses.
evidence: 4419-4420 `for cname in constraints: required_cols.add(cname)`; 4421 `_missing_columns_detail(required_cols, available_cols)`; 4422-4429 raises 400 if any required col missing. Hence at 4465 constraint_cols (when constraints is a dict) ⊆ available_cols always. Sibling projections at 4600-4601 (auto-range) and 4670-4671 (factors) do not apply the filter.

title: _validate_and_project iterates raw `constraints` for the required-column check but only projects constraints when `constraints` is a dict, so a non-dict `constraints` requires the columns yet silently omits them from the solver projection
description: The required-column existence check iterates `constraints` unconditionally: `for cname in constraints: required_cols.add(cname)` (4419-4420). But constraint_cols (used for value-contract validation, the cast map, and the solver projection) is only populated when constraints is a dict: `constraint_cols = list(constraints.keys()) if isinstance(constraints, dict) else []` (4431). The presence of the isinstance guard shows non-dict `constraints` is anticipated, yet the two derivations are asymmetric. If `constraints` were a non-dict iterable (e.g. a list ['income'] or even a bare string), required_cols would demand those names be present, but constraint_cols would be [] -> the columns are NOT validated for finiteness and NOT included in solver_cols, so the constraint is silently dropped from the projection/grid (the optimiser would solve as if that constraint did not exist) while still requiring the column to exist. By contrast _validate_and_project_auto_range derives required_cols from the dict-guarded constraint_cols (4561-4562: `required_cols = {qid_col, *constraint_cols}`), so it is internally consistent. config['constraints'] comes from the untyped graph node config (optimiser_node.data.config), not a pydantic-validated field, so the dict assumption is not enforced at the boundary. Reachability is low because the frontend always saves constraints as a dict; flagged as a latent silent-drop inconsistency, not a confirmed live defect.
evidence: 4419-4420 iterates raw `constraints` (works on dict keys, list elements, or string characters); 4431 guards `isinstance(constraints, dict)` for constraint_cols. 4458-4459 finite_columns/cast columns use constraint_cols; 4465-4467 solver_cols uses constraint_cols. Auto-range counterpart at 4561-4562 uses the guarded constraint_cols for required_cols, demonstrating the consistent pattern the solver path lacks. config is optimiser_node.data.config (arbitrary dict from the saved graph); _validate_config (4085-4117) does not type-check constraints.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

title: Malformed-field error says "is missing" even when the field is present but non-numeric, producing a contradictory diagnostic
description: _as_finite_float raises detail "field {field!r} is missing" on the type guard (line 384) whenever value is a bool or not an int/float. This branch is hit both for the genuinely-missing case (callers intentionally pass None, e.g. _frontier_point_constraint_value line 477 `_as_finite_float(None, field=total_key)`) AND for the present-but-wrong-type case. If a frontier point carries a stored value that is present but non-numeric (e.g. lambda_x = "0.5" as a JSON string, or total_objective = null serialised as a non-number), the 500 detail reports the field as "missing" when it is actually present with a bad type. The operator-facing message therefore contradicts the actual state, hampering debugging of malformed frontier_data. The separate non-finite branch (line 390) correctly distinguishes "is not finite", so only the type branch is mislabelled. A type-present value should report e.g. "is not a number" rather than reusing the "missing" wording.
evidence: Line 381: `if isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, int | float):` -> line 384 detail f"... field {field!r} is missing". Caller _frontier_point_lambdas (453-465) passes real point values (strings/None possible from arbitrary stored frontier_data); _scenario_stats_from_frontier_point (497) passes point.get(in_key) for each sv_* field; _frontier_point_result_dict line 570 passes point["iterations"]. Any of these being a present non-numeric value yields "is missing". Compare the adjacent finite-check branch (387-391) which uses an accurate "is not finite" message.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Online frontier-point /apply full-clears quote_grid/solver, ending the frontier session and breaking a subsequent apply of a different point
description: In apply_lambdas, the frontier-point branch (target_point_index is not None) calls _store.clear_result_data(body.job_id) with no keys argument, which defaults to the full _HEAVY_OBJECT_KEYS set = ('solver','solve_result','quote_grid','factors_df','ratebook_factor_contexts'). This wipes quote_grid and solver even though the user is mid frontier-analysis (they just applied a specific frontier point). Every OTHER frontier-session exit in this module deliberately preserves that heavy state: the non-frontier apply branch (line 1330) and the save/mlflow paths use _clear_result_data_after_user_action, which keeps quote_grid/solver when the job still has frontier points and only strips solve_result; and the ratebook frontier-select/apply paths (lines 1485, 1507) clear only ('solve_result',). The helper _clear_result_data_after_user_action exists precisely for this: its docstring says 'Slim result data without ending an active frontier-analysis session' (line 664), and _job_has_frontier_points gates retention. Consequence: after applying online frontier point 0, applying a DIFFERENT point N (which has no cached frontier_apply_result:N artifact) re-enters _materialise_frontier_point_apply and hits _store.touch_heavy_objects(job_id, required_keys=('quote_grid',)) at line 1025, which now returns False because quote_grid was cleared, raising HTTP 400 'Quote grid is not available for this job. Re-run the solve to materialise this frontier point.' (lines 1026-1042). The online apply path even persists per-point artifacts and carries its own re-run-the-solve copy, signalling an intended multi-point session, yet it self-destructs the runtime state needed for it after the first apply.
evidence: apply_lambdas line 1288: `_store.clear_result_data(body.job_id)` (full clear) vs the non-frontier branch line 1330 `_clear_result_data_after_user_action(body.job_id)`. clear_result_data default keys = _HEAVY_OBJECT_KEYS (optimiser.py imports / _job_store.py:30-31,508-511 includes 'quote_grid'). _clear_result_data_after_user_action (optimiser.py:663-670) retains heavy state when _job_has_frontier_points(job) is True, clearing only solve_result. Re-apply trace: _materialise_frontier_point_apply (online) line 1025 `if not _store.touch_heavy_objects(job_id, required_keys=('quote_grid',)): raise HTTPException(400, ...)` — touch_heavy_objects returns False when quote_grid is absent (_job_store.py:320-321). The intended-symmetry contract is pinned for ratebook by tests/test_optimiser_routes.py:9780-9858 (test_apply_ratebook_frontier_point_rejection_preserves_rate_table_switching), which asserts job['solver'], job['quote_grid'], job['ratebook_factor_contexts'] all survive an apply within a frontier session so other points can still be materialised; no test asserts the online path SHOULD full-clear quote_grid (the only online apply-then-state test, lines 8902-9005, applies a single point and re-creates frontier state).

title: mlflow_log issues two overlapping _touch_heavy_objects_or_raise calls where one with combined keys suffices
description: The non-frontier branch of mlflow_log calls _touch_heavy_objects_or_raise twice in sequence: first with required_keys=('solve_result',) (line 1667) and then with required_keys=('solver','solve_result') (line 1672). The second required-key set is a strict superset of the first, so the first call is functionally redundant — its only purpose is to emit the differentiated detail 'Job has no solve result' before the solver-specific message. Each call acquires the store _write_lock and runs _evict_stale (touch_heavy_objects, _job_store.py:313-314), so the first call is wasted lock-acquiring work. The same message differentiation can be achieved with a single touch on the combined keys followed by the existing explicit None-checks at lines 1682-1692 (which already raise the two distinct messages for maybe_solve_result is None and solver is None), making the leading single-key touch dead.
evidence: optimiser.py:1667-1678 two _touch_heavy_objects_or_raise calls; the explicit guards at 1682-1692 already distinguish missing solve_result (400 'Job has no solve result') from missing solver (400 'Solver is not available...'). touch_heavy_objects (_job_store.py:299-336) acquires _write_lock and calls _evict_stale each invocation. The first touch's reservation is immediately superseded by the second over a superset of keys.
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-preserving only if the combined-keys touch plus the existing None-guards reproduce the exact two HTTP 400 detail strings and the same heavy-object TTL refresh; current double-touch refreshes the window twice but the second (superset) refresh subsumes the first, so collapsing to one touch keeps the observable TTL outcome. Low confidence because the redundancy is defensible as an intentional message-ordering device and the saving is micro (one lock acquire); not worth changing unless touched for other reasons.
est_reduction: ~6 lines

title: Malformed list config (id_columns/feature_columns/exclude) returns HTTP 500 instead of a 4xx client error, inconsistent with the rest of the module
description: TrainService.start() calls _training_required_metadata_columns(config) at line 489 and _training_required_columns_by_node(body.node_id, config) at line 491, both inside the try block (opened at line 449). Those helpers call _string_list_config(config, key) for the user-supplied 'id_columns', 'feature_columns', and 'exclude' keys. _string_list_config raises a bare ValueError when the value is not a list, or contains a non-string/empty element (lines 197 and 202). A bare ValueError is NOT an HTTPException, so it falls through the admission handler (533) and the HTTPException handler (542) and is caught by the generic `except Exception` at line 579, which transitions the job to terminal reason 'error' and re-raises the raw ValueError. FastAPI then serialises that uncaught exception as HTTP 500. This is a user/config input error (a bad node config in the posted graph) being reported as a server error. It is inconsistent with: (a) _validate_config / _validate_glm_family_link, which raise HTTPException(400) for bad config; and (b) the training worker, which maps ValueError to terminal reason 'contract_error' (a 4xx-class state) at line 1193. The operator/UI therefore cannot distinguish 'my config is malformed' (should be 4xx + contract_error) from 'the server broke' (500 + error). A client can trigger this directly by POSTing a graph whose modelling-node config has e.g. `id_columns: "policy_id"` (string) or `feature_columns: [123]`.
evidence: Executed repro against the real helpers (PYTHONPATH=src, .venv python): _training_required_metadata_columns({'target':'y','algorithm':'catboost','id_columns':'policy_id'}) -> ValueError('id_columns must be a list of column names'); _training_required_columns_by_node('node1', {'target':'y','algorithm':'catboost','feature_columns':[123]}) -> ValueError('feature_columns must contain non-empty string column names'); _training_required_columns_by_node('node1', {'target':'y','algorithm':'catboost','exclude':'drop_me'}) -> ValueError('exclude must be a list of column names'). None of these are HTTPException, and the only handler that catches them in start() is `except Exception as exc:` at line 579 -> transition(to='error') + bare `raise` -> FastAPI 500. Well-formed configs return normally. TrainRequest (schemas.py:819) only validates graph/node_id/source; the node config dict is free-form (dict[str, Any]) and is not schema-validated for these list keys, so the malformed input is reachable from the public /api/modelling/train endpoint.
behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

title: CancellableJobRegistry entry leaks when training-job construction fails in _launch_background
description: _launch_background calls self._training_jobs.register_latest(...) at line 1043 (registering a JobCancellation token under key (_TRAINING_JOB_TYPE, job_id)), then performs an atomic_update (1048), build_training_job_kwargs (1092) and TrainingJob(**job_kwargs) (1097) BEFORE the thread-start try-block at line 1232. If any of those raise, the registry token is never released: the worker thread's finally (which calls _training_jobs.release at 1227) never runs because the thread was never started, and the thread-start except (which calls release at 1245) is not reached because the exception is raised before entering the try at 1232. The exception propagates to start(), whose except/finally only call execution_context.release_admission() (lines 588-589) and JobLifecycle.transition() to 'error' — start() never touches self._training_jobs. Because register_latest keys on the unique job_id, the stale entry is never superseded by a later job (different key) and is never TTL-evicted (CancellableJobRegistry has no TTL; only JobStore does), so _tokens_by_job_id and _latest_by_key grow unboundedly. cancel()/timeout() cannot clean it up later either: the job is already terminal ('error'), so cancel() returns early at lines 598-599 without releasing, and timeout() is only driven for running jobs.
evidence: register_latest at 1043; build_training_job_kwargs at 1092 can raise TrainingConfigError (ValueError subclass, _train_config.py:120 conflicting var_power / :98 missing target); TrainingJob.__init__ at 1097 can raise e.g. TypeError from SplitConfig(**split) (_training_job.py:361) on a malformed config['split']. Both raise BEFORE the try at 1232, so neither release path (1227 worker-finally, 1245 thread-start-except) executes; start()'s handlers (579-589) release admission but not the registry token. Grep confirms the only release call sites are 607 (cancel, guarded by running-status check at 598), 621 (timeout), 1227, 1245 — none cover the 1043–1232 window.

title: _check_gpu_fallback docstring/contract is false: it refuses (raises) and never falls back to CPU or mutates train_params
description: The docstring states 'Check GPU VRAM; fall back to CPU if insufficient. Mutates *train_params* in-place. Returns updated ram_warning.' The implementation does neither: when VRAM is insufficient it builds a warning, records it on the job, and raises _gpu_vram_http_exception (HTTP 507) — i.e. it REFUSES training rather than silently switching task_type to CPU. It also never assigns to train_params anywhere (it only reads train_params.get('task_type'/'border_count'/'depth') and passes the dict to _check_gpu_vram, which is likewise read-only, lines 361-394). The misleading contract is reinforced by start()'s comment at lines 1093-1095 ('threaded through the GPU feasibility check (which may adjust it in place)'). A maintainer trusting either comment could wrongly assume train_params was mutated (e.g. task_type flipped to CPU) and remove the apparently-redundant reassignment `ram_warning = self._check_gpu_fallback(...)` or mis-handle the refusal semantics.
evidence: Lines 758-794: branch returns ram_warning unchanged when task_type != GPU; otherwise on vram_check.warning it raises _gpu_vram_http_exception (783-788). No `train_params[...] = ...` assignment exists in the function; _check_gpu_vram (361-394) only reads params and returns a _VramCheck. Docstring at 754-757 vs. behaviour, plus start() comment at 1093-1095.

title: _execute_and_sink projection can drop a GLM feature column that is in both feature_columns and exclude, after it passed validation
description: The missing-column check (897-922) adds node_demand columns to required_training_columns, so a GLM feature listed in config['feature_columns'] (surfaced via required_columns_by_node, lines 903-906) is validated as PRESENT. But the subsequent projection drop computes drop_cols = [c for c in all_cols if c in exclude and c not in keep_columns] (line 929) where keep_columns is only the metadata set (target/weight/offset/id columns) from _training_required_metadata_columns — it does NOT protect node_demand feature columns. Therefore, for a contradictory config where a column appears in BOTH feature_columns and exclude (and is not a metadata column), the column survives validation but is physically dropped from the sunk parquet. TrainingJob then receives both feature_columns and exclude (build_training_job_kwargs lines 131-132) and will fail later with a missing-feature error against the parquet — a confusing downstream failure caused by silently discarding a required column, rather than a clear up-front rejection. CatBoost is unaffected because its node_demand is AllExceptColumns whose required_columns == keep, so required_training_columns reduces to keep and the drop only removes genuinely-excluded columns.
evidence: required_training_columns built at 897-906 includes node_demand (GLM frozenset of feature+metadata); validation passes if present (907-922). Projection at 927-932 protects only keep_columns, not the node_demand features, so a column in exclude ∩ feature_columns (∉ keep_columns) is added to drop_cols and removed via target_lf.drop(drop_cols). start() passes exclude=excluded for all algorithms (488,506) and keep_columns=metadata only (489,507).

title: Save-time apiInput cache mirror resolves data path only against project_root, diverging from the cache-build resolution for nested pipelines — committed/ is silently never promoted
description: `_mirror_api_input_caches` resolves each apiInput data file as `data_path = (self._root / path).resolve()` (project_root only). It then calls `mirror_cache_to_committed(str(data_path))`, whose first gate is `_is_working_consulted(data_path)` — a check keyed by `_path_hash` = SHA-256 of the canonical resolved path. The cache *build* path (`routes/json_cache.py::_resolve_data_path`) resolves the SAME logical apiInput path via `resolve_runtime_file_path(path, pipeline_dir=pipeline_dir(), project_root=Path.cwd(), prefer='project', enforce_project_root=True)`, which falls back to the *pipeline-relative* location when the project-root candidate does not exist, and marks THAT resolved path consulted via `_mark_working_consulted`. For a nested pipeline (`pipeline_root != project_root`, a first-class supported config — see `__init__` validating `pipeline_root.is_relative_to(project_root)`, and `pipeline_dir()` returning the configured `[project].pipeline` parent) whose apiInput references a data file relatively (e.g. `path='data/quotes.json'`) that physically lives under the pipeline directory (`<pipeline_root>/data/quotes.json`) and NOT under the project root, the two resolutions diverge: build resolves to `<pipeline_root>/data/quotes.json`; mirror resolves to `<root>/data/quotes.json`. Different paths -> different `_path_hash` -> `_is_working_consulted` returns False for the mirror's hash -> `mirror_cache_to_committed` short-circuits to a no-op (returns False). Result: the working cache the editor built is never promoted to committed/, so the committed/deployed pipeline serves a stale or missing cache while the editor shows the fresh one. The failure is silent (no warning — the mirror simply no-ops the consulted-gate).
evidence: _save_pipeline.py:620-627: `path = cfg.get('path',''); ... data_path = (self._root / path).resolve(); ... mirror_cache_to_committed(str(data_path))`. _json_flatten.py:84-91 `_path_hash` hashes `Path(data_path).expanduser().resolve()`; :111-113 `_is_working_consulted` returns `_path_hash(data_path) in _session_consulted_hashes`; :258-260 mirror returns False when not consulted. json_cache.py:146-159 `_resolve_data_path` uses `resolve_runtime_file_path(..., pipeline_dir=pipeline_dir(), prefer='project')` and the build marks `_mark_working_consulted(data_path)` with that resolved path. _path_resolution.py:101-128 shows the project candidate is tried first but falls back to the pipeline candidate when the project candidate doesn't exist. Existing integration coverage (tests/test_json_cache_integrity.py:196-206) uses `source_file='cache_mirror_pipe.py'` at project root, so `pipeline_root == project_root` and the divergence is never exercised.

title: _mirror_api_input_caches calls path.endswith without the isinstance(path, str) guard its sibling validator uses — a non-string apiInput 'path' crashes the whole save with AttributeError
description: `_mirror_api_input_caches` does `path = cfg.get('path', '')` then `if not path.endswith(('.json', '.jsonl')):`. If `node.data.config['path']` is present but not a string (config is `dict[str, Any]`; the VALID_KEYS allowlist in `_config_io._prepare_config_for_sidecar` filters key *names*, not value *types*, so a `path` whose value is an int/list/dict survives to disk and back), the `.endswith` call raises `AttributeError`. That call sits OUTSIDE the per-node `try/except` (the try at line 626 only wraps `mirror_cache_to_committed`), so the AttributeError propagates up through `save()`'s try block, triggers `_rollback`, and re-raises as a 500. The sibling method `_validate_api_inputs_have_schemas` handles exactly this field defensively at line 579-580 (`path = cfg.get('path','') or ''` then `if not isinstance(path, str) or not path.endswith(...)`: continue), so the two methods that walk the same apiInput `path` field disagree on robustness. The mirror is a non-essential, explicitly idempotent best-effort promotion (its own docstring at 609-612 says partial state is fine and failures are merely logged), so a malformed non-string path aborting the entire save (including the code+config+sidecar writes that already succeeded) is the wrong failure mode.
evidence: _save_pipeline.py:620 `path = cfg.get('path', '')` (no `or ''`, no isinstance), :621 `if not path.endswith((".json", ".jsonl")):`. Contrast :579-580 in `_validate_api_inputs_have_schemas`: `path = cfg.get('path', '') or ''` then `if not isinstance(path, str) or not path.endswith((".json", ".jsonl")): continue`. The mirror try/except begins at :626 and wraps only `mirror_cache_to_committed(str(data_path))`, so a non-string `path` raises before it is reached.

title: Embedded submodel graphs are re-validated from raw dicts (PipelineGraph.model_validate) four-plus times per save
description: `_iter_embedded_submodel_graphs` runs a full `PipelineGraph.model_validate(...)` over every nested submodel's raw dict each time it is called. Within a single `save()` of a graph that has submodels it is invoked from at least four independent walks over the same nested data: `_validate_no_load_errors` -> `_iter_nodes_recursive`; `_write_config_files` -> `_collect_node_configs_recursive`; `_collect_config_load_errors_recursive`; and `_compute_disk_prev_config_files` -> `_collect_node_configs_recursive` (on the freshly parsed disk graph). Each call re-parses and re-validates the same nested submodel dicts into brand-new Pydantic models, repeating identical validation work. The collectors are read-only, so this is purely wasted CPU, not a correctness issue; for deeply nested submodels the redundancy compounds with depth. Materialising the embedded sub-graphs once (e.g. caching the validated `PipelineGraph` objects per parent graph for the duration of the save) would remove the repeated `model_validate` cost while preserving behaviour exactly. For the common no-submodel case `graph.submodels or {}` is empty, so there is no cost there.
evidence: _save_pipeline.py:670-679 `_iter_embedded_submodel_graphs` calls `PipelineGraph.model_validate({...})` per submodel. Call sites that each re-enter it for the same graph during one save: :251 (`_iter_nodes_recursive` in `_validate_no_load_errors`), :656 (`_collect_node_configs_recursive` in `_write_config_files`), :659 (`_collect_config_load_errors_recursive`), :834 (`_collect_node_configs_recursive` in `_compute_disk_prev_config_files`). No memoisation of the validated sub-graphs exists between these calls.
behavior_preservation: Exact: caching the validated embedded sub-graphs (or iterating raw dicts only once) yields identical config/error maps and identical recursion order; the only change is fewer redundant model_validate calls.
est_reduction: Eliminates ~3x redundant full PipelineGraph validation of every nested submodel graph per save (proportional to submodel count x depth); no LOC delta required but removes repeated O(nodes) validation passes.

title: Binary column with non-UTF-8 bytes crashes the entire Explore materialisation via a strict cast(pl.String) in the value-counts aggregation
description: Binary is included in _TEXT_DTYPE_BASES (line 78), so _supports_categorical_value_counts(Binary) is True (line 139, via the `base in _TEXT_DTYPE_BASES` arm), and therefore _has_categorical_value_counts(Binary) is True (not numeric, not Object-unhashable, supported). In _build_frame_stats the `elif _has_categorical_value_counts(dtype)` branch (lines 445-448) appends _categorical_value_counts_expr(name), whose first step is `pl.col(name).cast(pl.String)` (line 331). That is a STRICT cast. For a Binary column holding any non-UTF-8 byte sequence (hashes, serialized blobs, image bytes, arbitrary payloads), Polars raises `ComputeError: invalid utf8`. Because all per-column aggregations run in ONE batched streaming_collect (lines 450-454), a single offending Binary column fails the whole collect, so the entire Explore job for that dataset errors out (caught by the generic Exception handler in _run_job -> job status 'error', message 'invalid utf8'). The user simply cannot explore any frame that contains a Binary column with non-text bytes. Note Binary correctly gets no min/max (_supports_min_max(Binary) is False) and n_unique works on Binary; the value-counts cast is the sole failure point. UTF-8-valid Binary, Categorical, Enum, String, Boolean and temporal columns all cast cleanly, so this is specific to non-UTF-8 Binary content.
evidence: Reproduced with the in-scope predicates and expression: `_has_categorical_value_counts(pl.Binary)` -> True, `_supports_min_max(pl.Binary)` -> False, `_column_kind(pl.Binary)` -> 'Text'. Building the exact aggregation list of _build_frame_stats for a Binary column `pl.DataFrame({'blob':[b'\xff\xfe\x00', b'\x80', ...]}, schema={'blob': pl.Binary}).lazy().select([pl.len(), null_count, n_unique, _categorical_value_counts_expr('blob').alias(...)]).collect()` raises `ComputeError: invalid utf8` (from `col("blob").strict_cast(String).value_counts()`). UTF-8-valid Binary and a Datetime column both cast/aggregate fine, confirming the trigger is non-UTF-8 bytes. No existing test in tests/test_explore_routes.py exercises Binary columns (grep for 'Binary'/'utf8' -> no matches), and the bucket's only 'known' findings (SIMP-6, SIMP-8) are about src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py, not this file.
behavior_preservation: n/a (defect). A fix should make the value-count cast non-fatal for non-UTF-8 binary (e.g. cast(pl.String, strict=False) so invalid bytes map to null, or exclude Binary from the value-count gate while keeping its 'Text' kind), pinned by a new failing test that materialises an Explore frame containing a Binary column with non-UTF-8 bytes and asserts the job completes with a sensible categorical profile instead of erroring.

title: preview_node: `else: relevant = set(results.keys())` branch is unreachable
description: In `preview_node`, after computing `node_map`, the code branches on `if body.node_id:` (line 574) vs an `else` (line 585) that sets `relevant = set(results.keys())`. The `else` branch can never execute. `PreviewNodeRequest.node_id` is a required `str`, and an empty `node_id` is rejected earlier at line 507 (`if body.node_id not in graph.node_map: raise HTTPException(404)`). Node-map keys are sanitised function names that are guaranteed non-empty (`_sanitize_func_name` returns `name or "unnamed_node"`, _graph_utils.py:125), so the empty string can never be a key and `""` always 404s at line 507. Therefore by line 574 `body.node_id` is always a non-empty string, `if body.node_id:` is always True, and the `else` (lines 585-586) is dead. The dead branch also implies the dropped `nid in node_map` guard on the `node_statuses` comprehension (the known finding) is practically harmless, because in the only reachable branch `relevant = ancestors(...)` is already a subset of `node_map.keys()`.
evidence: Line 507 guard rejects any node_id not in graph.node_map; _graph_utils.py:125 `return name or "unnamed_node"` proves node ids are non-empty; line 574 `if body.node_id:` is thus always truthy, leaving lines 585-586 (`else: relevant = set(results.keys())`) unreachable.
est_reduction: 2 lines (drop the else; assign `relevant` unconditionally from the ancestors computation)
behavior_preservation: Removing the unreachable else does not change behavior for any input that can reach this code; `relevant` is always taken from the `ancestors(...)` path.

title: _ensure_source_file re-implements `haute.toml [project].pipeline` read already provided by shared helpers
description: `_ensure_source_file` hand-rolls reading `[project].pipeline` from `Path.cwd()/haute.toml`: open + `tomllib.load(f).get("project", {}).get("pipeline")`. This exact TOML read is already implemented in at least three other places: `_project._toml_configured_pipeline(root)` (src/haute/_project.py:105, returns `root/pipeline`), `routes/_helpers.pipeline_dir()` (src/haute/routes/_helpers.py:139-167, returns the validated parent dir), and `discovery.py:28`. The shapes differ slightly (this caller wants the raw relative string to assign to `graph.source_file`, not a resolved Path), but the read+parse+extract is duplicated and could route through a single shared accessor. Two secondary defects in this duplicate: (1) the `except (..., KeyError)` arm is dead — the `.get("project", {}).get("pipeline")` chain uses defaults and cannot raise `KeyError` (contrast `pipeline_dir()` which deliberately does NOT catch KeyError so bugs surface). (2) Unlike `pipeline_dir()`, this assigns the unvalidated `configured` value to `graph.source_file` with no project-root containment check; it is read from the trusted on-disk toml (not an API field) so it is not an injection vector, but the inconsistency with the validated sibling is a footgun. Note this read also runs synchronously on the event loop inside async handlers (called at lines 406/503/721 before any threadpool dispatch), consistent with the existing in-handler I/O pattern but adding a file open+parse per request when `source_file` is empty.
evidence: pipeline.py:263-264 `with open(toml_path, "rb") as f: configured = tomllib.load(f).get("project", {}).get("pipeline")` duplicates _project.py:122-129 and _helpers.py:140-157; the `except (..., KeyError)` at line 267 cannot trigger because every access in the chain uses `.get(default)`.
est_reduction: ~10 lines, plus removal of one dead exception arm; consolidate to a shared `_toml_configured_pipeline`-style accessor that returns the raw relative value.
behavior_preservation: A shared helper returning the same `[project].pipeline` string preserves behavior for the present cases; the only change would be dropping the unreachable KeyError arm and the inconsistent error logging tag.

title: _ensure_module_deps rebuilds without the lock used to invalidate it; no double-checked locking unlike _ensure_pipeline_index
description: invalidate_pipeline_index() clears the module-dependency cache by assigning `_module_deps = None` under `_pipeline_index_lock` (lines 506-509). However `_ensure_module_deps()` reads and re-builds `_module_deps` with NO lock at all (line 585-607): it checks `if _module_deps is not None`, otherwise scans every pipeline (discover_pipelines() + ast.parse of every file + extract_submodel_calls) into a local `deps`, then assigns `_module_deps = deps`. This contradicts the design rationale stated for the sibling cache at lines 487-492 ('The lock below serialises the rebuild path so two concurrent readers that both observe a cold cache cannot scan the filesystem twice'). Because `_ensure_module_deps` omits both the lock acquisition and the double-checked re-test that `_ensure_pipeline_index` performs (lines 531-538), two concurrent readers that both observe a cold cache will each run the full filesystem + AST scan. The module-deps rebuild is strictly heavier than the index rebuild (it ast.parse-s and walks every pipeline source for submodel() calls), so the missing de-duplication is more costly here than in the path the authors did protect. No data corruption occurs (single reference assignment is atomic on CPython, and each rebuild reads fresh disk state), so this is a consistency/efficiency defect rather than a correctness bug — but it is an unintended asymmetry that a careful reviewer would expect the two caches to share. The fix is to reuse the same double-checked-locking pattern (acquire `_pipeline_index_lock`, re-check `_module_deps`, build into a local, publish) exactly as `_ensure_pipeline_index` does.
evidence: invalidate writes under lock: `with _pipeline_index_lock: _pipeline_index = None; _module_deps = None` (506-509). Reader has no lock: `def _ensure_module_deps(): global _module_deps; if _module_deps is not None: return _module_deps; ... for f in discover_pipelines(): source = read_user_text(f); tree = ast.parse(source) ...; _module_deps = deps` (585-607). Contrast _ensure_pipeline_index lines 524-538 which take the lock and re-check before scanning.
est_reduction: no net line change; aligns module-deps cache with the established locked rebuild pattern and removes the redundant concurrent rescan
behavior_preservation: Results identical for all single-threaded and sequential callers; under concurrency it removes a duplicate full-AST filesystem scan and makes invalidation/rebuild race-free with respect to the lock, matching _ensure_pipeline_index.

title: load_sidecar_positions returns raw, un-normalised coordinates; submodel route injects NaN/Inf/non-numeric positions unvalidated (asymmetry vs parse_pipeline_to_graph)
description: The main graph path normalises sidecar positions through `_normalise_sidecar_positions` (parse_pipeline_to_graph line 731), which rejects non-dict entries, booleans-as-numbers, non-numeric x/y, and crucially non-finite values via `math.isfinite` (lines 790-797). The submodel path does NOT: `load_sidecar_positions` (637-640) returns `dict(load_sidecar(py_path).get('positions', {}))` verbatim, and its sole caller routes/submodel.py:120-124 applies them via `node.model_copy(update={'position': positions[node.id]})`. GraphNode has no `validate_assignment` config (only PipelineGraph carries a model_config, and it is just `ignored_types`), and Pydantic v2 `model_copy(update=...)` performs a raw __dict__ update with NO validation.
