Therefore a hand-crafted submodel `.haute.json` containing e.g. `{"positions": {"n1": {"x": NaN, "y": 0}}}` (json.loads parses NaN by default) or `{"x": "abc", "y": 1}` flows straight into node.position. When the SubmodelGraphResponse is serialised back to the client this yields invalid JSON (`NaN`/`Infinity` tokens that break strict frontend parsers) for non-finite coords, or a 500 from response-model validation for a non-numeric coord. The main pipeline GET is immune to the identical corrupt input because it funnels through `_normalise_sidecar_positions`; the submodel GET is not. This is a real robustness/contract asymmetry whose root cause is that `load_sidecar_positions` does not reuse the normalisation helper that already exists in this same module. Fix: have `load_sidecar_positions` return `_normalise_sidecar_positions(load_sidecar(py_path).get('positions'))` (or have the submodel caller normalise), so both code paths share one position-hygiene contract.
evidence: load_sidecar_positions: `result = load_sidecar(py_path).get('positions', {}); return dict(result) if isinstance(result, dict) else {}` — no per-coordinate validation. parse_pipeline_to_graph instead calls `_normalise_sidecar_positions(sidecar.get('positions'))` (731) which drops non-finite via `if not math.isfinite(xf) or not math.isfinite(yf): continue` (796-797). Caller submodel.py:124 `node.model_copy(update={'position': positions[node.id]})`; GraphNode (_types.py:602-608) has no model_config → no validate_assignment; Pydantic v2 model_copy(update) skips validation. Tests TestLoadSidecarPositions (test_route_helpers.py:264-281) only cover valid + missing-key cases, never malformed coordinates, so the gap is uncovered.
behavior_preservation: Routing through _normalise_sidecar_positions leaves all well-formed positions unchanged (the existing valid-case tests still pass) and only drops/ignores malformed or non-finite coordinates, matching the main pipeline path.

title: Blocking artifact filesystem I/O runs while holding the global _write_lock
description: _cleanup_artifact_handles() invokes the registered artifact cleaner (cleaner(handle)), which performs blocking disk I/O (the production/test cleaners call shutil.rmtree / Path.unlink on a result directory). It is reached exclusively under self._write_lock, via two hot paths: (a) _remove_job_locked called from delete_job (line 473, lock held at 472), and (b) _remove_job_locked called from the stale-eviction loop in _evict_stale (line 104, lock held at 94). _evict_stale runs on EVERY create_job / get_job / update_job / atomic_update / has_job_with_status / has_job_matching / touch_heavy_objects call. Consequently, whenever a single routine status poll happens to trigger eviction of an expired job that owns artifacts, the cleaner's filesystem deletion executes while the store's one global mutation lock is held, so every other concurrent job operation (status polls for unrelated jobs, background-worker progress updates, new job creation) blocks for the full duration of the disk I/O. On slow or networked filesystems, or with large artifact directories, this serialises the entire job store behind unbounded filesystem latency. The cleaner can be moved outside the lock: _remove_job_locked could collect the job's artifact handles and the caller could run the cleaners after releasing the lock (mirroring the existing _schedule_heavy_object_cleanup_if_needed pattern, which is deliberately invoked outside the lock to avoid exactly this class of issue).
evidence: _evict_stale (94: 'with self._write_lock'; 104: 'self._remove_job_locked(jid)') -> _remove_job_locked (118: 'self._cleanup_artifact_handles(job_id, job)') -> _cleanup_artifact_handles (140: 'cleaner(handle)'). Test cleaners confirm I/O: tests/test_job_store.py:213-214 'shutil.rmtree(handle["directory"])'. delete_job also holds the lock around _remove_job_locked (472-473). The class docstring and _schedule_heavy_object_cleanup_if_needed show the codebase's own convention is to keep slow/external work OUT of the lock.

title: _aggregate_v2_build_response and _aggregate_v2_status_response duplicate an identical ~28-line per-port aggregation core
description: The two functions share a byte-identical aggregation body that walks `tables`, sums `row_count`/`column_count`, accumulates `size_bytes` and `cached_at` from each table's on-disk parquet stat, and builds the synthetic `columns` map. The only real differences are: (a) the input variable name (`summary` vs `meta`), (b) the `skipped` access style (strict `summary["skipped"]` vs tolerant `meta.get("skipped") or {}`), and (c) the response wrapper (build adds `cache_seconds`, status sets `cached=True`). The shared core can be extracted into one helper (e.g. `_aggregate_v2_tables(cache_dir, tables) -> (row_count, column_count, columns, size_bytes, cached_at)`), with each caller adding only its differing fields. This removes a two-way drift hazard in a cache-integrity hot path where the build and status responses are contractually required to report the same row/column/size numbers for the same cache.
evidence: Lines 268-284 (build) and 312-328 (status) are identical apart from the receiver name: `tables = X.get("tables", []) or []`; `row_count = sum(int(t.get("row_count", 0)) for t in tables)`; `column_count = sum(int(t.get("column_count", 0)) for t in tables)`; identical `for table in tables:` loop computing `label`, `parquet_name`, `parquet_path = cache_dir / parquet_name`, `if parquet_path.exists(): stat = parquet_path.stat(); size_bytes += int(stat.st_size); cached_at = max(cached_at, float(stat.st_mtime))`; identical `for ci in range(int(table.get("column_count", 0))): columns[f"{label}.col{ci}"] = "v2"`. Only the `skipped` line and the final return object differ.
est_reduction: ~28 LOC of duplicated aggregation collapsed to one shared helper; eliminates a build-vs-status divergence hazard.
behavior_preservation: The extracted helper reproduces the same iteration order, the same int()/float() coercions, the same `isinstance(parquet_name, str)` and `.exists()` guards, and the same `{label}.colN` key construction; each wrapper keeps its own strict/tolerant `skipped` read and its own response type and extra fields (`cache_seconds`, `cached=True`). Output is identical for every input.

title: _resolve_config_path reports an embedded-null-byte path as HTTP 403, while the sibling _resolve_data_path reports the same condition as HTTP 400
description: `resolve_runtime_file_path` raises `ValueError("Path contains an embedded null byte")` for a path containing a NUL (see `_normalise_path_text` in _path_resolution.py:19-21). `_resolve_data_path` deliberately discriminates this case: `status_code = 400 if "embedded null byte" in str(exc) else 403` — a malformed-input NUL becomes 400 Bad Request, a project-root escape becomes 403 Forbidden. `_resolve_config_path` collapses BOTH conditions into `HTTPException(status_code=403, ...)`. `config_path` is a client-supplied JSON string (`JsonCacheBuildRequest.config_path: str | None`, and the GET-status `config_path` query param), so a payload containing `�` is reachable. The result is an HTTP-semantics contract inconsistency: identical malformed input (a NUL byte) is reported as 'Forbidden' on the config-path code path but 'Bad Request' on the data-path code path. SIMP-4 (the known dedup item) addresses only the data-path except-body idiom (lines 155-159) and does not cover this config-path branch, so the asymmetry is currently unreported and unguarded.
evidence: _resolve_data_path:157-159 -> `except ValueError as exc: status_code = 400 if "embedded null byte" in str(exc) else 403; raise HTTPException(status_code=status_code, ...)`. _resolve_config_path:175-176 -> `except ValueError as exc: raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail=str(exc)) from None` (no 400 branch). Both call resolve_runtime_file_path with enforce_project_root=True, and _normalise_path_text (_path_resolution.py:19) raises `ValueError("Path contains an embedded null byte")` for either path argument, so a NUL in config_path yields a 403 whose detail literally reads 'Path contains an embedded null byte' — a 4xx mislabel relative to the data-path sibling.

title: Progress 'rows' field is seeded to 0 and never updated by any producer, so /progress always reports rows=0
description: `_start_build_progress` seeds the per-path progress dict with `"rows": 0` (line 76), and `_get_build_progress` reads it back as `int(current.get("rows", 0))` to populate `JsonCacheProgressResponse.rows` (line 104). However, nothing in the codebase ever writes `_build_progress[key]["rows"]` to a non-zero value — the only mutations to the progress dict are the full-dict initialisation (line 72) and `active_count` increments/decrements (lines 79, 92), and `build_per_port_cache` (the threaded builder) does not touch `_build_progress` at all (it has no reference to the module's progress state). Consequently the `GET /api/json-cache/progress` endpoint's `rows` field is permanently 0 — the same value the schema would default to. The `"rows": 0` seed and the `current.get("rows", 0)` read are vestigial plumbing for a row-count feed that was never wired up, which is mildly misleading to API consumers who may expect a live row count during a long build.
evidence: Grep for `_build_progress` in json_cache.py shows writes only at line 72 (init dict), 79 (`current["active_count"] = ...`), 90/92 (finish), with no `[...]["rows"] = ` assignment. build_per_port_cache (_json_shred.py:748+) returns a summary dict but never imports or mutates routes.json_cache._build_progress. Therefore _get_build_progress:104 `int(current.get("rows", 0))` evaluates to 0 on every poll for every build.
est_reduction: Either remove the `"rows": 0` seed and the `rows=` argument from _get_build_progress (the schema default keeps it 0), or wire a real per-build row counter through _build_progress; today the field is dead.
behavior_preservation: Dropping the seed and the explicit `rows=...` argument is behavior-preserving: JsonCacheProgressResponse.rows already defaults to 0, which is the only value the endpoint can currently emit.

title: train_status raises TypeError (500) when a job's timeout is non-numeric (e.g. JSON null) from user config
description: train_status reads `timeout = job.get("timeout", _DEFAULT_TIMEOUT)` and then evaluates `if start and (time.monotonic() - start) > timeout:`. The `timeout` value stored on the job is taken verbatim from the modelling node's free-form config: in _launch_background, `_store.atomic_update(job_id, {..., "timeout": config.get("timeout", _DEFAULT_TIMEOUT)})`. `node.data.config` is typed `dict[str, Any]` (src/haute/_types.py:599) with no validation/coercion of `timeout` anywhere (confirmed: no `timeout` handling in _train_config.py or schemas.py). If a user sets `"timeout": null` (a realistic value when clearing the field) the key is present with value None, so `dict.get(key, default)` returns None — NOT _DEFAULT_TIMEOUT — and the comparison `(time.monotonic() - start) > None` raises `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'float' and 'NoneType'`. A string value (e.g. `"3600"`) fails the same way. Because _launch_background sets `start_time` together with `timeout` for every started job, the comparison branch is taken on every poll once the job is running, so each /train/status/{job_id} request returns a 500 and the user can never observe the running job's progress or terminal state. This is strictly worse than failing loudly at config time because the job keeps running while its status endpoint is permanently broken.
evidence: Line 67: `timeout = job.get("timeout", _DEFAULT_TIMEOUT)`; line 68: `if start and (time.monotonic() - start) > timeout:`. _train_service.py:1052 stores `"timeout": config.get("timeout", _DEFAULT_TIMEOUT)` (returns None when config has `timeout: null`). _types.py:599 `config: dict[str, Any]` — no coercion. No `timeout` coercion exists in _train_config.py / schemas.py.

title: Identical TrainStatusResponse construction duplicated between train_status and cancel_training
description: train_status (lines 109-123) and cancel_training (lines 130-143) build a TrainStatusResponse from the job dict using the exact same 13 fields with the exact same `.get(...)` defaults (status=require_job_status(job), progress, message, iteration, total_iterations, train_loss, train_loss_history, train_loss_history_truncated, elapsed_seconds, result, warning, terminal_reason, execution_metrics). TrainStatusResponse is constructed in only these two places in the entire src tree (grep confirms). Extracting a single private helper, e.g. `_train_status_response(job: Mapping[str, Any]) -> TrainStatusResponse`, would remove ~14 lines of verbatim duplication and ensure both endpoints stay in sync if the response shape ever changes (today a new field must be added in two places).
evidence: Both blocks are character-for-character identical except the surrounding function. grep for `TrainStatusResponse(` returns exactly modelling.py:109 and modelling.py:130.
est_reduction: ~14 lines
behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: extract the shared TrainStatusResponse(...) builder into one helper called from both handlers. Output bytes are identical for any given job dict.

title: mlflow_check blocks the event loop by importing mlflow synchronously in an async handler
description: mlflow_check is declared `async def` but performs `importlib.import_module("mlflow")` (line 237) and `resolve_tracking_backend()` (which touches `Path.cwd()` / env, line 252) directly on the event loop. Importing mlflow is a heavy, blocking operation (pulls in numpy, pandas, sqlalchemy, etc.) that can take hundreds of ms to seconds on the first call, during which the single FastAPI event loop is blocked and cannot service any other request. The sibling heavy work in this module is correctly off-loaded: mlflow_log wraps log_experiment in `run_in_threadpool` (line 368), export_script and clear_model_cache use `run_in_threadpool`, and the optimiser route declares its mlflow_log as a plain `def` (so Starlette runs it in a threadpool). mlflow_check is the only handler that does a blocking import inline on the loop. Either declaring it `def` (so Starlette threadpools it) or wrapping the import/backend-resolution in `run_in_threadpool` would avoid stalling the loop.
evidence: Line 225 `async def mlflow_check`; line 237 `importlib.import_module("mlflow")` runs on the loop with no threadpool; contrast line 368 in mlflow_log which uses `await run_in_threadpool(log_experiment, ...)`. optimiser.py:1652 defines mlflow_log as `def` (threadpooled).

title: estimate_training GPU feature-count ignores the feature_columns allowlist, over-estimating VRAM
description: When computing the GPU VRAM estimate, estimate_training derives the feature count as `n_features = max(ram_est.probe_columns - n_non_feature, 1)` where n_non_feature = len(exclude) + 1 (+1 for weight). This assumes features = all columns minus excluded/target/weight. But training also supports an explicit `feature_columns` allowlist (config key consumed by TrainingJob: _training_job.py:1420-1427, _train_config.py:132). When `feature_columns` is set, the model trains on exactly `len(feature_columns)` features, which can be far fewer than `probe_columns - n_non_feature`. estimate_training never reads `feature_columns`, so the VRAM estimate (and the gpu_warning that can be shown to the user) is computed against the wrong, larger feature count, potentially warning that GPU training is infeasible when it actually fits. This is an advisory estimate only (no functional gate), so impact is limited to a misleading number/warning.
evidence: Lines 198-202 compute n_features purely from `probe_columns - n_excluded - target - weight` and never consult `node.data.config.get("feature_columns")`, even though _train_config.py:132 forwards `feature_columns` and _training_job.py:1421-1427 uses it as the authoritative feature set when present.

title: git_create_branch duplicates the empty-description guard already enforced by _git.create_branch
description: The route pre-validates `if not body.description.strip(): raise HTTPException(400, 'Branch description cannot be empty.')`. The domain function `create_branch` (src/haute/_git.py:444-449) already performs the identical check (`if not description.strip(): raise GitDomainError('Branch description cannot be empty.')`) AND a stronger follow-up check on the slug (line 448, which also rejects descriptions that are non-empty but slugify to empty, e.g. '---' or '!!!'). The `GitDomainError` is mapped to HTTP 400 with the verbatim same message by `_handle_git_error`. The route-level check is therefore a strict subset of the domain check and produces an identical observable result for whitespace-only input. This also contradicts the module docstring (lines 11-13) which states each route body 'collapses to a single return _git.<op>(...) inside the try/except'. Removing the route check and letting `create_branch` own all input validation would centralise the contract in one place (consistent with the project guidance to 'share functionality that's already been built').
evidence: Route git.py:132 `if not body.description.strip():` -> HTTPException(400, 'Branch description cannot be empty.'). Domain _git.py:444 `if not description.strip():` -> GitDomainError('Branch description cannot be empty.') -> _handle_git_error -> 400 same text. tests/test_git_routes.py:593 (test_whitespace_only_description) only asserts status 400 and 'empty' in detail, which the domain path already satisfies.
est_reduction: 2 lines
behavior_preservation: Behaviour-preserving for the common path (whitespace-only description still 400 'empty'). One edge-case ordering nuance: when NOT inside a git repo, removing the route guard would let _assert_git_repo (_git.py:442, runs before the empty check) surface 'Not a git repository...' for a whitespace description instead of the 'empty' message; both are HTTP 400, only the message text/priority differs. Tests pin only status+substring, so they stay green.

title: Module docstring overstates that every route collapses to a single `return _git.<op>(...)`
description: The module docstring asserts: '`_git` returns Pydantic response models directly, so each route body collapses to a single `return _git.<op>(...)` inside the try/except'. This is only true for 7 of the 12 routes. Four routes call `_git` functions that return plain values, not response models, and must wrap them after the try/except: git_create_branch (create_branch -> str), git_switch (switch_branch -> None), git_history (get_history -> list[GitHistoryEntry]), git_archive (archive_branch -> str). For these the body does NOT collapse to a single return — it assigns inside `try` and constructs the response model afterward. The docstring describes an aspirational uniformity the code does not actually have, which can mislead a maintainer about the contract of the `_git` layer.
evidence: git.py:135 `branch = create_branch(body.description)` then :141 `return GitCreateBranchResponse(branch=branch)`; git.py:153 `switch_branch(body.branch)` (returns None) then :159 `return GitSwitchBranchResponse(...)`; git.py:205 `entries = get_history(...)` then :211 `return GitHistoryResponse(entries=entries)`; git.py:257 `archived_as = archive_branch(...)` then :263 `return GitArchiveResponse(...)`. Confirmed in _git.py: create_branch -> str (line 440), switch_branch -> None (552), get_history -> list (640), archive_branch -> str (872).
est_reduction: 0 lines (doc-accuracy only)
behavior_preservation: No runtime behaviour change; documentation accuracy only.

title: Semaphore double-release (permit leak) when limiter acquire and supersession complete in the same event-loop step
description: In `_acquire_limiter_unless_superseded`, when `asyncio.wait(..., FIRST_COMPLETED)` returns with BOTH `acquire_task` and `superseded_task` in `done` (reachable whenever a limiter permit is available at the same moment the request is superseded), the permit is released twice. The body at lines 183-186 releases the just-acquired permit (`limiter.release()`) and sets `acquired = False`, then raises `SupersededRequestError`. That exception is caught by the `except BaseException` handler at line 189, which drains `acquire_task` (already done with result `True`) and, at line 191-192, re-derives `acquired = True` from the drained result (`drained_acquire_result is True and not acquired`). It has no memory that the permit was already released at line 184, so line 194-195 releases it AGAIN. Net effect: the semaphore permit count is incremented by one each time this race fires, silently and permanently raising the per-key concurrency cap (e.g. `_preview_work_slots` / `_trace_work_slots`), defeating the bounded-worker guarantee the coordinator exists to enforce. The overloaded `acquired` flag conflates 'task succeeded' with 'we still hold a permit needing release'.
evidence: Trace (both tasks in `done`): L177 `acquire_result=True`; L180 `acquired=True`; L182 superseded in done, L183 `acquired` True -> L184 `limiter.release()` (permit returned), L185 `acquired=False`, L186 `raise SupersededRequestError`. Caught at L189: L190 `_cancel_and_drain(acquire_task)` -> task already done so no cancel (L200), returns its result `True` (L202); L191 `True is True and not False` -> L192 `acquired=True`; L194 True -> L195 `limiter.release()` (SECOND release of the same permit). Reproduced against a real `asyncio.Semaphore(1)`: after driving this race the semaphore ends with `_value == 2` (was 1) and permits 2 concurrent `acquire()` calls without any intervening `release()`. The existing test `tests/test_request_supersession.py::test_superseded_limiter_acquire_race_releases_slot` asserts `releases == 2` but that counts one release from each of two separate `run_latest` calls (the obsolete call releases once via the cancel-returns-True path, the latest call releases once on worker completion); it never exercises the single-call both-`done` path, so this leak is uncaught.

title: _coerce_worker_terminal_reason hardcodes a fourth copy of the terminal-reason set
description: The valid terminal-reason strings are maintained in four independent places: the `TerminalReason` Literal in _job_lifecycle.py, the `WorkerTerminalReason` Literal in _worker_isolation.py, the `TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` mapping in _job_lifecycle.py, and this inline `{...}` set in `_coerce_worker_terminal_reason`. The set literal here duplicates exactly `TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS.keys()`, which is already imported into scope alongside `TerminalReason`. Replacing the inline set membership check with `reason in TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` would remove the fourth copy and make adding a new terminal reason a single-site change, while keeping the loud-coercion-to-'error' behaviour identical. Low priority: this duplication mirrors an existing project-wide pattern rather than being a localized defect, and the function is otherwise correct and well-guarded.
evidence: Line 232-241 enumerates {'completed','superseded','timed_out','cancelled','memory_limited','contract_error','error'}, which is byte-for-byte the key set of TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS defined in _job_lifecycle.py:34-42; that mapping is already importable (TerminalReason is imported from the same module at line 19). For all concrete IsolatedWorkerError subclasses the passed `exc.terminal_reason` is statically one of WorkerTerminalReason's 7 members, so the membership branch always succeeds and the `return 'error'` fallback (line 242) is unreachable under the type contract.
est_reduction: ~9 lines collapse to a 1-line membership test against an existing mapping
behavior_preservation: Identical: `reason in TERMINAL_REASON_TO_STATUS` accepts exactly the same 7 strings and rejects everything else, preserving the coerce-unknown-to-'error' contract and the cast.

title: JSONL row count is estimated even when the preview already read the whole file (<=5 rows), reporting a possibly-wrong count
description: For a `.jsonl` source, `_read_schema_blocking` ALWAYS goes through the size-ratio estimator whenever `n_preview > 0`, and always reports `row_count_estimated=True` with `row_count = max(1, int(file_size / avg_line_bytes))`. But the preview is `lf.head(5)`, so any JSONL file with at most 5 rows is fully materialised into `preview_df` and `n_preview` IS the exact row count. The code throws that exact value away and returns a heuristic instead, which can disagree with the true count when line lengths vary. Example: a 3-row JSONL where the three lines have unequal serialized lengths yields avg_line_bytes from the re-serialized preview; `int(file_size/avg_line_bytes)` can round to 2 or 4, so the API returns e.g. `row_count=4, row_count_estimated=True` for a file that demonstrably has exactly 3 rows already loaded in the preview. The fix is to short-circuit when `n_preview < 5` (file fully read) and return `row_count=n_preview, row_count_estimated=False`.
evidence: Line 90/104: `preview_df = _collect_file_preview(lf.head(5))`. Lines 110-122: the `if path.endswith('.jsonl')` branch runs the estimator for every `n_preview > 0`, with no special case for `n_preview < 5` (file exhausted). `row_count_estimated` is then `True` for any non-empty file (line 125, since `row_count >= 1`). tests/test_files_routes.py::TestGetSchemaJsonl only covers a 100-row file and asserts `row_count > 0`, so the small-file exact-count path is unpinned. read_source maps `.jsonl` to `pl.scan_ndjson` (src/haute/_io.py:534-545), and head(5) on <=5-row file returns the whole file.

title: Case-sensitive `.jsonl` detection (`path.endswith('.jsonl')`) is inconsistent with case-insensitive parquet/`read_source` dispatch and defeats the JSONL memory optimization for `.JSONL`
description: The parquet branch detects extension case-insensitively (`target.suffix.lower() == '.parquet'`, line 85) and `read_source`/`_source_format` dispatch case-insensitively (it lowercases the path), but the JSONL row-count special-case uses `path.endswith('.jsonl')` (line 110) against the RAW, un-lowercased user query string. For a file named e.g. `data.JSONL`: `read_source` still routes it to `pl.scan_ndjson` (case-insensitive), but `_read_schema_blocking` skips the parquet branch (suffix.lower() != '.parquet') AND skips the JSONL branch (`'data.JSONL'.endswith('.jsonl')` is False), falling into the `else` at line 127 which runs `_collect_file_preview(lf.select(pl.len()))`. Per the code's own comment (lines 106-107), `pl.len()` on `scan_ndjson` materialises every row — i.e. the exact whole-file read the JSONL branch exists to avoid. So an uppercase/mixed-case `.JSONL` file silently loses the bounded-memory row-count path and reads the entire file into memory.
evidence: Line 85 uses `target.suffix.lower()`; line 110 uses `path.endswith('.jsonl')` on the un-normalised user string. `_source_format` lowercases before matching (src/haute/_io.py:150-159), so `.JSONL` -> NDJSON -> `pl.scan_ndjson` (line 536). The else branch at files.py:127 does `lf.select(pl.len())`, which the comment at lines 106-107 documents as materialising every row for ndjson.

title: browse_files computes relative_to against an UNRESOLVED `base=Path.cwd()` while validate_safe_path returns a resolved target, raising an unhandled ValueError (500) when cwd is non-canonical
description: `browse_files` sets `base = Path.cwd()` (line 34, NOT resolved) and uses it for `entry.relative_to(base)` (line 43) and `target.relative_to(base)` (line 59). However `validate_safe_path` internally does `base = base.resolve()` and returns `target = (base.resolve()/raw).resolve()` (src/haute/routes/_helpers.py:88-102), so `target` and everything from `target.iterdir()` are symlink-resolved canonical paths. When the process working directory contains a symlinked component (so `Path.cwd() != Path.cwd().resolve()`, e.g. a deploy layout like `/var/app/current -> /releases/123`), `entry` (resolved) is not relative to `base` (unresolved), and `Path.relative_to` raises `ValueError`. `browse_files` has no try/except, so this propagates as an unhandled 500 for every `/api/files` request under such a layout. `get_schema` is unaffected because it never calls `relative_to(base)`. The fix is to resolve `base` once (use the same canonical base validate_safe_path uses) before computing relative paths.
evidence: files.py:34 `base = Path.cwd()` (unresolved); line 35 `target = validate_safe_path(base, dir)` returns a `.resolve()`d path (_helpers.py:96-102); line 43 `rel = str(entry.relative_to(base))` and line 59 `target.relative_to(base)` use the unresolved base. `Path.relative_to` raises ValueError when the path is not a subpath. No error handling wraps the loop, so the ValueError surfaces as HTTP 500.

title: Initial `avg_line_bytes = file_size / max(n_preview, 1)` is effectively dead and `max(n_preview, 1)` is redundant inside `if n_preview > 0`
description: Inside `if n_preview > 0`, the first assignment `avg_line_bytes = file_size / max(n_preview, 1)` (line 114) is immediately overwritten by `avg_line_bytes = sample_bytes / n_preview` whenever `sample_bytes > 0` (line 121). `sample_bytes = sum(len(line)+1 for line in preview_df.write_ndjson().splitlines())` is > 0 for any non-empty preview (even a row serialising to `{}` contributes `len('{}')+1 = 3`), so for every reachable input with `n_preview > 0` the initial value is discarded. The `max(n_preview, 1)` guard is also redundant because the enclosing `if n_preview > 0` already guarantees `n_preview >= 1`. The block can be reduced to computing `sample_bytes`, then `avg_line_bytes = sample_bytes / n_preview` (with sample_bytes guaranteed positive), removing the dead initial assignment and the redundant `max`.
evidence: Line 114 sets avg_line_bytes; lines 120-121 overwrite it under `if sample_bytes > 0`. write_ndjson of a non-empty frame always yields >0 bytes, making the `if sample_bytes > 0` always true and the line-114 value dead. `max(n_preview, 1)` is inside `if n_preview > 0` (line 113).
est_reduction: 2-3 lines
behavior_preservation: Identical for all reachable inputs: whenever n_preview>0 the preview is non-empty so sample_bytes>0 and the estimator already uses sample_bytes/n_preview; the removed branch only ever executed in the impossible 'non-empty preview serialises to 0 bytes' case.

title: JSONL size estimate uses character length (len(line)) against byte-denominated file_size, overestimating row count for multibyte UTF-8 content
description: `sample_bytes` is computed as `sum(len(line) + 1 ...)` over the lines of `preview_df.write_ndjson()`, where `write_ndjson()` returns a `str` and `len(line)` is the Python character count, not the UTF-8 byte length. This `sample_bytes` (chars) is divided by `n_preview` to get `avg_line_bytes`, which is then divided into `file_size` (real bytes from `target.stat().st_size`) to estimate the row count. For JSONL containing non-ASCII characters (each multibyte UTF-8 codepoint counts as 1 char but >1 byte), `avg_line_bytes` undercounts the true per-row byte size, so `row_count = file_size / avg_line_bytes` overestimates. Using a byte length (`len(line.encode('utf-8'))`, or summing over `write_ndjson().encode('utf-8')`) would keep both sides in bytes. The field is flagged `row_count_estimated=True`, so this is an accuracy defect rather than a hard contract break, but it can be materially wrong for heavily-unicode JSONL.
evidence: Line 116-119: `sample_bytes = sum(len(line) + 1 for line in preview_df.write_ndjson().splitlines())` — `write_ndjson()` is a str, `len` is chars. Line 111: `file_size = target.stat().st_size` is bytes. Line 121-122 mixes the two: `avg_line_bytes = sample_bytes / n_preview` then `row_count = max(1, int(file_size / avg_line_bytes))`.

title: Invalid table name / unsafe query on POST /fetch returns 500 instead of 400, masking user input errors as server faults
description: fetch_databricks_table does NOT call _validate_table_param (unlike its three sibling endpoints get_fetch_progress, get_databricks_cache_status, delete_databricks_cache, which all validate and return a clean 400). Table-name and query validation only happen deep inside fetch_and_cache, where they are raised as bare ValueError. Those ValueErrors propagate through run_blocking_with_response_timeout (which re-raises everything except TimeoutError/CancelledError) and are caught by the route's final `except Exception as e:` branch, which logs and raises HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=_INTERNAL_ERROR_DETAIL). The result is that a malformed client request (bad fully-qualified table name, or a query that fails _validate_select_clause such as a non-SELECT, a semicolon, an SQL comment, or a forbidden keyword) is reported to the client as a generic 500 'Operation failed. Check the server logs for details.' This is a wrong/contradictory error contract: (a) it is inconsistent with the sibling endpoints, where the identical invalid table (e.g. 'DROP TABLE foo') correctly yields 400 'Invalid table name' (see tests test_cache_status_rejects_invalid_table / test_delete_cache_rejects_invalid_table); (b) a 500 signals a retryable server-side bug and hides the actionable validation message, so the UI cannot tell the user their input is malformed nor surface the real reason.
evidence: Route databricks.py:150-180: try-block calls run_blocking_with_response_timeout(fetch_and_cache, table=body.table, ...); except order is TimeoutError -> ImportError -> HTTPException -> `except Exception as e: logger.error('fetch_table_failed', error=str(e)); raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=_INTERNAL_ERROR_DETAIL)`. No ValueError handling. _databricks_io.fetch_and_cache:297-301 raises `ValueError(f"Invalid table name: {table!r}. ...")` when `not _TABLE_NAME_RE.match(table)`, and :303-304 calls _validate_select_clause(query) which raises ValueError for unsafe queries. _timeouts.run_blocking_with_response_timeout only catches TimeoutError and asyncio.CancelledError, so ValueError flows straight to the route's `except Exception` -> 500. No test asserts a 400 for an invalid table/query on /fetch (grep of tests confirms only progress/cache/delete have invalid-table 400 tests).

title: publish() metrics callback lets KeyError/ValueError escape into the execution memory-pressure hot path and abort a live job
description: The `publish` closure installed as `ExecutionContext.memory_pressure_callback` wraps ONLY `store.require_job(job_id)` in `try/except Exception: return`. The two operations that run after the guard — `require_job_status(job)` (raises `ValueError` on a status not in `JOB_STATUSES`) and `store.atomic_update(job_id, {...}, expected_status=RUNNING_STATUS)` (raises `KeyError` when `job_id` is no longer present) — are OUTSIDE the try/except. `memory_pressure_callback(event)` is invoked unguarded from `ExecutionContext._record_memory_pressure_events` (`_execution_context.py:947-948`), which runs on the execution sampling path via `_observe_rss`. The `stage()` contextmanager only catches `ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError`, so a `KeyError`/`ValueError` raised here propagates up and aborts the running execution. The reachable trigger is a TOCTOU eviction/deletion: `require_job` succeeds, then the running job is evicted by TTL (`_evict_stale` for a stale running job, see `_job_store.py:106-111`) or removed via `delete_job`/`clear_result_data` on another thread, then `atomic_update` does `old = self._jobs[job_id]` (`_job_store.py:413`, documented `Raises KeyError if job_id does not exist`) and raises `KeyError`. A best-effort metrics publish thereby becomes a fatal execution failure. The `if status != RUNNING_STATUS: return` guard does not help because it runs before the window and does not prevent eviction of a running job.
evidence:
_job_lifecycle.py: `try:
    job = store.require_job(job_id)
except Exception:
    return
status = require_job_status(job)  # ValueError escapes here
if status != RUNNING_STATUS:
    return
store.atomic_update(job_id, {...}, expected_status=RUNNING_STATUS)  # KeyError escapes if job evicted`. Callback invoked unguarded at _execution_context.py:947-948 `if self.memory_pressure_callback is not None: self.memory_pressure_callback(event)`, reached from _observe_rss -> _record_memory_pressure_events; stage() at _execution_context.py:726-728 only catches ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError. atomic_update raises KeyError per _job_store.py:413 and its docstring.

title: childNodeIds persisted in non-deterministic set order, diverging from the parser sibling path
description: `child_node_ids = {n.id for n in child_nodes}` is a set comprehension. The set is correctly used for order-independent membership tests (e.g. `e.source in child_node_ids`), but it is then materialised three times via `list(child_node_ids)` — into the submodel placeholder node config, into `existing_submodels[sm_name]["childNodeIds"]`, and into the `SubmodelGraphResult`. CPython set iteration order is hash-seeded and not the graph node order, so the persisted `childNodeIds` lists are non-deterministic across processes/runs, producing churn in the saved `.haute.json` and the generated module for an otherwise identical create operation. The parse-time path that builds the same submodel metadata uses a deterministic, order-preserving list (`_parser_submodels.py:174` `child_node_ids = [n.id for n in sm_graph.nodes]`), so the two sibling builders — which `_submodel_graph.py`'s docstring says are meant to share submodel-construction logic — disagree on ordering. Behaviour is unaffected because downstream consumers treat the field as a set (`codegen.py:969` `set(sm_meta.get("childNodeIds", []))`, `projection.py:2224` `sorted(children)`), so this is a reproducibility/consistency defect, not a functional one. The fix is to derive an ordered list `[n.id for n in child_nodes]` for the materialisations while keeping a set for membership, matching the parser path.
evidence: _submodel_ops.py:48 `child_node_ids = {n.id for n in child_nodes}` (set); lines 83/96/113 each emit `list(child_node_ids)`. Compare _parser_submodels.py:174 `child_node_ids = [n.id for n in sm_graph.nodes]` (ordered). Consumers are order-agnostic: codegen.py:969, projection.py:2224.

title: Cancellation path silently swallows CancelledError and skips the structured failure log when the started worker raises after the request is cancelled
description: In run_blocking_with_response_timeout's `except asyncio.CancelledError` branch, the drain loop `while not blocking_task.done(): await asyncio.shield(blocking_task)` only catches asyncio.CancelledError (to re-loop on re-cancellation). If the already-started worker thread finishes by raising an ordinary (non-cancellation) exception, `await asyncio.shield(blocking_task)` re-raises that worker exception. Because it is not an asyncio.CancelledError, it is not caught by the `except asyncio.CancelledError: continue` arm: it propagates out of the while loop AND out of the entire `except asyncio.CancelledError` block. Two consequences follow: (1) the trailing bare `raise` (which re-raises the original CancelledError) is never reached, so the in-flight request cancellation is suppressed and converted into a domain exception, violating the asyncio structured-concurrency contract that a coroutine catching CancelledError must re-raise it; upstream cancellation/limiters may then treat the task as 'failed' rather than 'cancelled'. (2) `_drain_background_future_result(blocking_task)` is skipped, so the dedicated structured `route_work_background_failed` error log for a worker that failed after cancellation is never emitted (the failure is only visible as whatever exception type the caller did not expect). This contradicts the project's 'fail loudly / observable failures' principle. The normal-return cancellation path (worker returns a value) is correct and is the only behaviour the existing test test_run_blocking_with_response_timeout_cancellation_waits_for_worker exercises; the worker-raises-after-cancel branch is untested.
evidence: Lines 51-58: `except asyncio.CancelledError:` then `while not blocking_task.done(): try: await asyncio.shield(blocking_task) except asyncio.CancelledError: continue` then `_drain_background_future_result(blocking_task)` then `raise`. asyncio.shield's returned awaitable propagates the inner task's result/exception unless the OUTER await is cancelled; so a worker raising e.g. ValueError makes `await asyncio.shield(blocking_task)` raise ValueError, which the `except asyncio.CancelledError` arm does not catch -> escapes both the while loop and the outer except block, bypassing `_drain_background_future_result(blocking_task)` and the `raise`. Contrast the timeout branch (lines 47-50), which deliberately routes background failures through `blocking_task.add_done_callback(_drain_background_future_result)` so a late worker exception IS logged. The cancellation branch lacks that guarantee. The drain helper itself (lines 61-70) is the only place the `route_work_background_failed` structured error is produced.
behavior_preservation: n/a

title: Per-target output dir derived from config stem can silently collide and clobber another target's artifacts
description: `_safe_target_name(config_path)` returns `config_path.stem.replace('.', '-')` and is used as the per-target output subdirectory in `_run_target` (`target_dir = output_dir / _safe_target_name(target.config_path)`), which is then `shutil.rmtree`'d and recreated on each run. Target uniqueness, however, is only enforced on the full `config_path` and on `name` (`_load_target_specs` lines 204-207), never on the derived directory name. Two distinct config filenames can map to the same `_safe_target_name`, in which case the second target's run deletes (rmtree) and overwrites the first target's artifacts within the same output_dir, silently losing one target's results while both appear in the manifest.
evidence: stem of 'cosmic-ray.registry.toml' is 'cosmic-ray.registry' -> replace('.','-') -> 'cosmic-ray-registry'. Adversarial example: 'cosmic-ray.a.b.toml' -> stem 'cosmic-ray.a.b' -> 'cosmic-ray-a-b', and 'cosmic-ray.a-b.toml' -> stem 'cosmic-ray.a-b' -> 'cosmic-ray-a-b' collide. _load_target_specs only checks `len(set(names)) != len(names)` and `len(set(configs)) != len(configs)` (configs = config_path list), so the collision passes validation. In _run_target: `if target_dir.exists(): shutil.rmtree(target_dir)` then both targets write target-summary.json/session files into the identical directory.

title: Spurious 'survival rate could not be parsed' failure appended when a critical stage aborts before the rate stage runs
description: In `_run_target`, when a critical stage other than `baseline` aborts the loop early (the `break` at line 562-563 fires for `init`/`filter-pragma`/`exec`), `session.sqlite` already exists (it is created by `init`) but the `rate` stage never executes, so `rate.txt` is never written. `_parse_survival_rate` then returns None because the file does not exist. The guard at line 580 is `if session_file.exists() and survival_rate is None:` which is satisfied, so an additional failure string 'survival rate could not be parsed from rate.txt' is appended on top of the genuine '<stage> exited with code N' failure. The recorded failure reason is factually wrong (the rate was never attempted, not unparseable), producing misleading diagnostics in target-summary.json, mutation-summary.json/.md and the printed summary for a gate whose entire purpose is clear correctness signal.
evidence: Loop at 550-563: on `exec` returncode != 0, appends 'exec exited with code N' and `break`s (exec is in the critical set). `session_file` = target_dir/'session.sqlite' was created by the earlier `init` stage (cmd at line 514). `rate` stage (line 536-541, writes rate.txt) is never reached. Line 384-385 `_parse_survival_rate`: `if not rate_path.exists(): return None`. Line 580: `if session_file.exists() and survival_rate is None:` -> True -> failures gains a second, inaccurate entry.

title: Duplicated 'format rate as percent or n/a' logic with inconsistent defensiveness
description: The optional-rate-to-string formatting exists twice with diverging behavior. `_format_optional_rate` (lines 454-457) guards with `isinstance(value, int | float)` and returns 'n/a' otherwise, while `_write_summary_markdown` (lines 432-433) inlines `'n/a' if survival is None else f'{survival:.2f}%'` / `'n/a' if fail_over is None else f'{fail_over:.2f}%'`, which assumes the value is strictly float-or-None and would raise on any non-numeric, non-None value. The markdown writer could reuse `_format_optional_rate` for a single, consistently-defensive implementation.
evidence: _format_optional_rate: `if isinstance(value, int | float): return f'{float(value):.2f}%'` else `'n/a'`. _write_summary_markdown: `survival_text = 'n/a' if survival is None else f'{survival:.2f}%'` and `fail_over_text = 'n/a' if fail_over is None else f'{fail_over:.2f}%'` — same '%.2f%% or n/a' intent, different None-vs-isinstance handling.
est_reduction: ~3-4 lines; removes a second, less-robust formatter
behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving for the only values actually produced (survival_rate/fail_over are float|None); reusing _format_optional_rate additionally hardens the markdown path against unexpected types instead of raising.

title: Injected quotes() api_input fixture hand-rolls (and has drifted from) the shared load_v2_api_source helper, embedding a latent config-path bug
description: The _QUOTES_API_INPUT_BLOCK string is appended verbatim into the scaffolded rating/main.py as the body of the `quotes` api_input node. It hand-rolls the v2 per-port cache resolution: it manually computes _json_cache_dir for the 'working' then 'committed' layer, calls is_per_port_cache_valid twice, raises the stale-cache RuntimeError, derives _emit_labels, calls load_per_port_cache, and branches single-vs-multi return. This is exactly (and only) what the shared runtime/codegen helper haute._json_shred.load_v2_api_source already does (src/haute/_json_shred.py:968-1023). Production codegen for an api_input JSON node (_api_input_template, src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:234-249) now emits just `return load_v2_api_source(str(_data_path), _v2_config)` precisely so 'this generated/deploy path can't drift from the runtime builder'. The harness fixture has drifted: it duplicates ~37 lines of logic instead of calling the helper, so it can silently diverge from the real codec and stop faithfully exercising it. Worse, in copying the old logic it introduced a config-path-resolution defect: it uses `_config_path = Path("config/quote_input/quotes.json")` (a CWD-relative path), whereas production codegen uses `_config_path = Path(__file__).parent / {config_path_repr}` (module-relative, src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:240). The backend runs with cwd = E2E_PROJECT_DIR (project root; _start_backend sets cwd=str(E2E_PROJECT_DIR), and no os.chdir exists anywhere in src/haute/), but the config is written under rating/ (scripts/run_frontend_e2e_server.py:282-284 -> E2E_PROJECT_DIR/rating/config/quote_input/quotes.json). So a CWD-relative `Path("config/quote_input/quotes.json")` resolves to E2E_PROJECT_DIR/config/quote_input/quotes.json (missing the rating/ segment) and `_config_path.read_bytes()` (line 131) would raise FileNotFoundError. Every other injected block in this file correctly uses __file__-relative paths (e.g. _BROWSER_OPTIMISER_BLOCK line 46 and the same quotes block's own _data_path on line 129), which is what makes this one's bare cwd-relative config path stand out as a defect.
evidence: Fixture (lines 130-149) does: _config_path = Path("config/quote_input/quotes.json"); _v2_config = orjson.loads(_config_path.read_bytes()); _cache_dir = _json_cache_dir(...,'working'); if not is_per_port_cache_valid(...): _cache_dir = _json_cache_dir(...,'committed'); if not is_per_port_cache_valid(...): raise RuntimeError(...); _emit_labels = [...]; _bundle = load_per_port_cache(...); return single-or-dict. Compare production _api_input_template (src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:239-249): _data_path = {portable_path}; _config_path = Path(__file__).parent / {config_path_repr}; ...; return load_v2_api_source(str(_data_path), _v2_config). Cwd proof: _start_backend (line 387-405) uses cwd=str(E2E_PROJECT_DIR); grep over src/haute shows zero os.chdir calls; pipeline_dir()/path resolution (src/haute/routes/_helpers.py:159-167) keeps cwd at project root and only resolves the pipeline file relative to it. Config write location: scripts/run_frontend_e2e_server.py:282-284. The reason this latent bug isn't caught by the api-input-v2-native.spec.ts Preview step is that preview executes the GRAPH via execute_graph -> _build_api_input -> _make_api_source_v2 -> load_v2_api_source (src/haute/_builders.py:464-509), reading config from the sidecar via the route layer, and never imports/invokes the literal quotes() function body from main.py. The body therefore only runs under `haute run`/module-import, where the cwd-relative path breaks.
est_reduction: ~37 lines collapse to a body mirroring production codegen (Path(__file__).parent for the config path + a single `return load_v2_api_source(str(_data_path), _v2_config)`), removing the duplicated cache-resolution logic and the latent FileNotFoundError-on-`haute run` path-resolution bug.
behavior_preservation: For the exercised browser-preview e2e flow, behavior is unchanged because that flow never executes the injected function body (it runs the graph). Replacing the body with the production-equivalent call to load_v2_api_source keeps the file structurally identical for the UI tests while making `haute run` against the scaffold correct and keeping the fixture in lock-step with the real codec.

title: SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers registered after child processes are started, leaving an orphan window if interrupted during startup
description: main() starts the backend (line 507) and Vite (line 508) child processes BEFORE installing the cleanup signal handlers (signal.signal(SIGINT/SIGTERM, _shutdown) at lines 519-520) and BEFORE the try/finally that guarantees _cleanup() (the try begins at line 526). If the operator presses Ctrl+C (or the CI runner sends SIGTERM) during the window between _start_backend()/_start_vite() and the signal-handler registration, the default SIGINT handler raises KeyboardInterrupt which propagates out of main() with no _cleanup() ever running, orphaning the already-spawned uvicorn and/or `npm run dev` processes (each spawned with --strictPort 5173 / port 8000), which then leak and can wedge the next run by holding the ports. Even after handlers are registered, the additional setup before the try block is not covered by the finally. Because the children bind fixed ports, a leaked process turns a transient interrupt into a hard failure on the next invocation.
evidence: Order in main(): backend_proc = _start_backend() (507); vite_proc = _start_vite() (508); processes = [...] (509); def _cleanup()/_shutdown (511-517); signal.signal(SIGINT, _shutdown) (519); signal.signal(SIGTERM, _shutdown) (520); ... try: _wait_for_url(...) ... finally: _cleanup() (526-541). The only cleanup guarantees are the signal handlers (active only from line 519 onward) and the finally (active only from line 526 onward); neither covers the 507->519 window during which both child processes already exist.

title: Manual leading './' stripping loop is subsumed by posixpath.normpath
description: In _normalize_repo_path, the `while path.startswith("./"): path = path[2:]` loop preceding `posixpath.normpath(path)` is redundant. posixpath.normpath already collapses any number of leading './' (and '//') segments: normpath('./src/x.py') == 'src/x.py', normpath('././/src/x.py') == 'src/x.py'. The only adjacent case is a path like './../x.py': the loop reduces it to '../x.py', which normpath keeps and the subsequent `normalized.startswith('../')` guard then rejects with CriticalCoverageError; without the loop, normpath('./../x.py') is directly '../x.py' and trips the exact same guard. Removing the two-line loop (and keeping just the strip()+normpath+guard) preserves behavior on all inputs.
evidence: Line 53: `path = raw_path.replace("\\", "/").strip()`; Lines 54-55: `while path.startswith("./"): path = path[2:]`; Line 56: `normalized = posixpath.normpath(path)`. posixpath.normpath collapses leading './' and '//' itself, so the loop never changes the final `normalized` value nor the './..' guard outcome.
est_reduction: 2 lines
behavior_preservation: Identical: normpath subsumes leading './' collapsing for every input; the './..' edge still trips the same startswith('../') guard with or without the loop.

title: `--json` argument is parsed but never read; flag is a complete no-op
description: `_parse_args` defines a `--json` boolean flag (action="store_true"), but `args.json` is never consumed anywhere in the module. `main()` always emits `json.dumps(summary, ...)` to stdout regardless of whether `--json` was passed, and `run_smoke` knows nothing about it. The only formatting toggle is `--pretty`. The help text rationalises it as "the default and is kept as an explicit flag for CI", which makes it intentionally inert, but it remains dead surface: passing or omitting it changes nothing, and a reader/maintainer cannot tell that from the code without grepping the whole file. A Grep for `args.json` across the file confirms zero consumers.
evidence: Line 308-312 defines `--json`. `Grep 'args\.json'` over scripts/memory_smoke.py finds no read site. main() (lines 328-338) builds output solely from `args.pretty` (`indent = 2 if args.pretty else None`) and unconditionally calls `print(json.dumps(summary, indent=indent, sort_keys=True))`. The `--json` value is discarded.
est_reduction: 5 lines (remove the unused argument) or, if kept for CI compatibility, no code reduction but the no-op should be made explicit.
behavior_preservation: Removing the flag changes the CLI surface (callers passing `--json` would error). If CI relies on accepting the flag, behavior is preserved only by keeping it; the finding is that the flag currently has no behavioral effect at all.

title: Windows OpenProcess unnecessarily requests PROCESS_VM_READ alongside PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION
description: The primary `OpenProcess` call requests `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ` (0x1000 | 0x0010). `GetProcessMemoryInfo` only requires `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` on Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 and later (the legacy requirement `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ` is the fallback path at line 115). Bundling `PROCESS_VM_READ` into the modern request is unnecessary and strictly narrows the set of processes that can be opened: a target where the caller has query-limited rights but not VM-read rights will fail the first `OpenProcess`, fall through to the legacy `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ` request (which is even more restrictive), and then return `None`, silently dropping the RSS sample. In this script's own usage the targets are always `os.getpid()` (for peak, line 63) or the wrapper's own child (line 58/242), which grant full rights, so the defect is latent here; but `StdlibMemorySampler` is a reusable public sampler and the over-broad access right is a correctness hazard against any other PID.
evidence: Line 113: `handle = open_process(process_query_limited_information | process_vm_read, False, pid)`. `process_vm_read = 0x0010` (line 93). The modern documented requirement for GetProcessMemoryInfo is PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION alone; VM_READ is only part of the pre-Win7 requirement satisfied by the fallback at line 115. On failure to open, both helpers (`process_rss_bytes`, `process_peak_rss_bytes`) yield `None`, which `_sample_child_rss` (line 186) and the summary then treat as 'unavailable' with no error surfaced.

title: Two-step max over child RSS samples and resource peak is partially redundant
description: The child peak is computed as `child_peak_rss = max(child_rss_samples, default=child_resource_peak)` followed by a conditional `child_peak_rss = max(child_peak_rss, child_resource_peak)`. When `child_rss_samples` is empty, the `default=child_resource_peak` already sets `child_peak_rss` to `child_resource_peak`, and the subsequent `max(child_resource_peak, child_resource_peak)` is a no-op. When samples are non-empty, the second line does the real combine. The intent (overall max of all polled samples plus the resource-reported peak, or None if nothing is available) is expressible as a single filtered aggregation, e.g. `candidates = [*child_rss_samples]; if child_resource_peak is not None: candidates.append(child_resource_peak); child_peak_rss = max(candidates, default=None)`. The current form relies on the `default=` value overlapping the second `max` operand, which is non-obvious and easy to misread as a bug.
evidence: Lines 259-261. Trace: samples=[] -> child_peak_rss = child_resource_peak (default), then line 261 guard fires only if child_resource_peak is not None, computing max(child_resource_peak, child_resource_peak) == child_resource_peak (no-op). samples=[500,300], child_resource_peak=None -> line 261 guard skipped, result 500. samples=[500], child_resource_peak=700 -> max(500)=500 then max(500,700)=700.
est_reduction: ~2 lines net; primarily a clarity improvement removing the overlapping default/max interaction.
behavior_preservation: Equivalent for all input combinations: empty/non-empty sample list crossed with None/int resource peak all yield identical results to the proposed single-aggregation form.

title: Non-strict XPASS perf test is mislabeled as "xfailed" and triggers a false "no tests completed successfully" message, contradicting the JSON summary which labels it "passed"
description:
A perf test marked `@pytest.mark.xfail(strict=False)` that unexpectedly PASSES is an XPASS, not an XFAIL. pytest reports it with outcome="passed" and a populated `wasxfail` (empirically confirmed: such a test yields outcome="passed", wasxfail set, and pytest exits 0). The two consumers of this data disagree on its classification, producing inconsistent and misleading output:

(1) `_build_report` line 125 computes `key = "xfailed" if result.wasxfail and result.outcome == "skipped" else result.outcome`. For an XPASS the outcome is "passed" (not "skipped"), so it is bucketed under `"passed"` in the JSON `summary.outcomes`. The artifact therefore claims the test simply passed.

(2) `_budget_violations` line 71 defines `xfailed = [r for r in results if r.wasxfail]`, which INCLUDES the XPASS (its `wasxfail` is truthy). This emits the violation "Performance tests must not be xfailed; expected failures hide perf coverage: <nodeid>" naming a test that actually passed -- a wrong label and a wrong rationale.

(3) `_budget_violations` lines 88-90 require `result.outcome == "passed" and not result.wasxfail` to consider a test successful. The XPASS has `wasxfail` truthy, so it is excluded; if it is the only perf test, the runner additionally emits "No performance tests completed successfully." even though the test ran and passed.

The root cause is that the two code paths use divergent definitions of "xfailed": `_build_report` uses the correct `wasxfail and outcome=="skipped"`, while `_budget_violations` uses just `wasxfail`. Because the repo sets `xfail_strict = true` globally (pyproject.toml:143), a *plain* `@pytest.mark.xfail` that passes becomes a strict XPASS -> outcome="failed" -> caught cleanly via exit code; the inconsistency only surfaces when a test explicitly overrides with `strict=False`, which the global setting does not suppress. The lane still fails overall (exit 1 from the violations), so CI is not silently green, but the emitted reason and the JSON `outcomes` are mutually contradictory and misleading for whoever debugs the failure.
evidence: Empirical probe with pytest 9.0.2: a test `@pytest.mark.xfail(reason=..., strict=False)` whose body asserts True produced report row outcome="passed", wasxfail="...", and `pytest.main` returned EXIT 0. Tracing: _build_report:125 -> key="passed" (outcome != "skipped"); _budget_violations:71 -> wasxfail truthy -> appended to `xfailed` -> message at lines 80-87; lines 88-90 -> `not result.wasxfail` is False -> XPASS excluded from the success check -> if sole test, "No performance tests completed successfully." also fires. pytest's own pytest_report_teststatus (_pytest/skipping.py:315-321) classifies this same report as "xpassed", distinct from both "xfailed" and "passed".

title: Duplicated truncate-to-5 list-formatting for the skipped and xfailed violation messages
description: The blocks building the `skipped` and `xfailed` violation strings (lines 72-79 and 80-87) are near-identical: each joins `result.nodeid` over the first 5 entries, appends ", ..." when more than 5 exist, and formats a message. The shared shape (slice [:5], join on nodeid, conditional ellipsis) could be extracted into a small helper such as `_summarise_nodeids(results, limit=5) -> str` to remove the copy-paste and keep the two messages in sync. This is purely a readability/maintenance cleanup; it does not change observable behavior or output.
est_reduction: ~6 lines
behavior_preservation: Identical violation strings before and after; only the construction is factored into a shared helper. Covered by tests/test_perf_suite_script.py::test_budget_violations_fail_when_perf_tests_are_skipped_or_xfailed which asserts the exact message text.

title: _is_stale ignores Vite's root index.html and public/ assets, so edits there ship stale and skip rebuild
description: _is_stale only treats files under frontend/src/ (rglob of *.ts/*.tsx/*.css/*.html) plus a fixed config list (vite.config.ts, tsconfig.json, tsconfig.app.json, package.json) as build inputs. But the Vite build (frontend/vite.config.ts: outDir '../src/haute/static', emptyOutDir true) has two additional first-class inputs that are NOT scanned: (1) frontend/index.html — the actual Vite entry HTML at the frontend ROOT (it references /favicon.svg and /src/main.tsx and is transformed into static/index.html), and (2) everything under frontend/public/ (favicon.svg, vite.svg) which Vite copies verbatim into the output. Because src_dir.rglob('*.html') is rooted at frontend/src, the root frontend/index.html never matches, and frontend/public/ is never walked. Consequence, in two places: in initialize() line 50, when HAUTE_BUILD_FRONTEND=1 the rebuild is skipped (returns early) even though the entry HTML or a public asset changed; and in _validate_static_assets() line 85 a normal wheel build passes validation even though the packaged static/ is genuinely older than the changed input. This is exactly the failure the module exists to prevent (module docstring lines 1-6; _validate_static_assets docstring line 77: 'Fail clearly when a wheel build would package missing or stale frontend'). A developer who edits the page <title>, meta tags, favicon, or the script entry in frontend/index.html, then builds a wheel, silently ships the previous build's index.html. Secondary instance of the same gap: tsconfig.node.json (which exists in frontend/) is also absent from the config list, though its build impact is weaker than index.html/public.
evidence: vite.config.ts line 34-35: outDir '../src/haute/static', emptyOutDir true. frontend/index.html exists at frontend root (Vite entry) and references /favicon.svg + /src/main.tsx. frontend/public/{favicon.svg,vite.svg} exist and are copied to outDir by Vite. hatch_build.py:97 src_dir = frontend_dir / 'src'; line 98-101 rglob over src_dir only; line 103 config list omits frontend/index.html and any public/ path. tests/test_hatch_build.py covers only the 'missing assets' path, not staleness of root index.html or public/, so no test catches this.
